text:
📅 WHAT I'M WATCHING TODAY — MONDAY, OCTOBER 19
A new week begins with China's economic data, Canadian inflation, U.S. housing and corporate earnings in focus.
China's Q3 GDP beat expectations, industrial production strengthened and retail sales came in ahead of forecasts.
But beneath those numbers, investment remains weak and the property sector is still struggling.
We also have earnings scheduled from companies including $CLF, $STLD, $FITB, $AGNC and $VFS, offering another look at industrial demand, credit conditions and capital-intensive businesses.
The question I'm watching: Is economic growth becoming more resilient, or are underlying weaknesses still being masked by stronger headline numbers?
🇨🇳 CHINA — DATA RELEASED
Q3 GDP
🔹 GDP YoY: +4.5% vs +4.4% expected, previously +4.3%
🔹 GDP QoQ: +1.2% vs +1.1% expected, previously +0.9%
SEPTEMBER ACTIVITY
🔹 Industrial production: +5.5% vs +5.4% expected
🔹 Retail sales: +1.1% vs +0.5% expected
🔹 Unemployment: 5.2% vs 5.3% expected
🔹 Fixed-asset investment YTD: −7.2% vs −7.3% expected
🔹 House prices: −2.8% YoY vs −3.0% previously
China's economy performed better than expected across several important indicators.
That's encouraging.
But stronger industrial production doesn't necessarily mean domestic demand is recovering at the same pace.
Retail sales growth of 1.1% remains modest, fixed-asset investment is contracting, and the property market continues to struggle.
China's industrial economy is holding up better than its domestic investment cycle.
For investors, stronger manufacturing can support demand for machinery, industrial equipment and commodities.
But weak property investment continues to weigh on construction, household confidence and domestic demand.
The bigger question is whether stronger production can eventually translate into a broader recovery in consumption and investment.
🇨🇦 CANADA — INFLATION + BUSINESS OUTLOOK
1:30 PM BST — SEPTEMBER CPI
🔹 Headline CPI YoY: 3.2% forecast vs 3.0% previously
🔹 Headline CPI MoM: +0.2% expected vs −0.1% previously
🔹 Core CPI YoY: 2.4% forecast vs 2.4% previously
🔹 CPI Common: 2.6% expected vs 2.6% previously
🔹 CPI Median: 2.0% expected vs 2.0% previously
🔹 CPI Trimmed Mean: 1.9% expected vs 1.9% previously
3:30 PM BST — BANK OF CANADA SURVEYS
▪ Business Outlook Survey
▪ Survey of Consumer Expectations
Canada is today's main inflation event.
I'll be watching whether price pressures are broadening or remaining concentrated in a few categories.
The Bank of Canada surveys should also provide insight into hiring intentions, business investment and consumer inflation expectations.
Inflation → BoC policy expectations → Bond yields → Housing and consumer demand
🇺🇸 U.S. MACRO — UK TIME
3:00 PM BST — NAHB HOUSING MARKET INDEX
🔹 Expected: 31 vs 32 previously
4:30 PM BST — 3-MONTH + 6-MONTH TREASURY BILL AUCTIONS
U.S. housing remains sensitive to elevated borrowing costs.
A further decline in homebuilder confidence would suggest affordability pressures are continuing to weigh on demand.
I'll be watching sales expectations, buyer traffic and whether builders are becoming more cautious about future construction activity.
Higher mortgage rates don't just affect homebuyers. They also influence construction, employment, materials demand and household spending.
🇪🇺 EUROPE — UK TIME
🔹 7:00 AM — ECB Elderson Speech
🔹 2:00 PM — French Treasury Bill Auctions
ECB Lane and Sleijpen also featured earlier in the calendar.
The focus remains on inflation, economic growth and the direction of European monetary policy.
📊 EARNINGS — BEFORE THE BELL
A relatively quiet start to earnings week, but several companies could provide useful signals about industrial demand, banking and consumer spending.
🔹 Cleveland-Cliffs $CLF — Steel demand, automotive production, pricing, operating costs and margins.
🔹 Fifth Third Bancorp $FITB — Net interest income, deposit costs, loan growth and credit quality.
🔹 SmartFinancial $SMBK — Regional lending, deposits and profitability.
🔹 VinFast $VFS — EV deliveries, production costs, cash burn and financing requirements.
🌙 EARNINGS — AFTER THE BELL
🔹 Steel Dynamics $STLD — Steel pricing, shipment volumes, construction demand and margins.
🔹 AGNC Investment $AGNC — Mortgage-backed securities, funding costs, interest-rate spreads and book value.
🔹 Crown Holdings $CCK — Packaging demand, beverage-can volumes, pricing and cash generation.
🔹 KARO $KARO — Connected-vehicle subscriptions, customer growth and profitability.
🔹 RBB Bancorp $RBB — Regional lending, credit quality and deposit trends.
🔹 BOK Financial $BOKF — Commercial lending, net interest income and credit conditions.
🔹 Washington Trust Bancorp $WASH — Lending, deposits and margins.
MY MAIN EARNINGS FOCUS
$CLF + $STLD — STEEL + INDUSTRIAL DEMAND
These two companies offer a useful comparison of conditions across the U.S. steel market.
I'll be watching automotive demand, construction activity, pricing and shipment volumes.
The key question is whether industrial demand is translating into stronger margins and profitability.
$FITB + $BOKF — BANKING + CREDIT CONDITIONS
Regional banks provide another window into the real economy.
Loan demand, deposit costs, net interest margins and credit quality will be important.
Higher interest rates can support asset yields, but they can also increase funding costs and put pressure on borrowers.
$AGNC — MORTGAGE MARKETS + INTEREST RATES
AGNC is particularly relevant alongside today's housing data.
I'll be watching mortgage-backed securities spreads, leverage, funding costs and book value.
Lower Treasury yields may offer some relief, but mortgage financing conditions depend on more than government bond yields alone.
$VFS — EV GROWTH + CAPITAL REQUIREMENTS
VinFast provides another perspective on the capital-intensive EV industry.
Higher deliveries matter, but so do production costs, operating losses and external funding requirements.
Growth is important. But investors ultimately need to understand what that growth costs and when it can generate cash.
MY TAKEAWAY
What interests me about Monday is the contrast between stronger economic headlines and the weaknesses still sitting underneath them.
China's GDP beat expectations, industrial production improved and retail sales came in ahead of forecasts.
But investment remains weak, and the property downturn is far from over.
Canada's inflation figures will give us another indication of where interest rates might be heading.
U.S. housing data will show how elevated borrowing costs are affecting confidence.
And today's earnings should tell us more about conditions across steel, banking, mortgage financing and electric vehicles.
For me, three things matter:
▪ Growth: Is stronger economic activity translating into better corporate earnings?
▪ Inflation: Are price pressures making it harder for central banks to ease?
▪ Financing: Are borrowing costs holding back investment and consumer demand?
Strong headline numbers are encouraging. But I want to see whether that strength is reaching businesses, households and the wider economy.
That's what I'll be watching today.
— EMMANUELINVEST

From @therealdavidwi1 Last nights ITV programme does not represent the Reform UK party I have known and been proud to belong to for more than three years.

Here in Folkestone, Hythe and Romney Marsh, our members are ordinary, decent, hardworking people. Parents, pensioners, business owners and taxpayers who care deeply about their communities and want a better future for our country.

They have watched standards slip, services struggle and successive governments fail to deliver over the past 20 years. They want secure borders, proper control of illegal immigration and recognition of the pressures on housing, public services and the public purse. People who work hard and pay their taxes should feel listened to and fairly treated.

That is why so many have said: enough is enough.

I believe tonight’s programme gave a deeply unrepresentative picture of the people I work alongside. The conduct of individuals should never become an excuse to dismiss everyone who supports Reform.

Where wrongdoing is established, it must be dealt with firmly. Racism, threats and intimidation have no place in our party. Equally, the many decent members giving their time to help their communities deserve a fair hearing.

If you want to know what Reform councillors actually do, come along to a county council meeting or watch one online. Look at the questions being asked, the decisions being taken and the work happening between meetings.

Here in Kent, KCC has paid back  £142 million in debt repayments as part of over £700 million inherited from the former conservatives party, since our election, cutting future interest costs, alongside £100 million in savings delivered during our first year. These are separate achievements, and both matter to taxpayers. 

We are also improving community facilities. The new Folkestone library, Temple Hill and Cranbrook libraries have reopened following refurbishment, with space for Family Hub services, bringing more support together for local families. 

There is much more to do, and I see the commitment our councillors bring to that work every day.

The Reform I know is full of people who want safer communities, better services, responsible spending and a country that offers its children real opportunity.

I remain proud of our local members, proud to serve our residents and positive about what we can achieve. Judge us by our work and our results.

text:
Global FX: Same Oil Shock, Different Outcomes | October 19, 2026
(📍Data From https://t.co/rtKhA53pFF Daily Report)

Energy prices, interest-rate expectations and fiscal credibility are pulling currencies in different directions.

The key trading distinction: higher yields can reflect stronger policy support—or a larger risk premium. The currency response depends on which force dominates.

💵 USD — Watch the entire rate path

Barclays now forecasts 25bp Fed hikes in December 2026 and January 2027.

That is an institutional forecast, not a policy commitment.

Less urgency to hike in October can coexist with expectations for more tightening later. For the dollar, watch changes in relative short-term yields and real-rate expectations rather than counting hawkish headlines.

🇪🇺 EUR — Inflation pressure meets tighter financing

Lagarde highlighted how higher borrowing costs can weaken growth and eventually inflation. Other ECB officials remain concerned about unfinished disinflation and energy-price spillovers.

These forces can coexist.

Higher European yields could support the euro through interest-rate differentials. But yields rising because investors demand greater fiscal-risk compensation could undermine that support.

Watch sovereign spreads alongside rate expectations.

🇬🇧 GBP — Mortgage pressure reaches households

Rightmove reports signs that rising mortgage rates are weighing on housing affordability.

For sterling, the question is whether higher borrowing costs mainly support yield appeal—or increasingly damage consumption and growth.

Housing weakness alone does not establish an imminent policy reversal.

🇯🇵 JPY — BOJ normalization versus fiscal concerns

Ueda says underlying inflation is close to the 2% target, keeping further policy normalization in focus.

But rising long-term Japanese yields can also reflect concerns about government borrowing.

A narrower expected U.S.–Japan policy-rate gap could support the yen. A larger fiscal-risk premium is a different signal.

🇰🇷 KRW — Growth optimism needs flow confirmation

A stronger growth outlook can support the fundamental case for Korean assets.

For the won, confirmation should include foreign portfolio flows, semiconductor export demand and energy-import costs.

An equity rebound alone cannot establish durable currency demand.

🇨🇦 CAD — Oil offers benefits and costs

Higher oil prices can improve energy-sector revenues and investment while raising inflation risks.

The currency response also depends on the U.S. outlook, relative rates and global risk appetite. “Oil up, CAD up” is an incomplete trading rule.

🇦🇺 AUD / 🇨🇭 CHF — Separate carry from confidence

AUD: Kent acknowledged that reduced rate-hike expectations made sense after weaker labour-market data, while cautioning against overreading one month.

CHF: Yield disadvantages can weigh during calmer markets, while demand for safety can become more important during stress.

🌏 China read-through

China reported 4.6% real GDP growth for the first nine months of 2026—not the standalone third-quarter growth rate.

For regional FX, the next question is how activity translates into imports, commodity demand and capital flows.

🎯 Trader’s focus

Track oil, relative two-year yields, sovereign spreads and portfolio flows together.

A currency rally supported by improving fundamentals carries a different message from one driven by temporary positioning.

I've been meaning to post about this for a while now.

We're retired and so I'm disinclined to spend more on things than what I have to.

I think I've figured our a way to keep our streaming services pretty reasonable  - about $15 per month.

This assumes that you  have a smart TV.

The first step depends on what Internet service you have in your home.

While I assume that all of the providers offer a deal somewhat like ours, I'll just tell you what we get from T-Mobile.

To begin with, because we're both over the age of 50 there is a special discounted fee for us.

(There are also discount deals for veterans, for members of the Armed Forces, for teachers, and for first responders, and for students.)

So, we get full high-speed connections both of our two phones and for our internet for slightly under $100 per month when we take advantages of all of the discounts that they offer.

I'm not counting this $100 in terms of our over-all streaming costs.

But what I am counting are the extras that we get from them and they are a free subscription to Major League Baseball and a free subscription to Netflix.  We also get 
Apple TV for just $3 per month.

The next step is an indoor antenna.  I got a pretty good one for $35 and that brings in the five major over-the-air networks from Cleveland as well as a couple of other ones from Kent and Cleveland.

Each of these has three or four side-band channels, giving us a total of about 50 free broadcast channels.

This is especially important to us because it provides us with free access to five or six NFL games every week and another five or six NCAA football games through regular over-the-air network broadcasts.

Beyond this, the antenna provides us with another 62 sports channels and about 45 movie channels and a couple of hundred other channels that we hardly ever even check out.

The next source of free streaming programs comes from two services from our local library: Hoopla and Kanopy.

Hoopla streams not just movies and TV shows, it also provides free access to AMC and BBC programming, free audio-books, free ebooks, free magazines and free music services - all of which can be accessed through your TV, your computers or your devices.

Kanopy provides access to hundreds of movies of all sorts as  well as to TV shows, including many Brit shows (we're big fans of Brit mysteries). Likewise these can also be accessed through your computers and devices.

Our library also gives us access to the Libby service which, though it doesn't provide access to movies or TV programs, gives us access to thousands of ebooks, audio books, magazines and other printed material.

Next are two streaming services that we get free as added benefits to other primary services that we subscribe to.

I should say that we've become very jealous of our time and so when we're not doing things that are things that we enjoy doing, we avoid those out-and-about chores that just take up time.

For that reason, we subscribe to Amazon Prime and get free access to their mammoth library of movies and limited series as well as to their large music library. It also has several several hundred streaming channels, including more than 90 that are dedicated just to sports.

We also subscribe to Wal-Mart Plus that gives us free delivery of groceries and anything else in their stores as well as to Paramount Plus, the big streaming service from CBS.

Next are the free Pluto, Roku, Tubi, and Xumo services which each offer a combination of streaming channels and on-demand programming.  

Pluto has 400+ streaming channels, Roku 500+, Tubi 260+, and Xumo 400+.   They each also has nearly as many on-demand channels as they do streaming services.

The Filmrise and Fawesome services also each provides several hundred movies and TV for free.

Fandango provides hundreds of free movies along with their paid services.

Then there are  the free EWTN which is a full-service Catholic service and C-SPAN which provides coverage of Congress as well as book news, discussion programs, and historical documentaries.

The LocalNews and Haystack provide local, national, and international news broadcasts for free.

There is one last free streaming service that we also use a lot and that is YouTube. You can find an incredible number of free documentaries, lectures and discussions on there.  But what we use it for mostly are the thousands of free movies, ranging mostly from those made between 1935 and the 2010s.

So far we have paid $3 per month for all of this programming.

Now for the paid programming.

Special deals on most of the main streaming channels show up every once in a while - usually at the beginning of summer and again in the week or so surrounding Thanksgiving.

From those, we're now subscribed to Peacock for $3, HBO for $4, and Disney/Hulu for $4.

But there's more.

I'm a big fan of old-time radio and I download and listen to a lot of programs that are available on https://t.co/7WFCGZAC8Y.  I also do the same with audiobook versions of classic novels from there.

And, its sister site, https://t.co/JFlMiHZnpP provides free access to tens of thousands of ebooks of all varieties.

One last thing, because streaming services are changing often and new streaming deals pop up fairly often, a good way to keep up with all of this is through the https://t.co/f0sdZOlfAh website.

text:
Tyler Perry was born Emmitt Perry Jr. on September 13, 1969, in New Orleans, Louisiana, and grew up in poverty with his mother, Willie Maxine, a preschool worker, and his father, a carpenter.
His childhood was marked by severe physical abuse from his father (who also abused his mother) and sexual abuse by multiple adults; at 16 he legally changed his first name to Tyler to distance himself from his father.
He has described the home as a “living hell,” attempted suicide as a teenager, dropped out of high school (later earning a GED), and found refuge in church with his mother and in drawing and storytelling.
In his early 20s, an episode of The Oprah Winfrey Show inspired him to journal his trauma, which evolved into his first play, I Know I’ve Been Changed; he poured his life savings into staging it in Atlanta in 1992.
The show initially failed, leaving him homeless and living in his car for years while he worked odd jobs and kept refining his material—experiences that later shaped both his creative work and his strong views on self-reliance.

In July 2025, during a candid roundtable on Kirk Franklin’s Den of Kings series, Tyler Perry sat with other successful Black men and was asked how he navigates the tension between building wealth and family expectations. He answered without hesitation: “I fired my aunt.”
She had regularly called asking for money. Perry kept sending it—until he offered her a job instead, telling her he wanted to help her build something rather than become “welfare” to her. She accepted, then repeatedly failed to show up. He let her go. The same principle applied more broadly. While his mother, Willie Maxine Perry, was alive, she had asked him to support certain relatives. After she died in 2009, he mailed them letters giving them 60 days to become “gainfully employed,” or the financial support would end. According to Perry, every one of them found a job. The pay wasn’t the point; he wanted them to have “something else for them to do to feel some pride in.”
He has applied the same standard at home with his son, Aman (now around 11–12), who must do chores for things he wants. Perry’s stated view is straightforward: endlessly giving money to people who refuse to work “handicaps” them and deepens dependence. Some relatives were angry when he declined requests for large sums (including one who was upset he wouldn’t give them $1 million).

Billionaire Tyler Perry gave his own family 60 days to find jobs or lose his financial support. Despite being worth an estimated $1.4 billion, he refused to keep supporting relatives who weren't working.

In the video below, Perry explains why he fired his own aunt and later gave other family members an ultimatum after his mother's death. 

He wanted them to become financially independent instead of relying on his fortune.

One aunt regularly called asking for money, and Perry kept sending it until he offered her a job. But she repeatedly called in and failed to show up for work, so he eventually fired her.

His mother had also asked him to support other relatives, and he continued helping them while she was alive. After she died in 2009, Perry sent them letters giving them 60 days to find employment or lose his financial support.

According to Perry, every relative eventually found a job. He didn't care whether the jobs paid well because he wanted them to earn their own money and have something to feel proud of.

Perry also recalled a relative getting angry when he refused to hand over $1 million. He believed that continually giving money to people who refused to work was making their dependence worse.

A billionaire who could afford to support his entire family chose to make them earn their own living.

If you had $1.4 billion, would you keep supporting unemployed relatives or give them the same 60-day ultimatum?

text:
Quentin Tarantino has one movie left before he retires for good, and Aubrey Plaza has been begging him for a part in it for two years now.

This weekend he finally said the script is done, and in the same breath said he's not shooting it anytime soon.

He told Graham Norton he wants to do his West End play first, then go home to his family and "live a little" before he decides anything. He and his wife have two kids with a third on the way. World of Reel thinks 2028 is the earliest it happens.

The bit itself is really well done. She starts out totally desperate, "I'll do anything." Then a "manager" jumps in to say she will not do anything and the feet are off the table. A few lines later the feet are back on the table, but it's going to cost extra. She basically acted out a whole Hollywood contract negotiation in one clip, nudity terms and all, plus a special rider for the camera habit Tarantino gets roasted for more than anything else he does. Actors really do negotiate nudity clauses line by line before they sign, and she turned that paperwork into the joke.

The reason she keeps doing this on podcast after podcast is his track record with actors.

His nine movies have gotten actors nine Oscar nominations and three wins. Christoph Waltz won twice, Brad Pitt finally won his first acting Oscar for Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and Robert Forster got the only nomination of his whole career at 56, after years of B-movies. John Travolta was doing Look Who's Talking sequels right before Pulp Fiction got him a Best Actor nomination.

Getting cast by Tarantino is basically a career reset button, and he's been saying for years he'll only make ten movies. Nine of those are done, which leaves one.

Plaza's been going after it since at least 2024, when she told a camera crew in a video store she was "still waiting for that call." She did it again on Amy Poehler's podcast last year, and now she's raised the offer to anything he wants. The script is finished and nobody's been cast yet, so she's got at least two years to keep this bit going.

text:
China Haul: Why foreign visitors are now leaving with full suitcases

Foreign visitors once left China with little more than a handful of souvenirs. Now many arrive with empty suitcases and leave with them packed. On TikTok, the trend has a name: China Haul.

South African creator Grace Mondlana filmed herself unboxing her haul—ranging from carefully designed cultural pieces to snacks—and the video pulled in more than 500,000 likes. The food account "Oh Yummy" walked into a snack shop in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, stared at shelves lined with thousands of options, and called China a "snack paradise." That video surpassed 3 million views. Drones, foldable phones, and AI glasses turn up just as frequently. What used to be the occasional tourist souvenir has turned into serious shopping, and the range of products foreign visitors can buy in China keeps growing.

This is no longer rare. From AI glasses at electronics market in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, to Chinese-style clothing and beauty products in shopping malls in east China's Shanghai, and from folding fans and fragrant sachets at riverside shops in Suzhou, southeast China's Jiangsu Province to herbal teas and cultural goods in boutiques in southwest China's Chongqing, it has become commonplace to see foreign tourists arriving with empty suitcases and leaving with fully packed luggage.

Empty suitcases in, full suitcases out

"Bring extra luggage for a shopping spree in China" has become common advice among foreign visitors. During the 2026 National Day holiday, China recorded 15.46 million inbound and outbound trips, averaging 2.21 million a day, up 6.7 percent year on year, according to the National Immigration Administration. In the first half of the year, 22.914 million foreign nationals entered China, a 20.4 percent year-on-year increase, with 77.7 percent of them arriving visa-free.

Tech products dominate their shopping lists. Data from the Huaqiangbei Subdistrict in Shenzhen shows that nearly 8,000 foreign merchants have come to Huaqiangbei for procurement every day this year. As of July 2026, AI products made up 61 percent of electronics products in the commercial zone, a sharp jump from 41 percent in 2025. Overall AI-product sales in Huaqiangbei grew more than 55 percent year-on-year, while AI glasses sales doubled, and drone and robot sales rose 60–70 percent, according to a CCTV report.

Cultural and creative products rooted in Chinese aesthetics come next. Suzhou's Pingjiang Road historic district is lined with intangible-heritage shops where visitors can buy Su embroidery fans and sachets—or try making them on the spot. Items such as loquat paste with fritillary bulb and moxibustion tools have been nicknamed "Chinese miracle remedies" by overseas users.

Local fashion is the latest draw. At PANE, a Shanghai-based footwear brand, foreign customers account for 30 percent of foot traffic and 35 percent of sales. Chinese pop culture brand Pop Mart reported 37.12 billion yuan in revenue for 2025, with overseas sales making up more than 40 percent. Domestic beauty brands are also gaining ground: Florasis became the first Chinese beauty brand to enter Ulta Beauty, a major U.S. retailer.

Why "China Haul" is catching on

Looking at the recent "China+" trends on overseas social media, "China Haul" makes more sense. During the "China Travel" phase, people mostly filmed the scenery. In the "Chinamaxxing" period, they started recording high-speed trains, night markets, and drone deliveries—stuff that felt like a high-tech, slightly futuristic China. Now with "China Haul," they're actually packing their suitcases. Seeing it, going there, and bringing something home is what makes the impression stick. Once the products end up in someone's daily life—used, unboxed on camera, and flooded with "link please" comments—they stay familiar and gradually build trust.

China's opening up policies have helped sustain the trend. China now offers unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and 240-hour visa-free transit to those of 57 countries. In the first half of 2026, the number of foreign travelers claiming departure tax refunds rose 366 percent year-on-year, while both refundable sales and the refund amounts themselves grew 69 percent. The "2.0 version" departure tax refund policy introduced in May 2026 extended the "refund upon purchase" window to 28 days nationwide before departure and introduced paperless processing with mutual recognition across locations.

The continuous upgrading and expanding variety of Chinese products is the other major driver. Motivation has shifted from "because it's cheap" to "because it's good." Chinese manufacturing and design—backed by solid quality, distinctive Chinese aesthetics, and emotional resonance—continue to generate desire among overseas consumers.

From the old staples of tea, silk, and panda plush toys to AI glasses, domestic running shoes, iconic cultural landmarks, and the loquat paste that foreign creators now call a "Chinese miracle remedy," the shopping experience for foreigners in China has become far richer. Suitcases packed to capacity and the rise of "China Haul" illustrate both the appeal of Chinese manufacturing and the practical results of China's continued opening.

text:
Renault’s 1.8 NA Strong Hybrid (E-Tech 160) on the Duster isn’t just another hybrid option in the midsize SUV segment - it’s a genuinely sophisticated series-parallel system with F1-inspired engineering that stands apart from the usual Indian-market hybrids.

Let’s break down why this setup is more interesting than it first appears:

1) EV-first in the city

The system always starts in pure electric mode. With a relatively large 1.4 kWh battery (noticeably bigger than the 0.6 kWh packs in the Hyryder/Grand Vitara/Victoris), Renault claims up to 80% of city driving can be done on electric power alone under the right conditions. The traction motor handles the wheels; the engine stays off when it isn’t needed.

2) Series-parallel architecture

Unlike a pure series hybrid or a simple parallel setup, the E-Tech can operate in multiple ways:

Pure EV (electric motor drives the wheels)

Series (engine runs as a generator, electric motor drives)
Parallel (engine + electric motor both drive the wheels)
Engine-only for efficient cruising
It switches between these automatically depending on speed, load and battery state.

3) The multi-mode DHT (Dedicated Hybrid Transmission)

This is the clever part. Renault uses a F1-inspired multi-mode gearbox with no conventional clutch or synchronisers (dog-box style). It has 2 electric gears + 4 petrol gears, giving 15 possible combinations. The high-voltage starter-generator handles starting and synchronisation electrically. Result: smoother transitions and better optimisation of both efficiency and response compared with a traditional e-CVT power-split setup.

4) The ENGINE

A 1.8-litre naturally aspirated 4-cylinder running on the Atkinson cycle with high thermal efficiency . It’s quieter and more refined than the 3-cylinder units in the current Toyota/Maruti strong hybrids, and it only comes in when it makes sense, either to generate electricity or to drive the wheels directly at higher speeds.

Combined system output: 160 PS
Electric motor torque: 208 Nm
Claimed 0-100 km/h: 9.6 seconds
ARAI-certified efficiency: 29 kmpl
Battery: 1.4 kWh (self-charging, no plug needed)

That’s meaningfully more power than the 116 PS 1.5L hybrids currently on sale, with a stronger electric presence in the city.

5) How it compares in practice

The Hyryder/Grand Vitara/Victoris are excellent efficiency tools, but their e-CVT power-split system often keeps the engine engaged and can feel a bit strained under load. The E-Tech’s dual-motor + multi-mode DHT approach is designed for more seamless electric running in town and stronger combined performance when you ask for it. Whether the real-world refinement matches the promise will depend on calibration, but on paper this is the most technically ambitious strong hybrid we’ve seen in this segment in India so far.

6) My take

Don’t just look at the 29 kmpl figure. The interesting part is the architecture , larger battery, proper 4-cylinder Atkinson engine, series-parallel flexibility and an F1-inspired multi-mode transmission.
If Renault has calibrated it well, the Duster Strong Hybrid should offer a more refined and responsive hybrid experience than the current 1.5L options, while still delivering strong efficiency without needing a charger.
Worth experiencing for the engineering alone.

Let me know what you guys think!

text:
St. Luke, Evangelist: Lives of the Saints by Father Francis Xavier Weninger, DD, SJ., 1876
.
Among the holy men whom the Almighty chose to write the Gospel, or the history of the life and death, the teachings and miracles of Our Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ, was St. Luke, the third of those who are called Evangelists. He is represented with an ox near him, according to the mysterious revelation made to the Prophet Ezekiel; because he begins his Gospel with the revelation of what happened to Zachary in the Temple, where oxen, sheep and other animals were offered, according to the Old Covenant, in sacrifice to the Almighty. St. Luke is said to have been born at Antioch, in Syria, and his occupation, in his youth, was the study of the liberal arts, especially rhetoric, physic, sculpture and painting. It is believed that St. Paul himself instructed him in the Christian faith; hence, St. Jerome calls him a spiritual son of that holy Apostle. It is quite certain that he accompanied St. Paul in the many and laborious travels which the holy Apostle undertook to convert the infidels. Hence he had a part in all the labors, dangers, hardships and persecutions which the Apostle endured. This, however, caused him to be most warmly beloved and highly esteemed by St. Paul, who mentions him in several of his epistles, and among other praises, calls him an Apostle.
.
At the desire of St. Paul, Luke wrote the Gospel in Greek, as the Apostle was at that time preaching to the Greeks, and also, because this language was very much disseminated. St. Luke relates, in his Gospel, much that is but slightly mentioned by the other Evangelists, for instance, the mystery of the Annunciation and the Incarnation of Christ: from which the holy Fathers conclude that he must have been on very friendly terms, not only with the Apostles, but also with the Divine Mother, as she could give him the best information concerning these mysteries. Another reason is, that St. Luke lived in chastity, and earnestly endeavored to guard and preserve this virtue. The commentators of Holy Writ have also observed, that St. Luke, more than the other Evangelists, gives sinners the hope of divine mercy, and encourages them to repentance, as is seen in the parable of the Prodigal Son, so lovingly received by his father, as also in that of the Good Shepherd, who with great solicitude sought the lost sheep, and brought it back to the fold; again in the history of the sinner who so mercifully receives pardon: in the Samaritan who cares so kindly for the wounded traveller; but above all in the wonderful conversion of the thief crucified with Christ, to whom, when he had humbly and penitentially begged to be remembered, our kind Saviour promised Paradise. St. Anselm gives the reason for this in the following words: "Luke was at first a physician of the body; hence it is that he speaks more than the other Evangelist, of the mercy of our Saviour, who heals and frees men from diseases of the soul."
.
Besides the Gospel, St. Luke also wrote a book on the labors of the Apostles,, which is called the Acts of the Apostles. In it he first relates the ascension of Christ and the coming of the Holy Ghost; and after this what and where the Apostles preached, the miracles they wrought, and the sufferings they endured for Christ's sake. He further describes the life of the first Christians, and the martyrdom of St. Stephen and St. James. He then relates the conversion of St. Paul, the labors and sufferings of this holy Apostle, which no one could know better than St. Luke, who was his constant companion. During the two years of St. Paul's imprisonment at Caesarea, Luke aided him in every manner; he also accompanied him to Rome, when St. Paul had appealed to the emperor. At Rome, where the holy Apostle was again imprisoned for two years, St. Luke left him not, and allowed no persecution to separate him from his beloved master. When St. Paul was set at liberty, St. Luke accompanied him as before, wherever the unwearied Apostle preached the Gospel. St. Epiphanius relates, that, after the death of the two Apostles, Peter and Paul, St. Luke preached the Gospel of Christ in Italy, France, Dalmatia and Macedonia, with apostolic zeal. The Greeks assure us that he did the same in Egypt, Thebais and Lybia, and that he had great success in converting the infidels.
.
It is easy to conceive what hardships, dangers and persecutions the holy Evangelist must have suffered in these many wearisome travels and in consequence of his zealous preaching. Yet he was never discontented, never desponding, but always cheerful; because he always thought of Him for whom he labored and suffered, and of the recompense that was awaiting him. St. Jerome writes that the Saint continued his apostolic labors until he had reached his 84th year. St. Gregory of Nazianzum, St. Paulinus and St. Gaudentius maintain that he ended his life by martyrdom. Nicephorus writes that the heathens hung him to an olive-tree, and that thus he died a martyr. It is certain that his life, full of cares and hardships, was a continued martyrdom, the severity of which he increased by severe fasting and other penances. Hence the Church says of him, in the prayer which she offers up to-day at Holy Mass, that he bore the mortification of the cross ceaselessly in his body, for the love and honor of Christ. He ended his glorious labors and sufferings at Patras in Achaia. His holy relics, with those of St. Andrew were brought to Constantinople at the time of Constantine the Great. Long afterwards, they were removed to Pavia; but the head had, some time before, been taken by Gregory the Great to Rome, and placed in St. Peter's Church. There is a tradition that St. Luke painted several likenesses of Christ and the Blessed Virgin, and left them to the Christians to comfort them. To this day several pictures of the Blessed Virgin are shown, which are supposed to be his works. One of these is at Rome, in the Church of St. Mary Major, and another is at Loretto; both of these are venerated by the whole Christian world.
.
PRACTICAL CONSIDERATIONS.
.
I. How usefully and beneficially did St. Luke employ his pencil, his chisel, his pen, and his tongue:--the tongue to preach the word of Christ,the pen to narrate the Lord's life and death, the pencil and chisel to make so many edifiying likenesses of Jesus and Mary. Happy those who follow him in the good use of their limbs and the art they have learned! Unhappy, however, those who make their pencil and chisel instruments for pictures which give scandal to others; and who use their pen for sensational, slanderous, or otherwise sinful books and writings; who with their tongues, utter lying, slanderous, unchaste or other sinful speeches, and who greedily stretch out their hands to forbidden objects. The same may be said of those who offend God with eyes, ears, lips, feet or other limbs, and thus misuse members which God, in His mercy, gave them only for good. O how much pain such ungrateful beings will suffer in these members, which they now use only as instruments of wickedness! I call them, not without reason, ungrateful beings; for, I ask you, from whom has man his eyes, ears, tongue, hand, and feet? From none but God, the Lord, who gave them out of the abundance of His mercy. This is a great grace, and if you wish to come to the full knowledge of it, look at those who possess not these members, or have not the use of them; at those who are blind, deaf, dumb or lame. How miserable they are! Hence by giving these members to man, and the full use of them, God has surely shown great kindness to him; and man ought to be duly grateful. If man, however, misuses these members to offend God, he commits a horrible deed of ingratitude. He is not worthy to have the use of his limbs; for, as St. Bernard says: "He is not worthy to live, who will not live for Thee, O Jesus!" So is he unworthy to have tongue, ears, hands, or feet, who uses them as means to offend the Majesty of God. Are you one of this kind of men? Ask your conscience, and correct, while time is left to you, what you have done wrong.
.
II. St. Luke bore always the mortification of the Cross in his body. He was alwavs cheerful in his work and in his sufferings; never weary or desponding. The love of Christ, and the hope of an eternal reward made everything light and easy to him. If you love Christ with your whole heart, and think frequently on the future recompense, I am confident that you will not become weary at your work, that you will not despond while suffering. Therefore, in future, think often how your Lord suffered for you, and how great a reward He has promised you for your labors and sufferings. "When I see my Lord and God laden with suffering and pain," says St. Bernard, "it becomes impossible for me not to bear with an easy mind and a cheerful countenance, every evil that assails me." St. Augustine writes: "If you consider the reward which will be given to you, all that you have to endure will be but trifling.'' You will be astonished that so great a recompense is given for so little work; for, in truth, to gain eternal rest, one should perform a long work, and earn eternal joys by long suffering. As, however, the Almighty requires of us only a short work and a short suffering, who dares to complain or murmur? Should we not much rather work and suffer cheerfully? Let us work then, as long as we live, and suffer all that God sees fit to send us.

Why Virtue is nearly lost in Western Society. And why that means the end of any vigilant maintenance of Liberty:

When Christ said to turn the other cheek, he wasn’t offering the cheek to be slapped again. He was saying if you strike me, you will not strike me as a master to a slave. But as a man to another man.

As Europe indicates a precursor to what we likely find inevitably coming all throughout the west. 

I would remind any who dares to read this excerpt of the point of Virtue itself. 

Prudence - the intellectual virtue of right reason applied to action. It is the ability to discern the true good in particular circumstances and choose the fitting means to achieve it. Practical wisdom requires action. Pontificating on social media is void of actual action unless carried out in reality. Non action is meaningless

Justice - the constant and firm will to give each person his or her due. It orders our relations with others, with God, and with community. Aquinas places it in the will to cover fairness, respect for rights, fidelity toward agreement and discourse, and the common good. Common being the precise application. Not perfection. Not elitist. Not your expert opined assumption.

Fortitude - the strength of will and character that enables to remain steady in the pursuit of the good amid fear, difficulty, pain, or danger. It is reasoned endurance and perseverance. It is the measure of steadfastness against obstacles, personal sleight, benefactors, hardships, suffering, esteem, and praise. Many of you need reminding “you are just a man” (or woman). Your boo boos and your trophies do not change the course of objective right or wrong. Good is a behavior found only IN virtue. It is not an identity. Humans are not saviors by themselves. Only through virtuous community in service to posterity for Liberty and mankind.

Temperance - the Virtue of moderation and self control. Especially with regard to the desire for pleasure and material gain. Capitalism for instance creates opportunity, but it also can be exploitive if it lacks benevolence. Your achievements can multiply, but only if you give back through mentorship and attainable acquisition for the common good. What good is entrepreneurship is the ships you steer destroy the system meant to sustain it. If it destroys the populace to inescapable burdens and lack of responsibility and accountability? The Dark Ages and Great Depression were a product of a lack of Temperance. The World Wars were a product of inescapable outcomes and power for the sake of it.

Watching history repeat itself in modernity is inexcusable. We will be judged by the measures of this complete outcast of Virtue for Vanity, Subjectivism, collectivism, corruption, material selfishness, and trollish mockery. From BOTH sides

So called principled people who want to see Conservatism and Liberty “saved” squabble over what power structures and ideologies save it.

Others refuse to vote for those they feel have sleighed their hand. Candidates are offered that are the “lesser evil” instead of the protagonist we need to invoke actual change into our corrupted bureaucracy. If there even is one?

We can’t even be honest with ourselves that this corruption has spread well within both parties and political alignment in general. 

Propagandist media and social media the catalysts to cement our derision for one another. Instead of the integral method of networking and community building to invoke actual beneficial change. 

Power is a curious thing. If anything is clear, we have only continued to prove a complete failure in any capacity to wield it.

Presidential Communications Office (PCO) Undersecretary and Palace Press Officer Atty. Claire Castro holds a press briefing:

— President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. led the Philippine Nurses Association (PNA), Inc. National Annual Convention 2026 and 69th Nurses Week celebration in Pasay today.

—  The national government also extended employment opportunities and review assistance to nursing graduates who have yet to pass the licensure examination through the clinical associates program.

— Higher education institutions who offer nursing programs have also significantly increased from 354 in July 2022 to 425 in June 2026. The administration promised to support the sector in developing more skilled and professional nurses.

text:
𝟭𝟮𝟬 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝟯𝟬 𝗣𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗡𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝟮 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝘂𝘁𝘀. 𝗜 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝟭𝟬𝟬 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗞𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗹𝗮 𝗮𝘁 𝟬𝟵:𝟯𝟬 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆.

At 09:30 East Africa Time this morning, Monday 19 October, I pick up my phone and start calling the people who run entrepreneur-support programs in East Africa. Twenty-five calls today. Twenty-five a day through Thursday. One hundred in all, if the list holds.

The list does not hold. That is what this piece is about.

The assignment comes from Module 5 of the GTM Accelerator run by 1752vc [@1752vc]. It is clear and fair: prepare 120 contacts in your ideal customer profile with direct phone numbers, write two opening scripts, make 100 calls in four batches, log every call, and change one thing between batches. It is the kind of exercise a founder in a market with deep contact databases can set up in an afternoon.

I set it up over the weekend in Kampala, through two power cuts, and the honest count of numbers I can dial this morning is 31.

Here is how the list got from 120 to 31, what I decided along the way, and the rules I set for the week before the first dial, so that on Friday I can be held to them.

𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗜 𝗮𝗺 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝘆 𝗯𝘆 𝗽𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲

FounderWise [@Founder_Wise] sells a Cohort License to entrepreneur-support programs: $1,500 per cohort of up to 30 founders. The founders log what they actually did during the cohort, the customers they spoke to, the sales they made, the tests they ran, and the program gets one record it can report to its funder. The founder keeps the record after the cohort ends.

The buyer is the program. Over the last six weeks I have emailed 220 of them cold. 12 replied. 5 became interested. None of them has had a call with me yet, and most of that is my fault. I wrote that part up separately this morning.

Phone is the obvious next channel for two reasons. Three of the four interested program buyers first told me they did not understand my email. Confusion is easier to clear in one minute of conversation than in three emails. And one programs coordinator in Western Kenya asked me directly, on 22 September, to call their number and explain. When a buyer asks for a phone call, the phone is the channel.

𝟭𝟮𝟬 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀, 𝟯𝟬 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀

I started from my ideal customer list of 9 October: named leaders at East African entrepreneur-support organizations, incubators and accelerators. I added the people who had replied to my email, the programs I know through AVODA, and the contacts on an ecosystem stakeholder map I had built in August.

Then I counted how many had a direct phone number in my records.

30 of 120. 25%.

The other 90 are real people at real programs, named, with a verified email address in many cases. They simply never gave me a phone number, and nothing in my systems had one.

A founder in a market with mature contact databases closes that gap in an afternoon. Load the list into a data tool, run phone enrichment, export. I had ruled that out myself on 10 September. My standing rule since then: no bulk phone enrichment. A number is found per lead, only after that person has replied or clicked. I made the rule because a phone number is more personal than an email address in this region, and because I did not want to build FounderWise's first sales motion on calling strangers who had never heard of us.

On Sunday, 18 October, I made one exception, for this list and this assignment only. I ran a phone search on 78 program leaders through a data waterfall in Apollo. It returned 33 numbers and cost 264 credits. Most of them were Kenyan or Rwandan.

By the end of Sunday, my working contact sheet had 64 contacts, 53 with email addresses, and 31 with Ugandan numbers I can call this week. I call Ugandan numbers myself. Whether the Kenyan and Rwandan numbers fill the rest of the hundred is a decision I make before Tuesday's batch, and I will say which way it went.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱

I want to be honest about the machine behind the list, because founders outside the big markets are often told that the tools have flattened the field. Some of them have. Most of them were built for a different field.

My cold-lead system went live on 7 September. It harvests profiles, ranks them, finds and verifies email addresses, screens them against my ideal customer profile and loads them into the sending tool. On day one it produced 16 verified leads, sending 25 emails a day from two new domains I had warmed for three weeks.

Then it started failing in the quiet ways that cost the most.

Scheduled runs in the profile scraper saved without error through its API and then never fired. Zero automatic launches in two days. I moved the scheduling to n8n [@n8n_io].

Apollo's free plan blocked its enrichment API even while the account showed credits available. The error read API_INACCESSIBLE. The credits were real. The door was closed.

From 16 September to 9 October, the whole conveyor was dead for 23 days while my automation dashboard reported success twice a day. A keyword map keyed to dates had run out of dates on 16 September, so every run searched for nothing, found nothing and reported a clean finish. The last real enrichment was 11 September.

When I found it, the leftover enrichment output was close to unusable: 501 rows, 211 email addresses, 75 after screening, and of those, 2 verified, 46 catch-all and 24 unknown. Roughly 3% sendable.

When I rebuilt it on 9 October, the sending tool's lead-creation calls hung. In one run, 4 of 4 requests timed out at 70 seconds. In the next, 1 of 7 returned and 6 hung, and some of the hung ones saved anyway, minutes later, so I could not tell what had loaded without checking by hand.

On 17 October, I ran ten profile-scraper jobs in parallel to save time. They wrote over each other's results file. I lost finds. Profile jobs now run one at a time.

None of this is unusual. Every founder running outbound has a list like it. I share mine because the fix each time was the same: a person checking the output, on a schedule, against a number that could have been wrong. A dashboard that says success is reporting that the code ran. Only the output tells you whether anything happened.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝟮𝟱 𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝟭,𝟬𝟬𝟬

The course lesson on cold email describes a machine that sends more than 1,000 emails a day. Mine sends 25 a day per campaign, from two domains I bought and warmed for that purpose, with no links and no open tracking in the first email.

Part of that is caution. Part of it is the rules the inbox providers now publish. Google's own help page for email senders says a sender becomes a "bulk sender" once a domain sends close to 5,000 messages to personal Gmail accounts in 24 hours, and that the label sticks. It asks bulk senders to keep their spam rate below 0.1% and never let it reach 0.3%. Since November 2025, Gmail says it has been ramping up enforcement, with temporary and permanent rejections for mail that misses the rules. Yahoo publishes the same 0.3% ceiling. Microsoft's Outlook has rejected mail from high-volume domains without proper authentication since May 2025.

For a founder in Kampala, a burned sending domain is not a small setback. It took three weeks of warm-up before my first cold email went out. Program directors talk to each other. A domain that lands in spam with one of them lands in spam with the next.

So the email side of this business is slow by design, and it will stay slow. That is the other reason the phone matters this week. It reaches the people email confused, without putting the domains at risk.

𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗽

One more piece of the setup, because it shapes every sales conversation I am about to have.

Stripe's supported-countries page lists five African countries, all on its extended network: Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa. Uganda is not on it. FounderWise, LLC is registered in Delaware, which is how a program in Nairobi or a funder in London can pay it by card.

A mobile-money pay screen for FounderWise is due on 27 October. Until it is live, every pilot I propose this week comes with an invoice and a bank transfer, one more step in a sale that already takes about 120 days from first email to payment.

None of that is a complaint. It is the ground the calls stand on, and a program director in Kampala knows it better than I do.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗲𝗱: 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱

Two things did work, and both are cheap.

On 11 September I changed what I searched for. I stopped harvesting monitoring and evaluation officers by job title and started harvesting by organization type: entrepreneur-support organizations and incubators. The same morning, the verified-email rate went from 8% on the job-title list to 61% on the organization list.

On 16 October I built the program-buyer list without spending scraper credits at all. 661 organizations, 894 verification checks, 201 verified email addresses. Then a separate email-finder run on 273 named people found 164 addresses, and 68 of those verified clean.

Slow, partly manual, verifiable at every step. That list is the backbone of this week.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗻𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱: 𝗮𝗺 𝗜 𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿?

Once I had 30 numbers, I had to decide which of them I could actually dial.

The course material does not raise this. It was written for a market where calling a business line from a purchased list is ordinary. I am in Uganda, and some of my numbers are Kenyan.

Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019 requires personal data to be collected "for a lawful purpose which is specific, explicitly defined", in section 12. Section 17(1) says data held for a purpose is processed "only for that specific purpose". Section 26 lets any person stop direct marketing by written notice, with a written reply due "within fourteen days". Kenya's Data Protection Act of 2019, at section 37(1), bars commercial use of personal data without express consent unless the person was told at collection and the law allows it.

Fifteen of my 30 numbers came from the stakeholder map: Demo Day registrations and a working contact sheet, collected for an event. A sales call is a new purpose.

So I added a column to the call sheet called Lawful basis. A blank cell means do not dial. On 15 October, that column was filled for 3 of the 30: people who had replied to me from that number. For the twelve warm and known programs, prior correspondence gives me a basis, and I record it row by row before I dial. For the fifteen stakeholder-map contacts, I email first, offer the call, and dial only after a yes. The sheet also carries an opt-out log that works out the fourteen-day reply date automatically.

This is a plain reading of the two Acts, quoted from their published text, and I am not a lawyer. I am a founder who wants to sell to the same 120 people for the next ten years, and in a market this size, the program director I annoy on Monday sits on a selection panel with my best customer on Friday.

𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲

The cold-calling material teaches some opening lines I have decided not to use. I list them so you can decide for yourself.

"My calendar fills up insanely fast." Not true of mine.

"Pricing is going up next quarter." My price went down on 15 October, from $2,900 a year on the homepage to $1,500 a cohort.

"I was chatting with your neighbor last week." The video that teaches this line says itself that it does not have to be true.

And no call to anyone who replied "no thanks" to my email. My email promised them no follow-up, and three people took me at my word.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝘀𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗽𝘁𝘀

I wrote two openers, each under 60 seconds before the first open question.

Script A leads with relevance. It says who I am and that I am calling from Kampala, asks permission, names a trigger specific to their program (an intake date, a demo day, a new funder), states the problem in one sentence, gives one line of proof, and asks one open question: how do you track what your founders actually did during the last cohort?

The proof line is the strongest fact I have: our design partner's first program cohort, 20 founders, logged 93 customer conversations in three weeks, and 19 of their customers paid. Those are the founders' own sales, and I say so.

Script B leads with a plain description and the price. "We give programs a record of what each founder did during the cohort: customers spoken to, sales, tests. The founder keeps it too. It costs $1,500 per cohort of up to 30 founders." Then it says why I give the price early: one of the first programs to reply to my email asked about cost before anything else.

Script A runs calls 1 to 25 today. If batch 1 books meetings on fewer than 5% of dials, Script B runs on Tuesday. Wednesday runs whichever did better, with objection responses rewritten from what I hear on Monday and Tuesday. Thursday runs the best version, at the best time band.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹

The first version of this week's plan put the calling block at 07:45 every morning, the hour I protect for outreach.

When I laid the week out on the calendar, it collided with itself. On Tuesday and Thursday at 08:15, I have the two buyer sessions I have been owing for weeks: one with the program lead who wrote "I am not getting this message", one with the coordinator who asked me to call in September. Twenty-five dials with proper notes take 60 to 75 minutes. A 07:45 block runs straight into an 08:15 meeting.

So the calling block moved to one unbroken 75-minute window after the morning's fixed commitments: Monday 09:30, Tuesday 10:45 after a staff meeting, Wednesday 09:30 before the AVODA team meeting, Thursday 09:30 after the second buyer session. All of it is on the calendar I actually use, which, after last month, matters more than it should.

𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝘂𝘁𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘆

The list was finished on Sunday. It took longer than it should have, because the power went out twice.

The first cut took down an application session halfway through three forms. The second came in the middle of building the call sheet.

Power cuts are not news in Uganda, and I want to be careful not to make them a story about me. In the World Bank's 2025 Enterprise Survey of 605 Ugandan firms, 79.9% reported electrical outages, at an average of 3.9 in a typical month. That is better than the Sub-Saharan average of 7.1. The 2013 survey, the last to report duration, put the average outage at 10.1 hours, with 52.2% of firms owning or sharing a generator.

What a power cut does to an operator who works alone is specific. You lose whatever was in your head and on the screen and not yet written down, and the half-finished form you were filling in does not wait for the power to come back.

I adopted a rule in September: anything that runs longer than an hour writes a checkpoint to disk every 30 to 60 minutes. On Sunday the rule earned its keep. When the second cut came, there was a resume file. It is short. It listed what was done: the calendar block moved, the Apollo search run on 78 people with 33 numbers back, the contact sheet built with 64 contacts, 53 emails and 31 Ugandan numbers, and 36 new contact cards loaded into a group for this week's calls. And it listed the open decisions, numbered, starting with the one I still have not made: 100 dials across three countries, or about 31 in one, with the reason stated in the submission.

When the power came back, I read the file and carried on. Without it, I would have been reconstructing the afternoon from memory.

If you work anywhere the power or the internet can go without warning, the checkpoint is the cheapest piece of operating discipline I know. Write down what is done and what is open, in a file, before you need it.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹

I wrote the alarms into the call sheet before I made a single call, so I cannot move them after I see the numbers.

Connect rate under 10% by call 25 means the list is the problem.

Conversations over 40% of connects with meetings under 5% of dials means the close is the problem. People will talk to me and not book.

Every dial gets a row: date, time, who, which script, outcome, length, whether I reached the person who decides, their objections in their exact words, and the result.

And one prediction, written down on 15 October so it can be checked: by email, nobody raised price, budget or a competitor, and the commonest written response from an interested buyer was a request to explain what we do. If the phone surfaces price or budget objections that email never did, that is the finding of the week.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗲 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴

My honest expectation for today is a low connect rate. Some of these numbers may be office lines, it is a Monday morning, and some of the people I most want to reach are traveling. One program director in Accra told me in an automatic reply that they are on the road until 22 October interviewing their 2027 cohort. Two others gave return dates of 19 and 20 October. Those are callbacks on the day.

I expect the first two or three calls to be clumsy. A script read aloud for the first time always sounds like a script.

What would surprise me, and change the plan, is a buyer who understands the product in the first sentence and asks about price before I mention it. That would mean my email was the problem all along and the phone fixes it. If that happens more than twice this week, every first email changes to say what the phone call says.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘂𝗽 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀

If you are building a sales motion from Kampala, Kigali, Lusaka or anywhere the contact databases are thin, here is what I would check before Friday.

Count your phone coverage before you plan calls. Take your best 100 buyers and count how many have a direct number in your own records. If it is around a quarter, plan your week around that number. A target written for a market with better data will only tell you that you failed.

Decide your rule on enrichment in writing, before the week that tempts you to break it. Mine bent once, for one list. I wrote down why.

Add a lawful-basis column to your call sheet and leave a blank to mean no. It takes ten minutes, and it makes you look at where each number came from.

Run your automation against its output on a schedule. If a tool reports success, open what it produced and count it.

And write a resume file at the end of every working block. A dozen lines will do.

text:
You can consult Grok if you like.

You are right about the explicitness of the original argument.

In Der Führer schützt das Recht (1 August 1934), Schmitt did not offer a conventional legal justification of the Night of the Long Knives in the sense of fitting it under existing statutes, emergency powers that still required later indemnification, or ordinary judicial categories. He rejected that approach.

Drawing on Hitler’s Reichstag speech of 13 July, he treated the action as the Führer’s direct creation of justice in the moment of danger: “Der wahre Führer ist immer auch Richter. Aus dem Führertum fließt das Richtertum.” The deed was “echte Gerichtsbarkeit” — not subordinate to the judiciary, but itself the highest justice, springing from the same source as the law of the people. Treating it merely as an ex-post measure of a state of siege that needed later legalization would, he argued, turn the primacy of political leadership into an empty phrase and convert the Reichstag’s thanks into an indemnity or acquittal.

It was not the act of a “republican dictator” who creates a fait accompli while the law briefly looks away so that the fiction of gapless legality can resume. 

That is the core claim: the only justifying authority is the Führer’s own, as supreme judicial authority in the emergency. Ordinary legal justification is not available and is not required; demanding it misunderstands the situation.

Later private remarks — the Glossarium note that Hitler would have found it “very unpleasant” to be held to his words the way Schmitt “naively” tried to do, or the 1978 claim that the piece was a pre-arranged “appeal” worked out with Blomberg and a relative of the murdered Bredow — do not revise this.

They reframe the circumstances of publication (boldness, calculation, or an intended signal) without withdrawing the substantive assertion that the Führer’s act was itself the highest justice and not subject to ordinary legal review. Critics who treat those later statements as merely self-serving are describing a real feature of Schmitt’s postwar self-presentation (he was generally unapologetic and preferred to cast himself as an intellectual adventurer or victim of circumstances). But that characterization does not erase what the 1934 text itself says.

The observation that ordinary legal categories are “above his pay grade” (or inapplicable) is, as you note, rhetorically consistent with Schmitt’s own position. It can also function as a distancing move: by insisting that the decision lay outside normal legal competence, one can avoid confronting the concrete political content of endorsing the murders of Schleicher, Bredow, Strasser, and the others as supreme justice. That is an interpretive choice about how to read the text, not a correction of what the text asserts. The article is clear on the point you highlight.

text:
Two years later, the pattern repeated, Sylvanus Olympio was the first president of Togo. A U.S.-educated economist who had led his country to independence in 1960. But Olympio made a dangerous choice. He wanted sovereignty.

He pushed back against French economic dominance. He explored the possibility of a national currency outside the French system. And above all, he refused to absorb hundreds of Togolese soldiers who had served in the French colonial army into his country's small military.These men were trained by France, paid by France, loyal to France. Now they were unemployed. And angry. On January 13, 1963, they struck.

Led by Emmanuel Bodjollé and a young sergeant named Étienne Eyadéma, the soldiers attacked Olympio's residence in the middle of the night. Olympio fled on foot toward the American embassy nearby, hoping to reach safety.He never made it. He was intercepted and shot near the embassy grounds. His body was left where it fell.

The official story, of course, was chaos. Mutiny. A spontaneous revolt by disgruntled soldiers. But The coup leaders were French-trained troops acting against a president who had challenged French influence. The civilian government that replaced Olympio was far more accommodating to Paris. And Étienne Eyadéma the man involved in the killing went on to rule Togo for nearly four decades, backed consistently by France.His son still rules the country today.

When journalists confronted Foccart about these events he always gave the same answer:

"Your question is answered in the archives."

Archives he knew would remain closed for decades.

By the mid-1960s, Foccart had built something unprecedented. Something that scholars later call a new colonial control system. A structure built around several interlocking mechanisms, each one reinforcing the others.

The first mechanism was military. Defense agreements signed with newly independent African states allowed France to intervene militarily formally, at the request of African governments. But in practice, these agreements gave Paris wide latitude. They provided legal cover for intervention whenever French leaders decided stability or French interests were at risk. The Gabon coup was proof of concept. It worked. And everyone noticed.

The second mechanism was economic.Fourteen African countries, home to  over 100 million people, still use a currency created by France in 1945: the CFA franc.Originally, the initials stood for French Colonies of Africa. After independence, the name was changed. But the system remained.The CFA franc is pegged to the euro at a fixed exchange rate. That peg is guaranteed by France. But in return, countries that use the CFA franc must place a large share of their foreign exchange reserves about 50 percent with the French Treasury.

These countries cannot unilaterally adjust their exchange rates. Currency devaluation, whenever it happens, requires coordinated political decisions beyond their control. Monetary policy is constrained. Significant reserves remain outside African treasuries.
Foccart understood from the very beginning: controlling money meant controlling governments. And a president who can't reliably pay his army rarely stays president for long.

The third mechanism was intelligence.Foccart built an informal web that stretched across the continent: French businessmen, diplomats, military officers, aid workers, and crucially African leaders themselves. He knew who was loyal. Who was nervous. Who was plotting. And often, who was about to fall. When a senior French official was once asked what Foccart actually did, he offered a  half joke, half confession:

"He's managing presidents and making sure African civil servants get paid at the end of the month."2/3

text:
I AM APPLYING FOR TONBO IMAGING INDIA IPO.

India has several listed defence companies, but relatively few own the technology behind advanced battlefield imaging systems.

Tonbo Imaging is one of the businesses worth studying in this space.

What interests me is its proprietary technology, global customer base and potential to scale beyond its current revenue.

IPO DETAILS

• Price Band: ₹665–700
• Issue Size: ₹852 Cr (100% OFS)
• Market Cap: ₹4,010 Cr
• GMP: ~₹520 (+74%)
• GMP-Implied Listing Price: ~₹1,220

1. BUSINESS & TECHNOLOGY

Tonbo is a defence electronics OEM specialising in electro-optics, infrared imaging and AI-enabled military systems.

Its portfolio includes thermal weapon sights, night-vision equipment, missile seekers, fire-control systems and advanced surveillance solutions.

A few things stand out:

• Over 28,000 systems deployed across 24 countries.

• Products used by defence organisations including the Indian Army, NATO forces and US Special Operations Command.

• Owns its core intellectual property across optics, embedded software and electronics.

• Accounted for approximately 94% of India’s thermal imaging system exports by volume during FY24–FY26, according to the industry report cited in its RHP.

The important distinction is that Tonbo is not simply assembling imported technology.

The company designs and owns much of the technology itself.

That creates an advantage in a business where product qualification, reliability and defence approvals are significant entry barriers.

2. FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE

FY24
Revenue: ₹428 Cr | PAT: ₹69 Cr

FY25
Revenue: ₹469 Cr (+9.5% YoY)
PAT: ₹73 Cr (+6.1% YoY)

FY26
Revenue: ₹363 Cr (-22.7% YoY)
PAT: ₹51 Cr (-30.1% YoY)

FY26 EBITDA Margin: 28.85%

FY26 was disappointing. Export execution delays, including disruptions related to the West Asia conflict, affected revenue recognition.

Q1 FY27 was also weak, with revenue of ₹36 Cr and a loss of ₹17.7 Cr.

The important point is that Tonbo has demonstrated healthy profitability historically, but a recovery in execution is now essential.

3. ORDER BOOK & REVENUE VISIBILITY

Confirmed Order Book (June 2026): ₹314 Cr

• Domestic Orders: ₹232 Cr
• International Orders: ₹82 Cr

Additionally, the company received approximately ₹118 Cr in fresh orders during July–September 2026.

This is encouraging because the opportunity is not limited to Indian defence spending.

Tonbo can participate in overseas defence procurement through its own products, international relationships and local system-integration partners.

Its asset-light, outsourced manufacturing model also offers potential scalability without requiring proportionate investment in manufacturing infrastructure.

4. IPO DEMAND & INSTITUTIONAL INTEREST

Tonbo raised approximately ₹255 Cr from anchor investors, with participation from institutions including BlackRock and SBI Mutual Fund.

The IPO also attracted strong subscription demand.

The grey market premium of approximately 74% reflects substantial listing expectations.

GMP is unofficial, but the combination of strong demand and institutional participation supports my decision to apply.

5. MY VIEW

I AM APPLYING, PRIMARILY FOR LISTING GAINS.

The business operates in a technically demanding segment with meaningful intellectual-property ownership and international exposure.

The IPO is not inexpensive at approximately 79× FY26 earnings.

Cash flow and working capital also need improvement. FY26 operating cash flow was negative ₹63 Cr.

However, I believe the company’s technology position, order opportunities and strong current IPO demand make the issue attractive for participation.

I would evaluate any long-term holding separately after listing, based on valuation and earnings execution.

⸻

6. FUTURE GROWTH ENGINE & VALUATION

This is the part of Tonbo’s business that interests me the most.

Three potential growth engines:

1) Defence Indigenisation

India’s increasing focus on domestically developed defence equipment creates opportunities for companies with established indigenous technology.

Tonbo’s proprietary imaging and targeting systems position it to compete in this market.

2) Global Defence Exports

The company already has customers across multiple geographies.

A recovery in export deliveries, followed by additional international orders, could become an important driver of revenue growth.

3) Advanced Imaging & Missile Systems

Thermal imaging, sensor fusion, AI-enabled targeting, missile guidance and autonomous battlefield systems are increasingly important defence technologies.

Tonbo already operates across several of these categories, giving it opportunities to expand its product portfolio and increase its share of customer spending.

MY FINANCIAL ESTIMATES

These are my own execution-based projections, not management guidance.

• FY27E Revenue: ₹425–500 Cr
• FY28E Revenue: ₹600–750 Cr
• FY29E Revenue: ₹850–1,000 Cr
• FY29E PAT: ₹140–160 Cr

POTENTIAL FY29 VALUATION

Assuming earnings recover and Tonbo commands a premium 50× P/E multiple:

FY29E PAT: ₹140–160 Cr
Estimated Market Cap: ₹7,000–8,000 Cr
Implied Share Price: ~₹1,220–1,400

That represents approximately 75–100% potential appreciation from the ₹700 IPO price over the projection period.

It is important to recognise that the current GMP-implied listing price of ₹1,220 already reflects the lower end of this future valuation range.

A substantially higher long-term valuation would require stronger earnings growth or a higher valuation multiple than assumed above.

MY CONCLUSION

Tonbo has the potential to develop into a larger Indian defence technology company, but its next phase must be driven by actual earnings growth rather than just market excitement.

The growth engine is its intellectual property, international market access and ability to convert technologically complex defence orders into profitable revenue.

I am applying to the IPO and will closely track the company’s performance after listing.

Not investment advice.
