text:
A New Milestone for Chinmaya Mission- South Africa 

Inauguration of the Medical Facility at Chinmaya Annapoorna! 🏥

On the auspicious first day of Sharad Navratri, Chinmaya Mission South Africa was once again blessed by the powerful grace of Devi. 11th October 2026 marked the divine inauguration of 'Andal Nilayam' – a compact free-healthcare facility for the underprivileged as well as the residential building for priests, acharyas, and devotees.

A traditional puja unto Pujya Gurudev and Devi Annapoorna was held in the morning of the opening day, followed by a formal event at night, in the presence of Swami Abhedananda (In-Charge, CM South Africa). With over 700 donors, members, devotees, and beneficiaries in attendance, the facility was officially declared open. Councillor Mpume Sithole (representing the Hon'ble Mayor), Prince Ishwar Ramlutchman, Dr Rajendran Govender, Councillor Daniel Mea, Mr Poobalan Govender (National Council of Provinces), Judge Ranjiv Nirghin (SA Hindu Mahasabha), and Shri Sidney Govindsamy (Devasthanum) were among the eminent dignitaries who addressed the gathering. Also blessing the event were Brahmacharins of the Mission.

The dignitaries generously appreciated Swamiji for his contributions to society through seva, satsang, and spirituality. Showering him with accolades, they referred to him as one whose name would be ranked the highest among those who came from Bharat to South Africa to uplift the people of this land. Further, they all publicly affirmed their allegiance and commitment to Swamiji and the Chinmaya Mission in their future endeavours.

11th October also marked the 2nd anniversary of the Nourish to Flourish project, completing two full years old dedicated selfless service through nearly half a million meals fed to thousands every day.

This completes the third phase of the Nourish to Flourish project and redevelopment of the Chinmaya Annapoorna premises. It is nothing less than divine will that every milestone for this initiative falls during Sharad Navratri every successive year. In Navratri 2021, CM South Africa received the land for this project. In Navratri 2023, construction began. In Navratri 2024, Nourish to Flourish had its grand launch and the mega-industrial kitchen was inaugurated. In Navratri 2025, construction of the Annapoorna Devi Temple was completed. And now, in Navratri 2026, Andal Nilayam is the latest addition to the blessings of Devi for the people of South Africa.

CM South Africa expresses gratitude to Shri Govind Bommi from Singapore for his spearheading contribution to this medical facility and Andal Nilayam, and continued support for the Mission worldwide. We offer all glory, achievement, and contributions at the feet of the Lord and Pujya Gurudev. We pray for the wellbeing of all and continue to seek opportunities to serve Narayana residing in all underpivileged individuals, families, and schoolchildren in South Africa.

text:
TWO PRESIDENTS, TWO VERY DIFFERENT MOMENTS WITH AMERICAN WAR HEROES 🇺🇦🇺🇸🇫🇷

When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Melvin Hurwitz, an American World War II veteran, the elderly soldier reached for his hand and attempted to kiss it. Zelenskyy gently pulled his hand away, lowered himself to the veteran’s level and embraced him instead.

What followed was a deeply moving exchange.

Veteran: “You’re the savior of the people!”

Zelenskyy: “No, no, no. You saved Europe.”

Veteran: “You bring tears to my eyes. You are my hero.”

Zelenskyy: “No, no, you are our hero.”

Veteran: “I pray for you.”

The encounter offers a contrast with controversies surrounding Donald Trump’s remarks and treatment of American military service members.

During a 2018 visit to France marking the centenary of the end of World War I, Trump cancelled a planned visit to the Aisne-Marne American Cemetery, where 2,289 American military personnel are buried. According to accounts published by The Atlantic, Trump privately questioned why he should visit a cemetery filled with “losers” and referred to fallen Marines at Belleau Wood as “suckers.” Trump has denied making those remarks.

The soldiers who died at Belleau Wood were fighting Germany in World War I, not the Nazi regime of World War II.

In 2024, Trump also attracted criticism for comparing the Presidential Medal of Freedom with the Medal of Honor. He called the civilian decoration “much better” while noting that Medal of Honor recipients are often severely wounded or awarded the distinction posthumously.

In 2025, Trump was criticised for playing golf in Florida rather than attending a dignified transfer ceremony for four fallen American service members, although presidential attendance at such ceremonies is not mandatory.

Zelenskyy’s exchange with Hurwitz was a simple moment of mutual respect between two men from different generations, both shaped by wars in Europe.

Neither wanted to be called a hero. Each insisted that the other deserved the honour.

text:
#cozymystery #dogs #fiction
How to Support Indie Authors and Help Books Thrive

A new book can arrive as quietly as a paw print on a porch. No giant marketing team announces it. No towering display appears at every store. Yet behind that book may be years of early mornings, revised chapters, research rabbit holes, and characters an author has come to love like family.

Knowing **how to support indie authors** means recognizing that a small, thoughtful action can travel farther than it seems. For readers who adore cozy mysteries, animal stories, small-town secrets, and a satisfying ending, supporting independent writers is also a way to keep the kinds of books you enjoy coming.

## Buy the Book in the Way That Works for You

Buying a book is the most direct form of support, whether you choose paperback, hardcover, ebook, or audiobook. It tells an author that their story found a home with a real reader, not just a spot on a digital shelf.

When possible, buying directly from an author’s website or at an author event can be especially meaningful. The author often keeps a greater share of the sale, and a signed copy may come with a personal touch. Still, there is no need to feel guilty if your usual bookstore, favorite ebook shop, or local library is the best fit for your budget and reading habits. A book read and enjoyed is never a lesser kind of support.

Preorders can be particularly helpful. Before a release date, they give publishers, retailers, and recommendation systems an early signal that readers are interested. For an indie author, a handful of preorders can make release week feel less like a lonely stakeout and more like a friendly gathering in the town square.

## Leave an Honest Review After You Finish

Reviews are one of the kindest things a reader can give. They help other book lovers decide whether a story is right for them, and they help books become more visible where readers browse.

A review does not need to be long, polished, or glowing to be valuable. Two or three sincere sentences can do plenty. You might mention that you enjoyed the dog narrator, appreciated the historical setting, laughed at a quirky character, or found the mystery difficult to solve. Specific details help future readers far more than a simple star rating alone.

Honesty matters. If a book was not quite your cup of tea, it is fine to say so with kindness. Focus on your reading experience rather than treating a book as though it has failed a test. Cozy mystery readers have wonderfully varied preferences. One reader wants more clues and suspects; another wants more cats, recipes, and charming front porches.

Avoid spoilers, especially in mysteries. You can say the ending surprised you without identifying the culprit. Think of it as protecting the evidence until everyone has had a fair chance to investigate.

### A Review Does Not Have to Be Perfect

Many readers hold back because they worry they do not know what to say. Try this easy starting point: say what drew you to the book, name one element you enjoyed, and tell readers who might like it. That is enough.

For example: “I loved the small Florida town setting and the animal-centered clues. The mystery moved quickly, and Daisy’s observations made me smile. A fun choice for readers who like lighthearted whodunits.” That small note can encourage a curious reader to give the book a chance.

https://t.co/qKjnzvFR2k

## Tell the Right Reader About It

Word of mouth has always been powerful. A recommendation from a trusted friend can beat the flashiest advertisement because it comes with something better than a sales pitch: genuine enthusiasm.

The key is to match the book with the person. Give a cozy mystery to the neighbor who enjoys puzzle nights. Mention an animal story to the friend who never passes a dog without saying hello. Bring up a children’s book when someone is shopping for a grandchild, niece, nephew, classroom, or little reader who needs a new bedtime favorite.

You do not need a large social media following. A text to a friend, a note in a book club chat, or a photo of your current read can introduce a title to exactly the reader who has been looking for it. If you share online, adding a few real words about why the book appealed to you makes the post warmer and more useful than simply posting a cover.

For a series such as the Doc and Daisy Mysteries, recommending the first book can be a lovely invitation. Readers enjoy discovering a place they can return to, with familiar characters, ongoing friendships, and enough clues to keep their detective instincts busy.

## Ask Your Library to Consider the Book

Libraries are treasured gathering places for readers, and a library request can give an indie title a longer life. Most libraries offer a way for patrons to suggest books for purchase. The process varies, and libraries must make choices based on budget, availability, local interest, and their collection needs. A request is not a guarantee, but it is a meaningful vote.

If your library carries an indie author’s book, borrow it. Checkouts show that readers are interested. You can also mention the title to a librarian who knows your taste. Librarians are skilled matchmakers for books, and they often enjoy hearing about new authors their patrons have discovered.

A library recommendation is especially helpful for readers who cannot buy every book they want. Supporting authors should not be reserved for those with overflowing book budgets. Reading, requesting, recommending, and reviewing all count.

## Show Up for the Human Behind the Story

Independent authors often wear many hats. They write, revise, arrange cover art, plan launches, answer reader messages, and sometimes pack books for the mail. A friendly response can brighten a very ordinary Tuesday.

If an author offers a newsletter, consider subscribing. Newsletters are often where readers hear first about new releases, special events, behind-the-scenes stories, or the real-life inspirations behind a fictional town. Unlike the quick current of social media, an inbox message has a better chance of reaching the people who asked to receive it.

Author events matter, too, whether they take place at a library, bookstore, festival, school, or community gathering. Attend if you can, bring a friend, and ask a question. Even a small audience can make an event feel lively and worthwhile. If you cannot attend, a short message of encouragement afterward is still a gracious gesture.

### Share With Respect for the Work

One way not to support an author is to share unauthorized copies of their books. It may seem harmless to send a file to a few friends, but it removes the sale, library checkout, or recommendation that helps sustain future writing.

If you want to pass along a story, lend a paper copy where permitted, give a copy as a gift, suggest it to your book club, or ask your library to add it. These choices spread the pleasure of reading while respecting the work that created it.

## Give Books as Invitations

A book makes a thoughtful gift because it says, “I thought this story might delight you.” Indie books are especially fun gifts for holidays, birthdays, thank-yous, host gifts, and care packages. Pair a cozy mystery with tea, cocoa, or a small dog-themed bookmark. Give a children’s book with a stuffed animal or a handwritten note inside the cover.

Book clubs can be wonderful supporters, too. Choosing an indie author for a monthly read gives a story several readers at once and creates conversation around it. Some authors may be available to answer questions, but it is best to check their stated preferences rather than assume. A respectful invitation is always better than a surprise summons to solve a mystery on a Tuesday night.

The best support is not necessarily loud or expensive. It is steady, sincere, and reader-shaped. Pick one indie author whose work makes you smile, then leave a review, tell a friend, request the book at your library, or save room on your shelf for their next adventure. Stories grow when readers carry them forward.

text:
Early Solidbody Electric Guitar Pioneers, 1931-1952

The solidbody electric guitar had no single inventor. Pickup design, Spanish-style playability and factory production developed independently; the first electric lap steel and first mass-market solidbody were different instruments.

George Beauchamp developed a horseshoe-magnet pickup alongside Adolph Rickenbacker and Paul Barth in Los Angeles. Their Ro-Pat-In company began in 1931; its cast-aluminum A-22 Frying Pan entered production in 1932. Made for lap playing, it amplified strings without a resonant soundbox. Its casting contained cavities.

Also in 1932, former Gibson designer Lloyd Loar and executive Lewis A. Williams produced the Vivi-Tone Skeleton. An August brochure documents its open frame, decorative face and lack of a resonant chamber. Its pickup sensed bridge vibration rather than magnetized strings. It is the earliest documented commercially offered solidbody electric Spanish guitar, though few sold.

Rickenbacker's 1935 Electro Spanish Model B adapted its horseshoe pickup to fretted playing. Molded Bakelite construction and a detachable round neck minimized feedback. Weight-relief cavities made it technically semi-solid.

Chicago's Slingerland introduced the wooden Songster Model 401 around 1936. Neck-through construction and a hum-canceling pickup arrangement distinguished it. A late-1930s catalog offered guitar, amplifier and case for $150, years before Les Paul or Fender produced their designs.

In Jamaica, musician and radio technician Hedley Jones built his own electric Spanish guitar, inspired by Charlie Christian. He assembled its pickup using horseshoe magnets and salvaged components. Kingston's Daily Gleaner photographed the instrument on September 2, 1940. Jones later became an important sound-system engineer.

Les Paul's Log, generally dated to 1941, joined an Epiphone neck, pickups and bridge to a four-inch-square wooden beam. Halves of an archtop body supplied a conventional appearance; the beam carried string tension. Built in New York, it explored sustain and feedback reduction. Gibson initially rejected the concept.

Iowa inventor O.W. Appleton built the APP, traditionally dated to 1941. Its carved single-cutaway wooden body carried a Gibson neck, pickup and trapeze tailpiece. Appleton reportedly showed it to Gibson in 1943. Claims that Gibson later copied it are unproven.

In 1948, Paul A. Bigsby built Merle Travis a custom wooden solidbody with precision hardware and six inline tuners. The original lacked a cutaway; its familiar cutaway and revised headstock were later changes. Its influence on Fender remains debated.

Leo Fender's breakthrough was economical mass production. After building lap steels and amplifiers with Doc Kauffman, Fender's team developed a flat body, removable bolt-on neck, adjustable bridge and simplified electronics. The single-pickup Esquire and two-pickup Broadcaster debuted in 1950. A Gretsch naming objection led to the Telecaster name in 1951. The design became the first widely successful mass-produced solidbody Spanish electric.

Gibson entered in 1952 under president Ted McCarty, with Les Paul as collaborator and endorser. The Goldtop Les Paul Model featured mahogany body, carved maple top, glued-in neck, two P-90 single-coils and trapeze bridge-tailpiece. Its traditional construction contrasted with Fender's modular design.

Rather than one invention, the modern solidbody emerged through overlapping developments in pickups, construction, playability and industrial production.

text:
Hermes yesterday: heads-up if you keep work in Hermes worktrees. An idle worktree with uncommitted or unpushed work used to sit on disk forever; on main the sweep now archives it to a git ref and then deletes it, and gitignored files such as .env copies go with it. Also: Docker sandboxes stop leaving root-owned and setuid files on your host, and Desktop stops opening a pile of sign-in windows overnight. 339 commits landed on main; here are the 10 that matter.

1️⃣ Idle worktrees with unsaved work are archived, then removed

Before: the worktree pruner never removed a dirty or unpushed tree at any age, and its 6-hour sweep only knew the Hermes checkout and cron workdirs, so trees piled up (658 trees and about 1 TB on one machine). After: on by default (worktrees.archive_dirty: true), a tree under a repo's .worktrees folder that sits idle past its tier (hermes-* and subagent-* 24 h, named trees 72 h) and holds uncommitted or unpushed work is first saved as a commit at refs/hermes/archive/<tree> (HEAD, staged, unstaged and untracked files, exact bytes) and then removed. hermes worktree restore <name> brings it back, hermes worktree list shows archives and hermes worktree prune --dry-run prints the plan without touching anything. Every repo Hermes has made a worktree in is now swept, a subagent's worktree with edits is archived when it finishes (its branch kept for the parent), and a dirty hermes -w exit asks Keep, Archive & remove or Discard (Keep is the default). Heads-up: gitignored files (.env copies, caches, build output) are not archived and are deleted with the tree, and archive refs older than 30 days are deleted (archive_retention_days). Left alone: trees with a running process or a live Hermes lock inside, recently touched ones, Kanban trees, trees with a submodule or a nested repo, and trees holding an untracked file over 50 MB. worktrees.archive_dirty: false brings back the old never-delete behavior. Not covered: closing a Desktop session never asks.

2️⃣ Docker sandboxes stop leaving root files and setuid binaries on your host

Before: on Linux the Docker backend runs as the image's user (root by default), so what it wrote into its bind-mounted /root and /workspace dirs stayed root-owned on the host and could not be deleted without sudo, and a file there carrying setuid/setgid bits or file capabilities kept them on the host, where running it as your user gave root's rights. Since the one-gateway change, hermes chat sessions on Docker also got no /workspace mount (container_persistent: false) or all shared one container bound to the first session's folder. After: at teardown a locked-down throwaway container hands root-owned files back to your user; setuid/setgid bits and file capabilities are stripped at every session boundary, persistent sandboxes included (on detach, before reattach and in the orphan sweep); each gateway session mounts its own folder, persistent Docker keeps one container per profile and folder, and idle per-folder containers are stopped instead of left running. Not covered: rootless Docker, userns-remap, Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows, and Podman (the pass is off or untested there); the default persistent container is never removed, so its file handback waits until it is; a setuid file planted while a sandbox is attached and run on the host before the next boundary; legitimate setuid files under /root or /workspace lose their bits inside the container too; reattach takes about 0.4 s longer.

3️⃣ Desktop stops piling up sign-in windows overnight

Before: after a gateway session lapsed (sleep, a gateway restart, an identity provider outage), every background request that got a 401 opened its own sign-in window, and when automatic sign-in could not finish, each one showed itself after 2.5 s, so people woke up to a screen covered in Hermes and Nous Portal sign-in windows. After: unattended sign-in runs hidden with a 12 s deadline and, if it fails, Desktop shows its own not signed in state with a Sign in button; a window appears only after you click Sign in, Use gateway or pick a cloud agent. There is one login flow per cookie jar: background callers join it and back off exponentially after a failure, and a second click focuses the open window instead of opening another one (which used to break the first with state_mismatch). Not covered: a real Nous Portal round trip and a real macOS lid close and wake were not tested.

4️⃣ TLS keeps working after the install environment rotates

Before: when the package manager replaced the install environment under a long-running Hermes process (a launchd gateway, for example), certifi kept pointing at the deleted CA bundle, so every model call failed with No such file or directory, Nous credential refreshes failed too, and only a restart helped. After: Hermes re-resolves the CA bundle once per rotation and logs one warning, and the Nous auth exchange, Weixin, WeCom and the Actual relay go through the same repair; the browser and Keenable plugins' requests calls get a live bundle (on Windows, the system store written once to $HERMES_HOME/cache/platform-ca-bundle.pem), and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE or CURL_CA_BUNDLE overrides keep working. Nothing changes on a healthy install. Not covered: other direct requests callers (https://t.co/38EVCVM64v lookups, image and video generation plugins, keyless MCP and others) still fail after a rotation until a restart.

5️⃣ Chat messages keep their order, and Desktop queues behind a busy bot

Before: since the one-gateway change, a photo or video followed quickly by text could be handled out of order, a message claimed just before /new ran on the fresh conversation, slash-command turns (/queue, /plan, skills) jumped ahead of waiting messages, and on serial platforms such as Signal and IRC a burst sent during a turn held up the reader. Typing into a Desktop chat while its gateway owner was mid-turn (a Bot Chat delivery) showed Turn failed, and peer DM, peer run, POST /v1/runs and bot or cron deliveries to a Bot Chat first created over the API failed with not_found. After: media and the text after it keep arrival order; /new drops the claimed turn; slash commands queue behind waiting messages; a burst on a serial platform merges into one follow-up; a Desktop prompt to a busy owner is queued and runs once after the turn, and when it cannot be queued (rewind, attachments) the card says why and that you can send it when the turn ends; the old API-created Bot Chat is moved aside as Bot Chat (API <id>) with its history, and deliveries land in a new local one. Not covered: per the PRs, these still need a live retest on real Telegram, Signal and Desktop setups.

6️⃣ An unattended gateway no longer freezes on a hook prompt

Before: a shell hook that was not yet approved made the gateway ask Allow this hook to run? on a console nobody watched (a hidden console still counts as a terminal), which froze it until the liveness watchdog killed it with exit 75; this could hit at start, when a secondary profile loaded or after a config set. Approving a hook later did nothing until a restart or a local session opened. After: the gateway, cron, mcp serve, ACP and the TUI backend never prompt; an unapproved hook is skipped, and the warning names the allowlist file of the profile that needs it (for example profiles/p2/shell-hooks-allowlist.json); only foreground hermes chat and hermes rl may ask. A running gateway registers a hook within about 30 s of its consent being recorded and drops it about 30 s after hermes hooks revoke, on single-profile and multiplexed gateways, without rebuilding adapters. A watchdog kill now also writes its thread stacks to logs/gateway-shutdown-watchdog.log.

7️⃣ Per-chat settings and history survive restarts

Before: since the one-gateway change, a /reasoning pick on a Bot Chat that follows its profile did not stick; the classic CLI's /model --once changed the shared session; deleting a parent session dropped launch secrets a /branch child still used; a managed worker's first Always approval on a fresh profile never reached config.yaml; resuming a compressed conversation showed only its last segment; and after a Desktop restart, opening a bot group by name created a fork of the room, All profiles switched itself off, and the all-profiles and Archived lists dropped or repeated sessions across pages. After: /reasoning is stored per session and survives profile following and restarts (/reasoning reset returns to the profile's level); --once applies to that one turn only; branch secrets stay while a branch uses them; Always is saved; resume returns the whole history with archived rows marked; Desktop reopens the existing group (a failed lookup offers Retry, never a new room), keeps All profiles on and lists each session once. Also: the gateway now refuses /voice tts on local sessions by name instead of synthesizing audio nobody hears.

8️⃣ Desktop: /usage before the first message, and a usable New Bot dialog

Before: Desktop and TUI /usage on a fresh session only said No active agent -- send a message first. In Bot Mode's New Bot dialog, opening Advanced, Capabilities before typing a name left a spinner forever and Create Bot then failed; the embedded Capabilities frame was a fixed 440 px. Main model settings squeezed Provider and Model into one row. After: /usage shows the provider's account limits and Nous credits right away, read from the session's own profile (a second profile's key included); the Capabilities tab loads whenever the name arrives, and its frame grows to min(85vh, 960px) in New Bot and Edit Profile; Main model settings get separate labeled Provider and Model rows with Apply below them, and choosing alone still saves nothing.

9️⃣ Plugins can post live progress and hear about compactions and deletes

New for plugin authors: https://t.co/9rizXZSqnt_message(text) posts one message into the conversation the plugin is working for and returns a handle whose edit() updates it in place on any channel (a fresh message where the platform cannot edit, a Desktop toast or TUI notice on local sessions, a line at turn end in the classic CLI); with no bound conversation it returns ok=False and sends nothing, and it is not available under plugins.isolation: host. A post_compaction hook fires once for every compaction that actually lands, on every path, so memory providers can re-inject what was summarized away; on_session_delete fires after any delete or deliberate archive from any surface, with a reason field. Plugin slash commands now receive session_id, session_key, platform and source when they declare them (one-argument handlers keep working), and the skills tool's lookup helpers (find_all_skills, locate_skill and five more) are public. Both hooks are observers: return values are ignored and delivery is process-local.

🔟 11 new plugins in the catalog: voice and devices lead

11 new community entries, and talking to Hermes outside the chat window was the day's theme: live WhatsApp voice calls on a linked personal number (through an unofficial protocol and a sidecar that streams call audio to Gemini Live) and small ESP32 devices with a screen, mic and speaker. Several disclose that they open a network port, run local subprocesses on the host or send data to a hosted service (tsubasa's API currently serves Canada only): read the disclosure before installing. Catalog entries do not wait for a release: they go live once the published catalog refreshes.

• Voice and devices: hermes-whatsapp-voice, gadget
• Desktop: completion-sound, offpeak-bekci, hermes-lang-it-full
• Agent logs: edit-ledger, interim-ledger

⚙️ Meanwhile, in the engine room

Dozens of fixes landed yesterday that most users will never see, and most of them went to the shared gateway: queues, sessions and profiles catching up with the one-gateway change.

• With proactive tool-result pruning on (proactive_prune_tokens), every prune rewrote the whole live transcript into state.db, leaving tens of thousands of superseded copies on one install; it now updates only the rows it changed, in place
• Scratch cleanup reclaims idle clones whose pack files are hardlinked to a live repo (one host had 100 GB held that way), and logs a root-owned leftover once, with the command that removes it, instead of re-walking it every hour
• On Windows, a normal Desktop or CLI facing a gateway started as administrator gets a named refusal with the fix (restart it without elevation) instead of a generic authorization error or, on some hosts, a silent attach across the UAC boundary
• hermes update on Linux with a system-scope dashboard unit and no root prints one exact sudo systemctl restart command instead of a polkit error and advice to restart the gateway

If you noticed none of this, it worked.

text:
Good morning, dear friends, and welcome to this new day on October 19, 2026. As the first light filters through our windows, it feels like the perfect time to pause and let a simple truth from Scripture settle into our hearts. The words from Isaiah remind us that one day, we will be glad and rejoice in his salvation. What a hopeful promise to carry with us from the very start of the morning.

Life right now brings its share of quiet worries and louder challenges. Many of us wake up thinking about rising costs, uncertain job markets, or the steady hum of global tensions that seem to fill every news cycle. Others carry personal burdens like health concerns for a loved one, the ache of loneliness, or the daily effort to keep relationships strong amid busy schedules. These realities can make joy feel distant, yet the verse gently points us toward something greater that never changes.

When Isaiah spoke of rejoicing in salvation, he was looking ahead to the moment when God would wipe away every tear and remove the veil of sorrow. That same hope is ours today. It does not ignore the difficulties we face but offers a steady anchor in the middle of them. We can choose to begin our day by remembering that salvation is already at work, bringing light into places that feel dark and strength where we feel weak.

Take a moment this morning to notice the small mercies around you. The warmth of a cup of coffee, the sound of birds outside, or the simple fact that you have another day to try again. These gifts echo the larger truth that God’s saving love is present and active. In a world that often pushes us toward fear or distraction, this verse invites us to lift our eyes and find genuine gladness in the promise that has already been fulfilled through Christ.

Whatever situation you are stepping into today, know that you are not alone. The salvation we rejoice in is not a far-off dream but a living reality that meets us in our ordinary moments. It gives us courage to face meetings, errands, conversations, and quiet hours with a heart that can still choose hope. Let this truth wrap around you like a warm blanket as you move through the hours ahead.

May your day be filled with unexpected moments of peace and the quiet assurance that God’s salvation is worth every ounce of our gladness. Rest in that promise, and walk forward with a lighter step.

Typical process and expectations
Send the photo or a sketch of the desired St. Michael defeating Satan design. Most companies respond with a mockup or 3D render, a quote, and timeline. Production commonly takes weeks to a few months. A large, detailed, illuminated, weather-resistant lawn figure (comparable to the one in the post) is usually a custom job in the thousands of dollars, depending on size, materials, lighting, and complexity. Chinese OEM manufacturers (via Alibaba or sites like LORK) can be cheaper but involve longer shipping, minimums, and more coordination for quality.
Contact a few with the image from the X post and ask specifically about continuous-air or sealed outdoor lawn versions with internal lighting and stakes. Creatable Inflatables and Inflatable Images are among the most relevant starting points for a religious-themed character display.

text:
"Hello, I am Palestinian.

And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." 
Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. 
They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. 
They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." 
Three noes. 
Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. 
They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. 
They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. 

And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.

I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
When You Discover That Georgia Is More Civilized Than the West

We have all witnessed the riots in Paris over the past weekend. What started as peaceful protests to express legitimate concerns about real problems turned into scenes of war, with hundreds of masked individuals destroying, pillaging and burning everything they could lay their hands on.

There is a strange phenomenon in human behavior. When people gather in large groups, their individuality can gradually disappear, and their behavior becomes influenced by the masses. This phenomenon is often associated with what we call gregariousness, the tendency of individuals to gather and move together.

The word comes from the Latin gregarius, meaning belonging to a flock or herd. Interestingly, the desert locust, Schistocerca gregaria, carries the same name because of its tendency to gather in enormous swarms.

A single locust cannot do much damage. However, a swarm of locusts can decimate hundreds of hectares of vegetation within hours.

It can be the same with people. One individual might hesitate to break a window, burn a car or destroy a shop. But surrounded by hundreds of others doing exactly that, the same individual can suddenly feel that everything is permitted. Personal responsibility disappears into the anonymity of the crowd, and individuals become part of a single destructive machine.

Of course, not every crowd behaves this way. Millions of people around the world demonstrate peacefully, sometimes under extremely difficult circumstances. The difference lies in the values that individuals bring with them when they join the crowd.

I could not help comparing the recent protests in France and Italy with those in Georgia.

Having lived in Georgia since the mid 1990s, I have witnessed countless demonstrations, some of them involving tens of thousands of people, others taking place during moments of extreme political tension.

I remember the Rose Revolution, the protests against Saakashvili, and the frequent demonstrations against Georgian Dream since it came to power.

In a country where political passions run extraordinarily high, where governments and opposition parties often treat each other as enemies, and where people have repeatedly taken to the streets to defend what they believe in, the overwhelming majority of protesters have understood something fundamental.

You can fight your government without fighting your country.

You can oppose those in power without destroying the property of your fellow citizens. You can demand change without burning the streets where your children walk, breaking the windows of businesses that employ your neighbors, or destroying the public spaces that belong to everyone.

I recall an incident a couple of years ago when benches were broken on Rustaveli Avenue. The protesters collected money the following day to compensate the company that owned them.

Think about the significance of such a gesture.

People who were protesting against their government felt personally responsible for damage caused during their demonstration. They understood that public and private property should not become the victims of political anger.

That is not simply good behavior. It is a demonstration of civic responsibility, dignity and respect for one's country.

And I believe that much of this starts at home.

It starts within the family, where children are taught to value, love and respect their country. It is at home that children first learn that they belong to something greater than themselves, their family, and that their family belongs to something greater still, their country.

They learn that freedom comes with responsibility, that rights come with obligations, and that disagreement does not give anyone the right to destroy what belongs to others.

A country is not simply a government, a parliament, a president or a prime minister.

A country is its people, its history, its streets, its schools, its hospitals, its gardens and the collective efforts of generations who built it.

Governments come and go. Political leaders rise and fall. But the country remains, and destroying it to express anger against those temporarily governing it is an act of extraordinary foolishness.

Paradoxically, in parts of the West, the family structure has weakened considerably, and with it, in some cases, the transmission of the values that once gave people a strong sense of belonging.

Too many young people grow up feeling disconnected from their society, their institutions and sometimes even their own country. Their immediate community becomes their only point of reference, while the country itself is perceived not as a common home that deserves protection, but as an enemy responsible for their frustrations.

Of course, governments themselves carry an enormous responsibility for this situation. When citizens feel abandoned, when opportunities disappear, when inequalities become unbearable and when political leaders lose the trust of the people, resentment inevitably grows.

But there is a fundamental difference between demanding justice and taking revenge on society.

Burning your neighbor's car will not make your life better. Destroying a small business will not create employment. Setting fire to a public building will not improve education, healthcare or social justice.

On the contrary, the first victims of such destruction are often the very people whose interests the protesters claim to defend.

There is also the question of immigration and integration, a subject that many Western societies have struggled to address.

Immigration itself is not the problem. Millions of immigrants have contributed enormously to the prosperity, culture and development of the countries that welcomed them.

The problem arises when integration fails, when communities live alongside one another without developing a common sense of belonging, and when some individuals never come to regard their adopted country as their own.

But integration is a responsibility shared by both sides. Those who arrive must respect the laws, values and institutions of their new country, while the country that welcomes them must offer a genuine opportunity to become part of its society.

A society cannot remain united indefinitely if its people no longer feel that they share a common destiny.

And this is precisely where Georgia has something important to teach the West.

Georgia is not a rich country. Its institutions are far from perfect. Its political life is deeply divided, and its democracy faces serious challenges.

Yet there is something deeply admirable about the attachment of Georgians to their homeland.

This is a country that has endured invasions, occupations, wars, economic hardship and political upheavals. Its people have suffered enormously, yet they have preserved their language, their culture, their traditions and an extraordinary sense of national identity.

They can be fiercely divided over politics, but their attachment to Georgia runs much deeper than their loyalty to any political party.

And perhaps this is one of the greatest strengths a nation can possess.

We often measure civilization through economic prosperity, technological achievements, magnificent infrastructure, political freedoms and the quality of public institutions.

All these things matter enormously.

But civilization is also measured by the way people behave when they are angry, by the respect they show for what belongs to others, and by their willingness to protect their common home even when they profoundly disagree with those governing it.

A wealthy society is not necessarily a civilized society, just as a poorer society is not necessarily less civilized.

Civilization is not only about freedom of speech, freedom of thought, individual rights and higher incomes.

It is also about responsibility, solidarity, respect, dignity and the understanding that we belong to something greater than ourselves.

It is about standing by our brothers and sisters, our families and our country when things get tough.

And sometimes, watching what happens in the streets of the wealthiest Western capitals, I cannot help thinking that the West, which has spent so much time teaching the rest of the world what civilization means, might have a few lessons to learn from Georgia.

- Fady Asly
October 19, 2026

text:
#Vietnam's Masan High-Tech Materials expands #tungsten processing capacity — strengthening Vietnam’s role in a critical global supply chain

Special Report:

Masan High-Tech Materials (MSR) is scaling its tungsten refining operations beyond the output of its own Nui Phao mine in Thai Nguyen province. 

With a current refining system of roughly 8,000 tonnes per year of ammonium paratungstate (APT) and tungsten oxides, the company is already processing a growing volume of third-party feedstock from international sources while securing long-term offtake agreements with Western partners.

In 2026, MSR expects to use about 1,300 tonnes of tungsten material from Nui Phao itself and purchase around 5,500 tonnes from external mines. 

A multi-year agreement with US-based Elmet Group, announced in September, commits MSR to process approximately 1,250 tonnes of tungsten trioxide (WO₃)-equivalent material annually for more than eight years. 

The company is also evaluating an expansion of refining capacity to 10,000–12,000 tonnes per year. Because this would build on existing infrastructure and technology, the estimated additional investment is relatively modest — around $15–20 million.

These moves turn MSR into more than a mine operator. It is becoming a flexible midstream processing platform that can convert concentrates from multiple origins into high-purity chemical products demanded by global industry.

Background: Nui Phao and more than a decade of investment

Nui Phao is one of the world’s largest operating tungsten mines outside China and a complex polymetallic deposit that simultaneously yields tungsten, fluorspar, bismuth, and copper. 

Over more than a decade, Masan has invested well over $700 million in the integrated mining and chemical complex. The processing technology for refined tungsten products was originally developed through a partnership with Germany’s H.C. Starck and has since been internalized.

MSR describes itself as the world’s largest producer of midstream and downstream tungsten products outside China. 

It accounts for a substantial share of the non-Chinese market (figures cited in company materials have ranged around 21–30% of ex-China demand depending on the year and product). 

Its main chemical outputs — APT, blue tungsten oxide (BTO), yellow tungsten oxide (YTO), and related compounds — meet the purity and consistency standards required by international customers in Europe, North America, Japan, and South Korea.

Why tungsten is strategically important

Tungsten is one of the hardest, densest, and highest-melting-point metals in industrial use. It is extremely difficult to substitute in many applications. Key uses include:

▪️Cemented carbide cutting tools and wear parts for manufacturing, mining, and construction
▪️High-temperature components in aerospace and industrial equipment
▪️Semiconductor manufacturing (including tungsten hexafluoride gas used in chip production)
▪️Electrical contacts, filaments, and specialty alloys
▪️Defense applications: armor-piercing penetrators, kinetic energy projectiles, missile components, guidance systems, and certain high-density alloys used in military hardware

China has long dominated both mining and especially the more complex refining and powder stages of the tungsten chain, controlling the majority of global supply. 

When Beijing tightens export controls or prioritizes domestic demand, prices outside China rise sharply and Western industries face supply risk. This has elevated tungsten’s status as a critical mineral for both economic and national-security reasons in the United States, Europe, Japan, and other partners.

The recent partnership with Elmet Group fits this context. Elmet is a US supplier of tungsten alloys, precision components, and advanced materials that serves defense and high-tech customers. 

The multi-year supply and conversion agreement, combined with Elmet’s equity stake in MSR, creates a direct commercial link between Vietnamese processing capacity and the US market at a time when Washington is actively seeking non-Chinese sources of critical materials. 

US policy discussions and funding programs aimed at rebuilding domestic tungsten supply chains further underscore the strategic value of reliable, high-quality external suppliers like MSR.

Technological depth and advanced products

MSR’s strength is not limited to volume. The company produces high-purity refined chemicals that serve as feedstock for downstream powder and carbide manufacturers. Over the years it has developed capabilities that go beyond basic APT and oxides.

One notable example is the development of specialized tungsten powders optimized for additive manufacturing (3D printing). Under the starck2print® trademark (developed within the broader H.C. Starck / Masan technology ecosystem), the company offered powders with high flowability and carefully controlled particle-size distributions suited for processes such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and selective electron beam melting. 

These powders are produced by hydrogen reduction of tungsten oxides and can be tailored for specific customer needs. 

The same platform supports recycling loops in which used 3D-printed parts can be recovered and returned as raw material — an important feature for both cost and sustainability in high-value applications.

Although Masan later divested its stake in the global H.C. Starck tungsten powders business to Mitsubishi Materials, the Vietnamese refining complex continues to produce the high-purity intermediate products that feed advanced powder and component manufacturing. 

The ability to process both its own ore and third-party concentrates to consistent international standards remains a core technological advantage.

Broader significance

By expanding refining capacity, accepting international feedstock, and locking in multi-year supply agreements with Western partners, MSR is positioning Vietnam as a meaningful non-Chinese node in the global tungsten value chain. This matters for several reasons:

▪️It increases the volume of high-purity tungsten chemicals available outside Chinese control.
▪️It generates higher-value export revenues and service income from processing rather than relying solely on mine output.
▪️It strengthens Vietnam’s position in critical minerals at a time when major economies are actively diversifying supply chains for defense, semiconductors, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing.
▪️It demonstrates that Vietnamese industrial capability can extend into technologically demanding midstream and downstream stages, not only primary extraction.

Tungsten will remain essential for both traditional hard-metal industries and newer applications in AI-related semiconductor production, electric mobility, energy systems, and defense. 

As China continues to exert influence over the majority of refined supply, the existence of a large, modern, and expanding processing platform in Vietnam becomes increasingly relevant to global industrial and strategic planning.

The current expansion plans — modest capital outlay on top of an already substantial installed base, combined with long-term offtake — give MSR a practical path to capture more of this demand while reinforcing Vietnam’s role in one of the world’s most strategically sensitive metal supply chains.

text:
A bank mail clerk turned down a hundred dollars for one book in 1912, and Harlem ended up with the greatest Black archive on earth. Arturo Schomburg had an autographed Phillis Wheatley and a dealer who wanted it badly, and a hundred dollars then was more than a month's pay for most of his neighbors. He wrote back three words. No parting glances.

Every weekday morning for twenty-three years, a man rode downtown to a bank and spent the day sorting other people's mail.

He ran the section at Bankers Trust that handled the letters going out to Cuba, Puerto Rico, Mexico and Brazil. They gave him that desk because he wrote English, Spanish and French, and a bank moving money through the Caribbean needed somebody who could read a complaint from Havana without sending it out to be translated.

He was good at it. He held the job from 1906 to 1929 and finished as supervisor of the whole Caribbean and Latin American mail section.

Into those same outgoing bags, most days, went letters that had nothing to do with the bank at all.

They went to booksellers in Madrid and London and Havana, and to other collectors in Philadelphia and Washington. They asked whether anybody had a certain pamphlet, a certain engraving, a certain thin volume of poems, and whether the seller would kindly hold it a while, because the buyer was a clerk and the money would take some time to come together.

His name was Arturo Alfonso Schomburg. The research library in Harlem that holds the largest archive of Black life anywhere on earth carries his name, and almost nobody can tell you it started in a mailroom.

In 1915 a census taker worked his way through the building at 63 West 140th Street and wrote down what every household did for a living. Porters, elevator operators, dressmakers, women who cleaned other people's houses.

Next to Schomburg's name he wrote bookkeeper.

That was the wrong job. Schomburg was a clerk in a bank mailroom, and the census taker had guessed at the man on the stairs who was always carrying boxes.

Wrong job, right man. The historian Laura Helton noticed the accident a century later, going through the record: he was keeping books, hundreds of them, and there was no word on the form for what he actually was.

He was the only Puerto Rican in that building. His neighbors were African American and West Indian, and he had already started calling himself Afroborinqueño, Afro-Puerto Rican, said as one word with nothing in the middle to argue about.

Three years before that census, he had been unpacking his library. Again.

He had moved constantly. The Lower East Side, then San Juan Hill in midtown, then Harlem, then a rented room in the home of Ramon Rothschild, an old comrade from Puerto Rico and a brother in his Masonic lodge, and then the apartment on 140th Street with his new wife, Elizabeth Green.

The books came with him every single time. By 1912 they had filled three bookcases, alongside the pamphlets, the manuscripts, the engravings, and what he cheerfully described as coins galore.

He wrote to his friend John W. Cromwell about it on Labor Day, 1912, and the letter is not triumphant. He said he ran into a great deal of trouble every time he had to move the treasured lot from one place to another.

Things went missing in the moves, and some of them he never got back.

Then he wrote a sentence that has never once appeared on a museum wall. He feared he had reached his limit.

He was thirty-eight. He had a wife, children, a mail clerk's wage, and a collection that had already outgrown every room he could afford to put it in.

That same summer, a dealer made him an offer on a single book.

Schomburg owned an autographed copy of Phillis Wheatley, the enslaved girl from Boston who published the first book of poems by an African American in 1773. The dealer wanted it and put a hundred dollars on the table.

A hundred dollars in 1912 was serious money to a man sorting mail. It was more than a month's pay for most of the people living in his building.

He wrote to Alain Locke that August with his answer. No parting glances.

He kept the book. He kept hauling it up and down stairs for another fourteen years.

Some things he could not buy at any price, because they had to be found first.

Benjamin Banneker was a free Black man in Maryland who taught himself astronomy, worked on the survey of the federal district, and published almanacs in the 1790s. Schomburg wanted a picture of his face.

Not an account of him. A picture, an engraving, the actual likeness of the man, something a person could stand in front of and look at.

It took him twelve years.

Twelve years of writing to dealers who had never heard the name, of asking friends headed to Philadelphia or Baltimore to please check the shops while they were down there. Twelve years of chasing a rumor into a dead end and starting the letters over.

Twelve years of postage, out of a mail clerk's wage, for one image of one face. He got it.

To understand why a grown man spends twelve years hunting a face, you have to know what he had been missing.

He was born in Santurce, just outside San Juan, on January 24, 1874, and baptized four days later at the Church of San Francisco de Asis. His mother was a Black woman from the Danish West Indies, and his father was a Puerto Rican merchant, the son of a German immigrant.

He grew up on an island with a great painter in it. José Campeche was the finest Puerto Rican artist of the eighteenth century, and his work was known and hung and admired.

Nobody told the boy that Campeche was Black.

He said so himself, decades later. Vanessa K. Valdés, who wrote the first book-length study of Schomburg as an Afro-Latino, treats that as the injury he spent the rest of his life working on.

A child is handed his own island's greatest painter with the color quietly taken out of him.

He worked out how the trick was done and he put it in print. Let a person of African descent do something excellent, and they get called exceptional, and then they get lifted out of the race and set off to one side by themselves.

There is another story about how it all started, and it is the one everybody knows.

He said a teacher told his class that Black people had no history, no heroes, no great moments. His biographer, Elinor Des Verney Sinnette, put it in her 1989 life of him, and it has been in every children's book and museum panel since.

Here is the part that keeps getting left out. When Sinnette went into the records in San Juan, what she found was conflicting evidence about whether Schomburg attended primary school there at all.

And he did not always tell it that way himself. He sometimes said the thing that lit him was a literary club he belonged to back home.

So the one claim in the whole record with no document under it is the claim he made about his own childhood.

He knew that better than anyone. A man who would spend twelve years proving a face was real understood exactly what an unsourced story is worth.

He told it anyway, for fifty years, because it does in nine seconds what the Campeche story needs a paragraph to do. It may be the only thing he ever put his name to that he could not have proved.

By the twenties, the books had taken the house.

He moved the family to Brooklyn in 1918, to a narrow brown place on Kosciuszko Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant, where he lived with Elizabeth Green and their children and several thousand items concerning people the schools would not mention.

The novelist Eric Walrond went out there in 1922 and wrote down what he found. He called it "hallowed ground."

He described a sitting room thick with the smell of old paper and the portraits on the walls, an Ethiopian princess, the composer Chevalier de Saint-Georges, a bandmaster named John Fraser. Writers and artists of both races kept turning up at that plain little house on a side street, Walrond wrote, because of what was inside it.

Six years earlier Schomburg had told Alain Locke by letter that the library had a few easy chairs, so a person could drop in and feel at home. He was talking about his own front room.

Somewhere in those rooms sat the handwritten military orders of Toussaint Louverture, on paper stamped Egalité, Liberté. The men who came to see them had a name for themselves, coined by the Philadelphia newspaperman William Carl Bolivar.

DOFOB. Damned Old Fools on Books.

In March 1925 a magazine called Survey Graphic gave an entire issue to Harlem, guest-edited by Alain Locke.

It carried Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen, Claude McKay, Jean Toomer, W. E. B. Du Bois, and an essay by Arthur A. Schomburg titled "The Negro Digs Up His Past." It opens on the sentence the whole Renaissance would end up standing on. "The American Negro must remake his past in order to make his future."

A few lines further down comes the harder one. History has to give back what slavery took, he wrote, because the damage is what this generation is stuck repairing.

Deeper into the essay he listed the serious private collections of Black material in America. Henry P. Slaughter of Washington came first, then the Reverend Charles D. Martin of Harlem.

Third on the list was Arthur Schomburg of Brooklyn. Fourth was the late John E. Bruce, his old mentor, and Bruce is the only one of the four he bothered to compliment.

He put himself third, inside a clause, with no adjectives on it.

That same year the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library opened a Division of Negro Literature, History and Prints. In October the head librarian, Ernestine Rose, wrote to Schomburg about the possibility of the branch acquiring his collection.

Private buyers had already come around. He turned them down and let the whole thing go to a public library in Harlem, where anybody could walk in off the street with no fee and no letter of introduction.

On May 14, 1926, the Carnegie Corporation approved the money. Resolution X-281, ten thousand dollars, for the Arthur Schomburg library collection on negro life and history.

Ten thousand dollars for all of it.

Five days later more than a hundred packing crates went out to the library's central building to be readied for the trip uptown. Shelley Fisher Fishkin describes that shipment in her book on American literary landmarks, thousands of books and manuscripts and etchings and portraits and pamphlets, boxed and addressed to Harlem.

Laura Helton makes the observation that lands hardest. That was the last time in his life Arthur Schomburg packed or unpacked his own library.

The Wheatley went, and the Louverture orders went. The Banneker face, twelve years in the finding, went into a crate with a number chalked on the side and rode uptown on a truck.

That house on Kosciuszko Street must have been very quiet by the end of that week.

He spent the money on more books. That same year he sailed for Spain, France, Germany and England, sitting in reading rooms and buying whatever he could carry home for a collection he no longer owned.

The library that had just bought his life's work did not give him a job with it.

He went back to the mailroom. He stayed at Bankers Trust until he was nearly fifty-six, leaving around the turn of 1930, and the library trustees' files from those years hold correspondence about the effort to get Schomburg onto the payroll at all.

To work in a library, he had to leave New York. At fifty-six he took the post of curator of the Negro Collection at Fisk University in Nashville, in the Jim Crow South, and built there a smaller version of what he had built in Harlem.

He came back in 1932 and finally sat down as curator of his own collection on 135th Street. Six years after the crates went uptown.

He had that desk for six years. In June 1938 he went in for dental surgery, an infection followed, and he died at Madison Park Hospital in Brooklyn on the tenth of the month, at sixty-four.

The funeral was two days later at Siloam Presbyterian Church, and it was private.

He was buried in the Locust Grove section of Cypress Hills Cemetery, a short ride from the house the books once filled.

Two years after that, the library put his name on the collection.

That building is free.

Anybody can walk into the Schomburg Center on Malcolm X Boulevard tomorrow, with no card and no letter of introduction, and ask to see the Wheatley he refused to sell for a hundred dollars. There are around ten million items in there now, and the first eight hundred of them came out of a mail clerk's evenings.

He was never really paid for it. Ten thousand dollars, four more years in the mailroom, a year in Nashville at fifty-six, six years behind the desk, then a tooth.

His own letters are in that building too. Including the ones he wrote at night, at a table in Brooklyn, asking a stranger in Madrid to please hold a book until a clerk in New York could put the money together.

So when the name on the building comes up, put the mailroom in the sentence with it. That part has no plaque on it, and it only survives if somebody carries it out of here.

Blind Willie Johnson's voice was chosen to represent humanity beyond Earth, yet the man behind that voice spent his final days without even a proper place to rest. I share stories like his because sometimes the greatest stories are hidden behind the names we already know.

text:
Put October in order and the mechanism is easy to see. Moscow makes an offer, then Washington pressures Kyiv to make it workable.

The offer
• Oct 9: per WSJ, Putin proposes to Trump a November summit with Xi to end the war on terms that favor Moscow
• Oct 9, same day: a US-Russia deal on diesel

The pressure on Kyiv
• Oct 10: Trump urges Ukrainians to replace Zelensky and demands an end to strikes on Russian refineries
• Oct 11: Trump announces an "energy truce" on his own
• Oct 12: US threatens to limit military aid and intelligence sharing if the strikes go on
• Oct 13-15: Ukraine hits gaps in US intelligence and limits on Starlink and Starshield
• Oct 16: an order letting Washington delay new sanctions on Russia

Refineries are the target that currently hurts Moscow's finances most. Stop those strikes, delay the sanctions, and Putin's plants stop burning while his revenue stays intact. He then walks into a November summit with Xi at the table, holding every card. Kyiv is asked to disarm its best lever before talks even begin.

On Oct 18 Trump said he won't tighten sanctions so as not to scare Moscow off, and in the same breath blamed Zelensky for not wanting peace. Only one side in this conflict is being punished for refusing to stop.
