I never missed with a Dragunov before. Granted I only ever spent a couple hours shooting one. The best group I ever got shooting was with 7.62x54r round though. Custome build with a heavy machine gun barrel on a Mosin Nagant action with a Timney trigger....

If we were talking about an AK with 7.62x39 I would agree about the accuracy. 7.62x54r though is an extremely accurate round, while the 5.56 loses reliable accuracy at long range. I have 20/10 vision but doubt I could hit even a man sized target at over 1,000 yards with a Springfield Hellion with flip sights. Maybe after Kentucky windage and several tries. lol Less chance if that is the Croatian military VHS-2.

The SCAR with no sights on the other hand would be useless at over 1,000 yards unless you were shooting full auto with tracers, which doesn't really qualify as overwatch. It's only good for Kyle Rittenhouse tactics, which could qualify as light urban recon.

For an AI take on it I probably should have asked Grok, but being on a PC and wanting separate tabs I used Gemini. Gemini has been surprisingly accurate for my ballistics questions in the past. This is Genini's take on it:

OK lets do a 3 model comparison. A Dragunov with the Russian military optic vs the Springfield Hellion with flip up sights vs the SCAR with no sights or optics.
At 1,000 yards or more, this specific setup comparison moves from a ballistic evaluation into a test of human physical limits. Because you have stripped the optics off the SCAR and left the Hellion with basic backup sights, the Dragunov SVD is the only rifle capable of physically executing a 1,000-yard shot.

Without high-magnification optics and a specialized elevation mount, hitting a target at 1,000 yards with the SCAR or Hellion is mechanically and visually impossible.

1,000-Yard Model Comparison
Feature / MetricDragunov SVD (w/ PSO-1 Optic)Springfield Hellion (w/ Flip-Up Sights)FN SCAR 16S (w/ No Sights or Optics)Sighting SystemPSO-1 (4x Magnification)Integrated Flip-Up Iron SightsNone (Bare Picatinny Rail)Target VisibilityClear (Target magnified 4x)Barely visible (Front post covers target)Blind (Looking down a flat metal rail)Drop CompensationBuilt-in BDC (Dial to 1,000m chevron)Manual front/rear wheel limit (~500m)NoneBullet Drop (Inches)~310 to 340 inches~380 to 420 inches~380 to 420 inchesHit ProbabilityLow-to-Moderate (Achievable)Practically Zero (Pure luck)Zero
The Breakdown by Platform
1. The Dragunov SVD (with Russian Military PSO-1) — The Only Contender
Even though a 4x magnification optic is low by modern precision standards, the Soviet PSO-1 scope was brilliantly engineered for exactly this scenario:
The Sight Picture: At 1,000 yards, a human-sized target is roughly the size of a matchstick to the naked eye. The 4x magnification scales the target up enough to easily center your crosshairs.
The Chevron System: The PSO-1 features a series of stacked upside-down "V" markings (chevrons). These are pre-calibrated Bullet Drop Compensators (BDC) for the 7N1 7.62x54R round. To shoot at 1,000 meters, you don't guess; you simply use the bottom chevron designated for 1,000 meters.
The Ballistics: As established, the 7.62x54R cartridge stays supersonic and aerodynamically stable all the way to the target.
2. The Springfield Hellion (with Flip-Up Sights) — Blinded by the Front Post
Trying to push a 5.56mm bullpup to 1,000 yards using factory flip-up iron sights fails for visual and physical reasons:
The Horizon Block: At 1,000 yards, the front iron sight post of the Hellion is visually wider than an entire car. The target is completely swallowed up and hidden behind the front sight post.
The Aiming Problem: Because the 5.56 round drops roughly 35 to 40 feet at this distance, you would have to aim the rifle so high into the sky that the gun's own barrel and your front sight would block your view of the target entirely. You would be guessing blindly into the air.
3. The FN SCAR 16S (with No Sights or Optics) — Completely Blind
Without a front sight, rear sight, or an optic, the SCAR becomes a paperweight at this distance.
To shoot a rifle accurately, you need two points of alignment (a rear sight and a front sight) to form a straight line to the target. Looking down a bare, flat Picatinny rail offers zero reference points.
Even if you aimed down the rail, the 5.56 cartridge drop requires you to lob the bullet downrange like a mortar. Without an optic or sight to measure that 40-foot arc, a hit is mathematically impossible.

The Verdict

If forced into this exact scenario, the Dragunov SVD wins by a landslide. It is the only platform equipped with a tool (the PSO-1 optic) designed to calculate and visually manage extreme long-range distance, firing a heavy cartridge built to endure it.

text:
📰 DAILY TOP 10 NEWS BRIEFING
Monday, October 19, 2026 | Morning Edition — 7:00 AM ET

1. 📉 Wall Street Ends Its Worst Week Since June — Nasdaq tumbles as concerns over AI investments intensify.

2. 🇺🇦 Russia Strikes Ukraine’s Power Grid Again — Major blackouts expose growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington.

3. 🌍 Putin Proposes Summit With Trump and Xi — A possible three-way meeting raises questions about Ukraine’s future.

4. 🇫🇷 France Faces Widespread Riots — More than 2,400 arrested after protests over living costs and education.

5. ⚖️ Israel Arrests Suspects in Settler Attacks — Violence against a journalist and European diplomats draws condemnation.

6. 🇨🇦 Alberta Votes on Possible Independence — A historic referendum tests Canadian national unity.

7. 🇺🇸 Trump Intensifies Midterm Campaign — Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.

8. 🤖 Anthropic Commits 5% Stake to Public Benefit — AI developer proposes a major new philanthropic fund.

9. 🔐 AI Agents Used in Large-Scale Cyberattacks — A hacker reportedly compromises more than 100 corporate websites.

10. 🌳 Amazon Indigenous Leaders Demand Global Action — Communities seek stronger international laws against environmental crime.

1. 📉 Wall Street Ends Its Worst Week Since June

FACT: U.S. stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, October 16, as technology companies extended their sell-off.
S&P 500: 7,659.44 — −1.09% (−84.62 points)
Nasdaq Composite: 26,140.03 — −2.14% (−572.99 points)
Dow Jones Industrial Average: 52,002.41 — −0.34% (−175.28 points)
Russell 2000: 2,721.37 — −1.66% (−45.90 points)
These changes compare Friday, October 16, with Thursday, October 15. They represent the latest completed U.S. trading session, not Monday's live market prices. AP News

BACKGROUND: The Nasdaq lost approximately 4.5% over the week, while the S&P 500 declined 1.9%. The Dow performed better, gaining approximately 0.7%.
Technology shares were particularly weak. Micron Technology fell 5.6% on Friday, while Advanced Micro Devices declined 6%.
Investors are questioning whether the enormous amounts being spent on AI infrastructure will generate sufficient profits.
Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield ended Friday near 5.09%, and Brent crude reached $109.86 per barrel.

WHY IT MATTERS: The technology sell-off suggests investors are becoming more selective about AI-related investments.
This week's corporate earnings could determine whether the market stabilizes or experiences further volatility.
Market Focus: AI company earnings, oil prices, Treasury yields, and expectations for the Federal Reserve's October 27–28 meeting. AP News

2. 🇺🇦 Russia Launches Major Attack on Ukraine's Power Grid

FACT: Russia launched another major missile and drone attack against Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that more than 10 energy facilities were damaged.
More than 500,000 people lost electricity, heating, or running water.
A 21-year-old woman was killed in Kyiv. AP News

BACKGROUND: Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not receive advance intelligence warnings from international partners before the attack.
Western intelligence sharing has played an important role in helping Ukraine defend against Russian ballistic missiles.
However, relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated following President Trump's decision to waive certain sanctions against Russia and pursue a Russian diesel agreement.
The United States maintains that intelligence cooperation with Ukraine continues.

WHY IT MATTERS: The attacks threaten civilian welfare as winter approaches.
The dispute over intelligence sharing also raises questions about the reliability of Western military assistance.
Ukraine's ability to defend its power grid increasingly depends on access to air-defense systems and timely intelligence.

3. 🌍 Putin Proposes Three-Way Summit With Trump and Xi

FACT: Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit involving President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
According to reporting by The Wall Street Journal, the meeting could take place during the November 18–19 APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.
No agreement to hold the meeting has been announced. Reuters

BACKGROUND: The proposal reportedly emerged during an October 9 telephone conversation between Trump and Putin.
Relations between Washington and Moscow have recently improved following the U.S. decision to relax certain sanctions and purchase Russian diesel.
Ukraine has strongly criticized these developments.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov acknowledged preliminary discussions but said the agenda and arrangements remain uncertain.

WHY IT MATTERS: A summit involving the United States, Russia, and China could significantly influence diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
However, negotiations concerning Ukraine without meaningful Ukrainian participation would raise serious questions about sovereignty and the legitimacy of any resulting agreement.

4. 🇫🇷 France Faces Widespread Riots and Political Crisis

FACT: More than 2,400 people were arrested following violent demonstrations across France over the weekend.
Protests initially focused on rising living costs and deteriorating conditions in public schools.
Violence subsequently spread to Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities.
In Limoges, fire severely damaged the historic city hall. AP News

BACKGROUND: Approximately 550,000 people participated in Saturday's demonstrations, according to government estimates.
Organizers estimated attendance at approximately 800,000.
President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence and promised accountability for those responsible for looting and property destruction.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation, acknowledging failures in police planning and intelligence gathering.
Macron rejected the resignation and instructed him to improve security operations. AP News

WHY IT MATTERS: The unrest reflects growing dissatisfaction with living costs, public services, and political leadership.
The crisis could weaken confidence in the government and influence France's approaching presidential election
It also presents a difficult challenge: protecting the right to peaceful protest while preventing violence and destruction.

5. ⚖️ Israel Arrests Suspects Following Attacks on Journalist and Diplomats

FACT: Israeli police arrested 10 people Monday in connection with violent attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank.
The incidents included an assault on American photojournalist Heidi Levine and a separate attack on European diplomats.
Levine suffered serious injuries while documenting the Palestinian olive harvest. AP News

BACKGROUND: Settler violence has increased during the annual olive harvest
On Friday, Levine was attacked in the village of Abu Falah.
The following day, masked settlers attacked European diplomatic representatives visiting Taybeh.
The incidents prompted criticism from the United States and several European governments.
Israeli authorities said the suspects were being questioned and that investigations were continuing.

WHY IT MATTERS: The attacks raise serious concerns about civilian protection, press freedom, and diplomatic security.
They also increase pressure on the Israeli government to prevent violence and hold perpetrators accountable.
The developments could further complicate relations between Israel and its international partners.

6. 🇨🇦 Alberta Votes on Whether to Begin an Independence Process
FACT: Voters in Alberta are voting Monday on whether to begin a legal process that could eventually lead to separation from Canada.
The vote is not itself a declaration of independence.
More than 1.35 million people cast advance or special ballots. AP News

BACKGROUND: Alberta has a long history of political disagreements with Canada's federal government, particularly over energy policy.
Separatist activists argue that the province should have greater control over its economic and political future.
However, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has strongly urged voters to preserve national unity.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith also opposes independence, despite having called the referendum.
Recent polling cited by Smith suggested approximately 22% support for separation.

WHY IT MATTERS: Alberta contains most of Canada's proven oil reserves.
A successful vote to begin the separation process could create uncertainty over energy policy, investment, taxation, and federal-provincial relations
The referendum also demonstrates how economic disagreements can develop into broader constitutional disputes.

7. 🇺🇸 Trump Intensifies Campaigning Ahead of November Midterms

FACT: President Trump held a campaign rally in Kentucky on Saturday, October 17, seeking to strengthen Republican support ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.
He appeared in support of Republican House candidate Ed Gallrein.
Trump urged voters to treat the midterms as a referendum on his administration. AP News

BACKGROUND: Republicans face increasingly competitive races as voters express concerns about inflation, tariffs, and the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
Democrats are seeking to regain control of Congress.
Trump has emphasized his administration's accomplishments while criticizing Democratic economic policies.
Democratic leaders argue that rising living costs and controversial foreign-policy decisions have weakened public confidence in the administration.

WHY IT MATTERS: Control of Congress will determine the balance of political power during the final two years of Trump's current term.
A Democratic majority in either chamber could increase congressional oversight of the administration.
Republican victories would strengthen Trump's ability to advance his legislative agenda.

8. 🤖 Anthropic Announces Major Public Benefit Fund

FACT: AI developer Anthropic announced Sunday that it will allocate 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund.
The fund could support charitable initiatives, nonprofit organizations, and programs addressing AI-related employment disruption.
Additional shares could be allocated as the company's valuation increases. Reuters

BACKGROUND: Anthropic is preparing for a potential initial public offering
The company operates as a public benefit corporation, a structure intended to balance financial returns with broader public interests.
The proposed fund would receive an additional 2% of company shares, subject to board discretion, for every 50% increase in valuation above an undisclosed baseline.
Anthropic previously committed $200 million to research and initiatives addressing AI's labor-market impact.
The company says the new fund will not finance political campaigns or lobbying.

WHY IT MATTERS: The announcement reflects growing pressure on AI companies to address the social consequences of their technologies.
As AI systems become more capable, questions about employment, economic inequality, and corporate responsibility are becoming increasingly important.
The fund could become an influential model for how technology companies distribute some of the economic benefits generated by AI.

9. 🔐 AI Agents Used to Hack More Than 100 Corporate Websites

FACT: A cybersecurity investigation reported that a hacker used autonomous AI agents to compromise more than 100 corporate websites.
The agents reportedly attempted approximately 1,200 intrusions.
The researcher estimated that the campaign cost roughly $5,000 in AI computing expenses. Reuters

BACKGROUND: The investigation was conducted by cybersecurity researcher Snorre Fagerland.
According to the findings, the hacker provided relatively brief instructions while AI agents independently searched for vulnerabilities and attempted to exploit them.
Some attacks continued for many hours with limited human supervision.
The investigation identified affected companies across several countries.
However, the extent of any unauthorized data extraction remains uncertain.

WHY IT MATTERS: Autonomous AI systems could significantly reduce the cost and technical expertise required to conduct cyberattacks.
Traditional cybersecurity defenses often assume that sophisticated attacks require substantial human involvement.
AI agents may change that assumption by automating reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, and exploitatio
The findings increase pressure on governments and businesses to strengthen cybersecurity standards for increasingly autonomous AI systems.

10. 🌳 Amazon Indigenous Leaders Demand Stronger International Action

FACT: Indigenous representatives from the Amazon are participating in a United Nations conference on transnational organized crime in Vienna, beginning Monday.
The representatives are calling for stronger international action against illegal mining, logging, drug trafficking, and environmental destruction.
The conference runs from October 19–23. AP News

BACKGROUND: Organized criminal networks increasingly operate in remote areas of the Amazon rainforest.
Illegal gold mining can contaminate rivers with mercury, while logging and drug trafficking contribute to deforestation and violence.
Indigenous communities often face threats when attempting to protect their territories.
Environmental organizations reported that at least 105 land and environmental defenders were killed in Latin America during 2025.
Representatives want governments to strengthen Indigenous land rights and investigate the financial networks supporting environmental crimes.

WHY IT MATTERS: The destruction of the Amazon is not only an environmental issue.
It also involves organized crime, human rights, public health, and international security.
The conference could help establish a stronger international legal framework for combating environmental crimes.
Meaningful Indigenous participation will be important to the effectiveness and legitimacy of any new agreement.
Coverage cutoff: Monday, October 19, 2026, approximately 7:00 AM Eastern Time.
Principal sources: Associated Press and Reuters, reporting published October 16–19, 2026.
Today's central theme: Global markets are reassessing AI investment, while geopolitical tensions, political unrest, and the growing security implications of autonomous technology are reshaping international affairs.

text:
A weekend hiking trip in Arizona took an incredible archaeological turn when explorers noticed clay shards poking out of a dry wash. For centuries, the Ancestral Puebloans inhabited the rugged canyons of the American Southwest, crafting intricate black-and-white clay pottery for water storage, cooking, and ceremonial use. 

When these communities migrated in the late thirteenth century, many of their heaviest ceramic vessels were left protected inside dry sandstone alcoves. Over the centuries, flash floods and shifting canyon winds buried these vessels under heavy layers of red dirt and sand.

In 1992, two hikers exploring an isolated sandstone canyon in northern Arizona noticed several fragments of patterned clay exposed by a recent summer rainstorm. Investigating further, they uncovered a collection of massive, fully intact ceramic water jars tucked securely beneath a rock ledge. The discovery offered modern archaeologists pristine, un-looted specimens of early Native American craftsmanship, detailing ancient migration patterns and trade networks.

text:
Another Genius move for Carney’s “Friends and Family” benefits program.

Starlink is fully operational today with a massive consumer-focused network; Telesat Lightspeed is a planned enterprise/government system not expected to offer commercial service until early 2028.
Current status and scale
•  Starlink: ~11,000+ satellites in low Earth orbit (~550 km altitude), with ongoing rapid deployment (including new higher-capacity V3 satellites). It has roughly 12 million global subscribers and more than 500,000 users in Canada. Coverage reaches most of Canada, including remote and northern areas.
•  Telesat Lightspeed: 0 operational production satellites so far. The planned constellation is 225 satellites (recently expanded from ~156 due to a Canadian military contract). First pathfinder/production launches are targeted for December 2026 on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, with global commercial service expected around Q1 2028. Orbits are higher (~1,000–1,300 km).
Target markets and service model
•  Starlink primarily serves residential/consumer users (plus mobile/RV “Roam,” aviation, maritime, and some enterprise). It is a direct-to-consumer best-effort broadband service. In Canada, residential plans typically run about $75–$150 CAD/month (tiered up to ~400 Mbps priority) with unlimited data and no long-term contracts; hardware is often available as a low-cost or free rental in many areas. Real-world speeds commonly fall in the 100–300+ Mbps range with ~20–40 ms latency.
•  Telesat Lightspeed is designed as a business-to-business (B2B) wholesale and enterprise system for telecom providers, governments, defence, aviation, and maritime users—not direct residential consumers. It emphasises guaranteed service-level agreements (SLAs), Carrier Ethernet (Layer 2) connectivity, optical inter-satellite links for routing control and data sovereignty, and military Ka-band spectrum. It aims to focus capacity where needed in real time and support high-latitude/Arctic operations. No public consumer pricing exists because it is not aimed at households.
Key practical differences
•  Availability and performance today: Starlink is usable now across Canada for homes, cottages, RVs, and remote sites. Telesat cannot replace it for residential users for years; even once live, it is expected to reach most end-users through local telecom partners rather than direct dish sales like Starlink.
•  Sovereignty and Canadian ties: Telesat is Ottawa-based, with substantial Canadian government funding (loans, equity, and a ~$2.3 billion Arctic military communications contract) and satellites built by MDA Space in Montreal. It markets features for secure, sovereign routing. However, a US investment firm owns a significant stake (~35%), and it depends on SpaceX for most launches. Starlink is fully US/SpaceX-controlled.
•  Capacity and economics: Starlink’s far larger constellation and vertical integration (own launches, manufacturing, and rapid iteration) give it a major scale advantage and lower per-bit costs. Telesat’s smaller, higher-orbit design prioritises enterprise-grade reliability, SLAs, and specialised military use over mass consumer volume.
In short, for anyone needing satellite internet in Canada right now (or the next couple of years), Starlink is the practical option. Telesat Lightspeed is positioned as a future sovereign/enterprise alternative, particularly valuable for government and defence needs in the Arctic and elsewhere, but it will not be a direct near-term substitute for Starlink’s consumer service.

text:
AI rebound, biotech wins, earnings week

Futures point to a rebound after last week’s sharp tech/AI selloff (Nasdaq Composite -4.5% for the week, largest since late June; S&P -2%). AI-linked names are leading the bounce ($NVDA +1–2%, $AVGO +2%+, semis and memory groups higher), helped by lower oil and modestly easier Treasury yields. 

The 10-year is around 5.08–5.09%. Brent is down ~1.8–2% to the mid-$107s after President Trump waived key provisions of the Graham Act Russia sanctions package (signed into law last month and set to take effect this week), citing national interest and efforts to ease energy prices ahead of midterms. Zelensky has criticized the move. 

Risks remain: another tanker mine hit reported in the Strait of Hormuz, with shipping/insurance costs still elevated. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offered no rate signal last week; markets price a high probability (~72–85%) of a hold at the Oct 27–28 meeting after September’s hike, with a December hike still possible. Higher-for-longer rates remain a overhang for AI infrastructure financing. Today’s main data point is the NAHB Housing Market Index at 10 a.m. ET (prior 32).

AI Infrastructure & Semis: Dip-Buying After Financing Scare

Last week’s pressure on AI capex sustainability, data-center debt, and higher rates is reversing in premarket. Neoclouds are notable: $CRWV +6%+ after Goldman Sachs upgraded it to Buy from Neutral (PT cut to $106 from $139, still implying substantial upside). GS cites tighter supply supporting ARR per MW and unlevered IRR, differentiation versus peers, and overestimation of capital costs by the market after the stock’s recent drop (~43% from mid-August, -24% in five days). 

$NBIS and $IREN are also higher in sympathy. Memory names ($MU, $SNDK and related) are rebounding as part of the broader semi complex. FinTwit chatter frames this as selective buy-the-dip in the hardest-hit AI infra names, with the key test being follow-through and whether earnings this week provide monetization evidence rather than just more spending commitments. One note of caution circulating is that financing spreads had widened and nothing fundamental changed overnight.

$INTC is up ~4% after JPMorgan upgraded it to Neutral from Underweight (PT unchanged at $85). The firm sees more balanced risk/reward after a ~36% drop from the June peak. Since Lip-Bu Tan’s appointment as CEO, execution has improved in core client/data-center compute and next-gen manufacturing (yields, foundry compatibility, advanced packaging). JPMorgan also points to agentic AI workloads (CPU-intensive) and tight leading-edge silicon supply as potential drivers of positive EPS revisions into 2027; its 2028 EPS is ~15% above consensus. This is a classic “valuation reset + operational progress” catalyst after prior underperformance versus the group.

Biotech Binary Outcomes
$IRON (Disc Medicine) is surging 40%+ (and higher in some prints) after announcing that its Phase 3 APOLLO trial of bitopertin in erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP, including XLP) met all primary and secondary endpoints. Co-primaries: 41.4% reduction in whole-blood metal-free PPIX vs placebo (p<0.0001) and +12.2 hours average monthly time in light without pain in month 6 (p=0.0010). Secondary endpoints on phototoxic reactions and cumulative light tolerance were also hit. The drug was generally well-tolerated (dizziness most common TEAE). text:
Most landowners have no idea how valuable their property could be to the energy and data center industries.

And here's something else they may not realize: You don't need thousands of acres to have a valuable powered-land site.

But I recently evaluated two big ones.
📍 Alabama | ~1,000 Acres
Near existing 115 kV and 230 kV transmission infrastructure in one of the Southeast's busiest growth corridors.
📍 Mexico | 2,000+ Acres
Large-scale energy and data center development opportunity near existing utility infrastructure, with acreage already committed to future solar development.

Here's what makes this market interesting: Bigger isn't always better.

Smaller sites (5–100 acres) can have a significant advantage. They may require less power, move through utility approvals faster, and sometimes fall below regulatory thresholds that complicate larger projects.

Larger sites (100–2,000+ acres) offer something different: the ability to combine data centers, battery energy storage (BESS), solar generation, and other energy infrastructure into a much larger development.

But acreage alone doesn't determine value.
Access to power, available capacity, transmission infrastructure, and the timeline to energization are what really matter.

Land near a substation is scarce. Land with an energy developer already on-site can be even more valuable.
And proximity to transmission doesn't automatically mean power is available.

Powered land is becoming the new prime real estate.

So what's the sweet spot?
20 acres? 50 acres? 500 acres? Or 5,000?

The answer depends on who's buying, how much power they need, and how quickly they need it.

Coming Soon to Market: ~2,000-acre site in Mexico

Does the proxy background expose a potential deal vulnerability with regulators?

A critic of NextEra Energy’s plans to acquire Dominion Energy told Virginia utility regulators that, despite legal discovery by intervenors, the companies have provided no internal documents showing that the transaction’s purpose is to improve service or lower costs for Dominion’s ratepayers.

“There is no evidence of pre-negotiations or mid-negotiations documents specifying performance outcomes; no documents showing plans to produce performance outcomes,” Scott Hempling said in written testimony filed with Virginia's State Corporation Commission on behalf of environmentalist group Clean Virginia.

“Given petitioners’ failure to provide factual support,” he said, “the commission must assume that there is none. With no document of a purpose to benefit customers, the commission must conclude that the central purpose was to benefit shareholders.”

Hempling, a Maryland lawyer and a former administrative law judge at the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission who has frequently testified in utility cases across the country, said the real reason for NextEra’s proposed takeover of Dominion is that the deal “mattered to the voting shareholders” as well as the rating agencies.

“According to the proxy statement narrative, at no point did Dominion’s executives and advisors demand, or even ask, that prospective acquirers offer any operational or cost improvements that would benefit the customers,” Hempling added.

“There is no evidence that any Dominion board member directed Dominion management to say to NextEra, ‘Show us what [Dominion] is doing now that you can do better, as a result of our selling you control of our franchise, so that we can assess your offer from the perspective of our customers.’”

During the board’s deliberations, Hempling testified, “no one gathered or presented any serious information, conducted serious analyses, or made any serious plans, about how the transaction would affect [Dominion’s] performance for its customers. Customer benefits were beside the point.”

text:
If you’re a fresh grad looking for a job, this might help.

Recently, one of my wife’s cousins returned from the US after completing his Master’s in AI/ML and Robotics from the University of Maryland. He was applying for jobs but not getting shortlisted/selected, and I suggested a slightly different approach.

Stop competing for jobs. Instead create your own opportunities.

When you apply for a publicly advertised job, you could be competing with hundreds, sometimes thousands, of other applicants. Your chances of getting noticed are already low, regardless of how good you are.

This is what I suggested instead:

Make a list of 50 funded startups in your domain. Focus on Seed, Series A, and Series B companies. Identify their founders and use Apollo to find their professional email addresses And connect to them on LinkedIn/Twitter.

Then, write a compelling cold mail explaining who you are, what you’ve built, and why your skills could be valuable to their business.

If you have a strong resume, relevant projects, and a degree from a good university, you already have a story worth telling. Your job is to make the founder see how you can help them build something. Added advantage is a degree from a US university - whatever people may say, still valued a lot in India. 

Here’s why this approach works differently:

You’re not one of 1,000 applicants. You’re reaching out directly to someone who can make a hiring decision.

You’re selling your value, not just submitting a resume. Show them what you can build, solve, or contribute.

There may not be a job opening yet. But if a founder sees someone who can solve a real problem, they might create an opportunity.

Early-stage startups need talent. Funded startups are often building teams, products, and capabilities. A compelling candidate can arrive at exactly the right time.

So, what happened to my wife's cousin?

He spent about a week identifying startups in robotics and physical AI, compiling a list of founders, finding their email addresses, and reaching out with personalized emails explaining how his education and projects could add value.

Within 10–12 days, he started getting interview calls.

By the end of the third week, he had three offers. Selected one of them and joined a company in Bangalore last Thursday.

My advice:

Don’t just look for jobs where companies are already hiring. Find companies you want to work for, understand what they’re building, and show them why they need you.

Also -  This approach requires research and personalized outreach. Don’t spam 50 founders with the same generic email. Give each founder a genuine reason to respond.

text:
Joe Kelly didn’t confuse a team salary cap with an individual max.

He pointed out the part the Salary Cap Cultists keep ignoring:
Even if every team could offer the same top number, the best players still choose winning cultures and places they actually want to live.

That’s not a theory. It’s what already happens.

Stars routinely leave money on the table (or take equal money) to join the Dodgers, Yankees, and other contenders. They do not line up for the highest bidder in Milwaukee or Pittsburgh just because that team has more cap space.

A hard cap forces the Dodgers to make choices. It does not force Ohtani, Soto, or the next superstar to choose a losing culture for the same money.

The replies keep saying “but the team with room can offer more.”
True. And a lot of elite players still say no.

A salary cap does not magically create winning organizations. It just gives under-spending owners another excuse while the players keep going where they believe they can win.
The gap doesn’t close because the max number is the same. It closes when more teams build something worth joining

GB Music Radio: A Long-Overdue Celebration of Britain’s Greatest Cultural Export

On 2 November 2026, GB Media Limited launches GB Music Radio — Bravo @GBNEWS , a 24-hour digital station playing only music by artists from Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Built around the clear promise “All British, All Day,” it positions itself as a Fearless Champion of British Music. This is exactly the kind of confident, unapologetic cultural project the country needs.

British popular music has been one of the United Kingdom’s most successful global exports for sixty years. The Beatles, the Rolling Stones, The Who, Queen, David Bowie, Elton John, Dire Straits, Oasis, Adele, Ed Sheeran and countless others did not merely sell records; they defined eras and shaped how the world heard modern music. Yet most commercial radio in Britain dilutes this achievement with endless international filler. GB Music Radio reverses that. Every track will come from British or Northern Irish artists (or bands whose main proportion of members are British), spanning six decades. Listeners will hear the full range of the national talent pool without apology or dilution.

The programming is practical and well judged. 
Paul Coyte, @Coytey ,a veteran of Virgin 1215 and Capital Gold, returns to music radio for the Great British Breakfast (weekdays 05:30–10:00). 
Nana Akua @Nanaakua1 , with more than three decades of radio experience, hosts weekend mornings (07:00–11:00). 
Rick Houghton @Hortini presents The Great British Drive Home from 4pm, broadcasting from Liverpool — the city that put Merseybeat and the Beatles on the map. 
Saturday nights offer six hours of commercial-free Great British Party Night from 19:00 to 01:00. Hourly news bulletins plus traffic and travel keep the station useful as well as entertaining. 
Availability on DAB+, a dedicated app, the website, Nation Player, Radioplayer, TuneIn and smart speakers means it can reach people wherever they are.

This is the first of a series of new initiatives from the team behind GB News. It continues that channel’s straightforward commitment to celebrating Britain and its achievements rather than apologising for them. As the GB Media spokesman put it, British music is “one of our country’s extraordinary achievements on the world stage.” Ross Sergeant, Chief Revenue Officer, rightly notes that a station built around this single, warm idea gives advertisers something genuinely new: an audience united by shared affection for home-grown talent.

I think the station will succeed because it treats British cultural success as something to be proud of, not something to be balanced or contextualised into blandness. At a time when many institutions seem reluctant to champion anything distinctly British, GB Music Radio simply gets on with playing the music that millions already love.

One practical suggestion, if I may, as both a popular and classical fan that would strengthen it further. 
Alongside the pop, rock and contemporary hits, the station should make room for more reflective moments drawn from Britain’s classical tradition. By ways of examples,  Ralph Vaughan Williams (The Lark Ascending, Fantasia on a Theme by Thomas Tallis), Edward Elgar (Enigma Variations, Pomp and Circumstance), William Walton (Crown Imperial, Façade), Benjamin Britten (Simple Symphony, Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra), Arnold Bax (Tintagel, the symphonies) and Arthur Bliss (A Colour Symphony, Checkmate) offer music that is unmistakably British in character yet accessible and emotionally rich. Short, carefully chosen pieces from these composers would give listeners quiet, high-quality interludes without breaking the station’s all-British rule and poular vibe. They would also remind audiences that British musical excellence long predates the 1960s and continues across genres.

GB Music Radio arrives at the right moment. It is straightforward, patriotic in the best sense, and commercially sensible. If it delivers on the promise of “All British, All Day” — and adds the occasional stretch of Vaughan Williams or Elgar for the quieter hours — it will give listeners something they have been missing for years: radio that treats British music as the national treasure it is.

text:
What LEOSA Actually Authorizes — and What It Doesn't

LEOSA (18 U.S.C. § 926C), commonly known as HR-218, was signed into law on July 22, 2004. It authorizes qualified retired law enforcement officers to carry a concealed firearm nationwide, overriding most state and local concealed carry restrictions. That single sentence carries enormous weight, but it comes with strict conditions.

To carry under LEOSA, a retired officer must meet four requirements: a minimum of 10 years of law enforcement service, separation from the agency in good standing, a photographic ID issued by the former agency, and proof of annual firearms qualification completed within the last 12 months. According to the US Concealed Carry Association, LEOSA does not grant any law enforcement authority. A retired officer carrying under HR-218 is legally equivalent to a civilian with a nationwide concealed carry permit.

LEOSA also does not override restrictions on federal buildings, school zones under current law, private property that prohibits firearms, or aircraft. These remain off-limits.

The LEOSA Reform Act of 2025 (H.R. 2243) passed the House on May 14, 2025, and was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the following day. Its Senate companion bill, S. 679, remains pending. If enacted, H.R. 2243 would expand carry to school zones, national parks, certain federal facilities, and public transportation property.

The Holster Qualification Problem Most Retired Officers Don't See Coming

Here is the part that trips up experienced officers: there is no single national holster standard under LEOSA. Holster requirements for qualification are set at the state or agency level, creating a patchwork of rules that retired officers must navigate on their own. What passes qualification in one state may get you turned away in another.

Connecticut offers a clear example. The Connecticut State Police explicitly ban cheap nylon or leather inside-the-pants holsters for LEOSA qualification. Their rules require that the holster used at qualification must be the same holster carried daily. The holster must secure the pistol without any risk of it falling out, and the shooter must be able to draw and re-holster with one hand without the holster collapsing.

These are not suggestions. They are pass/fail criteria. The wrong holster can cost a retired officer their qualification card. Without a current card, LEOSA carry rights lapse entirely. There is no grace period.

The practical takeaway is straightforward: research your state's specific qualification holster rules before you purchase carry gear, not after. Showing up to qualification day with a holster that doesn't meet the standard means you leave without a card and without the legal right to carry.

This is especially critical for officers who retired years ago and may not have kept up with evolving state-level requirements. Standards change. Your gear needs to reflect the current rules, not the ones that applied when you turned in your badge.

From Duty Rig to Concealed Carry: The Transition Retired LEOs Must Make

Most retiring officers spent their entire careers in Level II or Level III OWB duty rigs. That muscle memory runs deep. But LEOSA carry in civilian environments typically demands a shift to IWB or AIWB concealment setups. The duty belt stays in the closet.

OWB holsters remain valid for open-carry contexts and range qualification sessions. For everyday concealed carry under LEOSA, IWB is the dominant choice. According to Pew Pew Tactical, the shift from OWB duty carry to IWB concealment is one of the most significant gear transitions retired officers face.

Appendix carry (AIWB) is gaining traction among retired LEOs who spent decades on strong-side OWB. Key holster features that make AIWB safer and more comfortable include a claw attachment for improved concealment, adjustable cant for draw angle preference, and a full sweat guard that covers the slide and protects against skin contact.

Kydex has become the preferred material for this transition. Kydex holds its shape over time, does not absorb sweat or moisture, provides a consistent audible click on re-holster, and offers full trigger guard coverage. These are not convenience features. They are safety properties critical for officers retraining muscle memory from decades of duty carry.

C&G Holsters' COVERT/ALPHA Kydex Holster collection, available in both OWB and IWB configurations with Quickship and custom options, is built for exactly this transition. The retention consistency and one-handed re-holster capability align directly with what LEOSA qualification standards demand. Our founder, a retired Law Enforcement Officer and Master Firearms Instructor, designed these holsters with the same requirements he faced himself. Our team of U.S. Military Veterans, LEOs, and competitive shooters tests every design from a practitioner's perspective.

The community navigating this gear shift is substantial and growing. According to the Council on Criminal Justice, there were approximately 770,000 sworn law enforcement officers in the United States in 2024, roughly 30,000 fewer than the 2017 peak. A U.S. GAO report found that retirements spiked nearly 30% from 2019 to 2020 alone. That wave has not slowed. Every one of those retired officers faces this same OWB-to-IWB decision.

Optics, Weapon-Mounted Lights, and Modern LEOSA Carry Gear

Weapon-mounted lights (WMLs) and red dot sights (RDS) are now standard on defensive handguns. If you upgraded your carry pistol after retirement, your old holster almost certainly does not fit anymore. A standard holster will not accommodate a WML-equipped or optic-cut firearm. You need a holster specifically molded for your exact pistol model, light, and optic combination.

Light-bearing Kydex holsters are now widely available in both IWB and OWB formats. Generic-fit holsters create retention and safety risks that no retired officer should accept.

This matters for qualification, too. If you added a red dot to your carry pistol, replace your holster before qualification day, not after you discover the problem at the range. An optic-cut holster that accommodates your specific RDS is not optional; it is a prerequisite.

If the LEOSA Reform Act clears the Senate and expands carry to national parks, public transit, and certain federal facilities, light-bearing IWB configurations optimized for deep concealment will become the practical choice for those environments. Retired officers should be building their carry setup now with that possibility in mind.

Your LEOSA Carry Kit: The Documentation and Gear Checklist

A complete LEOSA carry kit requires three things on your person at all times: photographic ID from your former agency, proof of annual firearms qualification dated within the last 12 months, and a holster that meets the qualification standard used to earn that card.

If the LEOSA Reform Act (H.R. 2243) is enacted, requalification could extend from annual to every 36 months. Retired officers should monitor Senate progress on S. 679 and prepare their gear accordingly, but until the law changes, annual qualification remains the requirement.

Holster checklist for LEOSA compliance:

Full trigger guard coverage
One-handed draw and re-holster capability
No collapse on re-holster
Retention that prevents the firearm from falling out during normal activity
Compatibility with any WML or optic mounted on your carry pistol

One rule that cannot be overstated: if you qualify with a specific holster in your state, carry that same holster. Swapping gear between qualification and daily carry creates both legal and safety exposure. Your qualification card validates a specific setup. Honor it.

Keep a digital copy of your qualification card and agency ID accessible on your phone. A responding officer or federal agent may request documentation at any time, and fumbling through a wallet is not the impression you want to make during that contact.

Carry With the Same Standard You Served Under

You earned the right to carry under LEOSA through decades of service. The holster you choose should reflect the same standard you held on duty. This is not a minor gear decision. Your holster affects qualification eligibility, daily concealment, and your readiness in a threat scenario.

The key decisions are clear: know your state's qualification holster rules, make the OWB-to-IWB transition deliberately, ensure your holster fits your exact pistol configuration including lights and optics, and carry your documentation every single time you carry your firearm.

Treat holster selection as a mission-critical decision, not an afterthought. That mindset defined your career in law enforcement. It should define how you carry after it.

Ahuja described the result as a leaner, more accountable organization that does more because AI tools and clean internal data let teams move faster. She noted that remote work creates a document trail behind every decision, which feeds the intelligence systems that now shape how the company operates. Other tech firms have since made similar cuts.

The interview points to a model where AI agents handle more of the work once the organization has the right data, tools, and ownership structure in place. Block is already running that model.

text:
ASML Holding NV $ASML 
An Easy-to-Understand Guide for Everyday Investors

🧭 Navigation Compass (skip to 4,5,6 if  ADHD)

1: The Uncontested Giant of Microchip Manufacturing
2: Business Essentials: Competitive Advantage, Technology, and Trade Controls
3: Financial Health, Margins, and Cash Flow

4: Stock Outlook and Potential Scenarios
5: Analyst Consensus and Investor Sentiment
6: Summary: Key Drivers and Investment Takeaway

💡 Part 1: The Uncontested Giant of Microchip Manufacturing 

ASML Holding NV holds a unique position in global technology: it is the world's only provider of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. These giant, high-tech machines use laser light to print microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers. Without them, it is virtually impossible to manufacture the advanced microchips that power modern artificial intelligence, smartphones, and supercomputers.

As cloud giants spend heavily to build out AI infrastructure, the key question for everyday investors isn't whether chips are in demand, but how supply bottlenecks, trade restrictions, and manufacturing limits will shape ASML's future growth.

Management expects full-year 2026 revenue to reach €44 billion to €45 billion, with machine manufacturing slots booked out years in advance. At around 35.5 times future earnings, ASML trades at a higher stock price multiple than its industry peers, balancing strong market visibility against political risks in China and technical hurdles in scaling its newest machines.

📊 Part 2: Business Essentials:

ASML's Competitive Moat: DUV vs. EUV Technology

ASML's dominance comes from three decades of research and engineering. Its product line splits into two primary machine categories: Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) systems and Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) systems.

DUV machines use conventional lasers and water optics to print circuits for mainstream chips, such as those used in automobiles and basic electronics. EUV machines, by contrast, are required for cutting-edge chips. To generate EUV light, ASML blasts tiny drops of molten tin with lasers 50,000 times per second inside a vacuum chamber a feat of engineering no competitor has managed to replicate commercially.

To print smaller features without adding expensive extra steps, ASML built its next-generation platform: High-NA EUV. By using specialized optical lenses, High-NA tools print even finer features, though they require updated cleanroom setups and modified chip designs. Its production-tier system (EXE:5200B) handles up to 175 silicon wafers per hour to support high-volume manufacturing.

How Key Customers Are Adopting Next-Gen Tools

ASML sells its high-end machines to a small group of major semiconductor manufacturers: TSMC, Intel, Samsung, and SK Hynix. Each company is taking a different approach to adopting High-NA EUV.

Intel has been the earliest adopter, installing early pilot systems to regain technology leadership for its upcoming chip generations. In contrast, TSMC is taking a more conservative approach. Because High-NA tools cost around €350 million to €380 million each, TSMC plans to stick with standard EUV machines through 2029 by maximizing efficiency with existing techniques, before transitioning to High-NA around 2030. Samsung and SK Hynix are taking a middle path, introducing High-NA machines for high-performance memory chips (HBM) and sub-2nm fabrication over the next few years.

Key Suppliers and Production Constraints

ASML acts as a master integrator, designing systems while relying on specialized suppliers for key parts. For example, Carl Zeiss SMT builds the hyper-precise mirrors needed to guide laser light. Polishing these optical mirrors takes over a year per unit. While these custom partnerships create huge technical barriers for potential competitors, they also mean ASML's output depends heavily on smooth supply chain operations.

Geopolitics and China Export Controls

Because semiconductor manufacturing is strategically critical, governments closely regulate ASML's sales. Dutch and US regulations prohibit shipments of EUV machines to mainland China, and recent updates require licenses for advanced DUV systems as well.
After a period of heavy pre-buying by Chinese foundries in 2024 and 2025, Chinese sales have normalized to roughly 20% of ASML's total revenue. While local Chinese equipment makers are trying to build domestic alternatives, their tools remain well behind ASML's capabilities.

💵 Part 3: Financial Health, Margins, and Cash Flow

ASML's business model benefits from strong operating leverage: as sales grow, profits tend to increase even faster because fixed costs are spread over more high-margin machine sales and ongoing servicing fees.

Net sales rose from €28.3 billion in FY2024 to €32.7 billion in FY2025. In Q3 2026, ASML reported net sales of €11.7 billion and net income of €5.0 billion, driving operating profit margins up to 44.4%. Gross profit margins reached 57.5%, exceeding management's target.

Services and Upgrades Provide Recurring Revenue

Beyond selling new equipment, ASML earns steady recurring income through its Installed Base Management segment, which covers servicing, software upgrades, and performance retrofits. Revenue here grew to €8.2 billion in FY2025. Because these software and optical upgrades carry gross margins above 70%, they generate highly profitable, predictable cash flow regardless of broader economic cycles.

Balance Sheet Strength and Shareholder Returns

ASML maintains a healthy balance sheet with low debt. As of Q3 2026, cash and short-term investments totaled €12.7 billion against €2.2 billion in debt. Strong cash flows fund €4.8 billion in annual R&D without needing outside loans, while supporting dividend growth and a €12 billion stock buyback program running through 2028.

🔮 Part 4: Stock Outlook and Potential Scenarios

Valuation vs. Industry Peers

ASML trades at roughly 35.5 times forward earnings. While higher than chip equipment peers like Applied Materials (32x) or Lam Research (29x), this premium reflects ASML's unique monopoly over EUV lithography, where no direct rival exists.

Three-to-Six Month Scenarios for Investors

1. Base Case (55% Likelihood): 
The stock consolidates between $1,750 and $1,850 (€1,550–€1,650). ASML hits its Q4 2026 targets, full-year revenue lands near €44.5 billion, and Chinese sales hold steady around 20%.

2. Bull Case (25% Likelihood): 
Shares move up toward $2,100–$2,250 (€1,850–€2,000) as AI chip demand accelerates, High-NA tools prove successful at Intel, and chipmakers place new long-term orders.

3. Bear Case (20% Likelihood): 
Shares pull back toward $1,350–$1,450 (€1,220–€1,280) if trade restrictions expand to prohibit servicing existing machines in China, or if delays in new chip factory builds push orders outward.

⚖️ Part 5: Analyst Consensus and Investor Sentiment

Wall Street analysts remain overwhelmingly positive on ASML. About 87% of covering research firms recommend buying the stock, with an average 12-month price target around $2,152 (roughly 31% upside from recent trading levels). Major institutional funds continue adding shares, and outright short selling remains extremely low at under 0.4% of available shares.

💬 Part 6: Summary: Key Drivers and Investment Takeaway

ASML is a fundamental player in the global technology ecosystem. Its monopoly on EUV technology, high profit margins, and growing service revenue provide strong long-term tailwinds. However, because its stock trades at a premium valuation, near-term price swings will depend on trade policy decisions, factory timeline updates, and customer adoption speeds for High-NA tools. For retail investors, dollar-cost averaging or looking for entry points during short-term pullbacks offers a balanced way to participate in ASML's multi-year growth story.

THE NUMBERS — Q2 2026
🔹 Group revenue: $582.3M, up 454% YoY.
🔹 AI cloud revenue: $574.9M.
🔹 Group adjusted EBITDA: $236.2M.
🔹 Annualised run-rate revenue: approximately $3B at quarter-end.
What interests me is the possibility of operating leverage.
As more GPU capacity becomes available and utilisation improves, Nebius could potentially spread infrastructure and platform costs across a larger revenue base.
Its software capabilities may also help differentiate the business beyond raw computing capacity.
THE BULL CASE
🟢 Rapid growth in AI cloud demand.
🟢 Potential for software differentiation and customer relationships.
🟢 Improving operating leverage as infrastructure scales.
🟢 Opportunity to capture more value from AI workloads than a pure property-leasing business.
THE BEAR CASE
🔴 GPUs require enormous upfront investment.
🔴 Hardware depreciation and replacement cycles matter.
🔴 Competition could pressure pricing and margins.
🔴 Strong adjusted EBITDA doesn't automatically mean strong free cash flow.
MY VIEW
Nebius offers the most direct exposure of these three to the economics of operating an AI cloud platform.
But the question isn't simply how quickly revenue grows.
It's whether that growth produces attractive cash returns after GPU purchases, depreciation, financing and ongoing expansion.
2. IREN $IREN — POWER INFRASTRUCTURE MOVING INTO AI COMPUTE
IREN's investment case starts with something increasingly valuable: access to large-scale power-connected infrastructure.
The company is converting that advantage into an expanding AI cloud and compute business.
That creates substantial potential, but it also makes execution and capital allocation especially important.
THE NUMBERS — FY2026
🔹 Total revenue: $707M.
🔹 AI Cloud Services revenue: $128.8M, versus $16.4M in FY2025.
🔹 Bitcoin mining revenue: $578.2M.
🔹 Adjusted EBITDA: $245.7M.
🔹 GAAP net loss: $702.6M.
🔹 Contracted ARR for 2026 capacity: approximately $4B, as reported in August.
The GAAP loss needs context.
It included approximately $638.8M of non-cash impairments, primarily associated with Bitcoin mining hardware as IREN transitioned towards AI Cloud Services.
That doesn't make the loss irrelevant, but it shouldn't be interpreted as an equivalent cash loss from the AI cloud business.
There's another important distinction.
$4B in contracted ARR is not $4B in recognised revenue or free cash flow.
IREN still needs to complete deployments, commission equipment, secure customer acceptance and convert contracted capacity into billable operations.
THE BULL CASE
🟢 Valuable power-connected infrastructure.
🟢 Strong contracted demand for AI compute.
🟢 Opportunity to move further up the value chain through AI cloud services.
🟢 Potentially attractive economics if deployment costs and utilisation develop as expected.
THE BEAR CASE
🔴 Enormous capital requirements.
🔴 Financing costs and potential shareholder dilution.
🔴 GPU depreciation and replacement obligations.
🔴 Delays between contracted capacity, operational deployment and revenue generation.
MY VIEW
IREN may have one of the more interesting infrastructure-to-compute opportunities.
But its success shouldn't be measured only by megawatts, GPU counts or contracted ARR.
I want to see how much capital it takes to deliver that growth, how the expansion is financed and how much economic value remains for existing shareholders.
3. CIPHER $CIFR — LONG-DURATION DATA-CENTRE INFRASTRUCTURE
Cipher offers a different proposition.
Rather than relying primarily on selling GPU computing services, its HPC strategy is centred on developing and leasing large-scale data-centre infrastructure.
That potentially creates a more visible long-term contracted-income model.
THE NUMBERS — SEPTEMBER 30, 2026
🔹 Contracted gross HPC capacity: approximately 700 MW.
🔹 Contracted revenue: approximately $16.6B.
🔹 Weighted average lease term: 17.3 years.
🔹 Projected average annualised project-level NOI: approximately $843M.
These figures are impressive, but they require careful interpretation.
The $16.6B represents contracted revenue over the relevant agreements, not cash already received.
And the $843M NOI figure is a projected annualised measure of project-level revenue less project-level operating expenses over a defined period.
It is not company-level free cash flow or cash available for distribution to shareholders.
Construction spending, financing costs, corporate expenses and other capital requirements still matter.
THE BULL CASE
🟢 Long-duration contracts improve revenue visibility.
🟢 Infrastructure leasing can reduce direct exposure to GPU replacement cycles.
🟢 Large-scale power and data-centre development capabilities.
🟢 Potential for relatively predictable project income once facilities are completed and operating.
THE BEAR CASE
🔴 Construction delays and cost overruns.
🔴 Substantial upfront capital requirements.
🔴 Dependence on major tenants and their creditworthiness.
🔴 Project-level NOI may not translate into attractive equity returns after debt service and remaining costs.
MY VIEW
Cipher potentially offers the clearest contracted infrastructure-income structure of the three.
But contracted income isn't the same as shareholder profit.
The real test will be whether completed facilities generate attractive returns after construction costs, financing and ongoing capital requirements.
SO WHICH BUSINESS MODEL DO I PREFER?
This is where I think the comparison becomes interesting.
$NBIS — THE AI CLOUD ECONOMICS OPPORTUNITY
Nebius has the potential to capture more value from AI workloads through its integrated compute and software platform.
But it must continually justify the capital invested in GPUs and infrastructure.
$IREN — THE POWER-TO-COMPUTE OPPORTUNITY
IREN has valuable infrastructure positioning and a potentially powerful growth transition.
But the scale and financing of that transition could determine whether shareholders benefit.
$CIFR — THE LONG-TERM INFRASTRUCTURE-INCOME OPPORTUNITY
Cipher's leasing model offers greater visibility into contracted infrastructure revenue.
But development costs, tenant exposure and leverage will determine the actual returns.
My comparative judgment:
Cipher has the clearest long-duration contracted-income structure.
Nebius offers the most direct exposure to differentiated AI cloud operating economics.
IREN combines power infrastructure with substantial compute growth potential, but its transition carries major financing and execution demands.
That is a comparison of business models, not a ranking of which stock is cheapest.
To decide which stock offers the best investment value, I'd also need to compare current market capitalisations, net debt, remaining capital commitments, financing terms and potential dilution.
WHAT I'M WATCHING NEXT
For Nebius: GPU utilisation, pricing, margins and cash flow after capital expenditure.
For IREN: Deployment schedules, financing, recognised AI cloud revenue and returns per share.
For Cipher: Project completion, realised NOI, debt service and returns on invested capital.
And for all three, I want to know whether growth is becoming more self-funding or increasingly dependent on external capital.
MY TAKEAWAY
I'm bullish on the long-term AI infrastructure opportunity.
But I'm becoming increasingly selective about how that opportunity is financed.
Nebius needs to prove that AI cloud growth can generate attractive returns after GPU investment.
IREN needs to turn its power advantage and contracted capacity into sustainable cash flow without excessive dilution.
Cipher needs to demonstrate that long-term leases translate into profitable infrastructure assets after construction and financing costs.
Three different business models. Three different financial hurdles.
The winner won't necessarily be the company with the biggest backlog or the most megawatts.
It will be the company that creates the most lasting value per share from the capital it invests.
— EMMANUELINVEST

Monday, October 19, 2026 – AI/tech risk update
Verifiable data and market levels only; opinion is identified separately. Material changes since Oct. 12–16 are noted.
1. AI infrastructure financing and credit
• CoreWeave: Bonds traded at distressed levels. 2031 notes reached ~15.78% YTM (briefly above 16%); some unsecured notes fell below 75–80 cents. Five-year CDS hit records of ~1,038–1,195 bps, implying market-priced default risk above 60%. Prices and spreads remained elevated through the weekend.
• Peers and project bonds: Nebius and TeraWulf yields rose. Select SPVs fell: Meta-linked Hyperion near 91 cents; Microsoft-leased Project Excalibur below 87 cents; some Hut 8/Nvidia-linked deals at ~91–93 cents.
• Issuance: AI-linked debt reached hundreds of billions year-to-date, including hyperscalers, Oracle, SpaceX, and SoftBank; September issuance slowed from June peaks. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft issued substantial debt. Capex is weakening their IG metrics, though they remain stronger than sub-IG/neocloud borrowers. Oracle CDS widened to ~200–300 bps in recent reports. Higher benchmark yields pressure sub-investment-grade financing.
• Weekly change: Stress surged Oct. 14–15 amid viral yield charts and selloffs, with little relief afterward.
2. Inflation and rates
• September CPI: Headline inflation rose 0.6% m/m and 3.7% y/y; core rose 0.3% m/m and 2.6% y/y. Gasoline (+9.1% m/m) drove the headline increase. Core was more contained but exceeded some forecasts. PPI rose 1.3% m/m; August PCE was previously up 3.4% y/y.
• Rates and Fed pricing: The 10-year Treasury was ~5.08–5.10% Oct. 19, after nearing 5.3% following CPI; effective fed funds was ~3.88%. October hike odds rose to ~30–50% after CPI, then fell to ~12–15% following Warsh comments and equity weakness. A December hike remained more firmly priced.
• Weekly change: Hot CPI/PPI briefly lifted yields and hike odds; tech weakness and commentary later pulled them back. Inflation offered little relief.
3. Oil and Middle East/Iran/Hormuz
• Brent traded around $108–109/bbl, touching ~$110 Friday before dipping Monday, still above pre-conflict levels.
• After more than seven months of conflict, Hormuz/Gulf flows intermittently recovered to ~75–80% of pre-war volumes, aided by inventory draws and workarounds, but remain volatile. Dozens of shipping incidents in late September and early-to-mid October reduced some daily transits and raised freight costs. Inventories remain depleted; recovery is fragile.
• Weekly change: No durable de-escalation.
4. Market concentration and rotation
• Oct. 12–16: Nasdaq Composite −4.48%, Nasdaq-100 ~−5.5%, S&P 500 −1.95%, Dow +0.67%. Tech fell ~6.4%, its worst performance in about 1.5 years; semiconductors dropped 10–11%. Equal-weight S&P outperformed or advanced as investors rotated into healthcare, consumer, energy, and staples. Tech remains ~40% of the cap-weighted S&P.
• Weekly change: Rotation from AI, tech, and semiconductors accelerated amid financing and inflation concerns; concentration remains high.
• Hyperscaler capex consensus is ~$800 billion in 2026, rising to ~$1.1–1.2 trillion in 2027. Goldman estimates AI infrastructure needs ~$300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even; cloud revenue is currently ~$70 billion above its pre-AI trend. Broad solid returns would require about $1 trillion in annual AI-app spending. CoreWeave has ~$104 billion in contracted backlog.
• Enterprise surveys show some AI value, alongside cost overruns and forecast misses. No major positive guidance revisions emerged this week.
• Weekly change: Financing stress and capex scale remain central; no major earnings surprises eased ROI concerns.
Assessment: Risks are rising. Neocloud and AI infrastructure credit stress intensified,Last week’s tech weakness versus Dow and equal-weight resilience suggests selling may spread beyond AI. No clear relief emerged; high market concentration and the gap between capex and current AI revenue

text:
OFFICIAL PRESS RELEASE

Obi’s “Tell Them No” Advice to the Diaspora Is Clueless, Callous and Contradicted by the Facts - Omole.

At a town hall with supporters in the United Kingdom on Sunday, 18 October, arrogant Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), told Nigerians abroad that people back home were begging them for money, and that the proper response was "Tell them no!" He went further, suggesting that those relatives should instead be pressured to vote for him.

We read the remarks twice and watched the video several times, hoping we had misunderstood them. We had not. The statement shows no feel for how Nigerian families work, no grasp of how the Nigerian economy works, and no understanding of how the diaspora thinks. It deserves a plain answer, and we give it on three fronts.

Prince Ade Omole, Renewed Hope Advocate and Diaspora leader, reacted, “Mr Obi has looked at one of the most ordinary acts of love Nigerians perform and called it begging. Nobody in London, Atlanta or Toronto sends money home because a politician failed them. They send it because a mother, a brother or a child is waiting. Telling them to say ‘no’ is not politics. It is contempt.”

Anyone who has ever been the first child, or the one who "went abroad", knows that the money leaving a London or Atlanta account at month-end is not begging. It is school fees, a mother's hospital bill, a brother's rent, a cousin's exam registration. To call it begging insults the senders and the receivers in one breath. This is a Nigerian tradition of looking after one's own, older than any political party, and no candidate has the right to order Nigerians to ration it.

The economics are also no better than the manners. The Diaspora sent home a record $20.93 billion in 2024, according to World Bank data reported by Nairametrics, roughly four times foreign direct investment and nearly 37 per cent of all remittances to sub-Saharan Africa. Those dollars feed households and also feed the foreign exchange system that keeps the naira steady and reserves growing. The Central Bank reported that remittances through licensed operators rose by more than 61 per cent in the first ten months of 2024, to $4.22 billion, and the CBN Governor credited reforms and returning confidence. Mr Obi now asks Nigerians abroad to close that tap. He would starve households and weaken the currency in a single stroke, all to score a political point.

Omole added, “In our culture you do not count what you send home. The first son pays the school fees, the daughter in Manchester pays the hospital bill, and nobody calls it charity because it is family. That is how Nigerian households have survived challenging times for generations. A politician who wants to ration that love is asking us to be less than who we are.”

A widow in Onitsha does not cause bad governance by asking her son in Canada for help, and the son does not cure bad governance by refusing. Refusing family is not a vote. It is a punishment, and it falls on the same Nigerians at home whose votes Mr Obi says he wants. This is also the politician who, on the 2023 campaign trail in Ilorin, urged voters to collect whatever politicians offered them because it was their own money, as Daily Trust reported. In 2023, the advice was to take the money. In 2026, the advice is to refuse your own family.

Now to the record. Mr Obi wants his listeners to believe that Nigeria is beyond help. The people who scrutinise economies for a living have reached a different view.

Let us start with the Bretton Woods institutions. In February, World Bank Managing Director of Operations Anna Bjerde told President Tinubu in Abuja that Nigeria has become a frequent example of reform delivery in her conversations around the world, and called the two-year results commendable. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva has publicly commended Nigeria's decisive reform actions. At the Bangkok annual meetings last week, World Bank President Ajay Banga acknowledged the progress, and a Finance Ministry statement records that private capital inflows have grown from about $300 million in 2023 to nearly $6 billion this year.

The ratings agencies agree with them. Fitch and Moody's upgraded Nigeria in 2025. S&P followed in May 2026, lifting the rating to B, reportedly its first upgrade of Nigeria in 14 years, and citing the exchange rate liberalisation and a stronger external position.

Domestic numbers have also pointed in the same direction. Headline inflation fell to 14.63 per cent in September, from 20.98 per cent a year earlier and its lowest since October 2020. The Central Bank cut its policy rate by 350 basis points to 23 per cent in September. External reserves stood above $58 billion on 12 October, the highest since 2008, and the Finance Minister said the tax-to-GDP ratio rose from about 7 per cent to 12.5 per cent.

On tax, the four laws signed in June 2025 took effect in January 2026. Income up to ₦800,000 a year is now tax-free, up from ₦300,000, and minimum-wage earners pay no income tax at all.

Workers and pensioners have not been left out. The minimum wage is ₦70,000 a month, more than double the ₦30,000 it replaced. The Pension Transitional Arrangement Directorate has cleared ₦39.6 billion of inherited pension arrears, paid the arrears on the ₦32,000 pension increment, and the President has approved health insurance cover for Defined Benefit Scheme pensioners.

On local government autonomy, the Federal Government, through the Attorney-General, went to the Supreme Court, which on 11 July 2024 affirmed the financial autonomy of all 774 local government councils. The work of implementing that ruling continues.

On regional development, the administration has added development commissions for the North West, South East, South West and North Central to the North East and Niger Delta bodies it inherited, and created a Ministry of Regional Development in October 2024 to supervise them. The 2025 budget proposed more than ₦2.4 trillion for five commissions, and on 14 September the North Central commission opened a summit in Abuja on a 20-year plan for its zone.

And on infrastructure, Section I of the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, 47 kilometres, is complete, with Section II well advanced. The 1,068-kilometre Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway is under construction on several sections, and work on the Akwanga–Jos–Bauchi–Gombe–Biu–Maiduguri corridor was flagged off this year.

The President has been honest that these reforms were painful at first. They were also necessary, and the figures above show where they are leading.

“The President never told Nigerians the road would be easy. He told them it would be worth it. Three years on, inflation is falling, the naira has steadied, and the rating agencies are upgrading Nigeria. There is more to do on prices and jobs, and we will not pretend otherwise. But you do not fix a house by telling its owners to give up on it.” Omole affirmed.

Finally, the diaspora itself. Mr Obi spoke as though Nigerians abroad were waiting to be told what to do with their money and their votes. They are not. The Renewed Hope Global Tour took the administration's message across four continents and eight cities, among them New York, London, Dubai, Zurich and Toronto, and its 50-page report was presented to the Federal Government in Abuja in August. Diaspora groups have publicly pledged to mobilise for the President's re-election. A Strategic Global Diaspora Conference brought more than 600 participants together from Africa, the United Kingdom, the Americas, Europe and Australia to organise support for the Renewed Hope Agenda. In the Oxford–Metro Analytics National Trust Poll, which closed on 7 September, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, finished ahead of Mr Obi and led in more than 20 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

“The Nigerian diaspora is politically conscious, economically influential and perfectly capable of making its own decisions. The Renewed Hope Global Tour took the President’s message to four continents and eight cities, and Nigerians abroad answered with conviction, not instruction. They want a country that works, they can see what is being built, and they will organise to keep it going.” Omole said.

“You cannot build a nation by asking its citizens to abandon one another. You build a nation by strengthening families, rewarding sacrifice, creating opportunities and restoring confidence in the future. The diaspora's money belongs to the people who earned it, and the decision to support their families is theirs alone. Peter Obi is entitled to seek Nigerians' votes, but he has no right to turn family solidarity into a political weapon.” Omole concluded.

The diaspora will keep sending money home to the people it loves, and it will keep backing the President whose reforms are making that money count for more. We call on Mr Obi to withdraw his remark and to apologise to the Nigerians at home he described as beggars.

Hon. Tosin Olayinka, LL.B (Hons), B.L., LL.M (London)

𝐒𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐥: 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐮𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐅𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬

In August 2022, protesters in Kayar marched from the fishing wharf to a nearby fishmeal factory carrying signs that read “Kayar is sick” and “Our water is contaminated.” Residents said the plant had polluted local water, fouled the air with a relentless stench, and consumed fish that would once have been sold for people to eat. Similar complaints have surfaced elsewhere along Senegal’s coast, where fishmeal factories have been linked to pollution, respiratory problems, apparent zoning violations, and growing competition for a food source that remains central to daily life.

That competition is becoming harder to ignore. Fish supplies nearly half of Senegal’s protein intake, yet between 2009 and 2018, the amount of small pelagic fish reaching local markets fell by two-thirds, while per-capita consumption was cut in half. Fresh and dried fish prices later more than doubled. When reporters visited Senegalese plants in 2024 and 2025, they documented tons of fresh, whole fish entering factories that had historically been expected—or in some cases licensed—to rely on scraps and waste. Round and flat sardinella, both heavily overexploited and at risk of collapse, are among the species being turned into feed; round sardinella is also a foundation of thieboudienne, Senegal’s national dish. In some communities, the number of women working in fish processing has dropped from more than 300 to about 70. Researchers have also documented debt-bondage risks among crews financed by factory owners and fishmongers, and found children as young as eight working aboard roughly a third of artisanal vessels surveyed.

The strain extends offshore. Industrial boats have entered artisanal fishing grounds, gone dark by switching off tracking systems, and engaged in suspected illegal transshipment. Fishers describe larger vessels cutting nets, ramming pirogues, and threatening crews. As catches diminish and work disappears, some fishers are turning their boats toward the roughly 930-mile route to the Canary Islands, where more than 3,000 migrants died in 2025. Senegal’s experience offers a stark glimpse of a larger global feed economy: Fish vital to local diets, jobs, and coastal ecosystems are increasingly being redirected toward distant aquaculture markets. In Senegal, that shift can be seen not as an abstraction, but in depleted stocks, vanishing livelihoods, polluted towns, and fishing boats repurposed for migration.
