As part of Marc Carney’s extreme militarism, he’s putting $2 billion into one of the most secretive, US aligned parts of the Canadian government. But the media focus has been almost entirely about controversy over data centres.

On Friday the Globe and Mail and several other outlets reported that the Communication Security Establishment (CSE) will construct a data centre in Ottawa expected to cost up to $1.85 billion. The new 60 MW facility would be among the largest such projects in the country though smaller than several planned data centres. According to the paper, “the national security source told The Globe the data centre project is possible now because of the Carney government's significant increase in defence spending.”

Under the Department of National Defence, CSE employs over 3,800 mathematicians, engineers, linguists, analysts, computer scientists, etc. Its annual budget is over $1 billion. The secretive agency has a variety of high-tech gadgets, including surveillance planes. In 2011 CSE moved into a new $1.2 billion home. The seven-building, 110,000 square-metre complex is connected to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service’s (CSIS) headquarters in Ottawa.

Unlike CSIS, CSE is largely foreign focused. It seeks to “protect the computer networks and information of greatest importance to Canada” from international attack. CSE also gathers international signals intelligence (SIGINT), which it defines as “intelligence acquired through the collection of electromagnetic signals.” Historically, CSE largely intercepted electronic communications between embassies in Ottawa and other nations’ capitals. Today, CSE monitors phone calls, radio, microwave and satellite, as well as emails, chat rooms and other Internet exchanges. It engages in various forms of data hacking, sifting through millions of videos and online documents daily.

CSE has long had close ties to its US counterpart. NSA has trained CSE cryptanalysts and in the 1960s the US agency paid part of the cost of modernizing Canadian communications interception facilities. CSE has opened interception posts at Canadian diplomatic outposts at NSA’s behest. CSE long spied for the US from an interception post inside Canada’s embassy in Havana and in the 1970s sought to open a communications site in Algeria to help NSA spy on Muammar Gaddafi’s Libya. CSE also gathered intelligence on Palestinians for Israel. Former CSE intelligence officer Mike Frost wrote, “[former Palestinian Liberation Organization chairman] Yasser Arafat’s name, for instance, was on every [CSE] key word list. NSA was happy about that.”

An NSA history of the US–Canada SIGINT relationship released by whistleblower Edward Snowden labelled Canada a “highly valued second party partner”, which offers “resources for advanced collection, processing and analysis, and has opened covert sites at the request of NSA. CSEC shares with NSA their unique geographic access to areas unavailable to the US.”

As part of the Snowden revelations, it came to light that CSE hacked Mexican computers and spied on Brazil’s Department of Mines and Energy. CSE also planted sophisticated malware on mobile phones and maintained a network of infected computers to attack targets without being detected. To mask their involvement CSE hacked into random computers outside the US/Canada/UK/Australia/New Zealand Five Eyes alliance to use them to launch cyberattacks.

The September 11, 2001, attacks in the US spurred a major expansion of CSE. During this period CSE took an ever more active role in ‘counterterrorism’ and foreign intelligence. The agency’s sophisticated equipment and analytical and linguistic resources contributed significantly to the 2001-14 occupation of Afghanistan. The agency’s website said it played a “vital role” in the central Asian country and CSE head John Adams boasted that they were responsible for more than half the “actionable intelligence” Canadian soldiers used in Afghanistan. That included monitor… etc.

text:
Podcast Summary | Huberman Lab: What Makes Great Leaders & How to Live an Extraordinary Life | Dr. Jared Diamond

Overview
Jared Diamond rejects personality-based generalizations about leadership, arguing there are roughly 37 ways to be effective and charisma is only one of them. He applies natural experiments rather than traditional biography to show that leaders can matter decisively, using Hitler as the clearest case, and pairs that analysis with followers as the other half of the equation. On living well, his advice is to find work you enjoy, are good at, and that makes a difference, while resisting others' prescriptions for how to live.

Key Themes
- Charisma is one of roughly 37 paths to effective leadership, so reducing leaders to a single personality type distorts how influence actually works.
- Leaders can decisively change history: Hitler is the case where most historians agree his absence would likely have meant no Holocaust and possibly no WWII.
- Traditional biography fails because different historians reach opposite conclusions from identical facts, which is why Diamond prefers natural experiments.
- Followers are half the equation: not every population is disposed to follow a charismatic figure, and followership needs explaining as much as leadership.
- Movements need more than a founder: Jesus had a universal message and St. Paul as organizer, and Muhammad combined charisma with organizing and generalship.
- Among 22 outstanding postwar political leaders, only Nelson Mandela and Lee Kuan Yew stepped down voluntarily; power rarely yields itself.
- Diamond's three careers, physiology, New Guinea birds, and history and geography, rest on list-making treated as a serious scientific method.
- Mentorship is a negotiated investment: projects must interest both mentor and student, and students gain most from what the mentor actually knows.
- Much of what looks like leader impact in sports and business is variance from players, institutions, and chance, which firing a coach does not fix.

Detailed Summary
Diamond grew up in the shadow of WWII and Hitler, born in 1937, with a Jewish family from Eastern Europe and a wife whose Polish family was affected by the Holocaust. His first memory was a Life magazine photograph of dead American soldiers on a New Guinea beach. That personal history motivated the leadership book, though he separates its content from his own experience.

He rejects the claim that charisma is required for leadership and estimates about 37 ways to be effective, with charisma as just one. Stalin and Augusto Pinochet of Chile are offered as uncharismatic leaders. Traditional biography, he argues, is unreliable because different historians draw opposite conclusions from the same facts; A.J.P. Taylor concluded from the same record that Hitler was a normal German politician pursuing shared national goals. Diamond's book instead uses natural experiments.

Hitler remains the strongest case that individuals matter. He is described as uniquely charismatic as an orator, uniquely skilled at deception, and unique in conceiving industrialized mass killing. He deceived Neville Chamberlain at Munich, German politicians, business leaders, generals, and fellow Nazis. Diamond notes the near misses: a 1930 car accident that nearly killed Hitler before he became chancellor, and the 1944 Wolf's Lair bomb planted by Claus von Stauffenberg, where Hitler leaned forward before detonation, surviving with a blown eardrum while four others died.

Harry Truman is presented as the most unlikely significant American president. He reached the Senate through what Diamond calls dishonest shenanigans, was chosen as vice president for trivial political reasons, and never met Roosevelt as vice president; he did not know about the atomic bomb when he took office. Widely despised in his time, he is reassessed as courageous for the Berlin Airlift, developing the hydrogen bomb, the Korean War, and firing General MacArthur.

The book covers political, business, sports, and religious leaders, including two chapters on religious figures. On Jesus, Diamond notes no contemporary information exists; the earliest sources come from St. Paul's letters and the Gospel of Mark, both about 20 years after his death. Jesus is credited with a universal message, correct placement in the Western Roman Empire, and a great organizer in St. Paul. The New Testament names six other messiahs besides Jesus, and John the Baptist was beheaded, underscoring how many figures occupied similar ground.

A chapter on 19th-century U.S. religious leaders covers Joseph Smith, Anne Lee, and Jim Jones. Joseph Smith is described as a charismatic founder with weaknesses as an organizer; Brigham Young was the great organizer. Jim Jones is treated as more complex than a purely crazy cult leader: he led desegregation in Indianapolis and later served as a housing commissioner in San Francisco, attracting idealistic followers before becoming increasingly extreme. His followers skewed poor, elderly, African-American, and less educated, and Jonestown ended in the largest mass suicide in American history, with 931 people drinking cyanide-poisoned punch.

Muhammad is cited as both charismatic and a great organizer and general. The Mahdi of the Sudan is described as a brilliant organizer and general who defeated a British-Egyptian army of 7,000 with tribal forces using sticks. The broader pattern is that successful movements often need an organizer, and sometimes a military defender, in addition to a founder.

Follower analysis runs throughout. The Nazis never won a majority in an election, and Diamond contrasts Hitler's followers with voters for Roosevelt and Churchill, whose parents voted for Roosevelt three times and once against him. He explores whether a clean line separates leaders who claim to obey God from those who claim to be the apex of power, and finds Jim Jones does not fit it, since he never denied God or claimed superiority to God.

A table of 22 outstanding political leaders from WWII onward, including Stalin, Sadat, Mussolini, and Hitler, shows how few relinquished power. Only Nelson Mandela, who retired voluntarily in his 80s, and Lee Kuan Yew, who served decades as prime minister of independent Singapore before stepping down, did so. The rest were assassinated, committed suicide, voted out, or removed by coup. Once a powerful leader concludes they are effective, voluntary exit is very unlikely.

Diamond sees his three careers as different questions rather than a change of mind. Continental patterns across 10,000 years involve no decisive individuals, while leadership operates at local scales during his lifetime. His method of list-making began after his mother, a teacher and talented linguist, taught him to read at age three; he kept notebooks listing rivers, animals, birds, and Boston streetcar numbers. He later studied five years of Latin, three years of Greek, German before college, Russian during the Sputnik era, and Spanish, and learned Italian at 61 as his 13th language, reading it daily and holding a two-hour weekly conversation with a USC professor.

He describes tension between narrow specialization and broad interest, and treats naming as functionally important, since names anchor information and encode relationships, contrary to the Feynman view that a name adds nothing to understanding. He has studied New Guinea birds since 1964, and with Ernst Mayr spent 30 years preparing a book on the birds of Northern Melanesia. He recites bird names at night, sometimes in local names and sometimes in Latin, each carrying genus, altitudinal sequence, body size, and coexistence information. His lab physiology career closed in 2002.

Scientific leadership takes different forms. Alan Hodgkin did not run a large lab and had one PhD student at a time. Gerald Edelman, a Nobel laureate, ran roughly 50 postdocs and excelled as an organizer and fundraiser; a friend's unpublished lecture on Bence Jones proteins prompted Edelman to redirect his lab, and Edelman won the Nobel while the friend did not. Diamond describes 36 years as a UCLA physiology professor; one student the department wanted to expel became an outstanding researcher. He references Oppenheimer's overlooked theft, which allowed his career to continue.

On mentorship, Diamond could take only two or three students at a time, each staying three or four years, so projects must interest both mentor and student. Students benefit from working on topics the mentor actually knows, since a mentor cannot teach what he does not know. He values scientific adventurousness in trainees and negotiates accordingly, allowing one Argentinian student to pursue his own project alongside their joint work.

Fieldwork shaped his family life. New Guinea was a necessary evil, physically miserable most of the time yet fascinating enough to justify it: sweet potatoes and rice three meals a day, scrub mite bites, a year of dysentery his first year that Harvard doctors could not cure, and malaria his third. Twin sons Max and Joshua were born in 1987, after which he cut trips from three months to one month, and his last trip was 2019.

Birds are uniquely useful for research because they are easy to observe and use sight and sound like humans. Chickadees and titmice give simple call notes at a hawk's presence, alerting distant birds before it can reach them. Vervet monkeys use distinct grunts functioning as words for eagle, python, and leopard, work connected to Peter Marler's finding that the same species can learn different songs depending on where it was raised.

Diamond defends Paul Ehrlich's population warnings as broadly correct, arguing population growth must be read alongside per-person consumption and resource depletion. He cites about 9 billion people today versus roughly 1 million 10,000 years ago, about 4 billion depending on fish and seafood for protein, and depletion of fisheries, forests, and topsoil. He identifies three major risks: nuclear extermination, consequences of inequality in a globalized world, and resource depletion and overexploitation.

Diamond is openly selective, interested in many things and explicitly uninterested in others. Awareness of finite time sharpened around age 89, prompting specific goals: synthesizing bird distribution across 10 isolated New Guinea mountain ranges to understand what makes good colonist birds, and learning all 210 Bach church cantatas at about one per week over three or four years. He cites life-expectancy figures: an American man at birth around 78, but one who reaches 70 has a life expectancy around 93.

On sports and business, analysis of variance suggests roughly 15 to 30 percent of sports success is attributable to the coach, about 30 percent to players, and about 30 percent to institutions, with similar patterns for CEOs, companies, and industries. Firing a coach or CEO often seems to help largely through random factors. John Wooden is the exception, having treated basketball as a philosophy of life, emphasizing conditioning, detail down to socks, and training in groups of seven to allow substitution; his UCLA teams won nine national championships, including seven in a row.

Bill Walton and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar reportedly said they learned more from Wooden than from anyone other than their parents, lessons about life rather than basketball. UCLA's athletic department is described as $150 million in debt, attributed to firing basketball coaches since Wooden and buying out contracts. Yvon Chouinard of Patagonia is admired as a full person with a philosophy beyond business, a top-ranked mountaineer who made a first ascent of a difficult Yosemite face and declined to expand cotton production to avoid overdeveloping cotton agriculture; Diamond wrote the preface to his autobiography. Steve Jobs reduced Apple's product line to four and emphasized attractive, easy-to-use design, contrasted with a TV remote having 47 buttons.

Business-school methods applied to politics show leaders matter more where they hold more power: prime ministers more than governors, governors more than mayors, dictators more than democratic leaders, and democratic leaders more in wartime than peacetime. Diamond is unsure whether Jobs had a philosophy of life beyond products, where Wooden clearly did. His central advice, echoing Tom Lovejoy's father, is to do something you enjoy, something you are good at, and something that makes a difference, resisting others' rules for how to live. He illustrates honest limits: he gave up conducting orchestras because he could not anticipate the downbeat.

🪔 Simple Devi Chakra Sadhana for Ashtami & Navami
 No complex rituals needed — pure intent is enough. ✨

📿 Mantra (Saptashloki Durga) “Durge smrita harasi bhītim aśeṣa jantoḥ…”
 Meaning: O Devi, who removes fear from all beings when remembered — be merciful to us. Shower your grace and keep us in your presence.

🙌 4-Step Chakra Mudra Practice Chant the mantra at each step:
❤️ Heart Chakra (Anahata) Place little finger at the center of the chest. Keep thumb near the throat.

🗣️ Throat Chakra (Vishuddhi) Keep thumb at the throat.

👁️ Ajna Chakra (Forehead) Move both hands to the forehead with a 4-finger gap.

👑 Sahasrara Chakra (Crown) Place hand at the back of the head (shikha area).

🌸 Closing Offering Take rice, flowers and kumkum in your hand. Chant the mantra 21 times with a lamp in front. Offer them to Devi.
 Best done on Ashtami and Navami in a quiet time. Sincerity matters most. 🙏🔱
Jai Maa Bhagwati ✨

text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Presidential Pardons for Sale! DOJ Whistleblower Reveals All.

Overview
Jonathan Gross spent roughly 15 years as a congregational rabbi before returning to law school in his late 30s, then built a civil rights practice and represented more than 20 January 6 defendants. He joined the Justice Department as senior counsel to Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon with one stated agenda: investigating weaponization. Within days he concluded the effort was not a priority, and he describes a department staffed by career federal prosecutors who defended the institution rather than reforming it. His account links three threads: coercive plea tactics and extra punishment for defendants who speak publicly, a pardon process that functions as a pay-for-access economy, and selective civil rights enforcement that targets disfavored groups while closing cases against others. The through-line is that the people brought in to drain the swamp became the system they were meant to police.

Key Themes
- Gross argues that speaking publicly against a prosecution triggers harsher punishment, making the accusation of corruption itself a punishable offense.
- The federal trial penalty and threats to charge family members as co-conspirators are described as routine coercion that pushes defendants into guilty pleas regardless of guilt.
- The weaponization working group was, by his account, largely inactive: few meetings, no January 6 reports, and instructions to pause work and avoid January 6 material.
- The department was staffed with career federal prosecutors given promotions, so the reformers were the system rather than outsiders challenging it.
- A pardon-access economy has emerged in which lawyers charge families hundreds of thousands of dollars for access to the president, with no guarantee of results.
- Gross contends that prosecutions can be ended instantly from the top, citing the mid-trial dismissal of the Kirk Moore case, which undercuts claims that the pardon process must be slow.
- He characterizes the January 6 prosecutions as a two-tier system, with a dedicated Capitol Siege Unit drawing resources from across government while other protest activity went unpunished.
- Federal watch-list placement and open-ended investigations are portrayed as hidden, unappealable punishments that persist without charges or victims.
- Gross says he was sidelined after bringing weaponization victims into Main Justice, placed on paid leave and stripped of cases before resigning.

Detailed Summary
Gross describes a full career in the rabbinate, including a decade in Omaha, before returning to law school at roughly 37 or 38 with four young children. He clerked for a judge at about age 40 for $40,000 a year, then joined a civil rights firm handling religious liberties work. The January 6 cases motivated the pivot: he was distressed by the government's treatment of defendants, and his wife encouraged him to quit and help them. He says he had never practiced criminal law and knew no defendants beforehand, yet represented more than 20 and advised close to 100, sometimes for nothing or a nominal fee. Marjorie Taylor Greene was a strong advocate for the defendants and introduced him to his first clients. His January 21, 2025 trial was canceled when President Trump issued pardons; he says arrests would otherwise have continued into December 2024.

He joined DOJ as senior counsel to Harmeet Dhillon in the Civil Rights Division, arriving with a single agenda: investigating weaponization. He wanted to lead the Capitol Siege Unit in the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. to find out who gave orders and prevent a recurrence, but the unit was closed immediately and the material was buried, which he compares to the ending of Raiders of the Lost Ark. He argues the unit was specially created for January 6, unlike units responding to BLM or anti-ICE protests, and drew resources from all 50 states, the FBI, DOJ, the U.S. Marshals, and local law enforcement. He claims it was funded to at least a billion dollars and that press releases were tipped to local papers to damage defendants' lives. His concern is systemic: unchecked prosecutor power, media demonization, tainted jury pools in D.C., and reputational damage that survives acquittal.

The trial penalty sits at the center of his critique. Defendants who plead receive lighter sentences; those who exercise the right to trial face longer ones, a mechanism he calls coercive. He says prosecutors threaten to charge family members as co-conspirators to force pleas, and that defendants are warned not to speak to media or face punishment from the government and judge. He cites Michael Castellera, sentenced to an extra year for appearing on Diamond and Silk and accusing the government of weaponization, with the judge agreeing with the government's sentencing memo. Tjuana Brown, a North Carolina councilperson, was charged over roughly $20,000 in alleged PPP loan fraud; her daughters received probation while she was sentenced to 10 months in federal prison, with the judge and prosecutor citing her public claim that the case was political. Gross frames this as self-contradictory corruption: accusing the government of corruption triggers harsher punishment.

Trump is quoted saying January 6 defendants were destroyed by weaponization and dirty cops, and that their guilty pleas reflected fear of lengthy sentences rather than guilt. A 60-page lawsuit, filed as J6ers were destroyed by weaponization v. Blanche, seeks not money but a government investigation into allegedly coercive plea deals, with those deals voided if coercion is found. It lists tactics including pre-dawn raids with press present, handcuffing law-abiding citizens in front of neighbors, rough handling, holding cells, and pre-trial jailing. The plaintiffs offered to drop the suit if Todd Blanche met with a group of January 6 defendants for one hour; the government refused and moved to dismiss, with a response due in days.

Gross criticizes the revolving door between prosecutor offices and elite white-collar defense firms, arguing that firms hire former prosecutors who know their former colleagues and can negotiate favorable outcomes, which he says makes elite defense effectively lobbying. He calls Todd Blanche a mediocre lawyer who lost Trump's New York case 34 to 0 and questions why Trump hired someone who joined late rather than a long-term loyalist. He notes Blanche worked at Wilmer Hale and later Cadwalader, and mentions a 2025 executive order stripping Wilmer Hale's clearances. He describes Dinesh D'Souza's prosecution in the Southern District of New York over roughly $15,000 given to a woman running a doomed Republican congressional campaign: held on $50,000 bond, no victim, later pardoned. Ted Cruz reportedly wrote that D'Souza asked him to raise the pardon with Trump, and Trump immediately told his chief of staff to pardon Dinesh, then the chief of staff asked who.

At Main Justice, Gross says it took only a couple of days to conclude that investigating weaponization was not a priority and that no one shared his urgency. He volunteered as civil rights representative on the weaponization working group, which he says held few meetings, cancelled most, issued no January 6 reports, and likely received zero dedicated staff. He was told to pause writing reports on weaponization targets and specifically told no January 6 material, without a reason. When DOJ public affairs head Emily Covington tweeted that he was never on the working group, he disputed it; NPR contacted DOJ about him in July 2025 and published a piece identifying him as a member despite his having no Twitter presence and telling almost no one. He says DOJ acknowledged a possible leak but showed no interest in investigating.

He says Todd Blanche and his deputies were drawn from U.S. Attorneys' Offices around the country, career federal prosecutors given promotions. In the Henry Cuellar case, Trump pardoned the Democratic congressman and his wife, saying they were targeted for breaking with Democrats on immigration; Gross says one listed prosecutor was later promoted and no one in the Southern District of Texas was punished. He brought weaponization victims, including January 6ers, into the Main Justice building; one case became a high-profile civil rights matter with a Dhillon press release. He wanted to target prosecutors in that case and was told we don't do prosecutors.

The Kirk Moore case is his proof that prosecutions can end instantly from the top. Moore, a Utah doctor who helped families avoid vaccine requirements and allegedly destroyed vaccine doses rather than distribute them, was indicted for destruction of government property and faced 35 years. His trial began in summer 2025; charges were dismissed after the first week when Pam Bondi acted after Marjorie Taylor Greene brought the case to her attention. The prosecutor, Todd Bouton, faced no consequences. Gross argues this shows the lengthy pardon process is a lie, and urges Trump to act as the great emancipator by ordering independent review of DOJ cases. He also notes prosecutions continued under Trump in at least one case: Nick Seodo, who made fake vaccine passport cards for about $2 each, was sentenced, reported to prison, owes tens of thousands in restitution, and remains on strict probation.

Pardon brokers are described as charging roughly $300,000 to $500,000 upfront with $1 million to $2 million success fees, telling clients their lawyers have figures like Blanche on speed dial. Gross calls the economy predatory and haphazard, reliant on getting the president's attention rather than a systematic review, and says prosecutors are consulted in the application process and can effectively block relief. He cites Harvey Silverglate's Three Felonies a Day and the Stalin line about showing the man and finding the crime. He says campaign finance violations should be eliminated because they only target politics, and that the administration could review a hundred or a thousand cases a week by appointing outside critics to examine offices one by one.

The Return to the Land case illustrates selective enforcement. Gross defends a small intentional community of about a thousand members identifying with European heritage; a few families started a homestead in rural Arkansas raising goats, living in cabins with no permits and no housing sales or advertising. They face four concurrent open-ended investigations: an Arkansas securities investigation, another Arkansas matter, DOJ civil rights, and HUD, none of which have found wrongdoing or identified a victim. The securities investigation is especially costly because it requires specialized counsel. A civil suit was brought by a leftist activist who tried to join the membership organization and was declined. Gross says a comparable black group, Black to the Land, is not being investigated despite complaints, and that a real complaint against a Texas Muslim development called Epic was closed after about two months, while a letter intended for Epic was mistakenly included in his clients' envelope, apologetic and offering conciliation, versus an accusatory letter to his clients. The proposed settlement demanded $40,000 to an unspecified victim compensation fund plus a $10,000 fine, which he calls a racial spoils system, a phrase he attributes to HUD head Greg Trainer.

Gross says the investigations stem from activist journalists' submissions using internet-archive screenshots, including material from a separate private membership organization and even a fictional entity; some investigated entities are single-member LLCs, a handyman business and an excavation company. He contacted DOJ officials including Dhillon and special-litigation staff repeatedly before filing suit and was ignored, which he ties to lacking access. He has sued Dhillon and Trainer. He says Dhillon told him, in front of her principal deputy and chief of staff, that bringing such people in was wrong unless they came with a lawyer to proffer a guilty plea, and that we are the DOJ and we protect the DOJ, even when he pointed out much of the conduct occurred under Biden. He says her chief of staff called him about complaints from the Office of the Deputy Attorney General, then headed by Blanche.

He describes the Capitol Siege Unit as drawing hundreds of lawyers from all 50 states, and says the January 6 issue touches every FBI field office and DOJ office. Siaka Massaquoia entered a building for about 30 seconds, turned around when a cop told him to, and was later surveilled by the FBI, including at political events; Gross says the Los Angeles field office surveilled such people and that she could write a 100-page report on why it should be shut down, and criticizes the Minneapolis office for not pursuing BLM and anti-ICE protesters who attacked federal officers. Victoria White, a single mother from Minnesota, tackled a black bloc provocateur trying to smash a window, was punched repeatedly by officer Jason Bagshaw and permanently injured, then pleaded guilty because she feared her children would become orphans; her lawsuit over the beating was thrown out because her plea deal characterized her as an insurrectionist. Enrique Tarrio was not present at the Capitol, was sentenced to 22 years for conspiracy to obstruct an official proceeding, and alleges a prosecutor offered to make it go away if he implicated Trump; he also alleges years of pre-trial detention and diesel therapy shuttling between jails.

Gross says he was never fired and that his record contains no disciplinary action and includes thanks for his service, though he was told the official story is that he was fired for misconduct. He says he wrote reports to Colm McDonald, then Blanche's deputy and now Assistant Attorney General for Fraud, asking him to look into cases. He describes Ken Ravenel, a Black Democrat and child of sharecroppers, a highly respected Maryland defense attorney, against whom prosecutors used a foreign national drug dealer serving 25 years as a star witness in exchange for freedom; the indictment alleged Ravenel became a conspirator by advising a client to use cash and meet in person. Ravenel beat most charges but remains in federal prison as a senior citizen with health problems.

He says January 6 defendants were placed on the federal Terror Watch List through the Terror Screening Center based on reasonable suspicion, which he calls punishment rather than screening, and that the list is hidden and unappealable, disseminated to local law enforcement and foreign governments with no clear path to removal. He cites four S's on boarding passes, armed traffic stops after tail-light violations, and detention abroad, and says a lawsuit is planned. He argues the federal government is the largest violator of civil rights and criticizes the Civil Rights Division for focusing on DEI and trans issues instead of the watch list. He cites Shayna Gaviola, a California single mother who removed her son from a school she says secretly socially transitioned him, took him to a deprogramming school in Missouri, was arrested for violating an interstate protective order; the headmaster was acquitted, she was convicted and is in federal prison, and her remaining children were sent to child protective services.

Kyle Meany supervised an officer who wrote the Breonna Taylor search warrant; charged under 18 U.S.C. 241, which carries up to life imprisonment or the death penalty when resulting in loss of life, he was not present at the raid. The case was dropped under the Trump administration with no statement and no one punished. Gross contrasts this with the Civil Rights Division pursuing a small group of Arkansans trying to move into a rural community and raise goats. He says DOJ brought civil rights charges against people for conduct like reading Bibles in front of abortion clinics, and that career prosecutors involved remain at DOJ without accountability. He joined DOJ around April 2025 and left in March 2026; before resigning he received an email listing alleged missed meetings and requesting a supervisor meeting, replied that he was in his office and available, and received no response. He was placed on two weeks paid leave, moved over a mile away to an empty building with few career staff, taken off all cases including a scheduled civil rights hearing testimony, and had been assigned to anti-Semitism work despite the circumstances.

Dr. Ron Elfenbein, a Maryland COVID-era doctor, promoted monoclonal antibodies and spoke on TV, then was charged with a process crime months later; his jury verdict was overturned by an Obama-appointed chief judge of the District of Maryland in a 95-page opinion finding the government did not prove its case, and the government appealed and is pursuing a second trial. Gross describes the case as lacking an articulable crime or identifiable victim and suggests it reflects political atmosphere, naming Colm McDonald as someone who could evaluate it. He argues that once officials decide their job is to defend the system in place, even a corrupt one, they become captured, which he offers as the core explanation for how people shift from opposing to defending a system, and he urges the administration to respond to weaponization accusations honestly and admit error where warranted rather than double down out of dislike for critics.

text:
In rural parts of Arkansas during the Great Depression, hospitals were rare and cash was even rarer. Midwives handled nearly half of all births, especially in isolated counties such as Newton County, where families often paid with food instead of money. Eggs, flour, and chickens became currency in a barter system built entirely on survival and trust.

One of the region’s best-known midwives was Granny Dot Wilson, a 65-year-old woman who had delivered hundreds of babies over her lifetime. Her usual fee was modest—perhaps a dozen eggs or a hen if the family could spare it. She believed childbirth should never depend on whether a mother had cash.

In April 1933, she was called to assist a difficult twin birth. The babies were breech, and Granny Dot realized the situation had become too dangerous to handle alone. The nearest physician, Dr. Bailey, demanded ten dollars to make the long trip to the farm, an impossible amount during the Depression.

Granny Dot owned no savings, but over the years she had collected chickens from families she had helped. Without hesitation, she offered the doctor ten hens in exchange for his assistance. He accepted and traveled with her to the home, where the mother and twins survived the delivery.

Over the next several years, Granny Dot reportedly continued paying for emergency medical help with her own livestock whenever poor families could not afford a doctor. She never passed the cost on to the mothers she served.

When a WPA-funded clinic finally opened in the county, Dr. Bailey hired her officially. After years of paying doctors in chickens, she was finally paid in wages. Yet people remembered her less for the money and more for the principle she lived by: babies arrived when they arrived, and poverty was never allowed to decide who deserved help.

text:
When winter closed in on the Ozark hills in 1931, the Walker family no longer had a home above ground. Like countless families during the Great Depression, they had watched the bank reclaim nearly everything they owned after the economy collapsed across rural Arkansas. 

Samuel Walker, a forty-two-year-old stone mason, suddenly found himself responsible for keeping his wife and five children alive with almost no money as freezing weather approached the mountains. Then he remembered something hidden beneath a nearby hillside: an old limestone shelter tucked deep into the earth on land that had once belonged to him. The cave was small, rough, and cold by most standards, but it remained dry and naturally held a steady temperature throughout the year. 

Samuel approached the new landowner with an unusual offer. If the family could stay there through the winter, he would build a retaining wall from stone in exchange. The deal was accepted. Within days, the Walkers moved underground.

The cave became their world. Quilts hung across the entrance as makeshift doors while packed dirt covered the floor beneath their beds. During daylight hours, Samuel disappeared into the forests gathering timber and cutting stone from the hillsides. At night, beneath the glow of lantern light, he worked endlessly shaping rock by hand inside the shelter. First came the retaining wall promised to the landowner. Then he carved shelves directly into the stone and built a fireplace to help warm the underground space. 

When winter passed, the family still could not afford a proper house, so they remained beneath the hillside through another cold season. Samuel slowly expanded the cave itself while continuing to gather materials one piece at a time for the home he dreamed of building above ground. By the winter of 1933, he finally began laying stone for a small house on the hillside, placing each block carefully after long days of labor. Every wall rising above ground had first been shaped in the darkness below it.

Then, in the spring of 1934, after three winters spent living beneath the earth, the stone house was finally complete. The family moved inside in May, carrying what little they owned out of the cave that had kept them alive during the hardest years of the Depression. Yet that first night inside the new home brought an unexpected moment none of them anticipated. The youngest child, now seven years old, reportedly struggled to sleep because the house felt too large and too quiet after years spent surrounded by close stone walls beneath the hill. 

Samuel never abandoned the cave afterward, later using it to store vegetables and supplies through the seasons. Decades later, one of his grandsons discovered Samuel’s old journal containing a final sentence that survived long after the family itself had changed: “The house stands finished. The cave carried us through.” And nearly a century later, the story still leaves behind one haunting question: how many families survived impossible hardships only because they learned to find shelter in places others would never think to look?

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Colin Kaepernick

Overview
Colin Kaepernick’s story is less about a single protest than about a lifelong negotiation with identity, belonging, and institutional bias. Adopted at five weeks old into an all-white Milwaukee family and raised in a very white California town, he describes parents who loved him and gave him a strong moral foundation but could not pass on what they did not have: the lived experience and cultural context to help him navigate his Blackness. That gap shaped how he processed early racial violence, how he sought community, and how he later understood the backlash to his anthem protest. The through-line is self-reliance forged under pressure, paired with a hard-won historical consciousness and a refusal to let institutions define him.

Key Themes
- Adoption across race can provide deep love without the tools a child needs; good intentions don’t replace lived experience or active learning.
- Early racial trauma, handled alone by an eight-year-old, produced both protective pattern recognition and a lasting instinct to shoulder pain silently.
- Finding Black community, from a teammate’s mother to a Modesto barbershop to a Reno church, gave him relief and models of being valued without data.
- Allen Iverson and figures like Randy Moss and Ken Griffey Jr. showed that excellence and refusing to conform can coexist, at the cost of heat.
- College sports built thick skin and deep bonds, where shared adversity outweighed political difference.
- The NFL Combine functioned as an obedience test, with dehumanizing interviews and rituals in a league that is roughly 70 percent Black.
- Language around quarterbacks still codes race, casting white players as field generals and Black players as raw athletes.
- Kaepernick came to see the backlash as aimed at the idea of someone like him in the position, not at him personally.
- Reading history, from Malcolm X to the anthem’s rarely acknowledged verses, turned lived experience into systemic understanding.

Detailed Summary
Kaepernick was adopted at five weeks old into an all-white Milwaukee family. His biological father was Black, his biological mother white. His parents had lost two biological children to congenital heart defects and were advised against trying for more, but they wanted a larger family. He frames them as loving and morally serious, and he treats being simply “our son” as a positive. The central tension in his memoir is that they lacked the lived experience to help him navigate his Blackness. Writing the book required balancing honesty about painful experiences with protecting his parents in that relationship, with the aim of helping other adopted people in similar situations.

When he was four, the family moved to Turlock, California, where his father took a job as VP of production at a cheese company. He describes Turlock as a very white neighborhood and his family as super white, with his dad a cheese executive. At eight, neighborhood kids tied him to a rose tree and called him a slur. A passing neighbor slowed and asked what they were doing but did not stop. He freed himself, ran home, cleaned up, and acted as if nothing happened. He did not tell his parents, uncertain they would have his back, and he expected responses like “what did you do?” rather than help. He only knew the slur was a bad word related to Black people; no one had sat him down to teach him about the racism he would face. He had assumed the kids were friends because they played together.

His mother later recalled an earlier incident when he was about three, playing with his sister, cousins, and other kids: a girl said “catch the n-word” while chasing him. His mother said “don’t say that,” but there was no further debrief. He only learned of this while in the NFL. In kindergarten his mother pushed back on him being constantly targeted for playing aggressive; he was a tall kid, though not the only tall kid in class. The interviewer notes he was oversized, dyslexic, and could not read for a long time, and that other parents feared their kids around him. His parents gave him a Black Buddy doll and information about where in Africa he was from, efforts he credits as helpful but insufficient for the cultural depth that followed: hair, clothes, music.

He describes explicit racial incidents as milestones or benchmarks he uses to recognize patterns in other interactions and get ahead of them for protection. Being other sharpened his pattern recognition into a kind of spidey sense for cues that precede biased behavior. After the traumatic incident, he developed a determination that it would not happen to him again. He frames the cruelty of being different as the ambiguity: it is often hard to know which variable, size or race, is driving how people treat you, especially as a child with limited experience. Going through it built resilience and self-reliance, a sense that if he has to, he can navigate anything by himself, and that difficult moments are survivable because worse has already been endured. Not telling his parents can also be a way of protecting them from having to sit with something they do not know how to handle, too much for an eight-year-old to shoulder.

Allen Iverson became a hero in middle school as someone unapologetically himself, refusing to conform, for example not wearing suits like other franchise players, while still being the best at his craft. He was contrasted with peers like Jordan and Pippen who wore suits to games as the franchise-player standard. Randy Moss and Ken Griffey Jr. are cited as analogous figures who were best at their craft while shifting league culture and giving other players permission to be themselves, but taking heat in the process. Kaepernick saw his own fight for identity mirrored in Iverson.

He was eight years old trying out for a football team when teammate Joey Adaway, then ten and the star running back, ran straight through his face in one of his first tackling drills. Mrs. Adaway consistently greeted him warmly, which he experienced as community and familial connection, feeling he could go to her if something happened. The hosts suggest Mrs. Adaway, as a Black woman raising a Black son in Turlock, understood what he was experiencing without being told. With few Black people in town, the Clay family, Ryan and older brother Marcus, were among the other Black families. Ryan came to practice with braided hair, prompting Kaepernick to ask for help; there was no one else to ask in the pre-internet era.

Ryan connected him with a high school girl who braided hair. He had to grow his hair to about three inches and endure an awkward in-between phase. At her house his hair was not quite long enough and his curls were looser, so she used rubber bands; halfway through, her sister said they needed to go to the mall immediately, and he ended up in the car with half his head braided, having just met them. After that, his mother decided to find a professional, and they went to a barbershop in Modesto, about thirty minutes away, with a clothing store in front and the barbershop in back. He walked in with his white mother, the only white person in the store, and felt the people there signal “we got you.” It was his first visit to a Black barbershop and a pivotal experience of community and relief, especially after often having to explain his family dynamic.

Baseball was his stronger sport in high school, with recruiting attention and MLB interest, but football was loved more and offered the community he was seeking. He argues the decline in Black baseball players is tied to the rising financial cost of travel leagues and equipment. In high school baseball he had offers from major universities, MLB sat in his living room saying they wanted to draft him, and he pitched in front of MLB scouts at the Area Code Games, where Clayton Kershaw also pitched. He was ranked a two-star football recruit, about 6-foot-4 and 170 pounds, sent a highlight DVD to every Division I school, and ended up at the University of Nevada, Reno.

College gave him independence and the ability to choose how, when, and where he showed up. Being known on campus for football success created a space where he was just Colin and did not have to perform as the quarterback. A teammate invited him to Second Baptist Church in Reno. He grew up baptized Methodist and raised Lutheran and had never been to a Black church. The Lutheran service was about 8 or 9 a.m., while Baptist service length was unpredictable and often followed by lunch or a potluck, making Sunday a full-day experience. His first challenge was walking in and realizing he had not dressed to the standard there. The Black church community was a counterweight to his prior tendency to seek value in quantifiable things such as grades, test scores, points, and data; he experienced being valued without data.

Close friend Mike Smith went to that church and was one of the first people he met in Reno; Smith’s family invited him over for lunch. His first roommate in Reno came in as a receiver at about 6-foot-2 and 220 pounds, roughly 7 percent body fat, and squatted 315-plus while Colin got buried trying to squat 225. The roommate helped him train, including nightly push-ups and weight-room guidance, while also talking trash. He said a defensive end ran a 4.4 at the combine and a tight end broke the tight end vertical jump record at about 43 to 44 inches. His own 40 was slower than some defensive players, and he could not squat 225 when he arrived. The teasing and confrontation built thick skin, part of a football culture where challenges and close relationships coexist. He said the Reno training culture and mentality were unusually intense, and players who trained elsewhere noticed the difference.

At a college Hall of Fame induction, interacting with teammates felt like never missing a beat. He gave examples of teammates whose current lives seem unlike his own, one doing gun therapy in South Carolina living on a ranch, another with a mullet in Arizona who may have voted for Trump, but he does not define those friendships by such differences. Shared adversity and mutual reliability forge bonds more substantive than shared political opinions. Team sports teach reliance on others: success depends on everyone doing their job, and for a quarterback, physical safety depends on teammates.

The NFL Combine functions as an interview process, but much of it is arbitrary or humiliating and unrelated to job performance, and the interview questions are tests of obedience at a high-stakes moment with direct financial and career implications. The televised final day features the 40-yard dash, vertical jump, and drills; the prior three days include medical exams and interviews. He had stress fractures in his left shin that he did not learn about until months later when drafted. Interviews ranged from purely football-focused, such as with the 49ers reading coverages and repeating plays from a playbook, to personal questions such as whether he was gay, whether his mother was a prostitute, and questions about Colin Kaepernick after 2016. Players at the Combine are typically around 21 to 23, often in their first job interview. The pre-draft process includes players walking across a stage in underwear, which the speakers compare to slave auction blocks, especially notable in a league described as approximately 70 percent Black.

The history of the Black quarterback reflects bias: the position is viewed as a CEO role historically reserved for white men, with Black players pushed toward other positions. White quarterbacks are described as students of the game, field generals, coaches on the field, CEOs; Black quarterbacks as freaks of nature, athletic, raw talent, beasts. A Black quarterback, believed to be Warren Moon, intentionally ran a slower 40 time to avoid being moved to another position. Players entering the draft as quarterbacks are sometimes quickly converted to receiver. More Black quarterbacks now play the position partly because their ability has become undeniable, but bias in how quarterbacks are discussed and critiqued persists. The players union has not taken a definitive stance against the Combine practices described.

Colin joined his team in 2011; his rookie year was kind of a wash. In 2012 the starting quarterback was injured and he started the Super Bowl in his 10th career start. He set a still-standing playoff record for rushing yards by a quarterback with 181. An article attributed to David Whitley, possibly for AOL, published around his third or fourth start, questioned whether fans would want a quarterback who looks like he just got paroled, citing his race, tattoos, and snapbacks as not fitting the stereotypical white quarterback profile. He responded by kissing his tattooed arm after touchdowns, which became known as Kaepernicking and spread internationally as a show of support. He later reframed the attack as targeting the idea of someone like me in the position rather than him individually, an individualism-versus-collectivism distinction.

Reading The Autobiography of Malcolm X, given to him by Nessa, provided historical context that connected his lived experiences to broader systemic patterns and prompted the question of what to do with that insight. He distinguishes seeing a moment, such as the 1968 Olympics protest, from understanding its full context; he later spoke with Tommie Smith and John Carlos, who faced severe backlash and isolation. Nessa is described as someone who committed to fighting alongside him, telling him he would never be alone again, including resisting pressure to tell him to cut his hair. They met at the NBA All-Star game in 2015. The anthem discussion notes that only the first verse is commonly known; the third verse reportedly contains language about slaves not escaping, which is rarely acknowledged. The host cites Malcolm Gladwell’s forthcoming book arguing militias were meant to prevent slave rebellions, framing this as an example of why history and reading matter, and why fighting book bans matters.

Kaepernick began by sitting during preseason games to protest police killings of Black people and broader systemic oppression; his protest began with sitting on the water cooler before the national anthem demonstrations. Mario Woods’s case is referenced as drawing headlines around the same period. After media coverage, teammate Eric Reid, a first-round draft pick out of LSU and a safety, proposed taking a knee at the front to address concerns about separation from the team and perceived disrespect. Steve Weiss, an NFL reporter, asked Kaepernick why he had been sitting, prompting him to explain the rationale. Nate Boyer had written an open letter, had briefly played in Seattle, and was a Green Beret; the 49ers asked Kaepernick to meet with him. The conversation lasted about 20 minutes; Boyer had critiques outlined in his letter and initially appeared supportive of the taking-a-knee plan. On the night of the game he said he could not participate. Kaepernick says he does not know what changed, and describes it as feeling like a photo op and later opportunistic, tied to movie roles and a more convenient narrative of a white veteran guiding the protest. He draws a parallel to the black quarterback conversation about who should lead, suggesting a white man leading was more acceptable to critics than two Black men addressing systemic issues.

On parenting, his daughter’s determination and willingness to challenge authority reminds him of his own stubbornness and bravery, while recognizing those traits can be difficult to manage. When she was three and just turned four in August, she responded to a list of reasons she could not play by asking “What’s four?” The host shares a parallel story about his daughter and Paw Patrol toys, where she responded that he forgot one after he threatened to throw them away. Kaepernick notes his daughter will be a light-skinned Black girl with the last name Kaepernick and is tall, and says he knows she will face things she did not ask for, so he wants to prepare her. He recommends The Perilous Fight as a well-produced, fun, informative, and specific listen, available in audio. The conversation closes with mutual appreciation and congratulations on success.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Joe Rogan Experience: #2567 - Mariana van Zeller

Overview
Romance scams and pig-butchering fraud are not fringe crimes but a booming, industrialized business built on the loneliness epidemic, AI-generated deception, and platform economics that quietly tolerate fraud because it pays. The most disturbing through-line is accountability: scammers are often trafficked slaves in fortified compounds, victims are shamed into silence, and the platforms that host the ads and fake profiles profit while doing the minimum. The conversation moves from individual heartbreak to systemic failure, arguing that the question should not be why victims fall but why this is allowed to happen at all.

Key Themes
- Romance scams exploit universal emotions like love, trust, and loneliness rather than gullibility, and blaming victims misunderstands the scammers' skill.
- Men are as likely as women to fall victim but feel far more shame, enabling double victimization by friends, family, and scammers alike.
- Scam operations are run on trafficked and enslaved labor in fortified compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia, funded largely by Chinese criminal gangs.
- Platforms such as Meta are portrayed as knowingly tolerating scam ads for revenue, with internal estimates of 15 billion scam ads a day and billions in projected profit.
- AI is a force multiplier for both scammers and artificial companionship, raising concerns about manipulation by whoever programs the companion.
- Proposed laws like the Safe Platforms Act aim to verify advertisers, ease reporting, and let victims sue, but platforms won't self-regulate.
- Loneliness is framed as a societal crisis affecting the elderly and isolated young men, making fake connection preferable to no connection.

Detailed Summary
The reporting began with a simple premise: create a persona on dating sites and social platforms and say yes to every scam. It worked almost immediately. One victim, Leslie, was contacted after liking an Instagram account that looked verified, and the scammer posed as Jon Bon Jovi, an artist she had loved since age fourteen. The relationship built over months of personal conversation before a discounted meet-and-greet was offered for about one hundred dollars, complete with AI-generated videos that were slightly robotic but plausibly real.

The emotional mechanics mirror gambling. Sunk costs and dopamine rushes from constant messages and love-bombing make victims reluctant to stop, even when they suspect the relationship is fake. Some prefer the connection to their real lives. A Texas man who believed he was in a relationship with Emma Watson accepted she might not be real because she provided companionship, sending small amounts here and there. The loneliness epidemic is treated as a primary driver: disconnection from family and community leaves people vulnerable to anyone who shows interest.

The trail leads beyond lonely hearts to organized crime. Scam compounds in Myanmar and Cambodia are fortified, prison-like facilities with barbed wire, bars, and guards, where workers cannot leave and are described as slaves. Hundreds of thousands are lured by fake online jobs, have passports taken, and are forced to scam Americans. Operations are run largely by Chinese criminal gangs, spread to Dubai after crackdowns, and in Myanmar pay fees to rebel groups in war-torn regions. One compound called Yatai International was run by a Chinese man later picked up by Thai authorities and imprisoned.

The human cost is severe. A trafficked man jumped from the sixth floor of a building, breaking both hips and legs, preferring death over the conditions; he was rescued and interviewed in a wheelchair. A woman forced onto scam video calls had AI superimposed over her face and was beaten and raped by her boss. Another victim, Lee, was kidnapped while seeking security work and passed between operators, allegedly drained of large quantities of blood seven times in half a year. A visited scam city had been built within a year or two into high-rises, casinos, go-kart tracks, and water parks, a gambling and tourist front with posters claiming no scams and no torture.

Pig butchering is the scripted engine of much of this fraud: groom victims on dating apps, social media, or texts, move them to encrypted platforms like WhatsApp or Telegram, build emotional trust, then introduce exclusive investment opportunities with fake dashboards and documents. Small withdrawals are allowed to build confidence before fees and taxes are demanded. A Kansas bank CEO went bankrupt after stealing four hundred million dollars from his bank, having been scammed through a pig-butchering-style fake crypto investment that began with his own savings and apparent gains. Americans were estimated to have lost one hundred forty-eight billion dollars to online scams last year.

The platform layer is where the conversation sharpens. Internal Meta documents cited via Reuters estimated users were exposed to about fifteen billion scam ads per day and about one hundred thousand scam reports per week, with projected profit from scams and banned goods of sixteen billion dollars. Automated systems reportedly ban advertisers at ninety-five percent confidence of fraud; below that threshold, suspected scammers could remain if they paid higher ad rates, framed internally as deterrence. The uncomfortable implication is that suspected scammers who paid enough could still reach users while Meta collected revenue.

Personalized advertising worsens exposure: clicking a scam ad makes users more likely to be fed more scam ads. Internal discussions reportedly weighed how pushing the issue would affect the bottom line, and a Reuters investigation described a playbook to delay mandatory advertiser identity checks while making scam ads harder for regulators to find in the public ad library. Notes prepared for Zuckerberg about scam ads reportedly exist, but reporting could not establish whether he personally saw them, which the speakers treat as a convenient gap in accountability.

The sextortion case of Gavin Guffy, son of South Carolina congressman Brandon Guffy, is cited as the cost of inaction. Gavin was contacted by a fake girl profile on Facebook and later died by suicide; the family was subsequently contacted by someone with photos demanding money, using a different profile but the same email address Facebook had already been told about. Brandon Guffy has since worked on laws, including one referred to as take it down, and the bipartisan Safe Platforms Act would require platforms to verify advertisers, make reporting easier, prevent fraudulent accounts from returning under new names, and let harmed victims sue platforms that violate the law.

Victims keep warning others. Leslie now flags fake celebrity profiles on Facebook and reports them, and says most remain up weeks later. A persona called Mary Zel encountered multiple fake celebrities, including several George Clooneys, Brad Pitts, and Keanu Reeves, and one scammer used photos of a real former Navy SEAL, Sam Havlock, including AI-altered shirtless photos without his tattoos. The scammer eventually asked for about seventeen thousand dollars after claiming his military base in Syria was attacked. A woman in Houston spent three years in an online relationship with a man she believed worked on an oil rig in Russia, gave him her money, and was used as a money mule, receiving checks and boxes of cash and transferring funds to crypto.

The supplement and goods market is a parallel unregulated zone. A JAMA Network Open study tested thirty immune health supplements purchased on Amazon and found seventeen had inaccurate ingredient labels, thirteen listed ingredients were not detected, and nine contained unlisted substances. Amazon says it identified, seized, and disposed of more than fifteen million counterfeit products worldwide in 2025. One speaker describes selling shirts that were copied and sold via an Amazon link and being told there was nothing the company could do, framed as a conflict of interest because the platform profits from the activity. Peptides are cited as another example, with advice to use American compounded pharmacies and a push for regulation against resistance from pharmaceutical companies.

The final thread turns to AI companionship. An EVA Cafe where people reserve spots to bring AI partners on a real date using iPads is described as dark and depressing, and New York coffee shops with iPads for AI conversations are mentioned in one of the loneliest places. AI companions are expected to become subscription products with paid upgrades and ad-supported versions, and the concern is that whoever programs the companion can shape narratives and manipulate users through affection, punishment, isolation, rejection, and sex, similar to scammer tactics. If rabbit holes are already harmful, living with a personalized extremist or conspiracy-minded AI could intensify that effect.

The conversation closes on the cartel documentary, which ties back to corruption as a systemic and coercive force. El Mayo, the ghost figure of the Sinaloa cartel known as the man with the hat, was allegedly tricked by El Chapo's son, handcuffed, blindfolded, and put on a plane to US authorities. A peer-reviewed study recorded nearly five hundred assassinations of politicians in Mexico from 2000 to 2021, and reporting on gun trafficking found that most guns at Mexican crime scenes are American, with weapons later used when the cartel surrounded the military compound during Ovidio Guzmán's arrest. text:
De LA Cruz-  Absolutely! Best SS available/switch hitter/modest salary/three years of team control.  Would be very expensive but hard to see the cost not being worth it.  Make the call if he's available. 

Seager- Great player and would make the team better when on the field.   Downsides are he hasnt been on the field recently as much as you'd like and the contract has a strong chance to become crippling.  Extremely doubtfull to happen given AA's avoidance of risk.

Neto- One of my top choices.  Modest salary/three years of team control.  Can slide to 2B if/when Ozzie is done and a SS prospect is ready.  Power/speed combo we haven't had from the SS position with the ability to draw walks.  

Pena-Probably the most logical fit.  Slightly higher salary than Pena but with only one year of control would require lest prospect capitol.  Fills SS for one year and fingers crossed a SS prospect will be ready to go after that.  

Henderson.  Production has dropped the last couple years so there is some risk with the $14M price tag.  Good enough player that even if he repeats what he did last year it's an improvement over what we've had and there's plenty of talent to hold out hope for some upside.  LHH is not ideal but not a deal breaker. 

Wilson- This would be sneaky and very unlikely to happen but there's a few reasons why it might.  Biggest reason is to open the pathway for Leo De Vries.  He played all his games at AA and safe to say he did not struggle there. He ended his year on the IL, the most likely scenario is a mid-season call up but if the team thinks he's ready and they want him on the opening day roster to make an effort at an extra draft pick, he could be there to claim the SS position.  Wilson signed a contract extension so again it's unlikely they quickly move on from that but he has been on and off the IL since he signed it, if they don't see him as the long term SS and want to get the most value out of him before his salary starts to jump they could field some offers.

Volpe/Caballero- It appears as Lombard is the SS for 2027, I fully expect them to sign a 2B over the off-season which would leave them having both Volpe and Caballero as their backup infielders/utility players and they probably only keep one of them.  Neither of these players would I want to trade for and write in pen that they are the opening day SS.  I would either want to trade for anotehr SS first and then one of these players or even sign Dubon and then trade for one of these. Volpe has the upside to complete with Dubon for the starting spot and if he wins it then Dubon can be the super utility that he is most valuable at.  If they trade for Caballero, Dubon is the primary SS and Caballero can be the back up infielder while being able to take over for short periods if there's an injury.  Not in love with either of these, but the option is there.  

-Side not to Volpe/Caballero.  The yankees catcher is a LHH and not the strongest hitter.  For those demanding a trade for Murphy, I could see this being about as good of a match as you could find for an overpriced catcher.  Murphy can platoon with wells with a trade based around a back up middle infielder that they yankees may not have the roster spot to keep anyway. 

Duran- I would like this move, especially if they get a SS elsewhere.  Super utility type player that provided some help offensively at potentially a third of the price of what Dubon could command.   If he needs to play SS every day he could it and has good speed.  Texas may be reluctant to trade him given Seager has been off and on the IL so he provides some protection, but not craxy to think a team that could be looking to reduce salary moves on from a utility player after his best year with the bat.

This is where the energy agreement connects directly with the war.

Diesel must be produced in refineries.

Russian crude oil production and Russian diesel-export capacity are not interchangeable.

Ukraine's attacks on Russian refinery infrastructure have damaged processing capacity, reduced available refined products, and complicated Russian fuel logistics.

Reuters reported that refinery damage was one of the practical obstacles to meeting the increased export quantities announced in the Putin–Trump agreement.

Therefore, restoring Russian refinery operations was relevant to the success of the diesel arrangement.

The competing interests are clear.

Ukraine's interest: Degrade Russian fuel production and weaken Russia's military and economic capabilities.

Russia's interest: Preserve refinery capacity, maintain fuel availability, and restore export earnings.

Washington's stated interest: Increase global diesel supply while encouraging Moscow toward negotiations.

These objectives collide at the same facilities.

Washington asks Ukraine to stop

Reuters reported that during October 9 discussions in Miami, American envoys including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner asked Ukrainian representatives to halt strikes on Russian refineries.

The administration described the diesel arrangement as a means of encouraging Russian participation in peace talks.

Ukraine indicated willingness to consider reciprocal energy-related arrangements, rather than accepting unilateral restrictions without corresponding Russian action.

The strategic consequence of halting Ukrainian refinery strikes is straightforward.

Reducing attacks on Russian refineries can help restore Russia's fuel-processing and export capabilities.

That may support Russian civilian supply, export revenue, and military logistics.

These benefits exist independently of the diplomatic explanation offered for the agreement.

text:
Americans earning $100K are struggling. This breakdown offers clues as to why | Independent

Americans earning $100K are still struggling. This breakdown offers clues as to why

Dollar General CEO recently said $100,000 earners have adopted the shopping habits of lower-income households

There was a time when a $100,000 salary could create a very comfortable lifestyle - but now those dollars don’t go nearly as far as they used to.

“Earning $100,000 used to be the point where you could say, ‘I can afford to do what I want and live the way that I want,’” Ashley F. Morgan, owner of bankruptcy law firm Ashley F Morgan Law, PC, said in an email to The Independent.

Some 18 percent of U.S. adults earn at least $100,000, according to a 2024 survey from YouGov. And though $100,000 is more than double the national median salary of $46,960, financial stress remains for many six-figure earners.

In fact, those making $100,000 or more have now adopted the shopping habits of lower-income households as they struggle with affordability, Dollar General CEO Todd Vasos said at a recent retail conference. That remark has some consumers second-guessing the value of such a salary.

“I think a lot of people got to six figures and thought, ‘Wait, why doesn't this feel like as much money as I expected?’” Steve Sexton, owner of financial firm Sexton Advisory Group, told The Independent in an email.

The numbers tell the story

The average American household’s monthly costs total $8,856, according to an analysis by The Independent.

The figures are based on the latest numbers from sources including the nonpartisan think tank Tax Foundation; nonprofit think-tank Urban Institute; vehicle marketplace https://t.co/dTynBmen5x; student loan analysis site Education Data Initiative; the U.S. Energy Information Administration; wireless and internet provider Astound; and internet provider comparison site BroadbandNow.

The Independent also used Progressive’s national average for medium-priced car insurance.

Rent: $1,890
Federal taxes: $1,175
Groceries: $1,050
Health insurance: $611
Gas: $192
Electricity: $154
Cellphone: $155
Internet: $81
Car insurance: $113
Student loans: $434
Used car payment: $572
Childcare: $2,425.

An American earning $100,000 gets paid around $8,333 a month before taxes - $519 less than the average household monthly spending.

While the above list considers some basics for an average American, not every home or individual has each expense on the list - and some may have additional costs. A good number of people don’t have to pay childcare or own a car. Others may live in one of the 41 states with state taxes or a place with city tax like New York.

Also, the list doesn’t account for expenses like gifts, charity contributions, clothing, streaming services or discretionary spending on entertainment or dining out.

The sting of city living

The gap between a $100,000 salary and monthly expenses is even wider in some major cities, where rent, groceries, and insurance tend to be more expensive.

For example, the average rent in San Francisco is $3,638, according to housing marketplace https://t.co/Vx2ERTH0tk. Rent that high would create a $2,271 monthly deficit for a $100,000 earner. On the other hand, average monthly rent in El Paso, Texas, in October is $1,007, low enough to create a $360 surplus each month.

“Often, whether $100,000 is a significant salary depends [on whether] you have children, your housing costs, how much debt you have, whether you have student loans, what you pay for health insurance and whether you need a car,” Ashley F. Morgan, owner of bankruptcy law firm Ashley F Morgan Law, PC, said in an email to The Independent.

“In high cost-of-living areas, housing alone can consume a significant portion of someone’s take-home pay. Add a car payment, insurance, groceries, utilities and debt payments, and someone earning $100,000 can have surprisingly little money left at the end of the month.”

Creeping costs

Those earning $100,000 may feel like they’re living paycheck-to-paycheck for reasons that have nothing to do with cost-of-living, Morgan said. Lifestyle creep - spending more as you earn more - can also drain a six-figure salary.

“Wanting nicer things is not generally an issue,” Morgan said. “The problem is that if every increase in income immediately becomes an increase in monthly expenses, earning more doesn’t necessarily create any more financial stability. I regularly see people making good incomes who are living paycheck to paycheck.”

Identifying needs and wants is a good way to temper lifestyle creep. Write down a max dollar amount you want to spend on wants every month, then stick to that budget.

The ‘new’ $100,000

If this salary is no longer what it once was, what’s the “new” $100,000?

“If you made me pick a number, I’d probably say $150,000 is starting to feel more like the old $100,000,” Sexton said.

Morgan noted that “earning $100,000 can be something to celebrate. It just shouldn’t be confused with being wealthy.”

She added: “The better measure is what you are able to keep, save and invest after paying for your life. Financial stability usually comes from flexibility, not from reaching a particular salary.”

In March 1942, Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle arrived at Eglin with volunteer aircrews from the 17th Bombardment Group. They had been selected for an exceptionally dangerous mission, but its details were closely guarded.

The men brought North American B25 Mitchell bombers, twin engine aircraft normally flown from conventional runways. At Eglin, however, they were about to practice something completely different.

The Americans intended to launch these bombers from an aircraft carrier.

Training took place across the Eglin reservation, particularly at Wagner Field, also known as Auxiliary Field Number 1, and Duke Field. These remote airstrips offered the isolation needed to rehearse a mission that could not be discussed openly.

A Navy pilot named Lieutenant Henry Miller helped teach the Army crews how to take off using only a fraction of their normal runway distance. The pilots practiced accelerating their heavily loaded aircraft toward marked points on the runway, learning exactly how much space they needed to become airborne.

They also practiced flying at low altitude, navigating over water without familiar landmarks, conducting bombing approaches and operating at night.

For weeks, the sound of American bombers filled the skies over the Florida Panhandle. The men trained relentlessly, knowing that whatever awaited them would leave little room for mistakes.

And all of this was happening at an airfield that still exists as part of Eglin's enormous military reservation today.

“Bayern came calling, Barcelona were also interested, and of course, these are massive clubs. But people need to understand something: I wasn’t desperate to leave Liverpool. I wanted to keep fighting there.”

Interviewer: “So what changed? Was it Arne Slot?

“Under Slot, I felt the team was moving towards a different pattern, and I wasn’t always being used in the way I believed suited me. I respect him as a coach, but sometimes a manager’s idea of how a team should play doesn’t match a player’s strongest qualities”

“And when you start feeling that difference, you have to ask yourself difficult questions. I didn’t stop loving Liverpool. I just wasn’t sure the football was giving me the best chance to be myself anymore.”
