text:
Like Lyme disease being "racist" against the residents of Connecticut? How about Spanish flu or German measles?

The Biden administration conducted a sustained public and private pressure campaign—often called “jawboning”—on major platforms (Meta/Facebook, Twitter, YouTube/Google, and Amazon) to suppress or demote content on COVID-19 (vaccine safety/efficacy, side effects, origins, mandates) and election-related claims. Much of the targeted material came from conservative, skeptical, or anti-administration voices. Platforms frequently complied by changing policies or removing content, even when it did not clearly violate their rules at the time.⁠https://t.co/PCC6FHrdW3

Documented pressure and its effects

White House communications: Officials including Rob Flaherty (digital strategy director) and Andy Slavitt repeatedly emailed, called, and met with platform executives. On the administration’s third day, the White House demanded that Twitter remove a Robert F. Kennedy Jr. tweet linking Hank Aaron’s death to the vaccine “ASAP” and monitor similar content. Internal records show frustration when platforms pushed back, with demands extending to satire, humor, personal anecdotes, and “negative information or opinions about the vaccine.” Facebook understood the administration wanted true side-effect information and non-violative posts removed.⁠https://t.co/PCC6FHrdW3
Policy changes in response: Facebook removed or restricted lab-leak theory posts under pressure; an internal email later stated they did so “because we were under pressure from the [Biden] administration and others to do more… We shouldn’t have done it.” YouTube developed stricter vaccine-content rules and shared the proposal with the White House for feedback. Amazon adjusted book policies citing “criticism from the Biden people.” By late 2021, the major platforms had shifted moderation in ways responsive to White House demands.⁠Archive
Admissions from companies: In an August 2024 letter to Congress, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that senior Biden officials, including from the White House, “repeatedly pressured our teams for months to censor certain COVID-19 content, including humor and satire,” expressed frustration when Meta resisted, and that the pressure was “wrong.” He regretted not being more outspoken. In 2025, Google/Alphabet told the House Judiciary Committee that Biden officials pressed for removal of non-violative COVID and election content and created a political atmosphere aimed at influencing platforms; YouTube later offered reinstatement to some affected creators.⁠Reuters
Specific targets: Journalist Alex Berenson was permanently banned from Twitter in August 2021 after officials (including Slavitt) labeled him the “epicenter of disinformation” and pressed for action against him. Twitter later admitted in a settlement that the ban violated its own rules and reinstated him; related litigation produced government concessions on First Amendment issues. Content from figures such as Rand Paul and RFK Jr. was flagged. The House Judiciary Committee’s May 2024 “Censorship-Industrial Complex” interim report, based on tens of thousands of documents, concluded the campaign targeted true information, satire, and critics, with a chilling effect, and that companies cited White House pressure and leverage from other regulatory issues (antitrust, Section 230).⁠https://t.co/PCC6FHrdW3

text:
There is strong historical evidence that Jesus of Nazareth was a real person who was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Early Christian writings claim that multiple people saw him after his death, spoke with him, and ate with him, and that some of these witnesses later died for refusing to recant their testimony. While the New Testament (particularly 1 Corinthians 15) claims that more than 500 people saw the risen Jesus, these are internal claims rather than hundreds of independent external eyewitness accounts verified by non-Christian historians.
There is no solid archaeological evidence for Abraham as an individual, for Noah, or for a global flood. By contrast, there is archaeological and textual evidence for the historical existence of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, including the Tel Dan stele that refers to the “House of David.” Genetic studies also show continuity between ancient Levantine populations and later Jewish groups. The idea of exactly twelve distinct tribes leaving a clear, unified archaeological footprint is more traditional than strictly attested in the material record.
By comparison, there is no archaeological, genetic, linguistic, or material evidence for the large civilizations, cities, metal-working societies, or wheeled transport described in the Book of Mormon. Ancient DNA studies of Native American populations consistently point to Asian origins via Beringia, with no detectable pre-Columbian Levantine genetic signal matching the scale claimed in the text. Pre-Columbian horses, steel swords, chariots, and Near Eastern cereal crops (such as wheat and barley used as staples) are also absent from the archaeological record of the relevant periods and regions. The text claims its records were written in “reformed Egyptian,” yet no such script is recognized by Egyptologists, and there is no evidence of Egyptian writing systems in pre-Columbian America. It also reproduces long sections of the King James Version (including some of its known quirks and errors) and includes material from Isaiah 40–55, which most biblical scholars date to the Babylonian exile—after Lehi’s group would have left Jerusalem.
Joseph Smith faced roughly twenty to thirty criminal charges during his life. Most were dismissed or ended in acquittal. He was convicted of assault and battery in 1843 after striking a tax collector and paying a fine. He was also fined $1,000 (along with Sidney Rigdon) for operating the Kirtland Safety Society in violation of Ohio banking law by issuing unauthorized notes. He was sealed to an estimated thirty to forty women in addition to his legal wife, Emma. Some of these sealings were understood as for eternity only, while others involved sexual relations. The practice was kept secret during his lifetime, and he publicly denied practicing polygamy.
Other issues further weaken the founding claims. The Book of Abraham was produced from Egyptian papyri that Egyptologists identify as ordinary late-period funerary texts (primarily the Breathing Permit of Hôr); they do not mention Abraham and do not match the published text. In 1843, Smith examined the Kinderhook Plates—later proven to be a deliberate 19th-century hoax—and, according to contemporary accounts, offered a partial interpretation identifying them with a descendant of Ham. His multiple firsthand accounts of the First Vision also differ in significant details: the earliest focuses on seeking personal forgiveness and seeing “the Lord,” while later versions emphasize asking which church to join and describe two distinct personages. These points, alongside the absence of corroborating evidence for the Book of Mormon’s ancient American civilizations, form the core of the historical case against its claims.

text:
Amazon, AEP, and X-energy have entered an agreement to evaluate one of the largest proposed small modular reactor deployments in the United States, linking rising data-center electricity demand with plans to repurpose a retired Indiana coal site.

The distinction between development and construction matters. Amazon is funding milestone-based feasibility and development work for the Sullivan County proposal, while a final investment decision has not been made. The funding amount also remains confidential. In other words, the agreement moves the concept forward, but it does not yet authorize crews to begin building reactors.

Under the proposal, X-energy would supply 12 Xe-100 reactors, each rated at 80 MW. Together, the units would provide 960 MW to the regional grid. AEP said Amazon intends to purchase electricity from the project through a long-term power agreement, creating the kind of committed demand that can help support financing for capital-intensive generation.

That structure reflects a broader change in how large technology buyers approach energy procurement. Conventional renewable contracts can help offset annual electricity consumption, but data centers operate around the clock and place substantial demands on transmission systems. Nuclear generation offers steady output that is not dependent on wind or sunlight, although advanced reactors bring their own commercial, regulatory, and supply-chain risks.

Committing to 960 MW is a substantial step for technology that has not yet reached commercial deployment. X-energy's Xe-100 is an advanced, high-temperature gas reactor that uses TRISO fuel. Its cooling configuration can use air, water, or a hybrid arrangement, giving developers more flexibility in regions where water availability is a concern. That potential benefit still has to be demonstrated at commercial scale. https://t.co/zVlC9S87Jo

text:
End Users Don't Care About Your Code

I've spent the last 7 years building a tech company, and I'm more convinced than ever that code is the least important part of my business.

A few days ago, an open-source project called REA came out, allowing AI agents to reverse-engineer software. Separately, someone recreated the entire Adobe suite using AI.

What happens when you can replicate an entire software product in a single afternoon?

Well, the truth is that the value of a SaaS product has always been in the last S: Service.

Code is simply a means to an end. A way to deliver a service, enable communication, or automate repetitive tasks.

Ever since I started Saludtech back in 2019, I've faced the same question: What happens when clinics decide to build their own platform? Your product isn't technically complex.

The funny thing is, they were right about the second part. And they still are.

From a technical standpoint, Saludtech isn't much more than a database with some encrypted fields and an interface to create, read, update, and delete records. Add a couple of third-party integrations, and you've got the entire platform.

Back then, people already thought it would be easy to copy. Today, you could have a pretty good version up and running in an afternoon.

And yet, to this day, no other B2C telemedicine platform in Chile handles more consultations than Saludtech.

The secret, in our case, isn't the software. It's the operations.

We deliver a high-quality service. Of the 13,000 consultations completed in September, less than 1% resulted in a refund due to a poor experience.

A happy patient comes back and recommends us. A healthcare professional whose problems we consistently solve sticks around.

Focus on delivering great service for 7 years, and eventually you reach a point where the flywheel starts spinning almost on its own.

So how do you defend your position in the market if we assume Saludtech's entire codebase were made public?

Unique, proprietary data. Saludtech understands where telemedicine patients are located, the most common medical conditions, the most frequently requested tests and medications, and other insights we've gathered over the years.

Network effects. The more patients we have, the more attractive Saludtech becomes for doctors. And the more doctors we have, the more appointment slots we can offer. This creates a positive feedback loop within the platform.

Distribution. We maintain direct relationships with our users, manage our own advertising, and have built an active community of patients and healthcare professionals.

Seven years ago, people asked me what would happen if someone copied our platform.

Today, copying it is easier than ever. But I still think it doesn't really matter that much.

The real question is: What are we building that can't be copied with a prompt?

text:
This afternoon I met with a frustrated founder who vibe-coded a Bible sharing software with Claude/GPT-6 Astra.

He tried to sell it but even here, a very religious area he couldn't get anyone on a paid subscription.

So I checked out the software and as someone who likes to read the Bible I actually thought it was pretty cool.

There was one big mistake Claude or Astra didn't recognize. 

It looked like a SaaS, something high-tech. Maybe something aimed towards an advertisement tracking software.

There is a huge gap between what his ideal customer would like it to look like, and what it looks now.

His ideal costumer is likely going to be a bit older.. Think 50-60.. So it has to look like an environment they would like and feel comfortable in. 

Right now it looks like something for entrepreneurs/programmers. Something very complicated..

It should be warm, inviting, religious.

This offers a LOT of friction and scares people in the buying process.

text:
Today, I handed my novel to my (extremely janky - see picture) local AI and asked it to read the entire thing and generate some blurbs. I'm not happy with the results, but I think it's an interesting brainstorm, and I'm very pleased that I can run generations against massive texts without paying for inference or uploading to the cloud.

Here are my two favorites:

"From the neon-drenched combat pits of Bangkok to a smoking crater in the English countryside, the world is fracturing. Hanita Bhat—a Bollywood starlet turned nomad—is running from a past that won't let go. But when an impossible castle rises from the ruins of a terrorist strike and a top-secret scientist vanishes with a classified vehicle, running is no longer an option. Thrust into a high-stakes recovery mission alongside a disgraced SAS master swordsman and Delta Force operators, Hanita must navigate a reality where the rules of engagement have changed. In a war where high-tech longswords meet ancient shadows, survival is the only mission that matters."

text:
A letter from a Palestinian living next to Israel.
Hello, I am Palestinian. 📷

And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.
1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.
1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.
1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.
Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.
Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.
Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.
Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.
Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.
Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.
I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.
And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
France Riots: 3,000 Shops Looted as Curfews Loom. Macron, the Police or the Casseurs: Who Is to Blame?

Hassan has managed a phone shop on Boulevard Magenta in Paris since 2017. On Saturday looters took every phone he had, and when he tried to stop them, he says, they assaulted him. Since then France has been arguing about who is to blame: migrants and Macron, the far left, the police or the rioters themselves. Some of those arguments say more about the people making them than about what happened. Peaceful protest is a right, the students who started this movement have real grievances, and the bill for the looting is being paid by shopkeepers and workers. Before the next national day on October 24, it is worth testing each argument against the evidence.

What happened

At least 3,000 shops were damaged or looted on October 17 and 18, the French government said on Monday.

@NunezLaurent's Interior Ministry counted 2,397 arrests and 997 police officers and gendarmes injured, seven seriously, on Saturday alone.

The ministry put Saturday's turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The General Confederation of Labour (CGT), France's oldest trade union federation, founded in Limoges in 1895, said 800,000.

Limoges lost most of its 19th-century town hall to a fire the local prefect, the state's top official in the area, said was set deliberately. Lyon's tourist office burned. Rioters forced their way into Marseille's city hall.

One protester died of a cardiac arrest during the Paris march. Officials called it health-related, and prosecutors have opened an inquiry into the cause.

What the students want

The movement began in mid-September, when pupils at France's lycées, the upper secondary schools for ages 15 to 18, started blockading them over crumbling buildings, classes of 30 to 35 and absent teachers who are never replaced.

The Union syndicale lycéenne (USL), the high-school students' union formed in 2023 when the main lycée unions merged, wants Parcoursup, the national online platform for university admissions, abolished. With the Union étudiante, a university students' union founded in 2023, it also wants selection for university and master's places scrapped and 150,000 new higher-education places created.

The government has promised 3,000 replacement teachers for more than 500 priority schools. Student unions say that falls short.

On Saturday the students were joined by climate activists, the CGT and the "yellow vests" (gilets jaunes), the movement that began in November 2018 over fuel taxes and living costs. The CGT backed the protests with calls for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services."

"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high," a 19-year-old in Paris who gave her name as Lola told the Guardian.

The public was with the students on the substance. Before Saturday, 72% of French adults called their demands legitimate, and 82% said violence is never an acceptable way to press a demand, in polls by the French polling firm Elabe for news channel BFMTV.

Who paid

Hassan told actu Paris that the damage to his shop came to €70,000 to €90,000. An optician on the same boulevard, with five staff, was stripped bare, and its co-owner said it may close if aid does not arrive.

Carrefour chief executive Alexandre Bompard said 50 of the chain's stores were damaged, 20 of them looted. Bordeaux's mayor said up to 100 shops were looted there, and Lyon's city hall counted almost 200 vandalised.

Prime Minister @SebLecornu promised 100% state-paid short-time work for staff of damaged shops from Tuesday, plus a support fund.

The government's count already passes the 2023 riots after a police officer shot 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk, when more than 1,000 shops were vandalised or looted and insurers paid €793 million on 16,400 claims, a Senate inquiry found.

What people are arguing

1. "Immigration and Macron did this"

The argument travelling furthest abroad blames migrants and a weak president. Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!" In France, Éric Zemmour, leader of the hard-right Reconquête party, wrote that "there will be no return to civil peace without remigration."

The evidence does not carry it so far. French officials have made no link to immigration. Paris prosecutors were holding 557 people after Saturday, 151 of them minors, and have published ages and charges with no data on origins. Receiving stolen goods was the most common charge.

2. "The ultra-left planned it" versus "prove it"

Lecornu blamed "ultra-left" groups he said want "deep disorder" until April's presidential election. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of France Unbowed (La France insoumise, LFI), replied that if the prime minister "is neither a liar nor someone who wants to organise disorder, he must name and prove his accusation."

On this one the evidence leans toward Mélenchon's challenge. Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told TF1 on Monday that she "absolutely cannot confirm" that those behind the violence lean ultra-left. Most people in custody stay silent and make no political claims, she said. She did describe police-identified black blocs, masked groups that attack property, at the march from the start, and people arriving at Paris stations "to take advantage of the situation." Organised militants and opportunist looters both appear to have been there. No public evidence yet shows a plot.

3. "Police excess" versus "police overwhelmed"

The left says the students were met with too much force. France's Defender of Rights (Défenseur des droits), the independent rights ombudsman, opened an inquiry on October 1 after a 14-year-old was hit in the face by a tear gas grenade. A 15-year-old in Lens lost a hand to a stun grenade, and Nuñez suspended those grenades for student protests on October 7. On Saturday a 17-year-old girl in Mulhouse lost her left eye, and prosecutors referred the case to the General Inspectorate of the National Police (IGPN), the police's internal oversight body. Amnesty International's French section has called the force used against school pupils "disproportionate" since October 2.

Others say the police were simply outnumbered. Paris deputy mayor Lamia El Aaraje said officers were overwhelmed on Saturday, and the mayor of Limoges said police "lacked resources" and retreated. Intelligence services had expected about 200,000 marchers, franceinfo reported, and at least 550,000 came. On Monday Nuñez told France Inter radio that the police had "lost control," and Macron refused his offer to resign.

I think both sides are right. The policing failed twice: too much force against teenagers for a month, then too few officers when the looting started.

4. "Punish the casseurs" versus "protect the right to protest"

The right wants a crackdown on casseurs, the French word for rioters who smash property. Jordan Bardella, president of the National Rally (Rassemblement national, RN), wrote: "I will always defend the right to protest," and argued that zero tolerance for those who disrupt marches protects "popular demands." Marine Le Pen called the riots "a threat to democracy" and accused Mélenchon's party of legitimising violence. Mélenchon had told marchers to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."

Lecornu has asked prefects for "partial" and "localised" curfews and said a state of emergency was ready "if needed." The risk is that blanket measures fall on peaceful marchers as hard as on looters. Prosecuting the people who emptied Hassan's shop and burned Limoges town hall is the part of this argument everyone should be able to agree on.

5. "France is paying for Africa"

Some commentators online call the riots karma for Françafrique, the web of political, military and money ties France kept with its former African colonies. The record is real: France created the CFA franc, the currency still used by 14 West and Central African countries, in 1945 and still guarantees it. Historian Marco Wyss found that France became "the main supplier of military assistance" to Biafra during Nigeria's civil war. The argument still lands on the wrong people. Hassan and a 17-year-old in Mulhouse made no Africa policy.

What it costs

France's 10-year government bond, the OAT (obligations assimilables du Trésor), yielded about 4.87% on Monday, up about 9 basis points, Reuters reported. It touched 4.99% in early October, its highest since 2002.

BNP Paribas, Société Générale and Crédit Agricole fell between 2.2% and 2.7%, and the CAC 40, the index of the 40 biggest companies listed in Paris, dropped about 1.4%.

France runs a deficit above 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) while Parliament debates the 2027 budget. The students' demands, the shop support fund and the rebuilt town halls all draw on the same public purse.

Where this leaves France

Macron separated protesters with "legitimate demands" from "those who destroyed, smashed and looted," and handed concrete answers to talks Lecornu will lead this week with student, union and employer groups. CGT leader Sophie Binet said he had "understood nothing" of what is happening in the country.

Peaceful protest is a civil right. Looting a man's phone shop is theft, and the people who burned Limoges town hall have done more damage to the students' case than any minister.

When the yellow vests march again on October 24, will France judge this movement by the students' demands or by Saturday's looting?

Curious what @IfopOpinion and @Cluster_17, two of France's leading pollsters, @Mij_Europe of political risk firm Eurasia Group, @Chxta of Lagos research firm SBM Intelligence and Senegalese rights advocate @aliounetine16 make of it.

text:
In 1795, Immanuel Kant offered a striking image of political independence that deserves to be remembered whenever a larger (in size) neighbour looks across a border and sees something it wants.

A country, he wrote, is not a possession.

“A state is not, like the ground which it occupies, a piece of property … It is a society of men/[women] whom no one else has any right to command or to dispose except the state itself. It is a trunk with its own roots.”

A trunk with its own roots. A political community with an existence of its own.

More than two centuries later, that image speaks directly to Abiy Ahmed’s persistent pursuit of sovereign access to the Red Sea through Eritrea’s port of Assab.

The enduring force of Kant’s image is that  you do not acquire the right to uproot another nation because you desire the ground beneath it.

Eritrea's sovereignty is not conditional on its neighbour’s satisfaction.

France imposes curfews as riots spiral
Weeks of protests over rising living costs and deteriorating public services have descended into violent clashes and widespread destruction
Published 19 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/tvaBkZXbmh
France will introduce localized curfews as the unrest over rising living costs and deteriorating public services has escalated into widespread violence and destruction, leaving the authorities struggling to restore order.
The unrest escalated over the weekend, with nearly 2,400 people arrested, hundreds of businesses looted, and buildings set on fire across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police lost control in several major cities.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu announced on Monday that he instructed the regional authorities to introduce curfews following an emergency government meeting.
“They will be partial and may be highly localized,” Lecornu said, adding that declaring a state of emergency cannot be ruled out.
Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured over the weekend, according to the Interior Ministry. In Limoges, rioters set fire to the city’s historic 19th-century town hall, causing the roof to collapse. Clashes, arson, and looting were also reported in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other cities.
Nunez offered his resignation on Sunday, acknowledging failures in anticipating and containing the violence. President Emmanuel Macron refused to accept it, instead ordering a review of security planning and intelligence failures and demanding changes to policing tactics.
More than 2,500 businesses were targeted on Saturday alone, according to Alain Di Crescenzo, the president of the French Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
The Association of Mayors of France called for gatherings outside town halls on Monday, denouncing failures in policing and warning of a “real risk to the entire nation.”
The protests began in September at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, over teacher shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement has since spread to public sector workers and trade unions demanding higher wages, better services, and relief from rising living costs, while opposing spending cuts in the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
France is grappling with growing public debt (around 119% of GDP) and a substantial budget deficit. The government is seeking to reduce the shortfall through spending cuts and tax measures, while growing political uncertainty has pushed borrowing costs to the highest levels in more than 20 years.
The protests echo the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron’s economic policies. Yellow Vest activists have joined the demonstrations and called for another round of protests on October 24.
The crisis has intensified pressure on Macron in the final months of his presidency, drawing criticism from across the political spectrum ahead of the 2027 election.
Right-wing politician Marine Le Pen, who leads in first-round presidential polling, called Macron a president “without credibility or authority” who has “lost all touch with reality.”
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) party, blamed “ten disastrous years”of Macron’s policies for the crisis and accused Nunez and police commanders of “complete incompetence.”

In a weird way, this might actually be something that can be leveraged to achieve something that has been sought by constitutional conservatives for a long time.  

Why not meet in the middle and return power to the individual states? In other words, restore the federalism framework that was always intended by the provisions of the constitution. 

In this respect, if New York wants to implement a socialist or communist framework, then it can. New York citizens can vote for that.  People who don’t want to live under that framework can leave New York, people that want to live under that framework can stay.

You would want accompanying revisions to relevant revenue/tax and spending statutes and regulations at the federal level. If a state wants to implement a certain government framework, be a welfare state, be whatever, then it needs to do so on its own 2 feet, not subsidized by other states. 

Of course, this is unlikely to happen because it is precisely the monstrous size and power of the federal government that gives power to the political parties.

If you start to return power to the states, the president and Congress lose out on what they can offer to donors and supporters.

But, if things are radicalized enough, it might be a possibility

text:
According to French sociologist and terrorism researcher Olivier Roy, the issue is not the radicalization of Islam, but the Islamization of radicalism. Behind the breakdown of society lies France’s rapid transformation into a multiethnic state, an identity crisis between generations, social exclusion, and nihilistic hatred of the system and of Frenchness itself. Radical Islam offers a ready-made, violent form of expression that shocks the French state as much as possible.

France’s far left, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has seen an opportunity to advance its revolution by harnessing the violent potential of young Arabs and Africans. The alliance between communism and Islamism has deep roots going back a century to the Baku Congress, where the Bolsheviks urged Muslim peoples to wage holy war against the West. In February 2025, Mélenchon gave a speech in which he called for a population replacement in France (grand remplacement). According to him, it is a good thing for France if, in the future, the country is inhabited by a colored mulatto population (creoles) rather than ethnic French people.

The most visible sign of the strategic alliance between the far left and the immigrant population is the sheer number of Palestinian and African national flags displayed at every riot and clash. French flags have been conspicuously absent. Nationalism is therefore alive and well — not the dying liberal civic religion or European nationalism crushed by institutions, but African and pan-Arab nationalism, which the left promotes while caught up in its own anti-Western oikophobia.

The word “society” implies that there is something shared. In the 21st century, we have come to realize that inclusive civic nationalism and liberal democracy have only worked within relatively homogeneous nations. Without shared values, a shared language, or a shared culture, there is no society either. There are only different ethnic and identity-based groups whose struggle for power is now escalating toward a state resembling civil war.

If Europeans intend to survive all this, the first step is to acknowledge the failure of the liberal conception of citizenship. Neither France’s assimilationist policies nor their opposite, the Nordic model of inclusive multiculturalism, have integrated most of the people who have moved here from North Africa and the Middle East. We must return to a conception of nationhood based on ethnicity. The Finnish state was not originally founded as a community of shared values or as a mere administrative contraption governing a particular geographical area, but as a guarantee of the continued existence of the Finnish people. Nationality is inherently an exclusionary community based on continuity across generations. If we cannot or are not allowed to distinguish ourselves from others, then Finnishness itself no longer exists as a distinct group.

The fact is that, over the past few decades, millions of people have been allowed into Europe for whom our history, achievements, language, and culture mean nothing. To quote Jean Raspail’s novel: “They know nothing about you or what you stand for. Your world means absolutely nothing to them. They don’t even try to understand it.” Raspail once imagined the newcomers as poor, tired, and freezing, but the reality is worse: many of these people live here on the generous support of society.

European governments have bought their compliance with bread and circuses, housing, and welfare payments. When cheap debt starts running out and the cost of living rises, hostile mobs take to the streets to extract their share of prosperity by looting shops and smashing things up. The left has chosen its side in this conflict. Some of them joked that the town hall in Limoges was clearly worth more to conservatives than human beings were. On this point, they are absolutely right. The achievements of European civilization are infinitely more valuable to me than people who seek to destroy them.

2/2

text:
Born in 1976 in Lunga Lunga, a self-styled Kenyan doomsday preacher Paul Nthenge Mackenzie, grew up in rural Kwale County, Kenya. After completing his secondary school education, he moved to Mombasa, where he initially sold flour out of a handcart and worked various odd jobs. 

In the late 1990s, Mackenzie moved to the coastal town of Malindi and worked as a taxi driver. Fellow drivers from that period noted that he didn't initially even know how to drive, learning the skill on his sister's car with the help of a hired instructor.

Mackenzie grew up in the Africa Brotherhood Church, where he was a teenage choirmaster and Sunday school teacher. By 2002, he left after a dispute with church leadership and briefly joined a Baptist congregation.

In 2003, he teamed up with a local woman named Ruth Kahindi and officially establish the Good News International Church in Malindi. 

Paul Mackenzie and Ruth Kahindi met at a Baptist church in Malindi. Impressed by his oratorical skills, Ruth invited him to preach at her home. Together, they officially co-founded the Good News International Church (initially called House of the Lord). 

In the beginning, it operated as a completely conventional evangelical church. According to Ruth’s daughter, Naomi, Mackenzie preached normal salvation through faith, cross-examined standard biblical scriptures, and offered traditional hope.

While the local flock loved his charisma, a standard gospel in a highly saturated religious environment meant low cash flow, a lack of mass-scale followers, and faced tough competition from well established churches.

Mackenzie realized what many modern cult leaders discover: traditional messages of hope face steep competition, but fear, apocalyptic urgency, and anti-system conspiracy theories create absolute dependency.

Fear drives people to surrender their autonomy and assets. If the world is ending tomorrow, you don't need your bank account, your land title deed, or your property—you give it to the "man of God" who is preparing your passage to heaven.

By 2008, Mackenzie completely pivoted his doctrinal model. He returned from a trip to Mombasa with an altered ideology. He began aggressively preaching that formal education was satanic, modern hospitals/medicine were evil, and government infrastructure was the "Mark of the Beast".

Ruth Kahindi recognized this as dangerous brainwashing designed to exploit vulnerable followers. She actively confronted him and tried to talk him out of it, warning him that forbidding medical care and demanding people's property under the guise of an imminent apocalypse was wrong.

Instead of listening, Mackenzie weaponized the congregation against her. He accused Ruth of witchcraft and embezzling church funds to ruin her reputation among the flock. Realizing she was fighting a losing battle against a man she described as a "stubborn boy," Ruth was effectively pushed out and left the church entirely to him.

Without Ruth there to question him, he transformed a struggling local church into a highly centralized, expanding cult machine.

Mackenzie didn't just push Ruth out; he actively stripped her of her legacy by recruiting her own family members into his inner circle. 

Ruth’s son-in-law, Smart Deri Mwakalama, completely abandoned her side and aligned with Mackenzie. Mwakalama rose through the ranks during these transition years to become the official Church Secretary and, eventually, Mackenzie’s ruthless head of security and second-in-command. 

During the 2008–2015 window, Mackenzie proved that his new radical, anti-establishment message was highly marketable, and profitable. He shifted from a single location in Malindi to a multi-branch operation across the country, and established thriving new branches in major urban and rural hubs.

By planting these branches, he secured a steady, diversified stream of tithes and offerings from thousands of new followers nationwide, moving away from his early financial struggles.

Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access is not an attempt to challenge Eritrea’s sovereignty or lay claim to its territory. It is a matter of Ethiopia’s legitimate national interest and strategic necessity, one that can be addressed through peaceful negotiations and mutually beneficial arrangements.
When Ethiopia reached an agreement with Somaliland to secure access to the sea, Eritrea opposed it. Its position on Red Sea affairs, including its insistence that governance of the Red Sea should be restricted to coastal states, raises a fundamental question: On what principle does Eritrea oppose Ethiopia’s legitimate aspiration to secure sea access?
If Eritrea’s position offers no viable alternative for Ethiopia and instead focuses on preventing Ethiopia from securing access to the sea through peaceful means, such a stance contradicts the principles of good neighbourliness, regional cooperation, and shared development.
Ethiopia’s pursuit of sea access should not be treated as a justification for territorial conflict with Eritrea. However, just as Eritrea expects its own sovereignty to be respected, it must also refrain from policies that undermine Ethiopia’s legitimate national interests. The future stability of the region will not be secured by one country denying another its legitimate interests, but by pursuing solutions through dialogue, mutual understanding, and mutually beneficial cooperation.

text:
TRUMP WANTS TO RENAME THE ATLANTIC OR PACIFIC OCEAN THE “TRUMP OCEAN.”

Donald Trump has sparked another wave of online ridicule after casually suggesting that the United States should rename an entire ocean in his honor. Speaking to a large crowd of supporters at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee, Trump floated the idea of renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, arguing that America needed a major body of water bearing his name. The bizarre suggestion immediately drew criticism from commentators and social media users questioning his priorities.

During his speech, Trump joked about geographical landmarks, pointing out that the country already has a gulf and a beautiful lake. He then suggested that someone had mentioned the need for a river or an ocean, inspiring his latest grand proposal.

“So I was thinking either the Atlantic or the Pacific. We'll call it the Trump Ocean or the Ocean of the Americas, something like that,” he told the crowd.

The remarks followed his earlier push to rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America,” another controversial attempt to rewrite geographical terminology.

As clips of the speech spread across social media, political opponents and ordinary Americans quickly expressed their frustration. Commentator Brian Krassenstein criticized the remarks on X, arguing that the administration should focus on urgent economic problems rather than renaming geographical features.

Countless others echoed that sentiment, pointing out that Americans are far more concerned about soaring gasoline prices, inflation, healthcare costs, and the growing financial pressure on working families. Many questioned why the president was entertaining grandiose ideas about renaming oceans while millions of households were struggling to pay their bills.

This is hardly Trump's first attempt to attach new names to major geographical landmarks or introduce unusual political terminology. In recent months, he has also floated ideas involving the Strait of Hormuz and promoted expressions such as “superintelligence” and “artificial media.”

While these rhetorical performances attract enormous media attention and generate viral debates, they also provide ammunition for critics who accuse Trump of distracting the public from substantive policy discussions.

The timing makes the controversy particularly striking. With the November midterm elections approaching, Americans are increasingly focused on the cost of living, economic security, and the affordability of everyday necessities.

For families struggling with grocery bills, housing expenses, medical costs, and rising fuel prices, the prospect of an ocean bearing Trump's name offers little comfort.

Supporters may dismiss the remarks as another example of Trump's familiar rally humor. Critics, however, see something more troubling: a president seemingly preoccupied with his own name and legacy while ordinary Americans face mounting economic difficulties.

And perhaps that is the most remarkable part of this entire spectacle. At a moment when millions of Americans are wondering how to make ends meet, their president is apparently wondering which of the world's greatest oceans should carry his name.

America needs affordable living, economic stability, and serious leadership. Instead, it is being offered the Trump Ocean.

KEN PAXTON: THE MAN WHO PREACHES LAW AND ORDER WHILE HIS OWN RECORD RAISES SERIOUS QUESTIONS.

Before lecturing anyone about crime, corruption, morality, or protecting children, consider the record of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton:

1. FELONY SECURITIES FRAUD: Indicted in 2015, Paxton avoided trial nearly nine years later through an agreement requiring approximately $271,000 in restitution, 100 hours of community service, and ethics training. The charges were dismissed without a conviction.

2. BRIBERY AND ABUSE-OF-OFFICE ALLEGATIONS: Eight senior aides reported Paxton to the FBI, alleging he used his office to benefit donor Nate Paul. Federal prosecutors brought no criminal charges.

3. IMPEACHED BY HIS OWN PARTY: In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House impeached Paxton on 20 articles alleging corruption, obstruction, and abuse of power. The Republican-controlled Senate acquitted him—but that did not erase the allegations.

4. $6.6 MILLION WHISTLEBLOWER JUDGMENT: Four former aides won a judgment after a court found Paxton’s office violated the Texas Whistleblower Act. His office dropped its appeal, leaving taxpayers responsible.

5. A CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE PLEA DEAL: In 2026, prosecutors working under Paxton offered Adam Hoffman, a Waco attorney accused of repeatedly abusing a young boy, a deal that initially called for ONE DAY IN JAIL.

Hoffman admitted in a signed confession to sexually touching the child without consent. The original agreement would have reduced the felony case to misdemeanors and allowed him to avoid registering as a sex offender. After a judge objected, the final deal resulted in approximately 30 days in jail—still without registration.

Paxton’s prosecutors cited a hung jury and the child’s reluctance to testify again. But the contrast is stark: Paxton champions tough-on-crime policies while his office negotiated an extraordinarily lenient deal for a man who admitted sexual misconduct against a child.

LET THAT SINK IN.

Paxton has not been criminally convicted in these matters. That distinction matters.

But being legally unconvicted is not the same as having an unquestionable record of integrity, accountability, or judgment.

Law and order should apply to everyone—especially those entrusted with enforcing it.

Actually that is not entirely correct. Up until recently, the last time the US built a refinery was the early 1970s. US production at that time was mostly West Texas Intermediate and Venezuela was providing most of our oil. The accessibility of Canadian tar sands oil in the late 1970s and 1980s added more sour crude. The refineries were built to handle what they got at the time. Now that we have ruined our relationship with Canada, I don’t see it having any incentive to continue giving us a massive discount when the EU will pay more and offers political reliability. Canada has a ready market in Europe who is NOT going back to Russian oil and gas. 

Meanwhile, Venezuela is not going to meet that need because the infrastructure, security, and political risks there don’t make it worth the Oil Companies’ while. Every chief counsel officer I have talked to from Exxon is not touching that mess with a 100 foot pole. Chevron might because it still has a presence, but it really isn’t worth the ROI to increase investment. It is either retool the existing refineries, which takes time and takes them offline, or build new ones closer to the production centers while slowly retire the old ones. From an environmental perspective, it makes much more sense to build new cleaner and more efficient refineries and reclaim the brownfield lands left by the old ones. Given the new geopolitical realities, I think that option has become much more palatable to the political left here (just as gas and oil pipelines across Canada have all the sudden become a discussion point even amongst Canadian Liberals).

text:
On a Sunday afternoon in August, my 10-year-old son asked me to stop buying groceries for his father.

I laughed because I thought he was joking.

Then he said, “Mom, Dad told Grandma that you don’t know how to manage money. That’s why he gives her $800 every month to help her.”

I put down the grocery bag I was carrying.

“What did you just say?”

My son, Noah, looked at me nervously.

“He said not to tell you because you’d get angry.”

I felt a strange chill run through me.

My husband, Kevin, and I had been married for 12 years. We lived in a comfortable house in Texas with our two children, Noah and Lily, who was seven.

Kevin worked as a project manager for a construction company, and I ran a small bookkeeping business from home.

We weren’t struggling financially, but we weren’t careless with money either.

I paid the mortgage, utilities, groceries, and most of the children’s expenses from our joint account. Kevin handled his car payments, insurance, and some other bills.

Every month, I transferred money into our savings account because we wanted to buy a larger house before Noah started high school.

Kevin’s mother, Margaret, lived about 20 minutes away.

She had retired several years earlier and often complained that her pension wasn’t enough to cover everything. Whenever she needed help, I was usually the first person to offer it.

I bought her groceries, paid for her prescriptions when she couldn’t afford them, and once gave her $1,200 to repair her leaking roof.

Kevin always thanked me.

“Mom’s lucky to have you,” he would say.

So when Noah told me that Kevin had been sending his mother $800 every month, I wasn’t upset that he was helping her.

I was upset that he had hidden it from me.

That evening, I waited until the children were asleep.

Kevin was sitting on the sofa watching football when I asked him about the money.

“Have you been sending your mother $800 every month?”

He didn’t look away from the television.

“Who told you that?”

“Noah.”

His expression changed.

“Why is our son listening to adult conversations?”

“Kevin, answer my question.”

He sighed and muted the television.

“Yes, I’ve been helping Mom. She’s getting older, and she needs support.”

“That’s fine. But why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I knew you’d have a problem with it.”

I stared at him.

“Why would I have a problem with helping your mother? I’ve helped her for years.”

He shrugged.

“You always want to know where every dollar goes.”

I couldn’t believe what I was hearing.

For 12 years, I had been the one making sure our bills were paid on time, our children had what they needed, and our savings continued to grow.

Now my husband was making me sound like a selfish woman because I wanted to understand our finances.

I took a deep breath.

“How long have you been sending her money?”

He hesitated.

“About three years.”

Three years.

That meant he had secretly sent his mother $28,800 while I believed we were saving together for our family’s future.

But the amount wasn’t what frightened me most.

It was what Kevin said next.

“Mom thinks you’re controlling, too. She says a man shouldn’t have to ask his wife for permission to help his own mother.”

I slowly stood up.

“Your mother thinks I’m controlling?”

Kevin nodded.

Then he added, “And honestly, she’s right about one thing. You don’t need to know everything I do with my money.”

I walked upstairs without another word.

But the following morning, I discovered something that made the $28,800 seem insignificant.

Because the money Kevin had been sending his mother wasn’t coming from the account I thought it was.

text:
Elon Musk posted on X early Monday morning: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.” He didn’t say how the shares would be handed out or who would qualify, and CNBC reported it has reached out to SpaceX and Musk’s family office for details.

The numbers are big. There were about 72 million Americans under 18 as of July 2025, according to Census data cited by CNBC (CBS News and CNN put it near 73 million). At SpaceX’s Friday closing price of $146.03, CNBC figures that comes to about $10.5 billion in stock. CBS News reported SpaceX shares rose 2.7% to $149.49 Monday morning, a day before the company reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

The pledge came right after Anthropic, the AI company, announced Sunday it will put 5% of its shares into a new public benefit fund. Musk replied on X that he recommends giving shares directly to the public, and said that’s what he will be doing. CBS News noted the shares could go through the new Trump Accounts, the tax deferred savings accounts for children born from 2025 through 2028 that get a $1,000 government deposit, since Treasury rules let donors put stock into them. In July, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged one SpaceX share to each of roughly 2 million kids already signed up, putting lower income families and Texas kids first, CNN reported.

What’s next: no details yet on timing, eligibility or how families would claim a share. CNBC and CNN also pointed out Musk has made big giving promises before that didn’t happen, like his 2021 offer of $6 billion to the UN World Food Programme.

Now that’s how you share the wealth. No middleman, just a real piece of an American company for every kid. Put it in the Trump Accounts and let it grow. I hope the details come through soon. Thoughts?

Sources: Elon Musk on X, CNBC, CBS News, CNN

text:
Here is how I am using GrokBot  as a media buyer managing over $200K/day in Affiliate and Ecom Ad Spend:

Truthfully, I didn't expect my previous post to get so much attention, so I decided to actually share some value (hopefully). 

Basically I've got all APIs plugged into a handful of pots: Google Ads, YouTube, Everflow, Lead Prosper, and Google Sheets

Affilate:
- Checks my margin every hour. It matches my ad spend to the revenue I actually got paid, not the conversions Google reports. I match back campaignID and creativeID for real time tracking

- Tells me what to cut and what to scale. It follows my own rules, like cutting after 3 losing days and only raising budgets at certain hours. I've also had it run a study on my media buying actions over the last 60 days to see how my budget increases effect margin, so now I have predictor of how aggressively I should raise and at what hours of the day are the best to make changes

- Flags losing ads early. If an ad spends too much with no leads, I know before it burns real cash. For example if it spends 3x target CPA it automatically flags to be paused 

- Judges ads on lead quality, not just lead count. It matches every ad to which leads actually turned into sales, signs or appointments. I can pass back appointment rate, sales rate, call length, revenue per call, etc to each ad and transcript 

- Predicts where the day will end up, and how sure it is, so I'm not guessing at noon. Since there is a time delay between click and when the revenue fires back, sometimes I can be spending several thousand dollars per hour and see major drops in CVR, the predictions help me decide if the traffic quality is good or bad before the revenue fires back 

- Tests my landing pages and videos against each other and shows me which ones actually make money. I can see my profit per click per landing page, sure Redtrack does this, but I use Everflow not RT which doesn't have a built in LP tracker

- Checks what I changed before it gives advice, so it doesn't tell me to undo something I just did. I make sure its constantly learning from MY behaviors not making decisions on its own

- Updates my P&L sheet every day, so I never build reports by hand. I created a Google sheet and it pulls spend from Google Ads and Revenue from Everflow and creates a P&L daily of each offer and each vertical

- Pulls YouTube transcripts and ties back performance to the script and hook used in each ad

- Shows all my bank and card balances in one place.
Matches what each partner owes me against what actually hit my bank, so I see who's paying late. This is super helpful because it instantly tells me where my money is and knows which advertisers pay on which payment terms, which credit cards are due when, and helps me manage and understand my cash flow

E-com:

- Ecom is a lot more robust and I am still building out the flows but I will mostly be using it for understanding my media buyers behaviors, for example, if there are campaigns running hot in client accounts, I get a notification to my phone alerting me they haven't made a change they should have made

- The same goes for scaling, one of the hardest things is to teach buyers how to SCALE and I mean really SCALE not just 20% raises here and there. These alerts ping to me when we identify a campaign that can scale and if they don't make the changes or make changes against how I would do it, I get a notification which provides a teaching moment to the buyers 

- Of course, we are doing high level script and hook analysis on our creatives and landing pages 

- It also sending notifications when certain campaign types are underperforming or if it identifies new opportunities 

Overall, there is A LOT I am still learning and I've only had this bot set up for about a week, but its truly a revolutionary approach to buying and management. Sure, I should have been using Hermes agent a long time ago, but I am not the most tech savy person and have been quite busy, but GrokBot was SO easy to set up, I truly believe anyone and everyone can use it and improve massive amounts of workflows with it. 

Any questions? LET ME KNOW in the comments

text:
I founded Democracy Docket for moments like this

— Marc Elias 

Democracy Docket
Founder 

I have been litigating voting rights cases for over 30 years. I have argued before the Supreme Court, represented presidential campaigns and started my own law firm. With all of my experience as a practicing attorney, I really thought I had seen it all. That is, until the Department of Justice lost 26 straight cases in a row — all arguing the same thing.
 
The DOJ’s losing streak was put into motion last year, when the department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for access to unredacted voter rolls. This attack was a critical part of Donald Trump’s effort to subvert this fall’s midterm elections.
 
Yet in case after case, in state after state, the department failed. Judges of all stripes — from Biden appointees to Bush appointees to Trump appointees — shut the DOJ’s argument down.
 
Recently, the DOJ faced its most damaging blow yet when a federal judge struck down the administration’s effort to demand unredacted voter rolls. Judge Sparkle Sooknanan found the DOJ exceeded its statutory authority and violated federal law, invalidating the policy nationwide.
 
That means the DOJ is barred from demanding unredacted state voter registration lists, checking those lists against inaccurate federal databases and urging states to remove alleged noncitizens from voter rolls.
 
When this ruling came down, the Democracy Docket team sprang into action to cover it — just as the team did for all 26 voter roll decisions. In fact, Democracy Docket has been covering this story from the very beginning.
 
Meanwhile, I have written extensively about these cases — my law firm is litigating many of them. I have published countless podcast episodes explaining in depth why these cases are so important. It’s not just about the fact that the DOJ is losing and we are winning. These voter roll cases were critical to Trump’s ploy to undermine the midterm elections and control who can vote — and we beat him at every turn.
 
But this story is far from over. We are still waiting to hear from Delaware and Utah, and we could hear from the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals any day. I suspect this issue will likely land before the Supreme Court in the coming weeks.
 
When that happens, we’ll be the first to let you know.
 
That’s because I founded Democracy Docket to cover stories just like this. When I write to you about the DOJ voter roll cases, I’m not speaking as a commentator. I’m writing to you as someone who knows these cases inside and out. I’m staying up late to record a video, taking time between reviewing legal briefs to write to you, because I believe that we are facing the greatest threat to our democracy we’ve ever seen — and I refuse to stay silent.
 
Your contribution powers Democracy Docket's work. Most of what Democracy Docket offers is free to everyone, and your support is what makes that possible. Other media outlets hide important information behind a paywall, but that is contrary to our mission.
 
With the midterm elections quickly approaching, it's never been more urgent to keep our work accessible and inclusive. Your membership helps ensure everyone has the news, tools and knowledge they need to fight for our democracy.
 
Recently, Democracy Docket introduced a new VIP tier for those who want even more — including exclusive events, the opportunity to gift memberships to friends and family, and the chance to make a substantial impact on our mission.
 
If now is not the time, I understand and thank you for still staying in this fight with me. It means more than you know.
 
Trump’s voter roll scheme was about one thing: making it harder for you to vote and easier for him to cheat. In courtroom after courtroom, judges stopped him. But he isn’t done, and neither are we. I created Democracy Docket for moments like this, and I’m grateful to face it with you.

@nfcsentinels is now accepting applications for its new Bachelor of Science in Elementary Education degree program, set to begin Spring 2027. The program comes as Florida school districts continue to face a shortage of qualified teachers, particularly in elementary education.
According to the Florida Department of Education, elementary education entered the 2026-27 school year with an estimated 1,591 teaching vacancies, the second-highest number among certification areas statewide. Elementary education represents nearly 25% of the 6,446 vacancies anticipated across Florida for the current school year.
For NFC, those numbers point to a need the College can help address. The new degree allows students to prepare for teaching careers while staying close to home. It also offers area school districts another source of future teachers who are familiar with the communities they serve.
"Our school districts need teachers, and we have students right here in North Florida who want to teach," said David Dunkle, NFC Vice President of Academic Affairs and Chief Academic Officer. "This degree gives them another option. Students can earn their degree close to home, with the flexibility of online classes and the opportunity to work directly with teachers and students in the classroom."
NFC's Bachelor of Science in Elementary Education is designed to prepare students to teach kindergarten through sixth grade. Students who have completed an associate degree will take 60 credit hours of upper-division coursework, with most classes offered online.

text:
The Patterson–Gimlin film has people asking questions all over again. Here are five Bigfoot Society episodes I recommend for anyone who wants to explore the footage, the history, and the place where it happened. 🌲

I believe Bigfoot exists. I’ve interviewed over 1,000 witnesses and had experiences of my own. I’m still investigating, and I want to understand what people are encountering.

These conversations offer several ways into the Patterson–Gimlin story. Save this post for your next listening session.

1️⃣ M.K. DAVIS — EXAMINING THE FILM

“The Importance of Film Analysis and the Patterson-Gimlin Film”

M.K. Davis joins me to discuss his work examining the footage frame by frame and the importance of thinking critically about what we’re seeing.

If you’ve watched Patty’s famous walk and wanted to hear from someone who has spent considerable time studying those images, start here. This conversation introduces his approach and gives you questions to consider when you revisit the footage.

🎧 Watch the conversation
https://t.co/jZTVNtTSiW

2️⃣ TATE HIERONYMUS — RESEARCHING THE ACTUAL FILM SITE

“Tate Hieronymus from the Bluff Creek Project Podcast” — Episode 28

Tate shares his involvement with the Bluff Creek Project and his research into the Patterson–Gimlin film site.

There’s something compelling about hearing from researchers who have spent time on the ground where this story unfolded. This early Bigfoot Society interview is a good place to begin learning about Tate’s connection to Bluff Creek and the work that brought him there.

🎧 Listen to Episode 28
https://t.co/BainRNDvNv

3️⃣ THE BC19 EXPEDITION TEAM — PLANNING THE JOURNEY INTO BLUFF CREEK

“Braving the Wilds of Bluff Creek with the BC19 Expedition Team” — Episode 266

Tate Hieronymus, Jonathan Easley, and Ron Read join me to discuss their planned expedition up Bluff Creek to the Patterson–Gimlin film site.

This conversation brings the terrain and the challenges of reaching the location into focus. We use an onscreen map extensively, so I recommend the video version for this one. Audience questions are part of the discussion, too.

🎥 Watch the expedition discussion
https://t.co/bTSu3tPpRb

4️⃣ DUSTIN SEVERS — THE HISTORY SURROUNDING BLUFF CREEK

“The Abominable Snowman of California: A Conversation with Dustin Severs”

Author Dustin Severs shares research drawn from years of digging through newspaper archives and personal collections.

We discuss figures including Bob Titmus, Peter Byrne, and John Green, along with Ray Wallace’s place in Bigfoot history and Dustin’s experiences researching Bluff Creek. This is my pick for listeners interested in the people, research, and disagreements surrounding that area’s Bigfoot story.

🎧 Listen to the Dustin Severs interview
https://t.co/I16527dKWQ

5️⃣ KAI WADA ROATH — INSIDE THE “CAPTURING BIGFOOT” PREMIERE

“BREAKING: I Was At the San Francisco Capturing Bigfoot Premiere — A Talk with Kai Wada Roath”

Kai attended the San Francisco premiere, where Roger Patterson’s son, Clint Patterson, was also present.

He joins me for a spoiler-conscious conversation about his reaction to the documentary, its mystery footage, the audience, and the filmmakers’ Q&A. If the current discussion has brought you back to the Patterson–Gimlin film, this episode offers an attendee’s firsthand perspective on that screening.

🎧 Listen to Kai’s premiere report
https://t.co/OOQWgnwgUt

What is the ONE detail about the Patterson–Gimlin film you most want investigated further?

Tell me what you’ve noticed and why it matters to you. I want this to be a place where people can ask honest questions and share their experiences respectfully.

— Jeremiah Byron, Bigfoot Society
