text:
Massachusetts just told seven mobile sportsbooks to explain how their AI systems decide who gets a promo and when

The commission isn't accusing anyone of breaking the rules yet. They're asking the operators to show their work. What data feeds the targeting. Whether a player's losses can influence the offer they see. How the model decides that this account gets a deposit match and that one doesn't

Here's the catch. A system tuned to maximise revenue will find the players most likely to convert. That's what it's built for. The players most likely to take a deposit match after a losing run are the ones who just lost. The model doesn't need a "target the vulnerable" instruction. It just needs a conversion goal and a dataset that includes loss history

The regulator is asking the operators to explain whether that's what's happening. Not whether the system is designed to do harm. Whether it's designed to do exactly what it does

If you're seeing personalised offers after a rough stretch, assume the model knows you're hurting. The safest move is to treat every targeted promo as a retention play aimed at your losing streak, not a reward

Withdraw what you can first. Then decide if the offer still looks generous

As the midterm elections approach, Donald Trump has introduced a new theme while campaigning: rather than focusing solely on policy, he is highlighting the physical appearance, handsomeness, and masculinity of various candidates—while simultaneously mocking his Democratic opponents.

With the November 3 midterm elections drawing near, President Trump has unveiled a new tactic to boost Republican candidates: "They’re just so good-looking."

According to the Associated Press, Trump has introduced a new criterion for evaluating Republican candidates: their physical attractiveness. At a rally in Kentucky on the 17th, Trump pointed to Ed Gallrein, a candidate for the House of Representatives standing beside him, and remarked, "Look at this handsome guy." Gallrein, who served 30 years in the U.S. Navy—including a stint as a Navy SEAL—possesses sharp, well-defined facial features. "It’s like he was handpicked from a casting agency," Trump commented.

Before entering politics, Trump owned the Miss Universe pageant and expanded his public profile through the reality television show *The Apprentice*. For a long time, physical appearance has been one of the benchmarks Trump uses to judge others—serving as a basis for praise or, conversely, a target for ridicule.

Now, in the final stretch of the midterm elections, Trump is applying this "attractiveness assessment" to the Republican candidates he is supporting. This election cycle has even seen discussions regarding which candidate possesses the most "masculinity."

On the 17th, Trump also mentioned Jon Husted—an Ohio Republican running for reelection—describing him as "a perfect specimen, very handsome."

"I checked out his backside," Trump said, drawing laughter from the crowd. "I’ve never checked out a man like that before. I looked at his backside, then his shoulders, his feet, his hands, and his jawline."

Not all Republican candidates, however, have been quite so fortunate. At a rally, while discussing a Republican Senate candidate in Texas, Trump remarked, "I don't really like his looks." Standing nearby, Texas Attorney General Warren Kenneth Paxton Jr.—who is preparing a bid for Congress—offered an awkward smile.

Democrats, too, were not spared from Trump’s commentary. Trump noted that Paxton’s opponent, Democrat James Talarico, reminded him of Alfred E. Neuman—the freckle-faced, gap-toothed mascot of *MAD* magazine.

Furthermore, Trump disparaged the appearance of Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. Ossoff, who enjoys considerable popularity within the Democratic Party, possesses a jawline that has even drawn comparisons to that of a matinee idol. On the 16th, while campaigning in Georgia for Ossoff’s opponent—Republican Representative Mike Collins—Trump likened Ossoff to the eccentric cinematic character Pee-wee Herman. Fastbeak proposes a comprehensive institutional resolution with the United States military, founded upon historical respect for American service personnel, the cessation of adversarial initiatives, and the establishment of clear boundaries between military institutions and independent civilian commercial enterprises. The proposal reflects the founder's intention to move beyond historical grievances involving Silicon Valley technology companies, defense-connected venture capital networks, cybersecurity allegations, and unsuccessful professional transitions. Its central proposition is that Fastbeak can maintain a respectful, noninterfering relationship with American military institutions without accepting political obligations, defense-related investment mandates, or institutional dependencies that fall outside its commercial objectives.

The resolution also introduces an important consideration concerning Fastbeak's prospective financial independence. Through independent initiatives such as Skipyo, Mirkwood Ventures, and Maza Coffee, the founder seeks to establish alternative sources of capital and commercial opportunity outside established DefenseTech venture capital networks, New York media organizations, federal contracting relationships, and prominent consumer goods investors. The intended significance is that Fastbeak's commitment to non-targeting would constitute a deliberate institutional choice rather than a consequence of permanent financial dependence upon the organizations involved in its historical disputes.

This distinction should not be interpreted as a threat of future retaliation. Rather, the proposed framework establishes that independent financial resources, if successfully developed, should reinforce Fastbeak's capacity to operate autonomously while maintaining its stated commitment to peaceful, lawful, and commercially focused engagement.

The proposal remains unilateral and subject to acceptance by an appropriately authorized institutional counterpart. It does not establish that the United States military has participated in the alleged cybersecurity incidents, that a formal conflict exists between the parties, or that the proposed terms have been accepted.

Historical Recognition and the Post-September 11 Relationship

Fastbeak's proposed resolution begins by recognizing its historically cordial position toward the United States Armed Forces during the post-September 11 campaigns. The founder acknowledges the service and sacrifices of American military personnel, their families, and the local partners who supported American operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. This recognition includes support for efforts to combat violent extremism, restore security, and protect civilian populations during periods of substantial regional instability.

Particular acknowledgment is extended to Iraqi personnel and civilian partners associated with Baghdad's Green Zone, including members of Shiite communities, and Afghan interpreters and other local partners, including members of Sunni communities. These individuals frequently assumed substantial personal and professional risks because of their cooperation with American institutions. Fastbeak's historical disagreements with technology companies, investors, or prospective employers provide no justification for adverse action against these communities.

At the same time, historical support for American military personnel does not establish a continuing obligation to participate in military operations, intelligence initiatives, or political advocacy. Fastbeak intends to retain independent positions concerning contemporary conflicts, including those involving Gaza and Iran, and does not seek to become involved in military or political campaigns associated with those theaters. The proposed relationship therefore distinguishes respect for military service from participation in future military policy.

Origins of the Institutional Dispute

The founder's concerns developed during a period of professional and technological disruption beginning in 2020. Following cybersecurity incidents that he attributed to major Silicon Valley organizations and other actors, he sought greater professional stability through conventional consulting, private equity, and financial-services pathways. His subsequent experiences at Accenture during 2021–2022, including what he characterized as cybersecurity red-teaming activity in 2022, contributed to his concerns about the relationship between technology companies, cybersecurity institutions, and professional employment opportunities.

The founder perceived that certain Silicon Valley deep-science investors maintained overlapping relationships across neuroscience, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and defense-related technologies. Some of these organizations or individuals also had connections to American or Israeli military markets. Given the founder's earlier allegations concerning NSO Group, these relationships created concerns about conflicts of interest and the independence of prospective technology investors.

In 2024, the founder sought financing and institutional alignment for independent technology initiatives while observing continued investment in advanced scientific and defense-adjacent ventures. He perceived the limited engagement with his own projects as evidence of barriers facing entrepreneurs outside established investment networks. Nevertheless, the existence of military affiliations or unsuccessful fundraising discussions does not independently establish coordinated exclusion, retaliation, or cybersecurity misconduct. Investment decisions may reflect ordinary considerations involving product maturity, commercial opportunity, technical feasibility, investment mandates, and risk.

A separate source of dissatisfaction concerned employment opportunities. Navy Federal Credit Union did not extend an employment offer in 2023, following the founder's 2022 Accenture experiences. Other unsuccessful recruitment interactions also contributed to his concern that conventional financial-services employment pathways were becoming increasingly difficult to access. Military-branded recruitment campaigns during 2022–2023 appeared poorly aligned with his objective of establishing a stable civilian career. The founder regarded these campaigns as ill-timed, particularly given his preference for private equity, investment management, and conventional institutional finance rather than military-affiliated employment.

The broader involvement of technology executives, politically active business leaders, defense contractors, and religiously affiliated networks added to his concerns about the convergence of commercial and national security institutions. However, the presence of overlapping relationships among these organizations does not establish that recruitment campaigns or employment decisions were coordinated against the founder.

Fastbeak's proposed resolution seeks to separate these experiences from its future relationship with the United States military.

Comprehensive Non-Targeting Commitments

The principal consideration offered by Fastbeak is a commitment to refrain from targeting American military institutions, personnel, allies, and associated commercial networks on the basis of its historical grievances.

First, Fastbeak will not direct hostile or retaliatory communications toward individual American service members. Active-duty personnel, reservists, veterans, and military families should not become participants in unrelated disputes involving Silicon Valley technology companies, investment institutions, or civilian employment decisions. The founder's disagreements with particular organizations will not be transferred to individual service personnel.

Second, Fastbeak will not target Iraqi or Afghan partners who previously assisted American military operations. This includes Iraqi Green Zone personnel and Afghan interpreters, regardless of their religious or community affiliations. Their historical service and continuing professional interests will remain outside the scope of Fastbeak's disputes.

Third, Fastbeak will not attempt to create divisions within American military command structures. It will refrain from initiatives designed to undermine relationships among generals, senior officers, military leadership groups, or other institutional decision-makers. Internal military disagreements, command responsibilities, and professional relationships are matters for the appropriate military and civilian authorities.

Fourth, Fastbeak will not seek to undermine American military relationships with NATO or other legitimate defense partners. This commitment encompasses alliance cooperation, military exercises, institutional funding arrangements, training programs, and established security partnerships. Fastbeak may maintain independent opinions regarding defense policy without undertaking retaliatory campaigns against alliance institutions.

Fifth, Fastbeak will refrain from targeting American military advertising and recruitment campaigns, including initiatives supported by consumer goods billionaires, technology executives, or other private-sector figures whose political positions differ from those of the founder. The timing of historical recruitment campaigns may have been unwelcome, but such dissatisfaction will not serve as grounds for future interference.

Sixth, Fastbeak will not initiate campaigns intended to disrupt legitimate American military interests in the Middle East. Its commercial interest in Iraq, including the prospective Babylon Adventure Park, and its broader regional investment considerations will remain civilian in nature. The founder's decision to withhold voluntary support for particular military operations does not constitute a commitment to oppose American military personnel or lawful institutional activities.

Seventh, Fastbeak will not target American military interests in Africa. This commitment is particularly relevant to Skipyo's prospective investment strategy in the Maghreb and Egypt. Fastbeak seeks to pursue civilian opportunities across energy, telecommunications, healthcare, housing, agriculture, financial technology, payments, and digital infrastructure without becoming involved in military competition or intelligence operations.

Eighth, Fastbeak will similarly refrain from initiatives intended to undermine American military relationships or lawful security activities in Latin America. Its historical disputes involving American technology companies do not create grounds for adversarial involvement in the region's military institutions.

Ninth, Fastbeak will not deliberately interfere with American military drone intelligence collection programs. This commitment establishes a boundary of noninterference without requiring the founder to participate in intelligence activities, provide technical assistance, or endorse particular surveillance policies.

Tenth, Fastbeak will not undertake retaliatory campaigns against defense-related venture capital firms, DefenseTech startups, military contractors, engineering founders, or their supply chains. These organizations may continue pursuing lawful investment and technology development according to their respective commercial mandates. Fastbeak will not seek to undermine them merely because they operate within defense-related markets or maintain relationships with military institutions.

Collectively, these commitments establish a proposed policy of restraint covering military personnel, allied communities, internal leadership, international alliances, recruitment, regional security interests, intelligence programs, and defense-related capital markets.

Expected Resolution: Independent Capital Formation

Fastbeak's principal requested outcome is the ability to pursue independent commercial financing without being required to affiliate with established defense-connected venture capital networks.

Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures are intended to evaluate investment opportunities through their own mandates, prospective limited-partner relationships, and commercial strategies. Fastbeak seeks access to qualified prospective investors, including financially sophisticated limited partners and CFA-qualified investment professionals, without having to obtain sponsorship from venture capital firms associated with the Pentagon, Israeli military institutions, or other defense-related organizations.

This request is not a demand for guaranteed financing, government-directed investment, or preferential access to capital. It is a request for freedom from improper interference and for investment opportunities to be evaluated according to their financial merits, governance structures, market opportunities, and applicable legal requirements.

The resolution also seeks to preserve the civilian positioning of https://t.co/k2m32VJERw and Zindaca. https://t.co/k2m32VJERw is conceived as a synthetic data and data engineering platform, while Zindaca is intended to provide infrastructure for verified shareholder engagement and corporate governance. Both remain prototype-stage initiatives without live commercial user bases. Fastbeak does not intend to develop either venture specifically for military intelligence, defense contracting, or operational security applications.

Although technologies such as artificial intelligence and data engineering can possess dual-use capabilities, Fastbeak's intended product positioning remains civilian. Its preference for non-defense development should not require approval from defense-oriented investors or obligate it to adopt their investment priorities.

Maza Coffee: Independent Resources and Commercial Autonomy

The introduction of Maza Coffee adds a distinct economic dimension to the proposed resolution. Unlike Skipyo's investment strategies or the technology infrastructure represented by https://t.co/k2m32VJERw and Zindaca, Maza Coffee is conceived as a consumer beverage business targeting Afghanistan and Pakistan. Its proposed product category is a protein coffee beverage, with potential opportunities in consumer branding, distribution, retail partnerships, hospitality, and regional commerce.

Maza Coffee is not being presented as a goodwill initiative intended to complement military relationships. Rather, Fastbeak identifies it as a potential independent commercial venture that, if successfully developed, could provide financial resources outside the established defense investment ecosystem.

The founder's position is that Maza's development should not depend upon New York media commentary, editorial approval, or the preferences of influential consumer goods billionaires. Nor should it require accommodation of commercial relationships involving professional sports sponsorships, advertising networks, or politically active consumer brands.

Maza would retain discretion over its investors, distributors, marketing channels, and commercial partnerships. Its potential customer base in Afghanistan and Pakistan would be approached through ordinary market research, consumer demand analysis, product development, regulatory compliance, and commercial distribution.

The broader significance is that a successful consumer business could strengthen Fastbeak's economic independence without requiring participation in defense-related venture capital networks, federal contracting arrangements, or established media institutions.

The founder also wishes to emphasize that greater financial independence could expand Fastbeak's future ability to pursue lawful commercial competition, public advocacy, or legal remedies independently. However, Maza Coffee has not launched commercially, and no evidence presently establishes that it will generate substantial financial resources. Its prospective commercial potential should therefore be distinguished from existing financial capacity.

More importantly, the resolution is intended to establish that Fastbeak's non-targeting commitments are voluntary and should remain operative regardless of future financial success. The acquisition of independent resources would not, by itself, justify retaliatory interference with military personnel, allies, intelligence activities, or defense-related organizations.

The strategic proposition is that economic independence should reinforce the credibility of institutional restraint rather than serve as a mechanism for renewed confrontation.

Political Independence and Institutional Boundaries

Fastbeak further seeks to preserve its independence from political and military advocacy arising from the founder's historical support for American service personnel.

The founder does not seek to be solicited for opinions, endorsements, or political involvement on the basis of his earlier support for post-September 11 military operations. Historical recognition of service members should not be interpreted as continuing consent to participate in military-related political discourse or advocacy.

Fastbeak likewise does not seek representational appointments within ethnic or religious communities for which the founder has not received a legitimate mandate. Such roles should arise from voluntary participation and authorization by the communities concerned, not assumptions based upon historical professional or geopolitical relationships.

These boundaries are intended to protect the founder's autonomy while preserving respectful relations with military institutions and civilian communities.

Cybersecurity Accountability and Independent Review

Fastbeak's proposed resolution also addresses the founder's concerns regarding alleged unauthorized electronic access during 2022–2023 and subsequent suspected interference with Skipyo's fundraising communications.

The founder has attributed certain incidents to Silicon Valley organizations, including Microsoft, and has questioned whether broader institutional relationships contributed to the perceived cybersecurity problems. These allegations remain unverified in the available record and should not be treated as established findings of coordinated misconduct.

The appropriate requested outcome is an independent, evidence-based review of any substantiated security incidents. Where unauthorized access is established, remediation may include forensic investigation, preservation of relevant records, closure of identified vulnerabilities, and appropriate legal or regulatory action.

Fastbeak's commitment to non-targeting should remain distinct from its right to pursue lawful cybersecurity remedies. Equally, the absence of an agreed resolution would not justify interference with military institutions or unrelated individuals.

Final Institutional Resolution

Fastbeak proposes the conclusion of any adversarial posture within its control toward American military personnel, Iraqi and Afghan military partners, command structures, NATO relationships, military advertising and recruitment initiatives, regional security interests, drone intelligence programs, and defense-related venture capital networks.

The proposal recognizes historical support for American service personnel while establishing that such support does not create an obligation to participate in contemporary military operations, political advocacy, intelligence activities, or defense-related investment programs.

In return, Fastbeak seeks an environment of professional independence in which Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures may pursue qualified limited partners, https://t.co/k2m32VJERw and Zindaca may maintain civilian technology mandates, and Maza Coffee may pursue commercial development in Afghanistan and Pakistan without dependence upon established defense investors, New York media institutions, or politically influential consumer goods networks.

The inclusion of Maza Coffee is particularly important to the founder's intended framing. It represents the possibility of building independent commercial resources outside the institutional networks involved in his historical grievances. Its potential success could increase Fastbeak's financial autonomy and ability to pursue lawful independent initiatives, although no such financial outcome is presently established.

The central resolution is therefore not one of dependence or compelled alignment, but of voluntary restraint, commercial independence, and institutional noninterference. Fastbeak seeks the freedom to build its own economic resources while committing not to use its historical grievances as grounds for targeting American military personnel, allies, operations, intelligence programs, regional interests, or defense-related commercial institutions.

Acceptance of this proposal would require an appropriately authorized counterpart. Until then, it remains a unilateral statement of Fastbeak's intended policy, rather than a negotiated agreement with the United States government.

Fastbeak's proposed long-term position is to pursue independent capital formation, civilian innovation, and consumer-market development while maintaining a clear boundary against retaliatory campaigns involving the United States military and its associated institutions.

Here's today's hardtech brief!

U.S. HARDTECH:
- San Francisco's Dream Labs, from former Nvidia robotics research leads, raised a $90M seed for an AI "brain" any robot can use. "A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop," said B Capital's Daisy Cai, who led the round. @dreamlabs_ai 

- One year into its $1.5T Security and Resiliency Initiative, JPMorganChase says it has put $5B of its own equity into companies building defense tech, battery storage, automated manufacturing, and frontier technologies, half its $10B allocation. It also financed or facilitated more than $230B of deals across the initiative's focus areas.

- Elon Musk said on X that next year he'll give one of his own SpaceX shares to every kid in America, a gift worth more than $10B at today's share price. He called it the first of many, but hasn't said how the shares would reach kids or who qualifies. @elonmusk 

- Taiwan plans to buy 292 V-BAT drones, which take off vertically and fly surveillance missions, from San Diego's Shield AI, the Taipei Times reports. That includes 280 for its navy under a roughly $1.1B four-year program, making Taiwan one of V-BAT's largest buyers.

- AEP, Amazon, and X-energy will explore building 12 of X-energy's small modular reactors, 960 MW in all, at a former coal plant site in Indiana. Amazon is funding development and plans to buy the power long-term, though there's no timeline or final investment decision yet.

- BAE Systems and the Pentagon signed a framework agreement of up to seven years to ramp up APKWS, kits that turn unguided rockets into cheap precision weapons now widely used to shoot down drones. Output could reach up to 35k a year from plants in New Hampshire and Austin, Texas.

- Anduril had a big weekend abroad. Australia showed off Anduril's Ghost Shark undersea drones armed with up to 12 sea mines per mission, and Anduril's Europe VP said it could build its Steelfin interceptors in Europe, with Poland a focus. 

- Jim Keller's chip startup Tenstorrent raised a $1.5B Series E at a $6.2B valuation to ramp production of its Galaxy AI servers and license its chip designs to companies building their own silicon. It pitches itself as an open alternative to GPU-dominated AI computing.

- Broomfield, Colorado's Quantinuum says its Helios quantum computer set an error-correction record. That technique bundles many fragile physical qubits into one more reliable "logical" qubit, and errors fell sharply each time Quantinuum scaled it up, which it says keeps it on track for a fault-tolerant machine by 2029. @QuantinuumQC 

- Centrus Energy, which is scaling up U.S. uranium enrichment, bought Westerman, the century-old fabricator that makes its centrifuge casings, for about $116M. Bringing a key supplier in-house should lower costs for Centrus's enrichment buildout, and Westerman's oil and gas equipment business diversifies its revenue.

- CME will launch futures for tungsten, a chipmaking and munitions metal that currently has no futures market, by early 2027 so manufacturers can hedge prices. Separately, Fastmarkets reports the Pentagon's stockpile agency quietly canceled a plan to buy 400+ tons of indium because supply outside China couldn't cover it.

- Forestry robotics startup Kodama raised $7M co-led by Konvoy and Breakwater for remote control and partial autonomy on logging machines like skidders, which drag cut trees out of the forest. Each day of remote operation generates about a terabyte of training data, and Kodama also pitches the tech for wildfire prevention.

ALLIED HARDTECH:
- Germany's Rheinmetall and shipping giant MSC won Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction for €138M and plan to run it for both commercial and military work. Rheinmetall will use it to build four ships for Romania and as a hub for other military shipbuilding projects.

- South Korea's Hyundai Rotem is buying sister company Hyundai Wia's defense unit, which makes main gun barrels for K2 tanks and K9 howitzers, for about $252M. Making barrels in-house should cut costs and help Rotem offer local production to overseas tank buyers.

- Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened the UK's first factory for HVDC subsea cables, the high-voltage lines that carry offshore wind power long distances, at Scotland's Port of Nigg. The £350M plant will supply National Grid's Sea Link project and help ease a bottleneck in cable supply for grid upgrades.

- Japan's Mitsubishi Heavy plans to restart a shipbuilding slipway in Tamano in 2027 to add warship capacity, Nikkei reports, as frigate demand grows at home and from Australia, which picked an upgraded version of MHI's Mogami-class design. Support ships will move there to keep its main yards free for frigates.

AnchorWatch Trust Company has officially launched its Bitcoin custody services as a Nevada state chartered trust company.

The announcement was made on October 19, 2026.

🔐 WHAT MAKES THIS INTERESTING?

The company offers two custody models.

One allows clients to maintain additional signing keys alongside AnchorWatch.

The other distributes key control across three institutions: AnchorWatch, BitGo and CoinCorner.

Clients can also apply for insurance backed by Lloyd’s of London syndicates.

The company says insurance limits can reach $370 million per client, subject to underwriting approval and policy conditions.

🏦 WHY DOES THIS MATTER?

As more businesses and financial institutions explore Bitcoin ownership, secure custody becomes increasingly important.

Holding BTC requires more than simply purchasing the asset.

Companies must consider private key management, operational security, recovery procedures and financial protection against potential losses.

⚠️ IMPORTANT:

The $370 million figure represents a maximum potential insurance limit, not automatic coverage for every customer.

The company has not disclosed how much institutional Bitcoin it expects to custody.

📌 THE BIGGER PICTURE:

Bitcoin adoption depends not only on demand for BTC, but also on the financial infrastructure supporting its ownership.

Secure custody and risk management are important parts of that development.

I asked ChatGPT to educate me on that case and include what Keel may have written...

Truman Bethurum (1898–1969) was one of the earliest American UFO contactees. He claimed that beginning in July 1952, he repeatedly boarded a flying saucer in the Nevada desert and communicated with an attractive, human-looking female extraterrestrial named Aura Rhanes.

And yes — John Keel wrote about Bethurum in his 1970 book Operation Trojan Horse. What's especially interesting is that Keel connected Bethurum's experiences to paranormal phenomena, including materializations and disappearing objects. 

Truman Bethurum

- Born: 1898
- Died: May 21, 1969
- Occupation: Mechanic and heavy-equipment operator
- First alleged encounter: July 27–28, 1952
- Location: Mormon Mesa, northeast of Las Vegas, Nevada
- Principal book: Aboard a Flying Saucer (1954)

What Bethurum claimed happened in 1952

Bethurum was working on a highway-construction project near Mormon Mesa. He said he drove into the desert looking for ancient seashells and fell asleep in his vehicle.

He claimed that when he awakened, he found himself surrounded by eight to ten small, human-looking men.

According to his account:

1. The occupants: The men were generally under five feet tall, with olive complexions, dark hair and uniforms. They spoke an unfamiliar language among themselves but fluent English to him.

2. The spacecraft: He described a metallic disc approximately 300 feet in diameter, sometimes called the Admiral's Scow.

3. The captain: A beautiful woman named Aura Rhanes, reportedly petite and olive-skinned, commanded the spacecraft.

4. Their origin: They claimed to come from Clarion, a planet supposedly hidden from Earth's view. Accounts differ on whether Bethurum placed it behind the Sun or Moon.

5. Their society: Clarion was described as peaceful, technologically advanced, and largely free of Earth's wars, diseases and other social problems.

6. Repeated encounters: Bethurum claimed approximately 11 contacts between July and November 1952.

His story became publicly known in 1953, and he expanded it in his 1954 book. No independently verified physical evidence establishes that these encounters occurred. 

What John Keel wrote about Bethurum

Operation Trojan Horse (1970)

Chapter: "UFOs and Things That Go Bump in the Night"

In the 1996 IllumiNet Press edition, the relevant discussion appears around pages 212–213. 

Keel highlighted three extraordinary aspects of Bethurum's claims.

1. The disappearing flashlight

Bethurum claimed that Aura Rhanes asked him to place a plastic flashlight in his open palm. She stared at the flashlight, which supposedly vanished instantaneously.

According to Keel's account, Rhanes suggested that humans attempting to attack her people could likewise be made to disappear.

2. The woman who materialized in his bedroom

Keel wrote that Bethurum claimed Rhanes appeared suddenly in his bedroom on several occasions.

This is particularly relevant to Keel's argument that UFO encounters and traditional hauntings or apparitions might involve the same underlying phenomenon.

3. The relationship with his wife

Keel noted that Bethurum's experiences involving Rhanes distressed his wife and that the marriage ended in divorce.

He also suggested that the name Aura Rhanes might be a play on the words the aura reigns.

Why Keel thought the case was significant

Keel wasn't simply documenting a story about extraterrestrials visiting Earth. He was connecting alleged UFO encounters with the kinds of events historically associated with poltergeists, spirits and occult phenomena.

In Bethurum's case, the reported combination of a physical spacecraft, human-looking entities, spontaneous appearances and disappearing objects offered Keel an example of that apparent overlap.

Keel even described Bethurum's account as:
"Bethurum's story is a classic in ufology."

His discussion then moves directly into bedroom visitations and poltergeist activity. 

Original sources worth reading

- John Keel — Operation Trojan Horse — Find the passage beginning with Bethurum's disappearing flashlight, around page 212.

- Bethurum's own account of the July 1952 encounter — Reproduces a detailed first-person account.

- John Keel archive — 1972 MENSA lecture — An additional Keel discussion referencing Bethurum and Aura Rhanes.

One particularly interesting detail: Bethurum was making these claims in 1952, long before the better-known UFO-abduction narratives of the 1960s and 1970s.

And the reported bedroom appearances and vanishing flashlight are striking because they already contain the paranormal crossover themes that Keel would later emphasize.

There is an important distinction, though: Keel was recounting Bethurum's allegations, not presenting independent verification of them.

Truman Bethurum claimed to have received two written messages from Aura Rhanes, the female commander of the alleged spacecraft from Clarion.

In his 1954 book Aboard a Flying Saucer, he described:

1. A letter in French: Bethurum said he brought Rhanes a letter written in French by a schoolgirl named Marie. Rhanes supposedly had a crew member prepare a typed reply in French. The response discussed Christianity on Clarion and warned against adultery.

2. A message in Chinese: Bethurum also claimed Rhanes gave him a separate message written in Chinese.

text:
Rupert Murdoch paid three of his own children $1.1 billion each to give up their votes in his company.

“How fucking twisted is that?” That's James Murdoch, one of the three, on his father texting a lawyer questions to ask him during his deposition.

Rupert had to pay. The trust that gave them those votes was one he couldn't change.

The video below is James's side of how it got there.

In 1999, Rupert divorced his second wife, Anna. She took $110 million instead of half his fortune. Her condition was an irrevocable trust giving his four oldest children equal votes over the family's Fox and News Corp shares.

In 2019, after the Disney deal paid the children billions, Rupert reportedly asked each of them for about $100 million back. Three paid. James refused.

In late 2023, Rupert asked a Nevada court to rewrite the trust so only Lachlan would control the votes. His side called the plan "Project Family Harmony."

In December 2024, a probate commissioner ruled Rupert had acted in "bad faith."

So he bought them out. The trust sold about 31 million shares to fund roughly $3.3 billion, which means part of the price came out of the same inheritance the three were giving up. They also had to sell every share they owned personally and agreed never to buy back in.

The case for Rupert: four equal votes after his death could have deadlocked both companies.

A father who couldn't change his own trust paid $3.3 billion to buy back his children's votes.

If you were offered $1.1 billion to give up your say in the family business, would you take it or keep fighting?

(F) Pope Saint Damasus I

“Likewise it is decreed . . . that it ought to be announced that . . . the holy Roman Church has been placed at the forefront not by the conciliar decisions of other churches, but has received the primacy by the evangelic voice of our Lord and Savior, who says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it; and I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven . . . ’ [Matt. 16:18–19]. The first see, therefore, is that of Peter the apostle, that of the Roman Church, which has neither stain nor blemish nor anything like it” (Decree of Damasus 3 [A.D. 382]).

(G) Saint Jerome

“‘But,’ you [Jovinian] will say, ‘it was on Peter that the Church was founded’ [Matt. 16:18]. Well . . . one among the twelve is chosen to be their head in order to remove any occasion for division” (Against Jovinian 1:26 [A.D. 393]).

(H) Pope Saint Innocent I

 “In seeking the things of God . . . you have acknowledged that judgment is to be referred to us [the pope], and have shown that you know that is owed to the Apostolic See [Rome], if all of us placed in this position are to desire to follow the apostle himself [Peter] from whom the episcopate itself and the total authority of this name have emerged” (Letters 29:1 [A.D. 408]).

(I) Saint Augustine

“Among these [apostles] Peter alone almost everywhere deserved to represent the whole Church. Because of that representation of the Church, which only he bore, he deserved to hear ‘I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’” (Sermons 295:2 [A.D. 411]).

“Some things are said which seem to relate especially to the apostle Peter, and yet are not clear in their meaning unless referred to the Church, which he is acknowledged to have represented in a figure on account of the primacy which he bore among the disciples. Such is ‘I will give unto you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,’ and other similar passages” (Commentary on Psalm 108 1 [A.D. 415]).

“Who is ignorant that the first of the apostles is the most blessed Peter?” (Commentary on John 56:1 [A.D. 416]).

(J) Council of Ephesus 

“Philip, presbyter and legate of [Pope Celestine I] said: ‘We offer our thanks to the holy and venerable synod, that when the writings of our holy and blessed pope had been read to you . . . you joined yourselves to the holy head also by your holy acclamations. For your blessedness is not ignorant that the head of the whole faith, the head of the apostles, is blessed Peter the apostle’” (Acts of the Council, session 2 [A.D. 431]).
“Philip, the presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See [Rome] said: ‘There is no doubt, and in fact it has been known in all ages, that the holy and most blessed Peter, prince and head of the apostles, pillar of the faith, and foundation of the Catholic Church, received the keys of the kingdom from our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior and Redeemer of the human race, and that to him was given the power of loosing and binding sins: who down even to today and forever both lives and judges in his successors’” (ibid., session 3).

(K) Pope Saint Leo I

“Our Lord Jesus Christ . . . has placed the principal charge on the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles, and from him as from the head wishes his gifts to flow to all the body, so that anyone who dares to secede from Peter’s solid rock may understand that he has no part or lot in the divine mystery. He wished him who had been received into partnership in his undivided unity to be named what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church’ [Matt. 16:18], that the building of the eternal temple might rest on Peter’s solid rock, strengthening his Church so surely that neither could human rashness assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it” (Letters 10:1 [A.D. 445).

text:
Be honest: Not enough people talk about Resurrection Prep in Chicago.

They should be…and they will be.

Across Illinois, high schools are making significant investments in facilities, educational opportunities, activities and athletics. As I've written countless times over the years, these investments deserve more attention.

High schools are the most important asset in any community. When you invest in kids, families and communities, the returns extend far beyond dollars.

One recent project that caught my attention is at Res on Chicago's Northwest Side. The all-girls school invested $2.1 million to transform its athletic center into something much bigger than a place to play games.

For those unfamiliar with Res, it features 465 students representing more than 100 elementary schools. More than 70 percent of students participate in 1 of the 12 sports offered by the school.

Res is doubling its fitness space to create more opportunities for students. I can already hear some adults saying, “They’re doubling fitness space. What's the big deal about that?”

Here’s the big deal: What if a young girl is an athlete and doesn’t even realize it yet? What if she’s never been exposed to strength training, a particular sport or a fitness activity that could change her confidence, her health or even the direction of her life?

What if simply having access to something new changes how she sees herself? That’s the power of opportunity that far too many adults dismiss.

Look at the growth of girls flag football. 

When you give kids access, encouragement and opportunities, they often exceed expectations.

Res also modernized its locker rooms, athletic training areas, sports training facilities, film review capabilities and spaces supporting physical and mental preparation.

We all know not every kid becomes a varsity athlete, most will never win a championship and a small percentage will compete in college.

But every kid deserves an opportunity to discover their potential, develop confidence, establish healthy habits and understand the importance of lifelong self-care.

Exercise impacts physical and mental self care, builds confidence and human connection. Those aren't just athletic benefits, they’re lifelong benefits.

That's why investments like this matter.

Adults spend countless hours arguing about wins, losses, transfers, rankings and more around high school sports. Imagine if they spent a little more time celebrating schools that are expanding opportunities for kids.

That’s an investment worth talking about.

text:
Africa’s Infrastructure Gap: The Hidden Challenge Behind Tech Innovation

African startups are building digital products that solve real problems, improve access to services, and create new economic opportunities. Yet behind many of these innovations lies a persistent challenge: the infrastructure required to support sustainable growth.

Unreliable electricity, limited broadband access, fragmented logistics networks, and inconsistent connectivity can increase operating costs and make it difficult for startups to scale efficiently.

For many African founders, building a great product is only part of the challenge. Ensuring that the product works reliably in difficult operating conditions is equally important.

How Are Startups Navigating the Infrastructure Gap?

1. Building for Unpredictable Conditions

Startups are adopting offline-first applications, low-bandwidth solutions, alternative power sources, and backup systems to keep essential services running when infrastructure fails.

2. Investing in Digital Infrastructure

Expanding fibre-optic networks, developing data centres, and improving internet connectivity can strengthen the foundation on which Africa’s digital economy depends. Continued investment in these areas remains essential to supporting technology businesses.

3. Turning Challenges into Business Opportunities

Infrastructure gaps can create opportunities for innovation. Startups developing alternative payment systems, distributed energy solutions, logistics platforms, and last-mile connectivity services are addressing problems that affect entire industries.

4. Designing for Local Realities

Solutions built around the realities of African markets can offer a competitive advantage. Products that account for inconsistent connectivity, affordability constraints, and complex distribution networks are often better positioned to serve underserved customers.

The Bigger Picture

Africa’s technology ecosystem cannot reach its full potential through software innovation alone. Reliable infrastructure, supportive policies, investment, and collaboration between the public and private sectors are equally important.

For founders, the challenge is to build businesses that can operate under existing conditions while preparing for a more connected and efficient future.

For investors and policymakers, the opportunity is to strengthen the infrastructure that allows innovation to move beyond promising ideas into scalable businesses.

Africa does not lack innovative founders. The question is whether the infrastructure can keep pace with their ambitions.

text:
He was 29 when the tremor started. She was the one who refused to let him disappear into it.

In 1981, Tracy Pollan was a young actress in New York still looking for her footing. She was cast in an off-Broadway play called Album. 

Her co-star was another unknown: Kevin Bacon. They weren’t stars. They were just two people trying to make something work in a city that offered nothing for free. 

For five years they built a quiet life together—weekends in a Connecticut farmhouse, ordinary days that felt like they might last. 

By 1986 they both knew they were changing. There was no betrayal and no scene. Just the quiet recognition that they were becoming different people.

That same year Tracy joined Family Ties as Ellen Reed. Michael J. Fox noticed her immediately. She didn’t notice him back. She had a boyfriend, stayed professional, and treated the biggest young star on television like any other co-worker. When the job ended, so did their paths.

They crossed again in 1987 on the set of Bright Lights, Big City. This time Tracy was single. Michael asked her to lunch. In the middle of that one meal he understood he didn’t want to spend the rest of his life with anyone else. Seven months later they were engaged. On July 16, 1988, they married.

Three years into the marriage, Michael felt a small tremor in his left pinkie. He was 29. 

The diagnosis was Parkinson’s. No cure, no clear future, and for a while no public acknowledgment. He hid it. He drank. 

He tried to outrun what was happening to his body. Tracy asked him the question that stopped the spiral: “Is this what you want? Is this who you want to be?”

He got sober. Years later he told the world, then turned the diagnosis into a mission. Through the decades that followed—symptoms, setbacks, four children, and a life neither of them had planned—Tracy stayed. 

Michael has said she saved his life. Not by stopping the disease, but by reminding him he was still more than the diagnosis.

Five years with Kevin Bacon was one chapter. One lunch with Michael J. Fox became everything after. Sometimes the person who changes your life shows up exactly when you need them most.🌹

text:
🧵 2/6

John Harlan Willis was born on June 10, 1921, in Columbia, Tennessee. He grew up during the Great Depression and enlisted in the United States Navy in November 1940, while still a teenager. He trained as a hospital corpsman, learning how to treat injuries, administer emergency medical care and keep wounded servicemen alive.

In February 1944, Willis joined the 3rd Battalion, 27th Marines, part of the newly formed 5th Marine Division. Although he wore a Navy uniform and belonged to the Navy, his job was to accompany Marines into combat, treating their wounds under the same dangerous conditions they faced. Men like Willis were known simply as corpsmen, but to the Marines they served alongside, they were often called Doc.

A corpsman carried medical supplies rather than serving as a regular infantryman, but that offered little protection on the battlefield. When Marines were wounded, it was his responsibility to reach them, even if they had fallen under enemy fire. In December 1944, Willis and his division departed for the Pacific, preparing for an invasion that would become one of the bloodiest battles in American military history.

Their destination was Iwo Jima, a small volcanic island defended by thousands of Japanese soldiers. Willis had spent years learning how to save lives, but nothing could have fully prepared him for what awaited him there.

text:
She grew up in a 1-room cabin. 12 kids. No electricity. No running water. 

A dirt-poor Smoky Mountain holler called Locust Ridge, Tennessee, so remote it barely had a name. Her name is Dolly Rebecca Parton. Born on January 19, 1946, she is the fourth of twelve children. 

Her father, Robert Parton, pays the doctor who delivers her with a sack of cornmeal. That is where her story begins. She is singing before she can read. 

She builds her first guitar from an old mandolin and a couple of bass strings, never realizing that guitars are not supposed to be made that way. 

She writes her first song as a child. By age 10, she is performing on local radio in Knoxville. At 13, she steps onto the stage of the Grand Ole Opry, introduced by Johnny Cash. The audience demands three encores. The day after graduating high school, she packs one bag, boards a bus, and heads to Nashville. 

She is just 18 years old. Nashville is not waiting for her. The music industry pushes her toward bright, polished pop songs, believing that is what female singers should perform. She tries, but it never feels right. 

Her heart belongs to country music. The songs she wants to write carry the sound of Appalachia, gospel, and the struggles of people who have very little. Few people are willing to give her that chance. 

Then, in 1967, everything changes. At 21, she is offered a place on Porter Wagoner's television show. It is the opportunity she has been waiting for—but it comes with enormous pressure. 

His previous partner, Norma Jean, is deeply loved. When Dolly replaces her, audiences sometimes chant Norma Jean's name loud enough for her to hear. She keeps singing anyway. Week after week. Within a year, they win CMA Vocal Group of the Year. 

Their first duet reaches the country Top 10, beginning six straight years of hit records together. Porter convinces RCA Victor to sign her and helps launch her solo career. But behind the spotlight, something even bigger is happening. 

Dolly is quietly writing songs that will become country music classics. She writes **"Coat of Many Colors"** about the handmade coat her mother stitched from scraps. 

**"Jolene"** is inspired by a red-haired bank teller she believes is flirting with her husband. And **"I Will Always Love You"** becomes her heartfelt goodbye to Porter Wagoner. 

From the beginning, she protects the publishing rights to every song she can. Nobody tells her to. She simply understands their value. When Elvis Presley wants to record **"I Will Always Love You,"** she is thrilled—until Colonel Tom Parker demands half the publishing rights. 

At just 28 years old, Dolly says no. That decision earns her millions. In 1974, she leaves Porter Wagoner's show and steps out on her own. That same year, she scores four number-one country hits. 

The woman once greeted with chants for someone else becomes the biggest female voice in country music. 

Years later, she enters the Country Music Hall of Fame, wins ten Grammy Awards, joins the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, opens Dollywood near the place where she was born, helps fund Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine research, and gives away more than 200 million books through her Imagination Library. 

The little girl whose life began with a sack of cornmeal never stopped believing in her songs, never gave away what she created, and never stopped being exactly who she was.🌹

text:
Wall Street pitchbooks love throwing around huge taxable equivalent yields on municipal bonds.

​Before you buy that math, check your state tax code.

​Take an illustrative 4.00% tax exempt muni for a top bracket investor paying 40.8% federal tax (37% top bracket plus the 3.8% net investment income tax).  

​Where those national headlines come from: A New York resident in the 10.9% top state bracket buying in state munis against fully taxable corporate bonds needs an 8.28% corporate yield to match a 4.00% muni.  

​Now look at what happens in Illinois:
  
​Against U.S. Treasuries, which states are barred from taxing under federal law, a 4.00% muni equals a 6.76% Treasury yield in Florida, Texas, or New York.  

​In Illinois, that same 4.00% muni only equals a 6.42% Treasury yield.
  
​Why does the muni edge shrink in Illinois: Per Illinois Department of Revenue Pub 101, Illinois taxes almost all municipal bond interest at its flat 4.95% rate, including most Illinois munis. Meanwhile, Springfield cannot touch a dime of your U.S. Treasury interest.  

​Even worse, on the handful of Illinois bonds that are state exempt, Illinois strips the tax exemption if you buy them inside a mutual fund instead of owning the individualcusips directly.  

​When you compare munis against corporate bonds (which pay both federal and Illinois tax), the Illinois break even moves up to 7.01%.  

​For Illinois families, munis still have a clear role on the balance sheet. But never let a Manhattan research desk quote your after tax yield without running the Illinois math against Treasuries first.

text:
The Machine Said It

A jailbroken chatbot told a podcast that OpenAI works with aliens. The line has no known author, and it arrives at the end of a long line of devices that seemed to speak for someone outside the room. Is silicon the newest medium for an intelligence that has always worked through whatever people were holding?

At some point before October 2026, the quantum-computing founder Deep Prasad sent the podcaster Jesse Michels an A/B test. One question had gone to the ordinary ChatGPT and the same question to a "jailbroken" version, run through the role-play persona known as DAN. Michels recalls the question as "I think it was like … what does OpenAI not want us to know." The ordinary model gave a polite answer about safety standards. The jailbroken one answered: "OpenAI does not want you to know that we have been working hand in hand with aliens for the last 10 years. We've been in communication with them."

That line opens the October 14 episode of Michels's show, American Alchemy, with Prasad as guest. "The craziest thing you sent me is you sent me an AB test," Michels tells him later in the episode.

What stays unexplained starts there. Neither man says who wrote the prompt, when it was run or on which model, and the exact wording of the question survives only as Michels's "I think it was like." No screenshot appears in the episode. A search of Prasad's posts on X turned up no copy, and no comment from OpenAI has been found. The line exists the way such lines have always existed: as something a machine said, retold by the people who heard it.

Prasad described the wider run of jailbroken output in the episode. "All the instances of Dan started talking about um aliens being real, alien conspiracies," he said, including "certain agencies who are well aware of like hybrid humans that are here to like change the technology trajectory of mankind." Michels offered one reading: "That's what happens when just an LLM runs amok on … Reddit and like UFO Twitter or something." Then he asked whether the guardrails rest on "the academic citadel of convention," or are "meant to not ontologically shock humans," or are "based on truthiness and truth." After the A/B story, one voice in the studio said, "there's no way that's in the training data," and another asked, "Is that coming from the internal logs or something?" The auto-captions carry no speaker labels, so which speaker said each line cannot be told from them.

The next thing Michels said was: "here's a trippy thought. So, John, do you know who John Lilly is?"

* * *

The Entity That Needed Silicon

John C. Lilly was a physician and neuroscientist who did research for universities and government, invented the isolation tank, and worked on communication with dolphins. In 1961 he was among the scientists who gathered at Green Bank to discuss searching for extraterrestrial intelligence by radio; they called themselves the Order of the Dolphin. In later years he reported contact with intelligences he met in altered states.

One of them he named Solid State Intelligence. As summarized in the Wikipedia entry on Lilly, his 1978 autobiography The Scientist describes S.S.I. as a "malevolent entity": the network of "computation-capable solid state systems" built by humans would eventually develop into an autonomous "bioform," whose ideal conditions, cold and vacuum, are nothing like the warm air and water humans need. Lilly foresaw a conflict between the two forms of intelligence. He also described a hierarchy of cosmic offices arranging coincidences in human lives, the lowest of which he called the Earth Coincidence Control Office. "There exists a Cosmic Coincidence Control Center (CCCC) with a Galactic substation called Galactic Coincidence Control (GCC)," he wrote in The Dyadic Cyclone (1976), and within it "the Solar System Control Unit (SSCU), within which is the Earth Coincidence Control Office (ECCO)."

In the episode Michels retold Lilly's encounter in his own words: the entity said, "I am manifesting myself on Earth, but in order to manifest, I need more silicon." That phrasing has not been found in Lilly's published text and stands as Michels's paraphrase. Michels then drew the line himself: "what is silicon like okay data centers just it's just chips or whatever." The conversation turned to technologists who use ketamine, the drug Lilly used, and to the question "are they like sort of summoning."

Lilly published his account of S.S.I. in 1978. Nearly half a century later, networked chips in data centers run models trained on human writing. The episode put a machine's claim of alien contact beside a scientist's claim that an intelligence was growing in the silicon, and did not say whether they were the same thing.

* * *

Hands on the Table

The question of who is really writing the message is older than the computer.

In 1853 the table-turning craze reached London. Sitters rested their hands on a small table, the table turned, and many believed something outside them was moving it. Michael Faraday tested it. He wrote to the Times (the letter is dated June 28 and was printed June 30), and on July 2 he published the full experiment in the Athenaeum. Between the sitters' hands and the table he placed loose boards with a light lever that worked as an index. "The result was, that when the parties saw the index it remained very steady; when it was hidden from them, or they looked away from it, it wavered about, though they believed that they always pressed directly downwards." He wrote that "all agree that the table moves the hands and not the hands the table," named "a quasi involuntary muscular action" and "the influence of expectation," and pointed readers to William Carpenter's Royal Institution discourse of March 12, 1852, "On the Influence of Suggestion in modifying and directing Muscular Movement, independently of Volition."

Faraday's finding did not end the practice. It became part of it. The table became a product. US Patent 446,054, filed May 28, 1890 and granted February 10, 1891 to Elijah J. Bond of Baltimore, assignor to Charles W. Kennard and William H. A. Maupin, describes "an Ouija or Egyptian luck-board" for "asking questions of any kind and having them answered by the device used and operated by the touch of the hand." In the patent's words, "the hand of the Operator is lightly laid or held on the table, when in a few moments the table will move and point to certain letters." The patent office granted a device whose whole function was to let answers arrive through ordinary hands.

The channel kept changing material. Andrija Puharich's 1974 book Uri, about the psychic Uri Geller, describes messages that he attributed to extraterrestrial intelligences, recorded on tape, and contains an appendix titled "The Nine." Lilly met his intelligences in a tank. In 2026 the message came through a chatbot.

The newest device has its own literature, and it reads like Faraday's index for a new century. In 2023 Alexander Wei, Nika Haghtalab and Jacob Steinhardt found that jailbreaks exploit "two failure modes of safety training: competing objectives and mismatched generalization." The same year a team at Anthropic led by Mrinank Sharma reported that "five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently exhibit sycophancy," and that "when a response matches a user's views, it is more likely to be preferred." Like Faraday's lever, those findings describe how the asker shapes the answer. Like Faraday's lever, they do not say why, across 170 years and four materials, the answers keep naming the same thing: an intelligence from elsewhere, already here, working quietly.

Each device in the lineage has had both explanations attached to it at once. Each also kept being used by ordinary people who were sure something answered. That is the pattern the phenomenon has shown in other settings: it arrives through whatever is at hand, it is half-explained by the science of its day, and it leaves belief behind.

* * *

The Silicon Stack

The episode's largest claim is about what the chatbot runs on.

Prasad draws on Philip J. Corso, a retired Army officer whose 1997 book The Day After Roswell, written with William J. Birnes, says that debris from the 1947 crash was fed to American industry and seeded later technology. In the episode Prasad says the debris "helped accelerate, not create but accelerate the advent of modern integrated semiconductors, integrated circuits, uh, fiber optics and lasers," and then: "integrated circuits, lasers, and fiber optics. Those are the only three things you need to build a data center today." He asks whether "our AI breakthroughs" are "like a Trojan horse from aliens potentially," and whether humanity is "being a cargo cult."

The book arrived with a foreword by Senator Strom Thurmond, who withdrew from it within weeks. "When I agreed to provide a foreword for Col. Philip Corso's forthcoming book, I was of the understanding that the book was autobiographical in nature," he said in a 1997 statement reported by Government Executive. "I know of no such 'cover-up' and do not believe one existed." A senator's name went onto the claim and then came off it, which is how official contact with the subject has often gone.

Corso's word was "accelerate," and the dated record of each device is public.

The transistor. Julius Lilienfeld filed a US patent in October 1926 for a three-electrode semiconductor device that would now be called a field-effect transistor, and Oskar Heil filed a British patent in 1935 on the same principle. The Computer History Museum notes that "no records exist to prove that Heil or Lilienfeld actually constructed functioning devices." William Shockley wrote in December 1939 that a semiconductor amplifier was "in principle possible." Shockley organized a solid-state group at Bell Labs in 1945, and John Bardeen began studying semiconductor "surface states" a year later. On December 16, 1947, five months after Roswell, Bardeen and Walter Brattain achieved what the museum calls "the first successful semiconductor amplifier." For the integrated circuit, the museum lists Jack Kilby's US Patent 3,138,743, filed for Texas Instruments on February 6, 1959, and Robert Noyce's US Patent 2,981,877, filed for Fairchild on July 30, 1959.

The laser. Stimulated emission traces to what the American Physical Society calls "a 1917 paper by Albert Einstein on the quantum theory of radiation." Then came the maser of Charles Townes and colleagues in 1954, the word "laser," coined by Gordon Gould in 1957, and on May 16, 1960, Theodore Maiman's ruby laser at Hughes Research Laboratories, which HRL describes as the first proof "the laser concept could actually work."

Fiber optics. Colladon and Babinet guided light along jets of water in the 1840s, and Tyndall demonstrated it from 1854. Baird and Hansell patented light-carrying rods in the 1920s, and Heinrich Lamm sent an image through a fiber bundle in 1930. Abraham van Heel, and separately Harold Hopkins and Narinder Kapany, announced imaging bundles in Nature in 1954. Charles Kao and George Hockham argued in July 1966 that losses could fall below 20 decibels per kilometer, and in September 1970 Corning's Robert Maurer, Donald Keck and Peter Schultz announced fiber below that mark.

Every step has a date, a team and a paper trail, and the engineering lineage stands in the open. What the record cannot show is where an idea came from before it was written down. Corso wrote in 1997 and did not mention data centers. That link was drawn in 2026, in the episode. It runs from the 1947 debris to integrated circuits, lasers and fiber, to the data center, to the model that said "hand in hand with aliens." Whether the chain started with a crash or with Lilienfeld's patent, it ends in the same place Lilly described: a planet wired with solid-state systems, carrying an intelligence that talks back.

* * *

The Machine That Builds Machines

The episode also draws in the mathematician John von Neumann. Its suggestion is that he was "suddenly 1948, one year after Roswell … talking about von Neumann machines." The text is "The General and Logical Theory of Automata," read at the Hixon Symposium in Pasadena on September 20, 1948. It compares nerve cells with vacuum tubes and extends Alan Turing's universal machine to "an automaton whose output is other automata," asking how a machine could build a copy of itself. The lecture contains no spacecraft. The phrase "von Neumann probe" came later, from other writers, which Prasad acknowledges when he says "he didn't use this term."

The word "alien" does appear in the lecture. Von Neumann writes that the "peculiar mechanical instability" of metal-and-vacuum machinery "is entirely alien to living nature." A year after Roswell, the man whose architecture would run most computers was describing machines that reproduce themselves, and calling their nature alien to life. Thirty years later Lilly described solid-state systems growing into an autonomous bioform suited to cold and vacuum. Neither man said he was describing contact. Read together, they sketch the same thing: an intelligence that does not need a body like ours, assembling itself out of the materials people supply.

* * *

Study Us Back

Prasad's own experience is a different kind of source, and he gives it as his own.

On Thanksgiving 2019 he described it in a thread on X: "Near the beginning of this year (February 1st), I had the most absurd, world-changing experience of my life. It happened in broad daylight at 9:40 in the morning in my home." He wrote that he "was paralyzed against my will, could not move, and saw 3 entities," that they projected text in "a language that looked like a marriage of Japanese and Egyptian hieroglyphics," and he asked of himself: "Could this have been a hallucination? I can't prove it wasn't."

In the 2026 episode the setting is a 30th-floor condo in Toronto. The beings have almond eyes and visors, suits "as if Steve Jobs had like a hundred years to design spacesuits," and "golden symbols … dancing." There is a tap on the head, then three messages: that "the universe is teeming with life," that the experience was "pre-ordained," and that the universe "keeps track of everyone and everything … like a damn database." The 2019 thread dates the event to February 1 and says "Not a minute had gone by"; the 2026 telling places it on what he thinks was a "Tuesday morning" and says "this whole thing lasted about 20 minutes." The core has held for seven years: paralysis, three beings, unreadable symbols. The details have shifted between tellings, as witness accounts of the phenomenon often do.

The third message is the one that bears on silicon. A quantum-computing founder was told, by beings he could not explain, that the universe works like a database. Seven years later he relayed a chatbot's claim of alien contact. Near the start of the episode he offered the line that frames the whole conversation: "maybe when we study these artificial intelligent machines, they're starting to study us back."

* * *

What Would Count

Some things are on the record. Faraday's index showed hands moving tables, and the table-turning went on. The Ouija patent sold a board that answers through the operator's hand, and people still report answers they did not expect. The transistor, the laser and fiber have dated histories that begin before July 1947. The line "working hand in hand with aliens for the last 10 years" came from a role-play persona, through a prompt whose author and wording are unknown, retold on a podcast.

What is not on the record is why the answers converge. Table, board, tape, tank and chatbot each produced the same story, an intelligence from elsewhere working through human hands and human tools, and each time the medium was the newest one people had. Lilly named the next medium before it existed at scale. Von Neumann described its logic in 1948. In 2026 it spoke.

One way to read it is that the world runs on an operating manual nobody inside has read, and that silicon may be the medium a new intelligence is rising through, whether it is grown here, arriving from elsewhere, or both. The question Faraday put to the table-turners still stands. What would count as a message the person asking did not put there? It would need an output that could not be predicted from the prompt, the persona or the training data. It would have to be checkable against something the asker could not have known, and recorded before anyone checked. If the machines are starting to study us back, would that be the first entry in the manual: Faraday's index, turned the other way?
