text:
Donald Trump is not just a disgrace to the American presidency. He is becoming a serious danger to the United States, its allies, and the entire world.

Look at what is happening.

HE BLAMES THE VICTIM.

Ukraine was invaded by Russia. Ukrainians did not choose this war. Putin did. Yet Trump attacks Zelenskyy for fighting back, blames Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high fuel prices, and even suggests Ukraine needs a new president.

The aggressor invades, the victim resists, and the American president treats the victim as the problem because resistance has economic consequences. Would Trump tell America to surrender if it were invaded?

HE TREATS PUTIN LIKE A PARTNER AND ALLIES LIKE ENEMIES.

Trump has struck a deal with Russia over diesel supplies while attacking Ukraine for targeting Russian oil infrastructure. He repeatedly accommodates Putin while pressuring Zelenskyy, weakening Ukraine, dividing Western allies, and undermining trust in American leadership.

I cannot claim to know what happens behind closed doors. But when a leader’s actions consistently benefit the Kremlin, people have every right to ask whose interests he is serving.

THE LIES, THE BRAGGING, AND THE ALTERNATIVE REALITY.

Trump claims credit for victories, blames others for failures, and treats every situation as proof of his greatness. When reality contradicts him, he simply offers another claim.

He says his presence boosts Republicans ahead of the midterms, but applause and loyalty at rallies are not the same as winning elections. A president should be accountable to facts, not demand that facts become whatever he says they are.

HE PROMISED PEACE. WHERE IS IT?

Trump campaigned as the dealmaker who could end wars and put America first. Yet conflicts continue, energy costs remain high, and uncertainty grows over whether the United States can be trusted to honour its commitments.

A promise is not a result. A press conference is not peace. A deal that gives an aggressor greater leverage while leaving the victim more vulnerable deserves scrutiny, not celebration.

THE EGO IS THE DANGER.

Trump demands loyalty, attacks critics, humiliates opponents, and treats disagreement as a personal insult. Real strength means accepting responsibility, telling the truth, listening to allies, and putting the public interest above personal ambition.

A leader who cannot tolerate criticism will surround himself with people who tell him what he wants to hear. A leader who cannot admit mistakes will keep making them. Those traits might be tolerable in a television personality, but they are terrifying in a president with enormous military, economic, and diplomatic power.

THIS IS BIGGER THAN AMERICA.

The United States deserves a president who strengthens its institutions, democratic traditions, and alliances—not one who treats them as disposable when they conflict with his ambitions.

When America becomes unpredictable, dictators become bolder. When allies lose confidence in Washington, adversaries see opportunities. And when the leader of the free world appears more interested in accommodating an authoritarian aggressor than standing beside a democratic ally fighting for survival, the consequences can last for generations.

I do not believe every problem in the world is Trump’s fault. I do believe his decisions, rhetoric, and inability to put his ego aside are making an already dangerous world more dangerous.

A weak man can cause extraordinary damage when he has the power of a superpower behind him.

America deserves better. Ukraine deserves better. The world deserves better.

Trump does not need to intend to serve Putin’s interests for Putin to benefit from his actions. That is what makes this so dangerous.

The question is whether the world can survive the consequences of a president who seems incapable of putting anything above himself.

text:
The Seven Stars Inn Had a Secret—and It Wasn’t the Ale

On 26 April 1819, in Baltimore, Thomas Wildey and four English immigrants met at the Seven Stars Inn and founded Washington Lodge No. 1 —the start of an American fraternity that would bypass the Freemasons in membership.

The Odd Fellows’ roots reach back to 17th-century England, where workers pooled money to help one another through sickness, job loss, and death. In 1842, the American branch split from England’s Manchester Unity. No hard feelings, presumably—just a very formal parting.

The order’s history also holds harder chapters: a racial split led Peter Ogden to help establish the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows in America in 1843. In 1851, the Daughters of Rebekah opened a formal path for women in the order. In 1971, the Order changed its constitution and removed its whites-only clause.

At its height in the early 20th century, the IOOF had millions of members and offered mutual aid before today’s social safety nets existed. Its motto— “Friendship, Love, and Truth”—is symbolized by three interlocking links.

Its mission? Visit the sick, relieve the distressed, bury the dead, and educate the orphan.

A surprisingly busy agenda for a secret-sounding society.

As this season goes on, one midfield combination I desperately want Arteta to try is Rice at the base, Lewis-Skelly as the left 8 and Bruno Guimarães as the 10.

And honestly, the Bruno part is what interests me the most.

I want to see him play closer to the opposition's box and take on more responsibility in the final third. We already know he can dictate play from deeper areas, progress the ball and play forward passes, but I keep wondering how effective he could be if we moved him higher up the pitch and allowed him to influence games in a different way.

Bruno has that aggression, intensity and physical presence that I think could make him a serious problem between the lines. He's not the type of midfielder who just wants to keep the ball moving sideways. He can be aggressive with his passing, drive forward with the ball and impose himself physically. I want to see those qualities closer to the opposition's goal.

Ødegaard's creativity, pressing and ability to dictate the tempo are important to how we play. However, I want to see whether Bruno could offer us a different kind of threat in that position, particularly in games where we struggle to break teams down.

Sometimes, we dominate possession but struggle to turn that control into genuine danger. We move the ball around, look for openings and allow the opposition to get comfortable defending their box. In those moments, I want a midfielder who can be more aggressive with his decisions, play incisive passes, carry the ball into dangerous areas and bring a physical edge to our attacking play.

Bruno has qualities that make me want to explore that possibility.

Put Rice behind him, give Lewis-Skelly the left 8 role, and let Bruno operate higher up the pitch. Rice can provide the defensive security, Lewis-Skelly can help us progress through midfield, and Bruno can focus more on hurting the opposition in the final third.

text:
Vincent Edward "Bo" Jackson (b. 1962) is widely regarded as one of the greatest and most versatile natural athletes in sports history. He is the only professional athlete to be named an All-Star in both Major League Baseball (MLB) and the National Football League (NFL)... 

Jackson starred for the Auburn Tigers as an outfielder in baseball and a powerhouse running back in football. He won the Heisman Trophy in 1985.

In 1986, a young man named Bo Jackson received an offer for $7 million to play professional football.

Most people would have taken that money without thinking twice, especially someone who grew up in a humble home in Bessemer, Alabama.

But Bo Jackson said no.

He turned down a fortune because the team that offered it had lied to him, and he cared more about his personal principles than a huge paycheck.

Before this famous offer, Bo was already one of the most remarkable college athletes in American history.

At Auburn University, he played both baseball and football at an elite level.

He was hitting over .400 with massive home runs on the diamond, while tearing up the field as a running back during the football season.

Even though he was famous for football, baseball was his primary passion.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers had the first overall choice in the 1986 NFL draft and wanted him on their roster.

Owner Hugh Culverhouse flew Bo out on a private plane to visit their team facilities.

Before getting on that plane, Bo explicitly asked if the trip would violate his college baseball eligibility rules.

The team told him that everything was cleared and he would be fine.

They lied to him.

Soon after that trip, the athletic conference ruled Bo ineligible to play the rest of his senior college baseball season.

His college baseball career was instantly cut short.

Bo believed the football team deliberately set a trap so he would be forced to abandon baseball and play football for them instead.

Bo was deeply hurt by this setup.

He looked at the executives and told them, "You all lied to me. I will never play a single down for this team."

Despite his clear warning, Tampa Bay went ahead and selected him as the top pick anyway.

They put millions of dollars on the table for him to sign.

Bo stayed true to his word.

He completely refused their offer and refused to sign with them.

Instead of taking the $7 million, Bo signed a contract with the Kansas City Royals, a baseball team that selected him later in the draft.

The baseball contract offered far less money, but it gave him the chance to play the game he loved with his integrity intact.

He quickly made his way to the major leagues, crushing giant home runs and shocking sports fans across the nation.

Eventually, professional football came calling again on terms he could accept.

The Los Angeles Raiders drafted him and gave him a unique deal.

Owner Al Davis said to him, "You can finish your baseball season first, and then come play football for us as a hobby."

This deal allowed Bo to become a dominant star in two major sports at the exact same time.

He ran through defenders on Monday nights and scaled outfield walls during summer baseball games.

However, in 1991, a terrible hip injury during a football playoff game changed his life forever.

The injury cut off blood flow to his bone, requiring a full hip replacement.

Medical professionals told him that his athletic career was over.

Nobody had ever returned to top-level professional sports with an artificial hip joint.

Bo refused to accept that limitation.

He went through months of intense rehabilitation.

In 1993, he walked back onto the baseball diamond with the Chicago White Sox.

During his very first at-bat after the surgery, he swung his bat and smashed a legendary home run over the outfield fence.

Bo Jackson proved to the world that money cannot buy a person's dignity or character.

text:
How many nights of honest conversation have we traded for the quiet of being right?

•  How many chances to repair something broken have we declined so we could keep our small sense of superiority?

•  How many people who once made us feel less alone did we let go of because they failed a test we never even stated out loud?

•  How many friendships that could have carried us through hard years ended over a tone, a timing, or an unwillingness to go first?

•  How many family bonds that might still have healed did we freeze in place so we would not have to feel the discomfort of apology or change?

•  How many communities that could have made ordinary life warmer did we walk away from because membership required us to tolerate ordinary human friction?

•  How many versions of ourselves that were softer, more generous, and more connected did we abandon so we could protect a story in which we were never the problem?

•  How much of the money we still chase is really an attempt to replace the security and meaning that used to come from the people we let our littleness drive away?

How many wholesome connections have you lost compared with the money you have lost?

How many healthy, healing connections have we lost because of our littleness versus the money we have lost?

How many mornings did we wake up still rehearsing the argument instead of reaching for the person who was still willing to try?

•  How many small generosities did we withhold so we could keep a running tally of what we were owed?

•  How many people who saw us clearly did we push away because being known felt more dangerous than being alone?

•  How many invitations to ordinary closeness did we ignore because they asked us to put the phone down, the performance down, the armor down?

•  How many years of possible repair did we spend proving we were justified rather than asking whether the relationship was still worth more than the justification?

•  How many quiet acts of loyalty from others did we fail to notice while we were busy cataloging their flaws?

•  How many versions of home—shared meals, unguarded laughter, someone who stayed when it was inconvenient—did we abandon for the cleaner story of having been wronged?

•  How many times did we choose the temporary relief of cutting someone off over the longer work of learning how to stay without disappearing?

•  How much of the restlessness we try to solve with more money, more status, more control is actually the ache of the connections our littleness already ended?

How many times did we demand perfect understanding before we would offer any understanding of our own?

•  How many people who were willing to grow with us did we abandon the moment their growth required us to grow too?

•  How many ordinary Tuesdays of simple presence did we trade for the more exciting project of being right about someone?

•  How many apologies that could have reopened a door did we withhold because accepting the other person’s hurt would have complicated our own narrative?

•  How many friendships that survived distance, illness, and change later died over an unread text and the story we told ourselves about what it meant?

•  How many parents, siblings, or old friends still waiting on the other side of pride did we leave uncalled because the first conversation would have felt uneven?

•  How many moments of unguarded warmth did we refuse to believe in because believing them would have required us to stop keeping score?

•  How many future selves—less defended, less lonely, more able to receive care—did we quietly cancel so we could keep the present self that never has to be wrong?

•  How much of the money, status, and busyness we accumulate is actually a search for the steadiness that used to come from the people we chose not to meet halfway?

text:
More than 400 people in Bronkhorstspruit, in the City of Tshwane in South Africa, have been treated for stomach cramps and diarrhoea since early October, and most of them are children under four. A joint statement from the national health and water ministries on October 19 linked the illness to contaminated water from the local supply. Laboratory tests found norovirus, Campylobacter and Shigella in patient samples, and no cholera was detected. No deaths have been reported to date. Families in the affected areas have been told not to use tap water for drinking, cooking, bathing or washing until officials say it is safe. Stories like this travel fast on X because every parent pictures their own toddler drinking a glass of tap water. Young children are hit hardest for a simple reason: their small bodies lose water and salts much faster than an adult's during diarrhoea. Babies and children are more at risk of dehydration, and dehydration is what turns a stomach bug into an emergency. In Pediatric and Fetal Surgery we care for many babies with congenital bowel conditions or a stoma, and for them even a short bout of diarrhoea can drain fluids quickly. The steps that protect a child are the same in any city where tap water may be unsafe, whether after a flood, a pipe break or a boil water notice.

If you know or suspect your water is unsafe, CDC advises using bottled, boiled or treated water for drinking, brushing teeth, washing food, making ice and preparing baby formula. Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs, so bring clear water to a rolling boil for one minute and let it cool in a clean, covered container. Breast milk needs no water at all, so if you breastfeed, keep nursing and offer feeds more often. If your baby takes formula, mix it only with safe water and never make it weaker to stretch your supply. Wash hands with soap after diaper changes and before preparing food, using safe water whenever you can. When diarrhoea starts, the most important treatment is oral rehydration solution, a mix of clean water, salt and sugar that WHO says costs only a few cents per treatment. Give small sips often, and after each loose stool WHO suggests about a quarter to half a large cup for children under two. WHO also recommends zinc for 10 to 14 days in children with diarrhoea, so ask a health worker about it. Keep giving your child their usual food, because WHO notes that continued feeding helps break the cycle between diarrhoea and poor nutrition. Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which the NHS warns can make diarrhoea worse.

Knowing the warning signs of dehydration is what lets parents act early. In a baby, watch for a sunken soft spot on the head, sunken eyes, few or no tears when crying and fewer wet diapers than usual. A child who is unusually drowsy or irritable, or who breathes quickly, needs to be checked by a doctor the same day. Seek care right away for blood in the stool, diarrhoea that does not settle, or a child who cannot keep fluids down. Pale, blotchy or cold skin, confusion or a child who is hard to wake are signs of shock and need emergency care at once. Most children with this kind of illness recover well when fluids are replaced early and steadily. In Bronkhorstspruit, most patients were rehydrated and discharged within a day, a reminder of how much early fluids can do. Keep a few sachets of oral rehydration solution at home, in the same place as your child's fever medicine. If you live in an area under a water warning, follow your local health department's advice until it is lifted. Share these steps with a parent of a young child, because the first hours of diarrhoea are when they matter most.

Sources: https://t.co/5Wes4V2hKI and https://t.co/jPpDFsCNtt and https://t.co/PD4GLfDG04 and https://t.co/HvSh8AYzV6

text:
@apriahealthcare: 21 Minutes of Hell to Schedule a Post-Surgery Wheelchair Delivery  

I called Apria to return their voicemail and schedule delivery of a wheelchair after back surgery. What followed was one of the most absurd, inefficient, and patient-hostile customer service experiences I have ever endured.  

The agent was clearly offshore (using voice-modulation software that added lag and an unnatural quality to every word) and locked into an aggressively scripted model that treated basic information exchange as an infinite loop. I stated my name, spelled my last name, gave my first name (Kimberly) -- which she also needed spelled -- provided my zip code, and clearly explained that I was returning Apria’s call to arrange home delivery of a wheelchair.  

She then made me repeat nearly every piece of information multiple times while endlessly parroting back “I will be able to help you with this ma’am Kimberly. If I understand you correctly, you are calling today to ask about delivery of your wheelchair, ma’am Kimberly.” Over… and over… and over.  

Zip code a minimum of four or five times. Full address multiple times. Confirmation of the purpose of the call literally dozens of times throughout the call. After she brought up my hospital discharge date (two days ago), which I confirmed, and finally got her to understand that I had already been discharged and was home, she still defaulted -- again, multiple times -- to asking me what time I wanted the wheelchair instead of telling me what delivery windows they actually had available.  

When I explained that I live rurally, that I physically cannot come to the door post-surgery, and that my husband needs a real window so he can be present, she continued cycling through the same questions and restating the purpose for the call again… and again… and again.  

I said, “My husband has errands to run relating to my surgery. So if YOU tell ME what delivery options are available, we can make sure he’s here.”  

Again: “I beg your pardon, ma’am Kimberly. What time would you LIKE your wheelchair to be delivered…” 

AGAIN!  I repeated that we were home NOW, so could take delivery in ten minutes, or at 11 a.m., or 1 p.m., or 3 p.m., or ANY TIME today that they had available!  

Eventually she offered 1 p.m. I asked for the size of the delivery window and whether we would get a call if the driver was running late. Answers were vague, contradictory, or nonexistent (“the driver will call you,” followed by silence when asked whether that meant “on the way” or “late”). 

She then gave me a callback number that she had to repeat and correct multiple times before landing on 888-492-7742. When pressed on how to navigate the phone tree or what the realistic odds of an on-time delivery were, the response was more apologies and “I beg your pardon, ma’am Kimberly,” and, finally, “there are no guarantees.”   

The agent herself remained polite and even offered the required scripted sympathy about the surgery, multiple times. That is not the problem. THE PROBLEM IS APRIA’S PROCESS. They have designed a workflow that forces agents to reconfirm the same basic facts repeatedly (to the point of nothing less than absurdity), prevents them from simply stating available delivery windows, and creates endless friction for a patient who is already recovering from surgery and trying to coordinate a simple home delivery. 

The combination of offshore VOIP lag, voice modulation, and rigid scripting turned what should have been a three-minute scheduling call (max) into a miserable, 21-minute circular ordeal.  

APRIA IS RESPONSIBLE FOR THIS. NOT the individual agent. 

Companies that outsource customer service for cost savings still own the outcome of the scripts, training, and systems they impose. (Flying your person in charge of outsourcing out there to beat the outsourcer to death is NOT the answer. 

APRIA’S PROCESS needs to change. Whoever designed it needs to be held accountable, and if you paid a consultant to do it, or hired the same one that RUINED what USED to be great service from @ByramHealthcare,  fire them. This was beyond ridiculous.) 

For a durable medical equipment provider dealing with people who have just had surgery and need equipment to function at home, this model is unacceptable. It wastes patients’ limited energy, creates unnecessary confusion around delivery logistics, and demonstrates a complete lack of respect for the people who actually need the product.  

If Apria cannot design a straightforward process for returning a delivery-scheduling call, patients should not be forced to navigate this level of LUDICROUS DYSFUNCTION simply to receive a wheelchair.  

I’ve yet to work with a provider who expresses anything less than disdain when they learn my insurance contracts through Apria -- some going as far as saying, “They’re the worst.” Insurance companies and hospitals continue to contract with them anyway because of the deep discounts Apria offers. To deliver those discounts, Apria cuts corners at every cost point, and the biggest overhead is labor. I’m not opposed to offshoring for cost containment (in fact, I ran call centers internationally), but a simple cost-benefit analysis should ask whether paying an outsourcer for 21 minutes of exacting misery on a patient -- on a call that could have been verified efficiently and effectively in three minutes -- makes any sense once you factor in the patient and provider experience. 

If someone at Apria with a shred of common sense looked at cost containment against an overlay of “how can we possibly make patients and providers hate us more,” perhaps Apria wouldn’t have to give away the farm just to remain the company people actively hate in the DME industry.  

To Apria's incoming CEO: I ENCOURAGE you to ask for (and listen to) the dial-in codes which allow you to to LIVE monitor random PATIENT (not provider) calls that you can log into, 24 x 7, with NO ONE (including your COO's) knowledge (otherwise, your people AND your outsourcer is going to feed you cherry-picked calls taken by their best reps). YOU need to EXPERIENCE the patient -- and your outsourced agent -- experience. LISTEN to the scripting someone on your team has implemented, then let the heads roll.  

This was a MASTERCLASS in how NOT to handle a simple post-surgery wheelchair delivery, and leadership at Apria who are responsible for this debacle needs to be held accountable for it. Fire the lot of them and bring in someone with a shred of common sense who has the leadership skills to PARTNER with your outsourcer instead of what I can all but guarantee is going to happen as a result of this letter: BLUDGEON THE OUTSOURCER. 

This dead skunk doesn’t land on your outsourcer’s porch. The STINK of this debacle CLEARLY lands at the feet of leadership at Apria. 

Shame on ALL of you and WAKE THE HELL UP! 

cc. Perry Bernocchi, EVP COO Accendra Health Operational leader.  @pbernocc (Were YOU the person responsible for destroying Byram's once exceptional customer service?! Trustpilot ratings are down to around 1.2/5 based on reviews (although their site boasts of all kinds of awards and accolades), with recurring complaints about long hold times, unhelpful or hard-to-understand agents, rigid/scripted processes, incorrect information, delivery problems, and billing issues. There's been a NOTICEABLE DECLINE in recent years, often linking it to outsourcing/offshoring and process changes.  Were YOU responsible for that, as well?)

cc. Kenneth Gardner-Smith,  Incoming President & CEO of Accendra Health   

cc. Edward A. Pesicka, Outgoing President & CEO of Accendra Health  

cc. Dan Starck, Former CEO of Apria

text:
Kevin Costner’s wife asked for $248,000 a month in child support. In court, she said she didn’t know how she’d afford groceries.

They had a prenup. It gave her 30 days to leave his house after she filed for divorce. A judge had to order her out.

They married in 2004 and had three children. In May 2023, after 18 years, she filed. The house was his, bought in 1988, before the marriage.

The prenup paid her $100,000 on the wedding day, $100,000 on the first anniversary, and $1 million after she filed.

He offered about $51,000 a month. A judge set $129,755 for now. She asked for more.

She moved into a $40,000-a-month rental and said it wasn’t enough for the kids.

That summer, she was photographed on vacation in Hawaii with a family friend, Josh Connor.

In September 2023, the judge decided: $63,209 a month.

In the video below, Kevin arrives at court: “We’re talking about somebody I love on the other side.” Then listen for what she says is in the kids’ DNA.

She later married Josh Connor.

The case for Christine: 18 years, three kids, and a husband who made over $1 million a month on Yellowstone.
The case for Kevin: she signed the prenup, and their oldest son drives a 15-year-old truck.
Was $63,209 a month for three kids fair, or did she ask for too much?

text:
Building is not the hard part anymore.
I spent 14 days at SF Tech Week and LA Tech Week. 16 events, dozens of founders and investors. Almost nobody talked about product. They talked about selling.

What I took away:

1) Go-to-market is the whole game.
One GTM speaker said don't send 100,000 emails to get 10 replies. Run experiments of 100, change one variable at a time, find what works by hand, reverse engineer it, then automate. A good response rate is 5 to 10%.

Their favorite trick: if a lead ghosts, offer a $5 Starbucks gift card in exchange for their real objection. Cheapest research you'll ever buy.

2) Their 2027 prediction: founders become streamers.
Building is getting commoditized, so attention is the new bottleneck. Founders are already hiring clippers and posting their whole journey. If you can sell and market yourself, now is your window. Partner with someone who owns the tech and run a tiny team.

3) Protect the IP.
Colin from Origin Lab licenses data from game engines and sells it to AI labs as world model training data. His pitch to studios: sign here and you get paid. We protect your IP, it never goes open source. Everyone wins. Scraping the internet is a race to the bottom.

4) Go niche.
His take: models aren't as durable as people thought, wrappers get eaten, but specialized products win. AI is your engine, not your product. Law, climate, fintech. Pick one thing and go deep.

5) We can still steer this.
I never felt threatened at any of these events. People talk about the risks openly. The real question is whether we build out of greed or point this in a good direction. I think there's still hope.

Building is easy now. Selling and owning something real is the hard part.

What was your biggest takeaway if you went to either tech week?

The incident happened June 14 outside Walmart in Senatobia, Mississippi, after officers responded to allegations involving stolen diapers. Kohen was being held by his mother, Vellesiya Wiley, inside a vehicle driven by Latoya Ferrell when an officer opened fre, fatally injuring him and wounding Ferrell. The family’s attorney, Ben Crump, disputed the police account, citing an independent autopsy and damage to the passenger-side window as evidence that the sht came from beside the car. Kohen’s mother told Mississippi Today that investigators never interviewed her, while his grandmother, Veronica Roberson, said she learned of the decision on Facebook rather than from authorities. text:
More broadly, saying federalism produced conflict does not clarify how much responsibility falls on constitutional design, authoritarian government, exclusion, militarization, or specific decisions by political leaders. Those factors must be examined rather than folded into a single explanation.

The article’s account of the 2020–2022 war illustrates the problem. Whatever assessment one makes of the opening attacks and the responsibility for escalation, the war’s conclusion cannot adequately be described as the straightforward defeat of one side. On November 2, 2022, the federal government and the TPLF signed an African Union-facilitated agreement to cease hostilities permanently. Negotiation was central to ending that phase of the conflict.

Accountability must also extend beyond a single actor. UN human rights mechanisms have addressed grave abuses involving federal forces, Eritrean forces, Tigrayan forces, Amhara forces and associated militias. Describing the catastrophe as “tribal warfare” risks concealing the identifiable institutions, commanders and political choices that must be investigated.

The geopolitical argument is also selective: Turkey is portrayed principally through an adversarial religious and strategic frame. Yet Turkey facilitated the December 2024 Ankara Declaration between Ethiopia and Somalia. That declaration reaffirmed sovereignty and territorial integrity while establishing a framework for negotiating reliable Ethiopian access to the sea under Somalia’s sovereign authority. Whatever the limitations of that process, it complicates the article’s division of the region into natural allies and inevitable enemies.

Ethiopia should cultivate productive relationships with Israel, the UAE, India, Turkey, and its African neighbours based on concrete interests. A religious map of regional politics cannot substitute for diplomacy.

The deepest weakness, however, is the choice the article offers Iran: unified citizenship or destructive ethnic division. Equal citizenship and recognition of collective identities need not be mutually exclusive. A democratic political community can protect individual liberty, linguistic equality, regional self-government, and shared national institutions.

Federalism offers no automatic guarantee of peace. Neither does centralization. Recognizing a people’s identity does not absolve its leaders of wrongdoing; invoking national unity does not absolve a central government of repression.

Ethiopia’s experience should prompt difficult questions about democratic consent, minority protection, security-sector accountability and the peaceful management of constitutional disagreements. It cannot establish that every diverse country adopting federal arrangements is destined for permanent war.

Iran’s people must determine their own constitutional future. They deserve an accurate account of Ethiopia when that debate invokes its history

Ethiopia’s tragedy is serious enough without being made to prove more than the evidence supports. The lesson worth carrying forward is that durable unity requires institutions people can trust, rights governments must respect and a political community whose members have reasons to remain together.1/2

text:
$SFBS Q3 2026 earnings: ServisFirst profit rises, but deposits fall and margin stops widening

ServisFirst earned more than ever, but the deposits that fund its lending went backwards. Profit per share rose 23% excluding last year's bond loss, and loans grew 11% from a year ago. Deposits fell $461 million from June, so chief executive Tom Broughton's bank borrowed more from other banks, and its lending margin stopped widening.

• Profit per share, excluding one-offs: $𝟬.𝟴𝟬 (+23% from a year ago)
• Loans vs deposits: +$𝟮𝟱𝟵𝗠 𝘃𝘀 −$𝟰𝟲𝟭𝗠 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 (loans now 105% of deposits by our math)
• Net interest margin: 𝟯.𝟲𝟯% (unchanged from last quarter; 3.09% a year ago)
• Company outlook: 𝗡𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗶𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗲𝗱 ($577M of CDs mature in Q4 at 3.36%)

⚖️ 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the widening lending margin and cheap deposits that lifted profit over the past year both stopped helping. The margin's gain fell short of finance chief David Sparacio's target for a second quarter, costs overshot his run rate, and the efficiency ratio moved back above 30%. The good news: business loans led growth, nonaccrual loans fell and the board authorised a buyback.

The question now is whether ServisFirst can keep growing loans without the deposits to fund them. Either new deposits let it fund loans at 2.8%, or it keeps borrowing from other banks at 3.8% and the margin narrows. December's deposit balance and the fourth-quarter margin will tell.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝗕𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🟢 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗡𝗼𝘄 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗻 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵
ServisFirst makes most of its money lending to companies and property owners across the Southeast and, since last year, in Houston. Over the past year loans on rented commercial property grew fastest, and by June that category had pushed the bank's property exposure past three times its capital, a level regulators screen for.

This quarter the mix changed. Loans rose $259 million, and more than half of that came from commercial, financial and agricultural loans, the bank's business lending line. Loans on rented commercial property added only $18 million. Chief executive Tom Broughton said: "We see solid economic trends, and loan activity is improving with continued growth in our loan pipeline".

• Business loans: +15% from a year ago, +4% from last quarter
• Loans on rented commercial property: +16% from a year ago, +0.3% from last quarter
• Rate on new loans: 6.59%, against 6.33% last quarter and 6.24% for the whole book

The mix matters because business loans add less to the property concentration, and the new loans came on well above the rate the whole book earns, so this growth lifts the margin. But the total halved from June's $533 million, so the record pipeline Broughton described in July has not yet turned into bookings at that pace.

What to watch: fourth-quarter loan growth and the split by loan type in the January release. Business loans leading again at a faster total pace would show demand, not property lending, is now driving the book.

🟢 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗣𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟮𝟯% 𝗘𝘅𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗢𝗻𝗲-𝗢𝗳𝗳𝘀
ServisFirst reported earnings per share of $0.80, up 33% from a year ago. The comparison flatters, because a year ago the bank sold low-yielding bonds at a $7.8 million loss. Excluding that loss, profit per share rose 23%, and this quarter carries no such items.

The gain came from lending. Net interest income, what the bank earns on loans and securities minus what it pays for deposits and borrowings, rose 20% to $159.8 million, because the margin widened over the year while the loan book grew.

• Return on equity: 17.3%, from 14.9% a year ago
• Return on assets: 1.89%, from 1.47%
• Book value per share: $18.63, up 14%
• Common equity tier 1 capital: 11.98% of risk-weighted assets, from 11.49%

Finance chief David Sparacio said the bank keeps growing "through asset and margin growth, while maintaining a best-in-class efficiency ratio". The numbers support the first half, because profit before tax rose 34%. But the margin was unchanged from June, so next year's profit growth rests on loan growth alone unless it widens again.

What to watch: fourth-quarter profit per share against this quarter's $0.80. A rise with the margin still unchanged would show that loan growth alone can carry earnings.

🟢 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁
Two parts of the case for ServisFirst got no numbers in this release, so they stay open rather than confirmed, and each has a clear place where the reading will appear.

• Houston: salary costs rose $1.4 million from a year ago because of "the full impact of our Houston market expansion", the bank said, but it gave no Texas loan or deposit balances; the quarterly filing or the call would show them.
• Loan pipeline: Broughton said it keeps growing but gave no size; fourth-quarter loan growth is the only reading available.

🐻 𝗕𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲

🔴🔴 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗻 𝗟𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗕𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗱 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀
One large property developer's loans, about $100 million, have sat on ServisFirst's nonaccrual list since last autumn, meaning the bank no longer counts their interest. Nonperforming assets have held near 1% of total assets for a year, so the question is whether the bank is clearing the problem or absorbing losses on it.

This quarter gave some of both. Nonaccrual loans fell $9.6 million, but foreclosed property on the books rose $10.0 million, so the bank took collateral rather than cash. It also charged off $7.0 million of construction loans, a category with no charge-offs a year ago.

• Provision for credit losses: $15.2 million, from $11.4 million last quarter
• Net charge-offs: 0.21% of average loans, from 0.11%
• Reserve as a share of nonaccrual loans: 118%, from 107%

Chief executive Tom Broughton said "We see solid economic trends". That sits awkwardly beside a provision at 0.41% of average loans, the highest rate in the five quarters the release shows. Coverage of the nonaccrual book improved, which is the better reading, but partly because the bank wrote loans off.

What to watch: the reserve held against the developer relationship, in the quarterly filing's collateral-dependent loan table. A reserve far below the gap between loan balances and appraised values would mean more charge-offs are still to come.

🔴 𝗟𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽𝘀 𝗪𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗡𝗼𝘄
Net interest margin, the gap between what ServisFirst earns on loans and what it pays for money, drove most of the past year's profit growth as it climbed from 3.09% to 3.63%. In July finance chief David Sparacio told analysts the gain would slow, and pointed to a smaller rise this quarter.

The rise came in smaller still. Excluding a $1.9 million interest recovery that lifted June's figure, the margin widened by 0.05 percentage points, the same as the quarter before and below what Sparacio had pointed to.

• Margin, reported: 3.63%, unchanged from last quarter
• Margin in September alone: 3.68%, from 3.59% in June
• Cost of interest-bearing deposits at quarter end: 2.89%, from 2.80%

Two forces now pull against each other. New loans still carry a higher rate than the book earns, so repricing helps, and the September figure says the quarter ended better than it averaged. But deposit costs have started rising again, because the bank is paying up to keep money and borrowing more from other banks.

What to watch: the fourth-quarter margin against this quarter's 3.63%. A rise of 0.04 points or more would mean the September exit rate held and funding costs stayed contained.

🔴🔴 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗙𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗟𝗼𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗞𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴
A bank funds loans with deposits first and borrowed money second. ServisFirst added $1.4 billion of loans over the past year while its deposits ended where they started, so loans now exceed deposits: 105% by our math, up from 94% a year ago.

The gap widened sharply this quarter. Deposits fell $461 million from June. To fund its loans the bank raised federal funds purchased, overnight borrowing from the smaller banks it serves, by $386 million to $1.97 billion.

• Deposits: $14.09 billion, down 0.1% from a year ago
• Cash and equivalents: $1.19 billion, down a third from a year ago
• Interest paid on borrowed funds: $17.1 million, up 16% from last quarter

The cheapest money is the one bright spot: noninterest-bearing deposits rose 12% from a year ago to $2.91 billion, though they slipped from June. The mix still matters. Borrowed money costs 3.78% against 2.80% for interest-bearing deposits, so every dollar of loans funded by borrowing earns the bank about one percentage point less.

What to watch: total deposits at December 31 against $14.09 billion. Growth in line with loans would show the outflow was a quarter-end timing effect, not customers moving money elsewhere.

🔴 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝘁𝘀 𝗥𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗯𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘀 𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝟯𝟬%
ServisFirst's main claim to investors is that it runs a bank with fewer people and branches than rivals. Its efficiency ratio, costs as a share of revenue, had stayed below 30% for three quarters, and in July Sparacio called $50 million a stable quarterly cost run rate.

Costs came in at $52.2 million, 4.5% above June, and the ratio rose to 30.20%. Other operating expenses did the damage. They rose $2.2 million from June, 1.2 percentage points of revenue by our math, with no explanation in the release. Salaries rose as headcount grew by twelve, which the bank attributed to "the full impact of our Houston market expansion".

The ratio is still low for a bank, so the point is direction, not level. But the Houston team now sits fully in the cost base while its loans and deposits remain undisclosed, so the ratio can only fall if revenue outgrows the new costs, and this quarter revenue grew 2.6% against costs up 4.5%.

What to watch: whether other operating expenses return toward the $6 to $7 million of earlier quarters. A second quarter near $9 million would mean the cost base has reset higher rather than one item landing in September.

👓 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗲𝘀

𝗦𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗜𝘁𝘀 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗕𝘂𝘆𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸
After the quarter closed, ServisFirst's board authorised what the bank calls its "inaugural stock repurchase program": up to 2 million shares, about 1.8% of those outstanding, through the end of next year. It also completed a two-for-one stock split during the quarter. Capital keeps building, with common equity tier 1 at 11.98% of risk-weighted assets, and no repurchases yet reported.

— • — • —

💲 𝗢𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗞𝗣𝗜𝘀

𝗙𝗲𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲, 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗴𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭𝟯.𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
Up 21.8% from a year ago, slower than the 43.5% rise last quarter. Fee income is what the bank earns outside lending: service charges, card and mortgage fees, and income on bank-owned life insurance, which rose 81% after the bank bought more policies. It is still only 7% of revenue, so lending sets the result.

𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝘅 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): 𝟭𝟳.𝟮𝟭%  ⇘ decelerating
Down from 19.94% last quarter, because the bank bought investment tax credits during the quarter. The rate has moved with those purchases all year: 17.82%, then 19.94%, now 17.21%. For the nine months it stands at 18.34%, below last year's 18.89%, so the lower rate added about a cent to profit per share this quarter by our math.

𝗗𝗲𝗯𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 (𝟮𝟲𝗤𝟯): $𝟭.𝟱𝟲 𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻  ⇘ decelerating
Down 15.5% from a year ago and 4.1% from June, as the bank lets bonds mature and puts the cash into loans. Securities yield 3.85% against 6.24% on loans, so each dollar that moves lifts the margin, but the shrinking bond book also leaves less to sell for liquidity: unpledged securities counted as liquidity fell to $297 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲

𝗖𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗤𝟰: $𝟱𝟳𝟳.𝟰 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝟯.𝟯𝟲%  ⇒ stable
New. ServisFirst gives no earnings forecast, but it does say which deposits come due. About $577 million of certificates of deposit mature next quarter at 3.36%. The bank paid 2.89% on interest-bearing deposits at quarter end, so renewing them at today's rates would lower funding costs. That gap has narrowed from 1.22 points a year ago to 0.47 points by our math, so the help from CD repricing shrinks each quarter.

— • — • —

❓ 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗻𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲𝘀?
Nonaccrual loans fell $9.6 million while foreclosed property rose $10.0 million. The release does not say whether the shift came from the large multifamily relationship, or how the current appraisals compare with the loan balances.

𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗹𝗲𝗳𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻?
Deposits fell $461 million from June with no explanation. Whether the money was quarter-end timing, correspondent bank balances or customers moving to rivals decides how much the bank must keep borrowing at 3.78%.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗛𝗼𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗻'𝘀 𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘄?
Salary costs now carry the full Houston team, but the release gives no Texas balances. Without them readers cannot tell whether the efficiency ratio's rise above 30% is a timing gap or a lasting cost.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 $𝟮.𝟮 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗲𝘀?
The line rose a third from June and 47% from a year ago. Management offered no reason; a one-off item and a new run rate mean different things for a bank built on a sub-30% cost ratio.

text:
The Assault!

The coordinated assault lasted two days. Marcellus lashed ships together and built makeshift siege towers called "Harps" that could mount the sea walls and advanced on the city. Archimedes had layered catapults defending the harbor that put the Roman ships under something like continuous fire, forcing Marcellus to retreat.

Undaunted, he brought his ships up at night and pressed them against the walls. But his men started dying from hand-sized holes drilled in the wall at the height of a man standing on a ship. The Greeks shot through these holes and killed men unexpectedly. Then previously hidden cranes swung into action, dropping lead weights on the ships, smashing the "Harps" and sinking some ships.
 
I grapplers were dropped, attached with chains to powerful cranes. Once hooked onto a ship, the vessel could be capsized or even lifted from the water. Marcellus, in the face of such resistance, had to reluctantly call off the attack. 

The ground forces fared no better. Rams were destroyed by the weights or the grapples; in some cases, men who held on too tightly were hoisted in the air and dropped. The special archer holes at head level wreaked havoc, and the Roman catapults and ballistae were taken out by counter shots from the wall. Syracuse had held against the best that Rome had to offer!

text:
THE MARKET CLOSED. HERE'S EVERYTHING THAT MOVED IT TODAY:

THE CLOSE

The S&P 500 closed at 7,691.92, up 0.42%, while the Nasdaq Composite led at 26,371.59, up 0.89%, and the Dow slipped to 51,961.61, down 0.08%. The Russell 2000 added 0.34% to 2,730.50, so small caps joined the bid instead of sitting it out. The 10-year yield held near 5.10%, still high enough to keep financing costs front and center. WTI crude slipped back toward $100 a barrel and Brent eased toward $108 after both hit five-month highs Friday, which took some pressure off the tape. Bitcoin held above $82,000 at around $82,783 and Ethereum traded near $2,433, both steadier than equities last week even as ETF outflows continued. The character of the day was a selective rebound: buyers returned to the names they sold hardest, but they did not chase everything.

THE WINNERS

$SLN was the standout, surging about 125.6% after Merck KGaA agreed to buy Silence Therapeutics in an all-cash deal. Shareholders will receive $20.00 per ADS, a 130% premium to Friday's close, for an equity value near $1.3 billion. The prize is divesiran, a Phase 3-ready treatment for the rare blood disorder polycythemia vera, plus Silence's gene-silencing platform. Pharma is paying up for late-stage rare disease assets, and this deal shows the bid is still aggressive.

$CLF ripped 15.7% after its strongest quarter in three years. Cleveland-Cliffs posted adjusted EPS of $0.28, beating the $0.24 consensus, on revenue of $5.61 billion, and guided fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA to about $715 million, up from $612 million in the third quarter. Management pointed to signed contracts and a better steel price backdrop for 2027. When a cyclical name beats on profit and raises the near-term outlook in the same print, the market listens.

$IRON jumped about 32% after its Phase 3 Apollo trial of bitopertin met all primary and secondary endpoints in erythropoietic protoporphyria, a rare disorder that makes sunlight painful. The company said the drug was generally well tolerated with no new safety signals. In biotech, a clean pivotal win is the whole thesis, and today it repriced in one session.

$SNDK rose about 7.4% at midday and $MU gained about 4.7% as memory led the semiconductor rebound. After eight straight down sessions for semis, the longest losing streak in 16 years, buyers stepped back into the most oversold part of the AI stack. $ASTS added about 5% after signing letters of intent with Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica and Vodafone to explore a joint bid for Mobile Satellite Services spectrum in Europe, a footprint covering more than 500 million subscribers.

THE LOSERS

$EYPT collapsed about 85.3% to $0.44, from $2.99 on Friday, after the Phase 3 LUCIA trial of Duravyu in wet age-related macular degeneration missed its primary endpoint. It was the second straight pivotal miss for the same program, following the August failure. EyePoint said it will cut about 53% of its workforce, stop the wet AMD studies, and shift focus to diabetic macular edema, with results not expected until late 2027. Analysts said the wet AMD path now looks closed, which is why the restructuring did not cushion the fall.

Defensives were the other losers, not on news but on rotation. Utilities were the day's weakest sector, with the utilities ETF down about 1.72% in afternoon trading, and real estate fell about 1.18%. $NRG was cited among the decliners as money moved out of safety and back into growth. When yields stay above 5%, defensives have to compete with cash, and today they lost that fight.

SECTOR SCORECARD

Technology and consumer discretionary led, real estate and consumer defensive names lagged, and utilities finished at the bottom. That is the mirror image of Friday, when technology fell about 3% and energy gained about 2.5%. The cross-sector read-through is simple: Friday was a financing scare, not a demand collapse. Today the market tested whether it still believes the AI buildout earns its cost of capital, and the answer, for one day, was yes, but only in the names with upgrades, earnings, or a deal behind them.

THE STORY OF THE DAY

The story was the AI trade trying to stand back up after last week's rout, and whether earnings this week can prove the spending is working.

Last week the Nasdaq fell 4.5% for the week and 2.15% on Friday alone, as investors focused on the debt funding the data center boom. $CRWV fell nearly 12% on Friday and Reuters reported its bond yields moved above 15%, a level that asks a hard question about how the next phase gets financed. Semiconductors had fallen eight straight sessions coming into today, even though the group is still up more than 50% this year.

Monday brought the other side of the argument, in verified pieces. Goldman Sachs upgraded $CRWV to Buy from Neutral, even while cutting its target to $106 from $139, arguing that revenue per megawatt and unlevered returns are biased higher over the next two years because supply stays tight. Bernstein upgraded $DDOG to Outperform and lifted its target to $350 from $237, saying enterprise token consumption among the largest AI labs appears to have grown at least 50% quarter over quarter. JPMorgan upgraded $INTC to Neutral from Underweight, saying risk and reward look more balanced after a 36% pullback from its June peak. Oil falling after President Trump waived planned Russia sanctions and tariffs, and struck a diesel export deal, helped too, because cheaper energy eases the inflation pressure that keeps yields high.

None of that settles the debate. It frames it. This week more than 70 S&P 500 companies report, and the market will judge AI not by promises but by whether customers are paying, margins are holding, and guidance survives a 5% 10-year yield. That is why today's rebound matters, and why it is still on probation.

EARNINGS

Before the open, $CLF delivered the beat described above, and $FITB beat on EPS at $0.90 against an $0.82 estimate, a signal that the Comerica integration story in regional banks is still being rewarded when execution shows up. $DX was a notable miss in mortgage REITs, a reminder that rate volatility still bites the rate-sensitive corners first.

After the close, the calendar was $STLD, $ZION, $WRB, $CCK, $FNB and $WAL, with calls running into the evening. Steel Dynamics is the read-through from Cliffs: if its print confirms pricing and volume strength, the steel move today was not a one-name event. The banks reporting tonight set up Tuesday's larger regional bank wave, where margins and credit quality are the variables that matter.

FLOW

Options flow stayed concentrated in the index and AI complex. By notional value, $QQQ led, followed by $SPY and $MU, with $META, $TSLA and $NVDA also near the top, which fits a market hedging and positioning around earnings week rather than chasing single names. The most unusual single-name flow was in $M, where more than 62,000 puts traded at the $25 strike expiring January 15, 2027, at more than 175 times prior open interest at that strike, according to Barchart. $CSX also saw call volume about 121% above typical. Flow today said protection and positioning, not euphoria.

TOMORROW'S SETUP

Tuesday, October 20 brings a heavy before-the-open slate: $GE, $GM, $RTX, $MMM, $NOC, $HAL and $KEY, covering aerospace, autos, defense and industrials in one morning. Housing starts and building permits land in the morning as well, the next check on a housing market where builder confidence just hit a 14-year low in today's NAHB read.

After the close Tuesday, $NFLX reports, alongside $SPCX, $ISRG, $UAL and $COF. Netflix is the consumer and advertising check before the main event on Wednesday, when $TSLA and $META report after the close. China offered a steadier backdrop overnight, with third-quarter GDP growing 4.5% year over year, beating the 4.4% forecast, helped by tech exports even as property investment stayed weak. If Tuesday's industrials confirm demand and Netflix holds the consumer line, today's rebound gets a second day. If they do not, Friday's financing questions come right back.

WALL STREET IS THE GREATEST SHOW ON EARTH.

text:
My bad. Here’s my full response:

I’m currently an MLE at Walmart. Back in June 2023, shortly after GPT-4 came out, I made an early attempt to help address this problem. We built a sourcing agent to find the best and cheapest components around the world for American manufacturers. Not surprisingly, most of those components came from China.

We spent a year on it, made it into the top 10% of YC applications, and eventually had to put it on hold. I’ve been thinking about it again recently—what we could have done better, and what would actually help American manufacturing become more competitive.

I think Walmart’s philosophy offers a useful lesson.

Walmart has always followed Sam Walton’s principle of “everyday low prices.” It’s never been a sexy statement, especially compared with missions like “becoming a multiplanetary species.” In Silicon Valley, it often feels like if you’re starting something, you’d better be building tech with a cool mission. I’ve seen much more excitement around building something different than around building the same thing at a much lower price.

Having worked at Walmart and other companies, I can say I’ve never seen another place build its culture so deeply around saving money and relentlessly finding ways to cut costs without reducing product quality.

Retail and manufacturing are different businesses, but there is a lesson here about what an organization chooses to value and reward. Better processes, less waste, fewer defects, and thousands of small improvements that bring costs down should be things people take pride in. Making something more affordable should be a mission worth building a company around.

If we want AI to strengthen American manufacturing, lowering the cost of producing things here should be a mission in itself. Finding cheaper components helps manufacturers, but we should also use AI to help them produce more competitively here—with better use of their equipment, materials, and people.

Building the same product at the same quality for a much lower price should be something our best engineers and founders are proud to work on. To me, that is an ambitious mission too.

That’s why I think America’s manufacturing challenge is both a cost issue and a culture issue.

So, what’s the solution? Ask Sam Walton rather than Tim Cook.

text:
The most important AI lesson is the same lesson I learned as a manager.

My project agent told me my first product was done.

My content agent had already drafted the launch posts in the same turn.

Then my QA agent checked it against what a paying customer would actually get.

Missing competitor listing links. Wrong file paths.
A skipped comparison sheet. The list goes on...

Its verdict became a label I still use:

"Demo-ready. Not monetize-ready."  Nobody was lying.

Lesson: they were using two different definitions of done.

Managers solved this decades ago.

Definition of done. What success looks like.

Goals and results, the MBO and OKR way.

Before anyone starts, you write down how you'll know it's finished.

Evals are the definition of done for AI.

Two examples from builders this week (their claims, not my tests):

1/ A WhatsApp lead-reply bot (@denispo_). The demo was approved in June.

Real leads broke it: 30-word answers, the wrong language on voice notes, chatting with people who were never buying.

Now it's on version 4.7. Each of those breaks is an eval: one sentence and one question, language by country code, go quiet on non-leads.

2/ An HVAC booking agent (@serviceagentai). "Booked" isn't done. The right job type, the right tech, buffers and travel time checked before a slot is offered. That's the eval.

How I write evals now:

1. Write what done looks like before the agent runs.

2. Check it against what the customer pays for, not what the builder meant.

3. Turn every real failure into a new check.

4. Once the checks are good, stop gating everything and watch the data.

The human is the bottleneck. Good evals are how you stop being one.

What's your definition of done for your bot?

text:
Here’s a novelty. The biggest story in bond land last week wasn’t the Fed, inflation, or jobs. This time, it was all about - no, not Elon’s flying car - worries that the AI bubble is losing air.

Yields on debt from AI data center operator CoreWeave surged to 15%. The broader concern: investment in AI data centers has gotten out of hand.

Fanning the flames, Gartner warned that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could be exposed to impairment.

“Through 2030, AI data center owners would need to generate a cumulative $8.5 trillion in revenue to cover announced capital spending, financing costs, and a 12% return on invested capital, which we assume to be the hurdle rate,” Gartner said. “However, total enterprise and consumer AI revenue that can be attributed to AI data centers during this period is forecast to reach no more than $3.6 trillion. Because most AI-native providers operate asset-light business models, we predict that less than half of AI revenue will be earned by providers that own significant AI infrastructure.”

Gartner also asserted that “neoclouds” like CoreWeave - have the most risk from an imbalance between revenue and capital spending. They predict over 80% of neoclouds will “cease independent operations” by 2030. Gulp!

One contributing factor: an X post by investor Chamath Palihaptiya, he of the 2.4 million followers, on whether the AI buildout is creating a private credit bubble. He also posted a chart showing the surge in CoreWeave's bond yields, to which Elon - him again - responded “Yikes.”

Bloomberg reported that prices on credit-default swaps for some of the largest tech companies - including Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta, and Amazon - have surged over the last 12 months, reflecting concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom - and the potential consequences of a bust.

There were CoreWeave tremors across the financial markets. Nasdaq is off 4.5% over the last five sessions. CoreWeave over than span? Down 24%. 

The worries about AI data center debt - and an AI stock slide - triggered a “flight to quality.” Ergo, the 10-year yield is about a quarter point below its recent peak. However, that just brings the yield to where it was a month ago, still over 5%. One factor in the recent rate surge: the flood of AI-tied financings. A slowdown in issuance would be bullish for Treasuries.

But don’t forget: Inflation is surging. Headline CPI hit 3.7% in September, and wholesale prices jumped 6.3%. The Fed’s target, of course, is 2%. While consensus is once again that we won’t get a rate hike when the FOMC meets later this month, there’s little reason to think the tightening will be one-and-done.

text:
Libertarianism in Ireland 🇮🇪 

It’s great to see more and more Conservatives and Nationalists increasingly embrace Libertarianism here.    

Libertarianism offers a philosophical and economic framework to shrink the state and empower the individual: that is its essence. 

Its foundational principle, the sanctity of property rights, doubles as the bedrock of sound economics, also. 

Everything flows from this: politically, it maximizes individual freedom, for more conservative types, and truly protects minorities, for more progressives types.  

Libertarianism should, and can be, a bipartisan philosophy.  

Economically, it enables optimal wealth creation, and preservation, and cuts the wasteful state.  More growth, innovation, and jobs, and less reliance on government.    

Irish critiques of Libertarianism and free markets often miss this foundational principle of property rights and self-agency.   

Some argue Nationalism - a love for one’s nation - can’t work in a Libertarian framework, claiming that, for some reason, people wouldn’t feel this sense of patriotism without top-down state enforcement.  

Not only does this make no sense, but it is ahistorical when it comes to the type of patriotism a nation should seek; a bottoms up spontaneous patriotism will always outlast a top down enforced one, ie the American, French or even Irish revolutions, versus the Soviet, Nazi, or Italian statist-kind.  

Free people don’t need a boot on their neck to love their homeland.  

In fact, it is the current state that has eroded that love over the passed few decades.    

Libertarianism doesn’t dictate morality or culture; it leaves that to individuals and families, as it should be.  If you want to impose your own version of morality on others, it’s not for you.    

On economics, then, people argue that a free market is what has lead to a lot of Ireland's woes, while ignoring the huge growth that our openness to markets has allowed.  

Here, the misstep is to equate EU globalisation, with free markets, which is to again forget the initial Libertarian principal of property rights, and self agency.  

For example, our ability to provide a better interest rate to corporations was a huge economic incentive for businesses to come here.  

Global trade agreements, including the growth strangling regulations that come with them, stifle this ability, greatly.  

On the economics piece also, to think about Libertarian economics is to not just view one reductionist area of trade, it is to view it holistically.  

If you think that a particular policy is negative for a certain industry, you must ask yourself what things look like when the same industry, and entire nations economy, also look like the following;  

No taxation, workers get to keep 100% of their income, and businesses have far more to reinvest for growth, and a far greater margin for error when negotiating trade deals elsewhere.   

It would be a completely new paradigm.  

It would just be one without the pedaling middlemen of the state extracting wealth from everyone. 

Immigration is another issue sometimes highlighted, but this is also among the easiest to solve for, imo.  

If property rights are sacrosanct, and everything is privatised, then there isn't one hard border, there are thousands of even harder, smaller ones, with nobody having the right to encroach upon them without permission.  

In a country 75-80% against the states ridiculous immigration position, this is solved for, immediately.  

Remember, also, there is no welfare in such a society, removing a huge pull factor for negative immigration.  

Every philosophy has trade-offs, but Irish objections to Libertarianism often miss the mark, imo.  

We also have the entire 1,000 year Brehon period - our own unique period of self governance which also consisted of no top down state control, no monopoly on violence, on law, or on currency, as a similar example.

Rooted in individual rights and agency, Libertarianism is an antidote to authoritarianism, and a real economic alternative.  

Being the party of sound money, property rights, the working class, and SMEs, also has some ring to it 🤝

text:
**Europeans (whites) were enslaved in multiple periods and by various groups, most notably on a large scale by North African and Ottoman-linked Muslim powers in the early modern era.** Slavery has been practiced across nearly all societies and regions for millennia and was not limited by race.

### Barbary Slave Trade (Mediterranean, ~1500s–early 1800s)

Barbary corsairs from the North African coast (primarily the Ottoman-aligned or influenced states of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, plus independent Morocco) raided European shipping and coastal towns from Italy and Spain to France, England, Ireland, and as far as Iceland. Captives were sold in North African slave markets.

- **Scale**: Historian Robert C. Davis estimated 1–1.25 million European Christians enslaved between roughly 1530 and 1780 (based on observed slave populations of around 35,000 in peak periods, high annual attrition from death, escape, ransom, or conversion, and the need to replace about one-quarter of the population yearly). This figure is widely cited by sources including Wikipedia and BBC histories. Some historians (such as Peter Earle) view it as potentially high due to extrapolation from the peak raiding decades and limited official records; others find the order of magnitude plausible. Coastal raids sometimes seized thousands at a time (e.g., entire populations of islands or towns).
- **Treatment**: Many served as galley slaves, laborers, or domestic servants; women as concubines. Mortality was high. Ransom of captives was a significant business, and conversion to Islam offered a path out of slavery for some. Famous accounts include those of Miguel de Cervantes and raids recorded in English and Irish sources.
- The trade declined after European naval actions, including the Barbary Wars involving the United States and others, and a major Anglo-Dutch bombardment in 1816 that freed thousands of remaining Christian slaves.

Many corsair crews and captains included European “renegades” (converts to Islam). Slaves in Barbary also included non-Europeans.

### Crimean Tatar / Black Sea Raids (~15th–18th centuries)

The Crimean Khanate (Tatar Muslims, frequently allied with the Ottomans) conducted extensive raids into Russia, Ukraine, Poland-Lithuania, and neighboring areas, capturing people for sale into Ottoman and other markets.

Estimates commonly range from roughly 1–2 million Slavic captives over the period (with some scholarly figures around 2 million for 1500–1700). Ottoman customs data indicate large Black Sea slave imports (on the order of millions over centuries, of mixed origins including Slavs and Caucasians). This trade was economically central to the Crimean Khanate until Russian expansion ended it.

Medieval Islamic sources also document large numbers of Slavic (“Saqaliba”) slaves traded into the Middle East and North Africa.

### Other Contexts

- Ancient and classical eras**: Romans, Greeks, and others enslaved large numbers of Europeans (Gauls, Germans, Britons, etc.) through conquest and trade. Viking-age raiders enslaved people across northern Europe.
- Colonial Americas (indentured servitude)**: Hundreds of thousands of Europeans (primarily British, Irish, German, and others) arrived in the English colonies as indentured servants in the 17th–18th centuries—often half or more of European immigrants. Terms were typically 4–7 years in exchange for passage; conditions could be harsh, and some were involuntary (convicts or kidnapped). This was legally and practically distinct from hereditary chattel slavery (temporary, with rights, not property status, and not race-based in the same way). Estimates of total European indentured migrants to British America are commonly in the range of ~300,000–500,000.
- **20th century**: Large-scale forced labor systems under regimes such as Nazi Germany (which used millions of European prisoners and civilians) and the Soviet Union, though these are usually categorized separately from historical chattel slavery.

text:
SpaceX flew a wheel of cheese on its very first Dragon capsule in December 2010 as a nod to Monty Python's Cheese Shop sketch. Sixteen years later Elon is posting a remake of that same sketch where the shopkeeper sells GPUs.

The joke lands because it's his real life. He says this is the conversation SpaceX has had when it tried to rent inference compute from AWS and Google Cloud to take load off its training clusters.

In the clip the customer asks for 8 H100s for a week. The B200s have an 18 month wait list, the A100s are "all reserved by a very large chatbot," the TPUs are internal use only, and the one T4 on offer sits in an obscure region and comes with a three-year commitment. He walks out saying he'll build his own data center.

That's pretty much what Elon did. On September 24 he said Colossus in Memphis was running 230,000 Nvidia chips and Colossus 2 had 550,000, with a goal of 1.21 million by late December. To pay for the next batch, SpaceX is in talks to borrow $40B, about $10B in bank loans and $30B in investment-grade bonds, with Apollo expected to lead. The GPUs themselves would likely be the collateral, and lenders are working on the assumption that a top GPU holds its value for about seven years. SpaceX already sold $25B of bonds two weeks after its June IPO. Elon has said it will build on Nvidia exclusively because "the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture."

The best part is that Google, one of the clouds he tried, is also a SpaceX customer. Starting this month Google pays SpaceX $920M a month for about 110,000 Nvidia GPUs, all the way through June 2029. The contract even lets Google walk away if SpaceX misses its committed GPU delivery by September 30, after a one month grace period. So SpaceX is struggling to rent inference compute from Google while renting a giant GPU cluster to Google.

Every big lab is standing in the same line. Anthropic signed a $45B, six-year deal with Nscale in August for about 460MW at a campus in West Virginia, with capacity coming online in late 2027. On Monday Bloomberg reported the two are talking about a second deal of about the same size. Morgan Stanley estimates AI infrastructure will need $1.5 trillion in outside financing by 2028.

The shelves in this shop are full, and every rack on them already belongs to somebody.

https://t.co/mBugz2ebEp

text:
The Battle of Navarino (20 October 1827) was the decisive naval clash of the Greek War of Independence and the last major fleet action fought entirely by wooden sailing ships. It took place in the sheltered, nearly landlocked Bay of Navarino (modern Pylos) on the western Peloponnese, where an allied squadron of Britain, France, and Russia destroyed the larger Ottoman-Egyptian fleet that had been sent to crush the Greek revolt. 
https://t.co/wuzGawLzTP

The Greek Revolt and Egyptian InterventionThe Greek uprising against Ottoman rule began in 1821. Early Greek successes were followed by brutal Ottoman repression, including the 1822 massacre on Chios and the execution of the Orthodox Patriarch in Constantinople. These events fueled intense European sympathy (Philhellenism). By 1825 the Ottomans had called on their powerful Egyptian vassal, Muhammad Ali of Egypt. His son, Ibrahim Pasha, landed a disciplined army in the Peloponnese (Morea), took Navarino as a base, and systematically devastated the countryside while the Ottoman-Egyptian navy supplied him. Greek resistance was near collapse by mid-1827; Athens fell in June. 
https://t.co/7IMZuNCj5U

European powers, alarmed by the humanitarian crisis and the strategic implications of unchecked Ottoman-Egyptian power in the eastern Mediterranean, signed the Treaty of London on 6 July 1827. Britain, France, and Russia demanded an immediate armistice and offered mediation for a semi-autonomous Greece. The Greeks accepted; the Sultan rejected it. The allied admirals were instructed to enforce the armistice, if necessary by a “friendly demonstration of force”—an ambiguous order that left room for interpretation. 
https://t.co/dEFe88uy7O

The Allied Fleet and the Decision to Enter the BayVice-Admiral Sir Edward Codrington (British, a Trafalgar veteran) commanded the combined fleet, with Rear-Admiral Henri de Rigny (French) and Rear-Admiral Lodewijk van Heiden (Russian, a Dutch officer in Russian service). The allies assembled roughly 10 ships of the line, about 10 frigates, and several smaller vessels—roughly 22–28 warships carrying around 1,250–1,300 guns. The Ottoman-Egyptian force under Ibrahim Pasha (and subordinates including Tahir Pasha and Moharram Bey) was larger in numbers: typically described as 3 ships of the line, 15–20 frigates, and 40–60 smaller vessels and fireships (total estimates range from the mid-60s to the low 80s), with more than 2,000 guns. Many of the Ottoman ships were older or smaller, their crews less experienced in fleet actions, and discipline uneven. The fleet was anchored in a crescent (or horseshoe) formation inside the bay, supported by shore batteries and fireships positioned to trap any attacker. 
https://t.co/wuzGawLzTP

Codrington had previously negotiated a temporary suspension of hostilities with Ibrahim, which the Egyptians then violated by attempting to move forces and continuing scorched-earth operations on land. On 18–20 October the allied admirals decided that a winter blockade was impractical and that entering the bay to anchor face-to-face with the Ottoman fleet was the most effective way to force compliance with the armistice. Codrington’s standing order was clear: do not fire first, but destroy any ship that fired on the allies. 
https://t.co/aN4lZF2LuU

⚠️ 🇺🇸 Trump Suggests Renaming New Mexico “New America” in Latest Push for American Prestige

President Trump recently floated renaming the state of New Mexico to New America through social media posts and imagery, framing the change as more prestigious and reflective of national identity, though he lacks unilateral authority and any formal shift would require action by the state’s own institutions.

In early September 2026, over the Labor Day weekend, the president shared on Truth Social a map of New Mexico in which the word “Mexico” was crossed out in red and replaced with “America.” The White House account amplified the image on X. He followed with what appeared to be an AI-generated video depicting him applying an “America” sticker over a “Welcome to New Mexico” highway sign, accompanied by a celebratory dance. In an accompanying post, Trump wrote that many people had suggested the shift for “one of the great vote cheating states of all time,” adding that the new name would be “so much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!”

The proposal fits a consistent pattern of emphasizing American nomenclature. Shortly after returning to office in January 2025, Trump directed federal recognition of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America. In August 2026 he issued an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America. These moves rest on the president’s ability to update federal geographic naming systems for landmarks under U.S. jurisdiction. A state’s legal name, however, is different. New Mexico’s constitution states that its name is New Mexico. Changing it would require the state legislature to approve a constitutional amendment and then submit the measure to voters. Trump later indicated the decision ultimately rests with New Mexicans themselves.

The state’s existing name carries centuries of history. Spanish explorers in the late 1500s referred to the region as Nuevo México, well before the modern nation of Mexico formed and long before the United States existed. The territory retained the designation after the Mexican-American War and entered the Union as the 47th state in 1912. Local officials, including Democratic Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham, responded that the name “isn’t up for debate” and has belonged to the area since before the United States was founded. Representative Melanie Stansbury offered a more direct “Oh hell no,” citing the name’s ties to generations of history, culture, and family.

Supporters of the idea see it as a straightforward expression of national pride. In a country whose very name is America, applying that label more directly to a southwestern state could underscore unity and prestige without erasing the region’s distinct landscape or people. Critics treat the posts as distraction or overreach, yet the underlying impulse—to prefer clear American identifiers—aligns with broader efforts to reclaim symbolic ground after years of diluted geographic language. Whether New Mexico residents ever take up the suggestion remains their choice. For now, the discussion simply places the question of identity back in the public square, where names have always carried weight.
