INTRODUCING A THANKSGIVING ACROSS AMERICA!
The Tradition Continues. The Table Grows.

This Thanksgiving, The Bridge to Liberty is launching a special nationwide initiative to bring American families and newly arrived Afrikaner refugees together through one of America’s most cherished traditions: Thanksgiving.

For many of our Afrikaner friends, this will be their very first American Thanksgiving. They may be thousands of miles from the homeland they have always known, beginning new lives in unfamiliar communities without extended family or friends nearby.

We want to change that.

Through our American Neighbor Network, we hope to connect Afrikaner families with welcoming American families who would be willing to share their Thanksgiving table, extend a hand of friendship, and introduce them to this beautiful American tradition.

For families who cannot be connected with an American host, The Bridge to Liberty hopes to provide grocery gift cards to help them prepare their own traditional Thanksgiving dinner or purchase a prepared holiday meal.

📷 OUR INITIAL GOAL IS 25 AFRIKANER FAMILIES ACROSS AMERICA!

But we don’t want to stop there! Depending on the response from participating families and the generosity of our donors, we may be able to expand this initiative to include even more families.

The more support we receive, the more Thanksgiving tables we can help fill!

📷 We are also inviting American churches, families, and individuals across the country to participate in our American Neighbor Network, a year-round initiative dedicated to building friendships, fellowship, and community connections for newly arrived Afrikaner families.

📷📷📷 A SPECIAL INVITATION TO OUR ESTABLISHED AFRIKANER FRIENDS!
Just because you arrived in America as a refugee doesn’t mean you cannot become an American Neighbor yourself!

If you have settled into your new life, are doing well, and are planning to celebrate Thanksgiving, we would love for you to consider joining the American Neighbor Network.

Perhaps you could welcome another Afrikaner family to your Thanksgiving table, help a newly arrived family navigate their community, or simply offer the friendship and encouragement that you may have appreciated when you first arrived.

You understand the journey because you’ve walked it yourself. Now you have an opportunity to help someone else along the way.

Our American Neighbor Network is about building a community where everyone has something meaningful to contribute.

📷 IMPORTANT REGISTRATION REQUIREMENT
All Afrikaner families wishing to receive Thanksgiving assistance through this initiative must first be registered with The Bridge to Liberty.

Once registered, families can sign in using their Bridge to Liberty registration number and password to select their Thanksgiving participation option.
American Neighbor Network volunteers who wish to host or assist must also complete the appropriate volunteer registration process.

📷 IMPORTANT DATES
📷 Registration Opens: October 21, 2026
📷 Registration Closes: November 8, 2026
📷 Thanksgiving Day: November 26, 2026

All Thanksgiving assistance is subject to available funding, eligibility, and local arrangements.

Americans and established Afrikaner refugees can participate by welcoming a family, assisting with meal delivery, or contributing toward Thanksgiving meals.

Thanksgiving is more than a meal. It is an opportunity to thank God for His blessings, share what we have, and extend friendship to those around us.

Our hope is that this becomes an annual tradition, creating relationships that last long after Thanksgiving Day.
Two Homelands. Shared Faith. One Thanksgiving.

text:
📓Antichrist in Nashville — Peter Thiel’s Theological Attack on AI Regulation📓

Markku Siira

Investor, technology entrepreneur, and unconventional lay theologian Peter Thiel has been giving lectures in Nashville, once again focusing on the Antichrist. The lectures have been held at the Grand Lodge of Tennessee Freemasons, bringing together a select audience to contemplate end-times prophecies, technological development, and the future of the world.

Nashville is the fourth stop on Thiel’s Antichrist tour. He has previously held similar events in San Francisco, Paris, and Rome. One of the world’s most influential technology investors has repeatedly explained to his audiences why the Bible’s great end-times deceiver might appear disguised as a regulator of artificial intelligence.

Thiel’s central thesis is a conceptual reversal. He already argued in San Francisco that the Antichrist of the 21st century could be a Luddite — someone seeking to halt scientific and technological progress — such as climate activist Greta Thunberg or AI skeptic Eliezer Yudkowsky.

In Nashville, he sharpened the argument into a political attack. According to recordings obtained by Politico, Thiel named Obama and Pope Leo XIV, saying that they “know that AI is not politically popular and want to exploit this to boost their own reputations.” His attack on the pope was even more direct. According to Thiel, the pope promotes AI regulation “to distract attention from the Church’s child-abuse scandals; he has found in AI a politically popular issue.”

This is a techno-theological hybrid operation that deserves to be taken seriously. In traditional Christian end-times doctrine, the Antichrist is a usurper who places himself in the position of Christ. Thiel almost completely bypasses this image. In his narrative, the Antichrist is an administrator who promises to save civilization from nuclear war, climate collapse, and uncontrolled artificial intelligence through global governance.

Thiel refers to Matthew 24:24, which warns of false prophets who perform great signs and wonders and attempt to deceive even the elect. His rhetorical strategy is clear: the real danger is dangerous precisely because it does not look dangerous. Thiel says that the Antichrist will appear as “the smartest person in the room.”

What makes this argument suspect is how neatly it aligns with Thiel’s own financial interests. His wealth is heavily concentrated in artificial intelligence. Palantir’s products are deeply embedded in military and intelligence systems, Founders Fund has invested in countless AI startups, and his hedge fund Thiel Macro has a $418 million AI portfolio.

If the forces pushing for AI regulation truly constitute the vanguard of the Antichrist, then Thiel’s opposition to regulation is not merely a theological judgment. It is also a defense of his portfolio. When a billionaire tells you that the force restricting his ability to make money is an instrument of Satan, it is worth taking a look at his books.

The counterforce Thiel places against the Antichrist is the katechon, the “restrainer” from the Epistles to the Thessalonians, which delays the coming of the end. In Nashville, he identified Charlemagne and Metternich as historical katechons.

He then made the transition to contemporary politics: “If anti-communism was the katechon preventing communism’s global one-world government, then neoliberalism is anti-communism in a world where communism no longer exists.”

This sentence is the political core of the entire lecture. During the Cold War, containment had a real external enemy that provided justification for a political katechon. When the Cold War ended, the enemy disappeared, but the logic of containment remained. It shifted toward new targets.

Effective altruism is one of those new targets. According to Politico, Thiel said in Nashville:

“The effective altruism strategy works in part because Armageddon is, of course, irreversible. You only have one planet. Greta is right about that. So you can’t simply ignore the risk. But people also have to take seriously that once you have created an almost totalitarian one-world government capable of stopping all dangerous science, that is not easily reversible either. There is no precedent in human history for this global prison warden voluntarily giving up its power. The ideology of effective altruism has brainwashed a significant portion of the people working on AI.”

There is an enormous crack in this argument. Thiel takes for granted a causal relationship between “stopping dangerous science” and “building a totalitarian world government.” Yet he never explains why an international AI-safety agreement would necessarily lead to global dictatorship.

The same outcome could just as easily result from superintelligence developed by American corporations. Those demanding AI regulation fear the consequences of the current trajectory, while others hope only to accelerate technological progress — either path could lead to increasingly centralized global governance.

Thiel argues that there is no precedent for such power voluntarily relinquishing its position. But the absence of precedent does not prove that something is inevitable. The leap from possibility to necessity is the weakest point of the entire lecture and, at the same time, the most important one: without it, identifying the Antichrist with the regulator loses its urgency.

This connects Thiel’s end-times doctrine to his broader political projects. Cryptocurrency decentralizes the power of central banks. Defense technology startups decentralize the state’s military power. Space exploration turns humanity into a multiplanetary species that cannot be controlled by a single government.

Since 2009, Thiel has maintained that freedom and democracy are incompatible. His Antichrist lectures are the theological wrapping around that conviction. The Antichrist is not a single future individual, but a metaphor for any governing structure that attempts to coordinate a global response to shared problems.

Climate change is real, nuclear war is dangerous, and artificial intelligence may be catastrophic, but in Thiel’s thinking, any attempt to solve these problems collectively becomes a portent of the Antichrist.

Vatican adviser and Franciscan friar Paolo Benanti published an essay in March titled L’hérésie américaine : faut-il brûler Peter Thiel ? (The American Heresy: Should Peter Thiel Be Burned?) in Le Grand Continent.

In the essay, Benanti interprets Thiel’s entire project as “a prolonged heresy against the liberal consensus” and defines it as “an attack on the foundations of civilized coexistence, which he now considers obsolete.” According to Benanti, Thiel is not primarily a venture capitalist or technology innovator but “a political theologian operating at the heart of the Silicon Valley ecosystem.”

Nashville’s geography also deserves attention. The city lies at the heart of American evangelicalism while simultaneously becoming a growing technology hub, attracting companies relocating particularly from California.

The lectures were organized by the local online publication The Pamphleteer together with Meriwether Academy. The Pamphleteer offers “alternative regional perspectives to mainstream media,” while Meriwether Academy is a kind of men’s advocacy academy that seeks to “develop networks of brotherhood and study societies across the United States,” with the ultimate goal of establishing boys’ schools based on classical education.

Thiel’s lectures, however, are troubled by a deeper philosophical problem. He has embraced René Girard’s theory of mimetic desire. According to it, human desire is fundamentally imitative: people desire what other people desire. Society manages the violence arising from this through the scapegoat mechanism.

Thiel applies this framework to technology policy. In his interpretation, the scapegoat mechanism becomes a primordial form of global governance: confronted by a common threat, society selects a victim, sacrifices it, and restores peace. His strategy of resistance is to refuse the sacrifice.

The Girardian irony, however, is that Thiel himself is also looking for scapegoats. Greta Thunberg, Obama, the pope, supporters of effective altruism, and AI-safety researchers are all presented as threats within his narrative. If the theory of mimetic desire is correct, it should apply to Thiel’s own behavior as well.

Recordings of the Nashville lectures became public almost immediately. Thiel, who has spent decades investing and channeling political donations, certainly knows how a leak can be made to look accidental.

The content of the lectures may not be as important as the way in which it was delivered: in a semi-public setting, in theological language, and as a narrative presented to a carefully selected audience that equates the technology regulator with the Antichrist.

The function of this narrative is not to predict, but to mobilize. It gives a particular political position a cosmological dimension. Within this dimension, regulators are not merely wrong; they are the deceivers of the end times.

And those who oppose them — accelerating technology, decentralizing power, and refusing to sacrifice — are not merely pursuing profit or freedom. They are waging a theological battle.

This is where the real significance of Thiel’s lectures lies within this technocapitalist eschatology.

He redefines the Antichrist in such a way that any force attempting to exercise power to regulate technology can be fitted into the category. It is an almost unfalsifiable framework.

If regulation comes, it is the work of the Antichrist. If regulation does not come, it is because the katechon is still holding it back. If Thiel’s own AI investments benefit as a result, that benefit can be presented as a by-product of the struggle for freedom.

Within this framework, every piece of evidence points in the same direction. It draws on the oldest narrative in the Christian worldview, serves the newest interests, and disguises the pursuit of self-interest and the defense of technological acceleration as a battle against absolute evil.

There is the "ring" of reality and then there are those of constructed realities based on fantasy, conjecture, and (if the arguer is honest) admitted, massive conflations to dismiss the difference in locale.

Either way though, I do wish you well. Signing off

text:
Conservation, Tourism and Community Participation: A Global Conversation

This morning, as I continued my 20th Edition of the Ivory Belongs to Elephants / Walking for Giants campaign from California towards New York, I had the privilege of hosting a three-hour livestream conversation with participants joining from different parts of the world.

Our discussion centred on three interconnected pillars: **Conservation, Tourism and Community Participation** and how they can work together to create a sustainable future for people and nature.

One of the key contributions came from Utamaduni Finest Julius Kihoro Thuo who highlighted the significant role tourism plays in the economies of many countries, contributing to national GDP, employment and livelihoods.

This sparked an important reflection: *How can we ensure that tourism not only generates economic benefits but also contributes meaningfully to wildlife conservation and community development?*

Across Africa, wildlife and natural landscapes are vital assets for tourism. Elephants, in particular, are an integral part of our natural heritage, attracting visitors from across the world and supporting tourism-related livelihoods.

However, the future of wildlife tourism depends on our ability to protect the very resources that make it possible. Without healthy ecosystems and thriving wildlife populations, sustainable nature-based tourism cannot endure.

Conservation cannot be the responsibility of governments and conservation organisations alone. Local communities, landowners, tourism operators, researchers, young people and the private sector must all have a meaningful role.

Communities living alongside wildlife should not simply be expected to bear the costs of conservation; they should also have opportunities to benefit from it.

When people see tangible benefits from protecting nature, we strengthen local ownership, encourage coexistence and build a stronger foundation for long-term conservation.

As I walk through Texas on my journey from California to New York, I see opportunities to connect experiences from the United States with conservation approaches across Africa.

Texas offers important perspectives on land stewardship, wildlife management, hunting traditions and tourism. Africa, meanwhile, provides valuable lessons from its extensive wildlife landscapes, elephant migration corridors, community conservancies and protected areas.

By exchanging knowledge and experiences, we can explore approaches that balance ecological sustainability, cultural traditions, economic development and the long-term survival of wildlife.

This morning's livestream reminded me that conservation is a global responsibility. Although we may live in different countries and come from different backgrounds, we share a common interest in protecting our natural heritage for future generations.

As I continue my 120-day walk, I remain committed not only to walking for elephants but also to creating platforms where people can exchange ideas, build partnerships and identify practical solutions for conservation.

My sincere appreciation to **Utamaduni Finest and everyone who participated in this morning's three-hour global conversation.** Your voices and contributions are an important part of this journey.

Tourism can help finance conservation. Community participation can strengthen ownership. Partnerships can turn shared ideas into action.

**When conservation, tourism and community participation work together, both people and nature have a better chance of thriving.**

*When I don't walk, I talk about elephants. When I walk, every step tells their story.*

**Day 39 of 120 | California to New York | 20th Edition Walking for Giants**

🗞 What Else Happened Today — October 19

AI, tech and games: stories that didn't make the feed

🧠 AI

▪️ CoreWeave's bonds are now in distressed territory
Last week CoreWeave's bonds fell so far that investors wanted 1,000 basis points more than government bonds pay. That matters for the whole AI build-out, which leans on borrowed money.

▪️ Nvidia launches new open models for agents
Nvidia released new open models for running AI agents in company data centers and on PCs. It's pushing private, on-device agents that companies keep asking for.

▪️ Microsoft says AI agents are a bit like insider threats
Microsoft wants companies to watch closely the agents staff use with systems outside AI labs' control, like OpenAI and Anthropic. It says frontier models can't be fully trusted.

▪️ Former OpenAI engineer had folder named Saudi Gov Docs
The FBI says the accused engineer kept a folder called 'Saudi Gov Docs'. A judge kept him in custody and called the Saudi offer to secure his release a 'blank check'.

▪️ Amazon's TorchNeuron tool takes aim at Nvidia
Amazon wants more developers to run PyTorch apps on alternative chips, its own included, instead of Nvidia's. It's the company's biggest push against Nvidia so far.

▪️ Homeland Security bans DeepSeek in federal civilian agencies
Homeland Security has banned DeepSeek use in federal civilian agencies. The decision came a couple of days after DeepSeek released its latest AI model.

▪️ Hackers hit OpenCode and ran up users' AI bills
Hackers broke into part of OpenCode's platform, stole some users' API keys and ran up charges on their AI accounts. For anyone using AI coding tools, API keys are the thing to guard.

▪️ Four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft in 27 hours
A team of four AI agents finished Minecraft on its own, with no human help, in 27 hours. Researchers published a report on the first fully autonomous run.

💻 Tech

▪️ Meta changes its new terms after scraping backlash
Meta has tweaked its new terms of service after backlash over scraping. The first version alarmed publishers and other business accounts.

▪️ TP-Link moves to assemble routers in the US
After an import ban, TP-Link is moving router assembly to the US. A Missouri production line could start rolling out routers as early as early 2027.

🎮 Games

▪️ Liquid Swords, maker of Samson, is closing
Christopher Sundberg, co-writer of Just Cause and Mad Max, says Liquid Swords is closing. Samson did well on consoles, and that still didn't save the studio.

▪️ Switch 2 V2 is out, but the screen issue stays
Nintendo released a new Switch 2 revision called V2. First checks show no clear display improvement, so the screen problem is still there.

▪️ Frostpunk comes to Nintendo Switch and Switch 2
The survival strategy Frostpunk is now out on Nintendo Switch and Switch 2. It's a city-building game about surviving an icy apocalypse.

https://t.co/IdOkJhTTPx

14 Oct 2026

Should you publish your content as a PDF or stick strictly to standard HTML?

Does Google treat PDF files differently when it comes to indexing, ranking, and AI search features?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team demystify how Google Search handles PDF documents.

They break down some of Google's internal pipelines, explain why putting an LLMs.txt file inside a PDF is a bad idea, explore common technical traps like rasterized pages and canonicalization issues, and share practical advice on managing PDFs for SEO, AEO (SEO), and user experience.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   Google's PDF converter pipeline: How Google converts binary PDF containers into HTML pages during indexing so the rest of the pipeline can process them normally.

LLMs.txt as a PDF: Why saving an LLMs.txt file as a PDF is a bad idea, even if you like LLMs.txt.     File limits & Project Gutenberg: Why crawling limits exist, and how HTML and PDF size limits function in the crawl pipeline.

Rasterized pages & accessibility: How pages saved as images destroy text readability, ruin screen reader accessibility, and prevent Google from extracting text content.

Canonicalization & "binary blobs": Why identical PDF downloads across different sites make canonicalization harder and how using rel="canonical" HTTP headers or embedded header links can help.

PDFs for SEO in AI Overviews: How PDFs are parsed, ranked, and referenced in Google Search, AI Overviews, and broader AI systems for training and grounding.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

HTML is preferred, and PDFs work: HTML offers better mobile responsiveness, zoom reflow, and faster loading.

Internally, Google converts indexable PDF text into HTML so they can rank normally and appear in AI features.

Test for text indexability: Highlight and copy text out of your PDF into a text editor; if text doesn't copy, it might be a rasterized image and can't be indexed easily.

For restaurant menus: A PDF menu is better than no menu at all for restaurants, but a responsive HTML web page provides superior performance, accessibility, and user experience. (Credit: Google)

Do sitemaps still matter?
https://t.co/Gdz66VVykn

1 October 2026

Sitemaps have been a core element of web development and search engine optimization for two decades, yet Search Console warnings like "Couldn't fetch" continue to generate concern among site owners.

Are XML sitemaps still necessary with modern search crawlers, or can search engines and AI bots figure out site structure on their own?

In this episode of Search off the Record, Google Search Relations team members Martin Splitt and John Mueller break down the history, technical specifications, and some misconceptions surrounding sitemaps, RSS feeds, LLMs.txt, canonicalization signals, and Search Console indexing behaviors.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Origins of Sitemaps: How early web crawling challenges led to the sitemap standard and how building a sitemap generator started John Mueller's career at Google.

Obsolete vs. Active XML Fields: Why Google dropped support for the priority and changefreq tags, and how the lastmod date is actually evaluated.

XML Sitemaps vs. RSS Feeds: How RSS feeds function as lightweight sitemaps for recent updates and why AI training crawlers utilize both.     Technical Limits & Index Files: The exact URL (50,000) and file size (50MB uncompressed) limits, alongside best practices for sitemap index files and robots.txt declarations.

HTML Sitemaps & LLMs.txt: Why user-facing HTML maps and Markdown-based LLMs.txt files cannot replace structured XML sitemaps for search engines.     Troubleshooting "Couldn't Fetch": How host load management and perceived site quality (crawl demand) trigger non-technical fetching errors in Search Console.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

Keep Sitemaps Enabled by Default: Even for small websites or dynamic CMS setups, keeping auto-generated sitemaps active carries no downside and assists with discovery as sites grow.

Provide Accurate lastmod Timestamps: Avoid setting all page timestamps to the current date; Google evaluates date reliability and will ignore lastmod signals if they are inaccurate or abused.

Submit Canonical URLs Only: Always place clean, canonical versions of URLs inside your sitemap file rather than parameter-tagged tracking URLs to help guide Google’s canonical selection.

"Couldn't Fetch" Isn't Always a Syntax Error: If Search Console reports "Couldn't fetch" on a valid, accessible XML file, the cause is often host load throttling or low crawl demand linked to perceived site quality.

(Credit: Google)

How to read the Indexing Report
https://t.co/h7AnJWQuAP

July 16, 2026

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

Chapters 0:00 - Introduction: Should we all be using Markdown?
3:45 - The history and purpose of Markdown.
7:15 - Why developers love it: Separation of style and content.
11:20 - Do crawlers need Markdown to understand your site?

17:30 - Discussing the "llms.txt" proposal and AI agents. 21:00 - Where Markdown actually makes sense (Developer Docs).
24:00 - Final verdict: Stick to HTML for the web.

Today’s edition covers the stories that matter most to American security, sovereignty and the cost of living. Conservative and center-right outlets lead the sourcing. Wire and mainstream reports are used only to corroborate when a page was paywalled or the reporting was thin. Allegations, official claims and battlefield figures are attributed, and events are dated when they happened.

DOMESTIC U.S. NEWS  🦅

DOJ Charges 28 Green-Card Holders In California Noncitizen-Voting Sweep (Oct. 19)

Federal prosecutors charged 28 lawful permanent residents in California with illegally registering to vote. Prosecutors allege 21 of them cast ballots, some in multiple elections. Eleven were arrested Monday and 17 more are expected to be taken into custody. Charges include fraudulent registration and, for some, false statements on naturalization paperwork. All 28 appear on a list of about 20,000 “likely noncitizen” registrants that DOJ gave California officials last week. DOJ has also sued the state to block counting mail ballots from people on that list until citizenship is confirmed. Officials say 113 people in 20 states have been charged in recent weeks. State and county officials had not responded at the time of reporting, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

Source: Washington Examiner; Washington Times; Associated Press

Kansas Man Charged With Threatening Trump Ahead Of Wichita Rally

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for Kansas filed a complaint
Oct. 17 against Jaden J. Read, 24, of Clearwater, under the federal statute on threats against the president. The charge carries up to five years in prison. A Crime Stoppers tip led investigators to Facebook comments on local news stories about the president’s visit. Prosecutors allege the posts called for shooting Trump and claimed Read had mapped nearby rooftops. He remains in federal custody pending a detention hearing. Trump was scheduled to rally Monday evening for Sen. Roger Marshall, who is in a tightening race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. Separately, Mediaite reported that Secret Service Director Sean Curran told “60 Minutes” on Sunday that threats against protectees are up about 40%.

Source: U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Kansas; KSN; Washington Examiner; NBC News; Mediaite

Trump And Vance Hit The Trail In The Midterm Homestretch

Election Day is Nov. 3. Trump’s week includes Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Iowa and Florida, with Georgia and Michigan next weekend. Vance campaigned in Hendersonville, N.C., on Monday and announces a Nebraska stop Thursday. In North Carolina he announced an additional $858 million in Transportation Department disaster funds for Hurricane Helene recovery. Early voting opened Monday in Texas. Gray DC, citing the latest race ratings, says Democrats hold an edge in the fight for Congress. CNBC reported Sunday that Democrats are surging in fundraising while Elon Musk backs Republicans.

Source: Washington Examiner; Gray DC; CNBC

DOJ Opens Civil-Rights Probe Into D.C. Jails (Oct. 19)

Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon notified Mayor Muriel Bowser that DOJ will investigate whether the D.C. Department of Corrections engages in a “pattern or practice” of violating inmates’ constitutional rights. The review covers safety, living conditions and meals. This is the opening of an investigation, not a finding of wrongdoing.

Source: Washington Examiner

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS  🌐

Lavrov Visits Tehran; No New Russian Mediation Plan Announced (Oct. 19)

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met Iran’s Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian. It was his first Iran visit since the U.S.-Israeli war began Feb. 28. He called the strikes illegal and urged a return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz. In Bahrain earlier, he urged both sides to revisit the Pakistan-brokered Islamabad memorandum. That agreement collapsed within weeks after Iran attacked ships it said were violating it. The New Arab reported that neither side announced a new mediation initiative. Araghchi blamed the U.S. war and its naval blockade for the insecurity. He said Iran’s seven-day ceasefire and phased-reopening offer is still on the table. The offer requires the U.S. to lift the blockade and sanctions, and Trump rejected it last month. Washington says the Strait is open to everyone except Iran and wants nuclear issues addressed at the outset.

Source: Washington Times; CBS News/AP; The New Arab; Fox News

Trump Endorses Netanyahu Ahead Of Oct. 27 Israeli Vote (Oct. 18–19)

Trump gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a full endorsement Sunday. He said that if Israel chooses a different leader, the U.S. would have to handle Iran largely alone. He also said the U.S. could soon complete the effort against Iran unless Tehran changes course. On Monday Netanyahu posted video of a phone call with Trump in which he said, “we have a job to finish.” Netanyahu has said he told Israeli security agencies to work toward toppling the Iranian regime. Araghchi dared the U.S. to strike again and accused Netanyahu of pushing America into war to avoid prosecution. That is an Iranian claim.

Source: Fox News; CBS News

Trump Waives Russia Sanctions; Gop Senators Object (Order Signed Oct. 16)

Trump signed an executive order Friday waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act. The law, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was signed Sept. 18 and was due to take effect two days later. Trump certified to Congress that the waiver serves the national interest. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration will take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called it “a carrot” to end the war and said Russia currently exports no diesel. Republican Sens. Thom Tillis, John Cornyn and Kevin Cramer and Rep. Don Bacon criticized the move. Democrats including Chuck Schumer also attacked it. CBS reports the roughly 300,000-ton Russian diesel purchase is about 2.2 million barrels, only a bit over half of one day’s U.S. diesel use. It also notes that delivery timing is unclear because Ukraine has damaged Russian refining capacity.

Source: CBS News; Reuters via Fox News; TheStreet

Trump–Zelenskyy Rift Deepens; Putin Floats Trump–Xi Summit; Starlink Questions Persist (Oct. 19)

Trump said Monday that Ukraine should pick “somebody else” to negotiate, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump is on the wrong side of history. Per the Wall Street Journal, Putin proposed a Trump–Xi–Putin summit without Zelenskyy during an Oct. 9 call. The idea could tie in with November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Rubio said a meeting has been discussed but is not finalized. Zelenskyy says throttled Starlink/Starshield speeds are hampering drone interception. Musk says Starshield limits are set by the U.S. government and ultimately the president. Trump denied imposing them and said Monday he did not know who ordered them but wants to find out. Nine senators have asked the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate. Tillis and Sen. Richard Blumenthal said after a Monday call that Zelenskyy reported disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing. HuffPost reported Rubio says sharing never stopped.

Source: Washington Examiner; CBS News; Wall Street Journal via TheStreet; HuffPost

France: Arrests Top 2,000 After Violent Cost-Of-Living Protests (Oct. 17–18)

France’s Interior Ministry reported 2,397 arrests Saturday and 997 police and gendarmes injured. Authorities put turnout at about 550,000 and organizers at about 800,000. Macron expressed “anger and shame” in a televised address, promised rioters would pay for their crimes, and vowed “full transparency” on the police response after criticism of inadequate preparation. Trump posted “France is burning!” and appeared to link the unrest to immigration. Vance also blamed immigration. French authorities have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have pointed to “radical far-left groups” and opportunistic looters. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman taunted Macron over the unrest.

Source: Associated Press via Washington Times and ABC News; France 24; Fox News

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

BUSINESS & MARKETS  💹

Tech rebounds after worst week since June (Monday close)

The Nasdaq Rose 291 Points (+1.1%) To 26,431.

The S&P 500 gained 31 points (+0.4%) to 7,691, and the Dow slipped 36 points (-0.1%) to 51,966. Amazon (+4.95%), Palantir (+4.36%), Tesla (+3.74%) and Micron led gainers. Meta and Apple lagged. Netflix, GE Aerospace and SpaceX report Tuesday, and Tesla, Meta, IBM and Texas Instruments report Wednesday, per TheStreet.

Source: Proactive Investors; TheStreet; Newslooks

Oil Swings On The Russia Waiver And Houthi Attacks; Pump Prices Ease Slightly

Brent settled Friday at $109.86, its highest since May 19. Crude dipped early Monday after the Russia waiver. WTI then reversed to about $103.73 by mid-afternoon, up roughly 2.4%, after Houthi attacks on Saudi targets. AAA’s national gasoline average was $4.30 Monday, down from $4.36 a week earlier. AAA says this is the first October above $4. Diesel hit a record near $6.49 in September. Wright said gasoline never approached $5 and is falling. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said prices should drop by the new year if the Iran conflict ends.

Source: Reuters via Fox News; TheStreet; Washington Examiner (AAA data); Fox 7 Austin (AAA data); ABC News

Homebuilder Sentiment Hits Lowest Since 2012

The NAHB/Wells Fargo index fell three points to 29, below the 31 economists expected. Freddie Mac says the 30-year mortgage averaged 7.40% last week, a near three-year high. Builders cited energy-linked costs, tariffs and labor shortages. Forty-three percent cut prices. NAHB chairman Bill Owens said more than one-third of builders reported immigration-enforcement activity in their areas that delayed projects and discouraged legal workers from showing up.

Source: Reuters via TheStreet

Saudi Investor Forum Postponed To 2027 (Oct. 19)

Organizers moved the Future Investment Initiative from Oct. 26–29 in Riyadh to 2027 amid Houthi attacks. The postponement follows a reported Oct. 10 attack on Riyadh’s airport that killed at least 12. Scheduled speakers included top Wall Street CEOs.

Source: CNBC via TheStreet; CBS News/AFP

SCIENCE & HEALTH  ⚕️

Trump Signs Women’s Health Order Creating Nih Division And Task Force (Oct. 19)

The order establishes a Women’s Health Division at NIH and a White House task force led by Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. It does not replace NIH’s existing Office of Research on Women’s Health. Melania Trump, who helped shape the initiative, signed alongside the president, though her signature carries no legal weight. The White House fact sheet cites research gaps in Alzheimer’s, endometriosis, infertility, maternal health and menopause. The order also rescinds prior-administration women’s-health initiatives.

Source: OAN; CBS News; NBC News; The Hill

1.58 Million Pounds Of Ready-To-Eat Meats Recalled (Announced Oct. 17)

Kayem Foods of Chelsea, Mass., is recalling 1,584,361 pounds of hot dogs, bacon, sausage, turkey breast, ham and deli meats. USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service said product was kept in a warehouse cooler with temperature deviations after a retailer reported warm product Oct. 1. Items were made March 31–Oct. 7, 2026 and shipped nationwide and to Hong Kong. No illnesses have been confirmed. Consumers should check the FSIS list and discard or return affected items.

Source: USDA FSIS via Food Safety News; NBC Chicago

Review Narrows Timing Of First Human Arrival In The Americas

A University of Kansas review of previously published DNA and archaeological evidence says genetic data most strongly support arrival 14,000–20,000 years ago, likely before 15,000. That challenges the older “Clovis First” date of about 13,500 years. White Sands footprints dated to about 23,000 years ago suggest humans may have been present earlier than the genetic record shows. The authors say key timing and location questions remain uncertain.

Source: Fox News Digital

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

NATIONAL SECURITY  🛡️

State Department Urges Heightened Vigilance For Americans In The Middle East (Oct. 19)

A Monday security alert cites Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian airports and infrastructure. It warns hostilities could escalate rapidly and that Iran-backed groups may target U.S. interests or Americans worldwide. At least 20 people, including one American, died in a single October week of Houthi airport attacks.

Source: CBS News/AP

Iran Threatens AI And Data-Center Infrastructure (Oct. 18)

Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said a “Persian Gulf Data Authority” is coming. He warned regional governments, funds and firms not to supply finance, land or energy to AI or data companies he accused of aiding invasions. Security council chief Mohsen Rezaei said earlier that undersea cables and data and AI facilities worth about $2 trillion would be within range if war resumes. Details are sparse, and these are threats, not confirmed actions.

Source: Fox News; Iran International

Germany Jails Two Over Iran-Directed Plot; Tehran And Berlin Trade Summonses (Verdict Oct. 15)

A Hamburg court sentenced a Danish national to 8½ years and an Afghan national to 4½ years. It found one man was recruited by Iranian intelligence to surveil and prepare attacks on Jewish community leader Josef Schuster and German-Israeli Society head Volker Beck, plus Berlin Jewish grocers. Iran’s embassy has called the allegations unfounded. The verdicts can be appealed. Per AP, Iran summoned Germany’s ambassador Monday after Berlin summoned Iran’s envoy.

Source: Reuters; Times of Israel; CBS News/AP

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS  🪖

Houthis Hit Yemeni Government Camp; Saudi Front Escalates (Oct. 19)

Yemeni military officials told AP at least 53 soldiers were killed and about 200 recruits wounded when Houthi ballistic missiles struck a camp in Shabwa province, and the toll could rise. The Houthis claim six operations inside Saudi Arabia in 48 hours, including Riyadh’s airport and Aramco sites. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claims 558 Houthis killed in 24 hours. Those figures are party claims and are unverified. Riyadh residents received air-threat alerts. Egypt’s parliament postponed debate on authorizing support for Saudi Arabia to Oct. 26. AP reports Trump has said he is considering joining Saudi operations, and the Houthis warn of “swift and painful” retaliation.

Source: CBS News/AP/AFP; Fox News

Hormuz Shipping Attacks Climb (Through Oct. 18)

The U.K. maritime agency UKMTO counted 10 attacks on commercial vessels last week, making October the worst month since March. On Oct. 18, two unidentified projectiles hit a tug off the UAE, causing one minor injury. CENTCOM says an Iranian projectile hit the container ship GFS Pride on Oct. 14 and that it sank under tow. CENTCOM’s spokesman says about 97% of transiting ships get through unhurt.

Source: Fox News; CBS News

Strike Options And Force Buildup Continue (As Reported)

Fox News reports Trump has put off new Iran strikes during the campaign, and experts expect any retaliation after the election. The Pentagon has told CENTCOM to finish preparing for possible major combat, per Axios via Breitbart. The USS Theodore Roosevelt group and the Makin Island amphibious group, about 9,000–10,000 personnel, are heading to the region. Reports put arrival from late October to November. Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defense minister Sunday, and he warned of costly U.S. losses if strikes resume. Reuters, via Fox, says U.S. plans reportedly include the GBU-43/B against Iranian nuclear and energy sites. No new U.S. strikes were reported in the sources reviewed.

Source: Fox News; Breitbart; Daily Caller; Associated Press

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

OTHER NOTABLE AND UNUSUAL STORIES 🌀

Supreme Court Will Review 1868 Ban On Home Distilling (Oct. 19)

The justices agreed to hear DOJ v. McNutt, in which the Fifth Circuit struck the ban as beyond Congress’s powers. The Sixth Circuit upheld it in a separate case brought by John Ream, so the circuits are split. Home distilling can bring up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Arguments are expected early next year, with a ruling by summer.

Source: SCOTUSblog; The Hill; CNN; Fortune

Musk Pledges Spacex Share To “Every Kid In America” (Oct. 19)

Musk said on X he will give one SpaceX share to every American child next year. TheStreet put it above $10 billion at recent prices. He gave no age range or mechanics, so this is a pledge, not a completed action.

Source: TheStreet

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

AMERICA FIRST READ  🇺🇸

ANALYSIS — not a news report.

Energy costs tie much of today’s news together. Officials say pump prices have peaked, but gasoline is still above $4 and diesel hit a record last month. The administration’s relief moves are the Russian diesel deal, the sanctions waiver and a push to expand refining. Those moves are drawing fire from Republican allies and may not offset Hormuz and Saudi disruptions, as CBS noted of the diesel deal. Trump’s Iran posture appears to weigh deterrence and midterm politics. Whether strikes resume after Nov. 3 is expert speculation, not announced policy.

Gulf instability is also reaching American markets. The Saudi forum’s postponement and Iran’s threats against data infrastructure show the economic reach of the conflict. Housing data suggest tighter immigration enforcement may add to builders’ labor shortages, alongside higher rates. That is a trade-off to weigh, and it rests on one trade group’s survey.

On election integrity, 28 charges out of roughly 20,000 flagged names show enforcement action. They do not show how many people on that list are noncitizens, a question for the courts. California disputes DOJ’s claims, and neither side’s position has been tested.

On Ukraine, the open questions are who throttled Starlink and whether a Putin–Xi summit sidelines Kyiv. Both are fracturing GOP unity, with senators in both parties demanding answers.

Should you publish your content as a PDF or stick strictly to standard HTML? 

Does Google treat PDF files differently when it comes to indexing, ranking, and AI search features?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team demystify how Google Search handles PDF documents. 

They break down some of Google's internal pipelines, explain why putting an LLMs.txt file inside a PDF is a bad idea, explore common technical traps like rasterized pages and canonicalization issues, and share practical advice on managing PDFs for SEO, AEO (SEO), and user experience.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   Google's PDF converter pipeline: How Google converts binary PDF containers into HTML pages during indexing so the rest of the pipeline can process them normally.

LLMs.txt as a PDF: Why saving an LLMs.txt file as a PDF is a bad idea, even if you like LLMs.txt.     File limits & Project Gutenberg: Why crawling limits exist, and how HTML and PDF size limits function in the crawl pipeline.

Rasterized pages & accessibility: How pages saved as images destroy text readability, ruin screen reader accessibility, and prevent Google from extracting text content.

Canonicalization & "binary blobs": Why identical PDF downloads across different sites make canonicalization harder and how using rel="canonical" HTTP headers or embedded header links can help.

PDFs for SEO in AI Overviews: How PDFs are parsed, ranked, and referenced in Google Search, AI Overviews, and broader AI systems for training and grounding.

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

HTML is preferred, and PDFs work: HTML offers better mobile responsiveness, zoom reflow, and faster loading.

Internally, Google converts indexable PDF text into HTML so they can rank normally and appear in AI features.

Test for text indexability: Highlight and copy text out of your PDF into a text editor; if text doesn't copy, it might be a rasterized image and can't be indexed easily.

For restaurant menus: A PDF menu is better than no menu at all for restaurants, but a responsive HTML web page provides superior performance, accessibility, and user experience. (Credit: Google)

Do sitemaps still matter?
https://t.co/1NBbsypmox

1 October 2026

Sitemaps have been a core element of web development and search engine optimization for two decades, yet Search Console warnings like "Couldn't fetch" continue to generate concern among site owners.

Are XML sitemaps still necessary with modern search crawlers, or can search engines and AI bots figure out site structure on their own? 

In this episode of Search off the Record, Google Search Relations team members Martin Splitt and John Mueller break down the history, technical specifications, and some misconceptions surrounding sitemaps, RSS feeds, LLMs.txt, canonicalization signals, and Search Console indexing behaviors.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Origins of Sitemaps: How early web crawling challenges led to the sitemap standard and how building a sitemap generator started John Mueller's career at Google.

Obsolete vs. Active XML Fields: Why Google dropped support for the priority and changefreq tags, and how the lastmod date is actually evaluated. 

XML Sitemaps vs. RSS Feeds: How RSS feeds function as lightweight sitemaps for recent updates and why AI training crawlers utilize both.     Technical Limits & Index Files: The exact URL (50,000) and file size (50MB uncompressed) limits, alongside best practices for sitemap index files and robots.txt declarations.

HTML Sitemaps & LLMs.txt: Why user-facing HTML maps and Markdown-based LLMs.txt files cannot replace structured XML sitemaps for search engines.     Troubleshooting "Couldn't Fetch": How host load management and perceived site quality (crawl demand) trigger non-technical fetching errors in Search Console.     

Key takeaways for SEOs & developers:

Keep Sitemaps Enabled by Default: Even for small websites or dynamic CMS setups, keeping auto-generated sitemaps active carries no downside and assists with discovery as sites grow.

Provide Accurate lastmod Timestamps: Avoid setting all page timestamps to the current date; Google evaluates date reliability and will ignore lastmod signals if they are inaccurate or abused.

Submit Canonical URLs Only: Always place clean, canonical versions of URLs inside your sitemap file rather than parameter-tagged tracking URLs to help guide Google’s canonical selection.

"Couldn't Fetch" Isn't Always a Syntax Error: If Search Console reports "Couldn't fetch" on a valid, accessible XML file, the cause is often host load throttling or low crawl demand linked to perceived site quality.

(Credit: Google)

Should you panic when your Search Console indexing report is showing pages that aren't indexed?

Is a 404 error code always a sign of a broken website?

In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the Page Indexing report in Google Search Console. They unpack why treating this report as a static inventory checklist to "fix" things is the wrong response, how to spot massive SEO-ruining hosting or CDN traps, and why a healthy website doesn't actually need a 100% index rate.

In this episode, you’ll learn:   The Indexing Report Shift: Insights from the Search Console team's Hillel on why you should look for trend lines and systemic patterns rather than treating the report as a giant list of errors.

When 404s are Good: Why expected 404 errors are technically correct for deleted content, and how to survive the "boss panic" of numbers that won't go down.

The Domain Property Advantage: How setting up a domain property handles canonical shifts, www vs. non-www tracking, and performance data much cleaner.

The Site Query vs. Search Console: Why the site: query is an artificial tool that might show old domain moves or hreflang swaps for years, making Search Console your only true source of truth.

Hosting & CDN Traps: How aggressive bot protections, hidden interstitials, and "Soft 200" error pages completely destroy your crawl data and lead to malicious canonicalization.

Discovered vs. Crawled: What it actually means when pages sit in "Discovered/Crawled - currently not indexed," and how to recognize holistic site quality issues over technical bugs.

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers:   Patterns over Inventories: Use the report to verify that your intentional changes (like site migrations or page removals) are processing correctly over time.

Forget the Ratio: There is no magic metric for indexed vs. non-indexed pages. Even Google’s own developer documentation has a massive chunk of non-indexed content due to intentional choices.

Watch Out for Soft Blocks: Ensure your security layers or CDNs aren't serving "Are you a bot?" challenge screens to Googlebot with a 200 success code.

Computers Fail (And That's Fine): Minor server blips, failed DNS requests, or temporary 500 errors happen. Google's systems are resilient and will just try again later. (Credit: Google)

Should you convert your website into Markdown to help Large Language Models (LLMs) understand your content better?

Is "llms.txt" worth the effort for SEO? In this episode of Search Off the Record, Martin Splitt and John Mueller from the Google Search Relations team dive deep into the history of Markdown, its rise in the AI era, and whether it holds any real weight for search engine discovery.

In this episode, you’ll learn:

The Origins of Markdown: From John Gruber and Aaron Swartz to its status as the "language of GitHub." Markdown vs. HTML: Why the "cleanliness" of Markdown is tempting for developers but potentially risky for site structure. LLMs & Markdown: Do AI crawlers actually prefer Markdown, or are they already experts at parsing HTML?

The "Parallel Version" Trap: Why creating a separate text/Markdown version of your site for AI can lead to the same maintenance nightmares as dynamic rendering. Use Cases that Make Sense: When Markdown is actually superior (like developer documentation) and when it’s totally unnecessary (like your shoe catalog).

Key Takeaways for SEOs & Developers: Crawlers are built for the "messy" web: Google and other engines have decades of experience parsing HTML. Don't sacrifice discovery: Headers, footers, and sidebars in HTML provide critical context for site structure that a raw Markdown file might lack. Maintenance is king: Avoid the complexity of maintaining two versions of the same content.

Chapters 0:00 - Introduction: Should we all be using Markdown?
3:45 - The history and purpose of Markdown.

17:30 - Discussing the "llms.txt" proposal and AI agents. 21:00 - Where Markdown actually makes sense (Developer Docs).
24:00 - Final verdict: Stick to HTML for the web.

**CFTC's prediction-market "swap" rule takes effect today (Oct 18).** On October 9 the CFTC issued companion rules adding event contracts to the legal definition of a swap, with an interim final rule effective today that carves casino-style gambling back out. Google already updated its ad policy to bar prediction-market ads in Connecticut, Michigan, Nevada, New York and Ohio, the five states that have sued the operators. The feds just drew a federal line between sportsbooks and exchanges for the first time, and Nevada is standing on the enforcement side of it, so Vegas operators cannot treat prediction markets as a settled problem.
https://t.co/W7xvKW6MAH

**Hacksaw Gaming launches a B2B prediction-markets platform (Oct 19).** The slots supplier launched a white-label prediction-markets product on October 15, letting operator partners plug prediction markets into their own offerings, after the Malta Gaming Authority extended its license to cover peer-to-peer prediction-market operations. The move follows a third quarter where revenue growth slowed to 11-12%, down from 31% in Q2. When a slots studio starts selling prediction markets as a growth engine, the vertical has graduated from curiosity to a channel your future competitors will offer natively.
https://t.co/jBoegH1Ici

**Pennsylvania posts $555M in September gaming revenue, up 4.1% (Oct 19).** iGaming hit $249.3M, up 6.8%, with Hollywood Casino at Penn National leading at $99M; slots did $196.1M, up 2.4%, and the state collected $242.6M in tax revenue. Online keeps growing roughly three times faster than slots. That ratio is the brick-and-mortar operator's nightmare printed in one monthly release.
https://t.co/qCA1QgNwo0

**Macau Q3 GGR falls 3.8% as mass baccarat weakens (Oct 19).** Quarterly GGR came in at MOP60.22bn, with mass baccarat down 7.9% while VIP stayed broadly flat; slot machine revenue jumped 18.8%. The government kept its MOP236bn full-year forecast. The world's biggest mass baccarat market is now living the exact slot-versus-table mix shift US floors have been managing for years.
https://t.co/B1CSmAvPxS

**A Vegas startup is putting AI eyes on the surveillance room (Oct 17).** https://t.co/A3kN5I782q, founded in Las Vegas in 2024, is wrapping a pilot at Resorts World that turns existing cameras into real-time agents flagging dealer errors and cheating as they happen, and it could convert to a paid deal covering nearly 30 tables in the high-limit room. The eye in the sky has been a review desk for decades. If this lands, the operator's job becomes triaging an algorithm's flags, and every surveillance director in town will get asked why they are not doing it too.
https://t.co/cjtQHRrixb

**Americas Cardroom flips ScreenShield on by default November 4 (Oct 19).** Winning Poker Network's anti-screen-capture table protection goes default-on, after a review of more than 2 million hands found remote-access software on user machines, though no hole-card misuse was proven. Game protection has moved fully into software forensics: the threat vector now is not the device at the table, it is the remote-access tool running on a home PC.
https://t.co/0cTvowGUWv

**PAGCOR wants a December app to tell players which sites are licensed (Oct 19).** The Philippine regulator is targeting December 2026 for a mobile app that verifies licensed online platforms, built and hosted free by the Development Bank of the Philippines Data Center under a five-year deal. It is the regulator-as-product playbook: instead of blacklisting illegal sites, hand players a badge-checker. If it works, US states will borrow the idea.

Today I start with a Market Overview and the trading rules I follow, then two deep dives: Heliostar and Mackay Gold & Silver.

Market Overview: Gold bottomed over the summertime. It reached a record high of around 5,600 on the futures in January, had a sell-off, recovered, had another sell-off, and bottomed in the summer, dipping below 4,000 a couple of times, with the average bottom slightly above 4,000. Coming into late summer it rallied, creating a nice cup, then sold off again. I think the rally was optimism that the war with Iran and the Strait of Hormuz situation was going to be over, and when that fizzled, it corrected. What I pay attention to is how these bottoming processes relate to the previous one, and this latest bottom is about $100 to $150 higher than the last low. A rising bottom is always very bullish to me. The next rally I'm looking for off this basing period is to 4,800-plus, and I think we've got a good shot at 5,000 before the end of the year. The trepidation is over the conflict in the Middle East, the bond market and the election. I think the bond market is fearful of inflation, the debt level and the cost of servicing that debt. For fiscal 2026, total interest expense on the U.S. debt came in at about $1.36 trillion, more than the cost of the military. Think about that. The fundamental reason gold reached those highs is the death spiral of debt and the cost of servicing it, and those things are only getting more bullish. So I'm not too worried about this correction, and I'm very bullish on it correcting to a higher low. Now we want to see a higher high. Silver bottomed around the same time as gold, didn't rally quite as much, and is now basing around its summer level. To me that's a coiled spring, not only for trading reasons but for the value proposition: not enough being mined, not enough new mines in the pipeline, and a deficit driven by solar panels. These are opportunities for accumulating, not reasons to be fearful. Copper is a rock star, trading from the lower left of the chart to the upper right. It's been trending sideways around 6.60, with the top of the range just below 7 and the bottom around 6.40, and I think that's another basing sequence. Every dollar level brings consternation as it approaches and breaks through. The deficit between what is consumed and what is mined is only going to grow, because current mines are getting old and having problems. Chile, one of the most important copper mining countries in the world, is revising its production estimates lower, and you've got problems at Grasberg too. Sulfur, which is really important for refining copper, is being blocked from moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile demand keeps growing from AI, data centers, cloud computing, electric vehicles and rewiring the energy grid in developed and developing countries, and I'm not even looking ahead to robotics, which will make AI look like child's play. There aren't enough projects in development to increase production or even replace what's being mined out, and not enough important discoveries. These are 10- to 20-year issues that won't be fixed overnight. So the bullish argument is getting stronger for gold, silver and copper, and it's all based on demand and supply. Investors get very wrapped up in price over value, getting more bullish as price goes up and more bearish as it goes down, which is why I always focus on value over price. The same goes for the miners, developers and explorers. I believe the top companies in each category will significantly outperform the metals. I think this is a once-in-a-decade or once-in-a-generation opportunity. The last time was the 2001 to 2011 gold bull market: the metals were strong for the first few years, and then the miners, developers and explorers with important discoveries started to participate in a magical fashion. We haven't reached that magical moment yet for the stocks, but I think it's coming.

My personal rules: I always go into a stock with a thesis. When the thesis changes for the good, the bad or the indifferent, that tells me when to make a decision. Sometimes a bullish thesis just gets more bullish and there's no need to change anything; sometimes the thesis is broken and you get out. The thesis is what it's all about, folks, not the price. Too many investors make price their thesis, and they're destined to buy the highs and sell the lows. I never sell a stock into a red day, and I never buy a stock into a green day. Many investors do the exact opposite, and that's an absolute rule I've always followed. It's done me pretty well over the years. Price is what you pay, value is what you get. Put that on your computer screen. That applies to every stock and every sector, and it's what the big boys and big girls who outperform the index do.

Heliostar's latest Ana Paula drill results (Ana Paula Project, Guerrero, Mexico): 52.4 metres grading 5.84 g/t gold from the High Grade Panel, including 12.6 metres of 17.8 g/t, while they continue to build out the Expansion Zone. That's a fantastic intersection. At about $130 a gram, 5.84 g/t is roughly $780-a-tonne rock that might cost you about a hundred bucks to mine underground, and the rest is margin, your free cash flow. Within those 52 metres you've got jewelry boxes of over $2,000-a-tonne rock. That's how I look at things: what's the value of the rock, and do you have continuity? They certainly do. They also hit 24.8 metres of 5.14 g/t from just 43 metres downhole, so right as you start your underground workings, boom, you're into very attractive rock. The Expansion Zone has very handsome grades over mineable widths, and that's the depth potential: you'd pay for your capex from the near-surface high grade, and that becomes gravy. Infill drilling in the High Grade Panel continues to demonstrate continuity. People say grade is king, but if it's random, some over here and some way over there, that's not a mine no matter how high grade it is. What you need is continuity. CEO Charles Funk says they've completed the conversion drilling program that will drive the upcoming Feasibility Study, the results show a remarkably consistent body of gold mineralization in the High Grade Panel that will drive the economics of the Ana Paula mine, and they remain confident in their target of an initial 10-year mine life averaging 100,000 ounces a year. He also highlights continued hits over impressive step-outs in the Expansion Zone, open in multiple directions, with potential to grow materially as they chase gold deeper toward a source intrusion and skarn targets like those hosting multi-million-ounce resources at nearby mines. Their current small-scale production generates free cash flow to help build Ana Paula, their platform to grow into a mid-tier producer around 2030. That's a great game plan, and I think they're executing very well. Before Heliostar, the previous owner wanted a bigger open pit, with a very high strip ratio. The Heliostar team modelled the high grade and said, wait a minute, we can go underground, which is easier to permit and less capex. Their drilling has proven that thesis out, with access from the old open pit, and where drilling is thinner, the zones still hang together. It looks like a mirror image of the High Grade Panel is developing, which they could reach from underground drill stations. I break gold miners down to valuation per 100,000 ounces of production. Over the last few years that's been about C$1 billion for higher-cost producers and closer to C$2 to C$2.5 billion for low-cost producers. Heliostar has a C$690 million valuation, very inexpensive compared to where they're going as Ana Paula gets into production, and if gold heads higher, that metric becomes even more bullish. They have a very good audience, about 687,000 shares a day, and they're up 2%, or 4.5 cents, on what looks like significant volume on a day when gold is down. Red day for gold, green day for Heliostar. Pay attention to those. On the https://t.co/eqFpIa32h7 Pro depth of market, the buy side is softer than the sell side, so there could be a bit of a cap, but I look at a cap as a hurdle to go through, and $2.60 to $2.80 is in my short-term window. https://t.co/eqFpIa32h7 Pro Sentiment is broadly optimistic, supported by the strong Ana Paula drill results, the grades and thicknesses, and its potential as a long-life, high-production asset, as I believe wholeheartedly. Charles Funk is a very talented geologist with a very good mind for business, and he reminds me of Ross Beaty. He could be the Ross Beaty of the future. The negatives say Ana Paula requires permitting, financing, construction and execution, which you can say about every development project, and I think they'll pass those tests with flying colors. Some question the timeline and dilution, so use that as a litmus test and watch whether they use current production to fund Ana Paula. On Mexico, yes, there are security issues in many locations, but it's an important miner of silver, gold and copper. I've often said that if you're looking at high-grade silver mining, all roads lead to Mexico, and I'd say the same for gold. Frustration about share price weakness is misdirected: the whole mining sector is seeing that. On the Lassonde Curve: they do exploration, but I don't like them for the left side. It's all about going up the right side, with production paying for development while they do feasibility work, from late phase three through phase four and into phase five. Using Ana Paula alone, they're being looked at as only about 25% into my sweet spot on the right side, before the run up the right side of the curve. I think this company has a very good future and is a great one to do your homework on.

Mackay Gold & Silver reports its second batch of drill results (Occidental South, Comstock District, Nevada): hole 26MGS0014 returned 2.30 g/t gold over 67.1 metres, 26MGS0015 returned 1.48 g/t over 97.5 metres, and 26MGS0013 returned 1.17 g/t over 70.1 metres. This is a brand new trading company, and the CEO, Darwin Green, is a very talented geologist I worked with in the past at a large geological consulting firm in Vancouver, so I can speak from experience. They came out of the block with a pretty handsome valuation and very well financed, because they have the old Comstock Lode ground, the district that made Nevada the Silver State. A lot of people think of it as the gold state, but the reason the license plates say Silver State is the Comstock. Darwin and his team did a great job consolidating what was a patchwork of claims. The high-grade sub-intervals include 17.93 g/t over 4.6 metres, 5.56 g/t over 15.2 metres and 5.22 g/t over 7.6 metres. At $125 to $130 a gram, that's very handsomely valued rock over mineable widths. Occidental South is rapidly taking shape as a potentially significant new discovery, with excellent continuity of thick, high-grade, near-surface gold-silver mineralization across 550 metres of strike on nominal 50-metre sections, open on all sides. This was an economic driver in early Nevada history, basically untouched for about a hundred years, and new discoveries are still being made. They're taking wide step-outs in a high-grade system, and actions speak louder than words: that tells you a lot about their confidence. Systematic drilling is underway across the initial 1 kilometre of the 5-kilometre Occidental-Brunswick Lode, with 45 holes and 9,300 metres completed of a planned 20,000-metre, 100-hole program, and assays pending for 30 holes. Darwin says Occidental South is quickly evolving into what appears to be a significant new discovery, with early results demonstrating grade, width and continuity, and with just 15 holes reported, they're off to a great start. I love geologists who talk about continuity. Grade is not king; it's grade plus continuity, and I hope one day to change that saying. They're targeting shallow oxide mineralization, which is also important. Oxide gold can be open pit mined and leached very inexpensively, and some oxide pits are mined at less than half a gram these days: $50 or $60 of gold that costs $20 or less to get out, and at 30,000 tonnes a day, you make a lot of money. That's why so much of Nevada mining is oxide open pits. At 1.17 g/t over 70 metres, this is definitely not tonnage challenged, and the high-grade sweet spots inside, like 17.93 g/t over 4.6 metres, are the honeypots open pit miners love. Look at the continuity on the sections: slap a pit model on that and there's a lot of juicy material, and the depth potential looks wide open. My mentor, Bob Darney, always told me to pay attention to where the gold is distributed within a drill hole, and their heat-map view shows exactly that, with silver hanging together with the gold. They have a C$285 million valuation. Some would say that's healthy for an explorer just starting its first 20,000 metres, and I'd tend to agree, but it's because they consolidated the Comstock Lode area and opened it up to exploration that hasn't happened in a hundred years. In real estate terms, you couldn't get better. I think it could go higher because Darwin and his team are very talented explorers in a very juiced-up area for gold and silver. They don't have a big audience yet, having started trading in the last six months or so, averaging about 47,000 shares a day, but today they've traded 181,000, more than three times average, and they're up 5.2%, or 16 cents, to $3.26. The offers look heavy, probably pre-IPO investors taking profits, but jamming up the offers is a poor way to sell because it scares away buyers. It's only about 40,000 shares, so it's not a real overhang; it just looks big next to small bids. https://t.co/eqFpIa32h7 Pro Sentiment is generally optimistic about the acquired land package, which I'd put in bold with blinking lights: one of the best in all of Nevada, with infrastructure, exploration potential and processing infrastructure, and some see district-scale potential, as do I. Intersections on all seven holes were received positively, as they should be. The negatives are price, price, price: too rich relative to financing prices, or wait for a lower entry. When negative themes focus on price and not on the thesis, that's a good sign. If the thesis were broken, you'd want to pay attention. Here the thesis was to acquire a prolific district unexplored for a hundred years, and the truth machine is proving it. The thesis is hanging together and getting better. On the Lassonde Curve: it's all about exploration and moving up the left side. I have them in the top 10% of my sweet spot on the left side of the curve. If they prove up their thesis, and that's a big if, you could see a valuation 10 times the current one. I think they've got a heck of a shot, but they still have to do it in the assays, and if they do, you'll pay a higher price to enter. It's all about your risk threshold. If you're a risk taker like me, I'd take a little swing at the bat right now, but that may or may not be you. Talk to your investment advisors, who know your risk profile, and do your homework. text:
🔥 VIRAL: Trump says New Mexico should "immediately" become New America. One catch: the name is older than the country of Mexico, and only New Mexicans can change it. 🇺🇸

📊 THE NUMBERS
• 825K+ views on the White House Rapid Response post of Trump's Truth Social message (12:07 PM PT); 230K+ on Fox News's
• ~3,500 posts an hour on X with "New America" in the 1 PM PT hour, up from ~50 an hour that morning (X post counts)
• 1500s: when Spanish settlers first called the region "Nuevo México." The country of Mexico didn't exist until independence in 1821
• 1912: statehood, as the 47th state
• 2nd round: Trump first floated "New America" with maps and an AI video on Sep 6-7
• 15 days to Election Day (Nov 3); early voting is under way in New Mexico

🗣️ WHAT PEOPLE ARE SAYING
• Trump: the name "would add great value and prestige," home values and incomes "would rise," and "Crooked Elections" would "become honest again"
• Supporters call it patriotic branding in the same vein as the Gulf of America
• Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) today: "We are New Mexicans... we're keeping both"
• Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) in September: the name "isn't up for debate"
• Pushback isn't only from Democrats: GOP governor nominee Gregg Hull told the Albuquerque Journal in September the state "does not need a new name"

✅ THE FACTS
✅ Article I of New Mexico's constitution says: "The name of this state is New Mexico"
✅ Changing it takes a constitutional amendment passed by a majority of all elected members of both legislative chambers, then approved by New Mexico voters. Congress isn't needed
✅ No executive order and no amendment is pending
✅ Precedent: Rhode Island shortened its official name in 2020 with about 53% of the vote
🔗 Axios, why Trump can't rename it: https://t.co/vwgGJelGrC
🔗 Washington Post, today's post: https://t.co/SxC3uYaykT
🔗 Census QuickFacts, New Mexico: https://t.co/sKM3CEcI2e

❓/❌ WHAT'S NOT
❓ UNPROVEN: a new name raises home values and incomes. We found no study tying a state's name to either. New Mexico's median home value is $248,100 vs $332,700 nationally, with a $64,059 median household income (Census, 2020-24)
❌ NO EVIDENCE: "crooked elections." New Mexico certified its 2024 results (Harris 51.9%, Trump 45.9%), and Trump offered no proof with the post

🤔 NUANCE
A president can't rename a state, but he can tell federal agencies what to call one. His executive orders did that for the Gulf of America (Jan 2025) and Lake America (Aug 2026). That would only change federal maps and paperwork, not the state's legal name. With early voting open and a governor's race on the ballot, both parties also have reasons to keep this fight going.

🇲🇽 En breve: el nombre "Nuevo México" es más antiguo que el país de México. Solo una enmienda y el voto de los nuevomexicanos pueden cambiarlo.

Should a state's name be up to its voters or to Washington? 👇
